President Boakai Dedicates Reclaimed Unity Party Headquarters, Hails “Return of Integrity” in Liberia’s Governance

By: Julius Konton 

Liberian President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. delivered a powerful and emotional address on Saturday as the Unity Party (UP) held its Homecoming, Fundraising, and Headquarters Dedication Ceremony at its reclaimed compound in Oldest Congo Town, marking a symbolic triumph after years of political turbulence.

The event drew senior government officials, lawmakers across the political spectrum, UP Alliance members, diaspora representatives, and hundreds of supporters who packed the compound many calling the day “a full-circle moment” for the governing party.

“More Than a Building, A Testament to Resilience”

Addressing the gathering, President Boakai said the moment represented far more than the opening of a refurbished structure.

 “Today, we gather not merely to dedicate and move into a building, but to celebrate a defining chapter in our journey,” the President said. “A chapter that speaks to resilience, unity, and the unwavering commitment of our loyal partisans.”

Boakai used his speech to reflect on the party’s painful 2021 eviction from the same headquarters, an event widely perceived as politically motivated. 

According to him, critics believed the episode signaled “the end of the Unity Party.”

“They counted us out,” Boakai said. “They underestimated our resolve. They did not understand that no one can eliminate conviction, silence purpose, or destroy a movement sustained by the will of its members and the grace of God.”

The President described the return to the compound as “a biblical reversal.”

 “The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone,” he declared.

Honoring Founding Icons and Fallen Heroes

In one of the most solemn segments of the ceremony, Boakai honored the founding visionaries of Liberia’s multiparty democracy figures he said must remain “immortalized” in the nation’s political history.

He paid tribute to Dr. Edward Binyah Kesselly, William Gabriel Kpolleh, Jackson Fiah Doe, and others whose courage helped birth Liberia’s contemporary political pluralism.

The President then turned to the more recent tragedy: the deaths of five supporters during the 2023 election campaign.

Three; Sulaiman Vanja, Mariama Koroma, and Peter were killed when a speeding vehicle rammed into joyous supporters at the party’s Broad Street headquarters on November 20, 2023. 

Two others died during the massive “September 17 Rally,” one of the largest political gatherings in modern Liberian history.

 “These five fallen heroes are not just names in our history,” Boakai said. “They are part of our story, our struggle, and our soul.”

The crowd observed a moment of silence in their honor.

Reclaiming the Compound: A Political Resurrection

Boakai highlighted the symbolic weight of returning to the compound from which the party was once ousted.

 “The building we were forced to leave is now the most welcoming foundation of our future,” he said. “What was once taken away has now been restored not by chance, but by perseverance and unity.”

He praised UP Chairman Dr. Luther Tarpeh and former and current party officials for rebuilding the institution despite internal and external challenges. 

He also applauded the National Headquarters Steering Committee, chaired by Senator Dabah Varpilah, for what he described as “tireless and historic work.”

Boakai Highlights Liberia’s Rising International Profile

Turning to national affairs, Boakai said Liberia’s global reputation was recovering significantly since his administration took office in January 2024.

Among the achievements he cited:

Liberia’s re-election to Category A of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Council placing it among the world’s top maritime nations for the 2026–2027 term.

Liberia’s inauguration next month as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council, a rare diplomatic milestone for the country.

A renewed sense of dignity for Liberians traveling abroad, with passports “regaining respect.”

Rising investor confidence and improving economic stability.

Greater national connectivity, with roads opening across the country and southeastern travel constraints easing.

 “Liberia now sits with dignity among nations,” Boakai said. “Respect and reverence for Liberia are rapidly rising again.”

“Transformation Is Not an Event”

The President cautioned that while progress is visible, sustainable change demands discipline and collective sacrifice.

 “A single battle victory does not amount to winning a war,” he said. “Transformation is not an event.”

He called on supporters to strengthen the party through “time, energy, and honestly earned resources,” emphasizing that the ARREST Agenda; Accountability, Reform, Recovery, Economic Stability, Service Delivery, and Transparency remains the administration’s guiding framework.

Boakai Reaches Across Party Lines

In a rare bipartisan gesture, Boakai publicly acknowledged opposition and independent lawmakers attending the ceremony, thanking them for “genuine national commitment.”

He extended an open invitation:

 “To our colleagues across the aisle, hop on board and make the Unity Party your political home. We will welcome your expertise and work side-by-side with you.”

A Renewed Mission

The President concluded by thanking the Unity Party’s 23 Alliance member parties and the broader “Rescue Mission” coalition that brought him to power.

 “Rest assured, we will not let you down,” he vowed.

As supporters chanted victory songs and fireworks lit the Monrovia sky, many said the day symbolized not just a party’s return, but a promise of national renewal.

Statement and Appeal for the Release of Tunisian Opposition Activist Shaimaa Issa, Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison

December 3, 2025

The political activist and outspoken critic of the rule of Kais Saied, Shaimaa Issa, has been arrested and sentenced to 20 years in prison on charges of “conspiring against state security.” This comes at a time when she, together with many lawyers, activists, and members of the National Salvation Front to which she belongs, has been calling for the defense of freedom of expression and protesting the systematic repression carried out by the authorities, as well as the policies of President Saied to monopolize power after dissolving parliament, dismissing the prime minister, and referring activists to military courts over the past four years.

While women around the world mark the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence from November 25 to December 10, by organizing activities and events aimed at ending violence against women, the Tunisian government continues to deploy violence, detentions, and prison sentences against women activists and political dissidents.

Tunisia, the country that sparked the Arab Spring and overthrew the dictatorship of Zine El Abidine Ben Ali in a revolution against injustice, tyranny, and poverty, is today, more than a decade after its revolution, facing a fierce assault on freedoms and rights following the president’s consolidation of unchecked authority since July 2021.

Women’s organizations, including the Tunisian Association of Democratic Women and Aswat Nisaa, alongside other groups, have organized protests against these oppressive policies. It was during the most recent demonstration, held on November 29, that Shaimaa Issa was arrested.

We, a collective of women activists and organizations inside and outside Iraq, declare our support and solidarity with the activist Shaimaa Issa, as well as with the entire women, liberationist, and pro-freedom movement in Tunisia defending political rights and freedom of expression.

We call on the Tunisian government to immediately release all detainees who exercised their democratic right to express their opinions, and to annul all unjust convictions and prison sentences handed down to those accused in the so-called conspiracy case, immediately and unconditionally.

We demand political safety for women and the protection of their freedom to express themselves, whether through writing, peaceful demonstrations, or political participation, all of which constitute basic civil and political rights guaranteed under international human rights conventions.

The very spark that ignited the revolution more than a decade ago is capable of igniting once again in the face of even the harshest dictatorships.

We call for the widest possible solidarity from women’s organizations and human rights groups across the region and the world.

A very, very long time ago—long before clans, kingdoms, and bride price negotiations—the Cow and the Buffalo lived deep in the forest with their mother. Life was peaceful until one tragic day when humans, hunting for meat, killed their mother.

The two siblings mourned. Then the Cow broke the silence.

“We must avenge our mother,” she said.

“Yes!” roared the Buffalo. “I will kill any human I see in this forest. They will learn to fear my anger!”

The Cow shook her head gently.
“No, brother. Don’t be so furious. If we fight them directly, they will kill us just like they killed Mother. Think, please.”

“I know it is war,” said the Cow calmly, “but there is a smarter way. Listen—this is how we shall defeat humans: we will surrender to them.”

The Buffalo blinked.
“Surrender?? To the killers of our mother?? Have you gone mad?”

But the Cow continued, “Yes! We shall give them milk. Feed them. Help them. And slowly, they will value us so much that they will start fighting over us. Clans will quarrel. Brothers will kill each other. Entire tribes will go to war for our sake. That way, they will destroy themselves without us lifting a hoof!” 😂😂

The Buffalo snorted loudly.
“What nonsense! Me? Surrender? Never! Do it your way, I’ll do it mine.”

And so they parted ways.
The Buffalo remained in the wild, roaming the forests, forever angry.

It is the Cow.

Brothers kill brothers over cows.
Clans feud over cattle.
Tribes wage wars over them.

The Cow’s revenge has succeeded more than anyone could have imagined.
She didn’t just avenge her mother—
She enslaved humans!

“NHỮNG BẢN NHẠC VIỆT NAM LÀ KINH VIỆT NAM –
CA SĨ HÁT LÀ TỤNG KINH VIỆT NAM”
“VIETNAMESE SONGS ARE OUR VIETNAMESE SCRIPTURE –
AND SINGERS ARE CHANTING OUR NATIONAL SUTRA”
(*Please read the English version below.)
Tôi là Tu sĩ Thích Huyền Việt, sinh năm 1947 tại miền Trung – Quảng Nam.
Thế hệ của tôi là thế hệ đã sống qua chiến tranh, chia cắt, đổi đời, vượt biên, tỵ nạn, và lưu vong. Mỗi người trong thế hệ ấy mang theo một câu chuyện khác nhau, nhưng chung một nỗi đau: nỗi đau mất quê hương và mất tự do.
Năm 1980, tôi vượt biển thoát khỏi chế độ Cộng sản, đến trại tỵ nạn Songkhla – Thái Lan.
Năm 1981, tôi được chính phủ và nhân dân Hoa Kỳ đón nhận, cho tôi định cư và bắt đầu một cuộc đời mới.
Từ ngày ấy đến nay, tôi chưa từng trở về Việt Nam.
Nhưng quê hương thì lúc nào cũng hiện diện trong tim tôi – từng nhịp đập, từng hơi thở, từng giọt mồ hôi trên đất Mỹ này, đều mang hình bóng quê nhà.
Tôi vẫn theo dõi từng biến động tại Việt Nam, nhất là sự tồn tại đầy gian nan của Giáo Hội Phật Giáo Việt Nam Thống Nhất – UBCV, mà tôi là thành viên.
Với tôi, làm người Việt lưu vong là mang một sứ mạng kép:
giữ gìn văn hoá Việt Nam và góp phần nâng đỡ dân tộc Việt Nam.
⸻
1. Người Việt lưu vong – ai cũng mang một vết thương
Lưu vong không chỉ là sống xa quê hương.
Lưu vong là mang trong mình một vết thương tinh thần.
Đó là:
 • nỗi nhớ quê cha đất tổ,
 • nỗi đau phải bỏ lại mồ mả tổ tiên,
  • nỗi lo văn hoá Việt bị phai mờ theo dòng thời gian.
Chúng ta nhớ nhà, nhưng không thể về.
Nhớ tổ tiên, nhưng không thể đứng trước bàn thờ.
Nhớ hương lúa nếp, nhưng chỉ có thể cảm nhận qua ký ức.
Và trên tất cả, chúng ta nhớ tự do – thứ đã bị tước mất khỏi bàn tay dân tộc Việt Nam.
Trong tình cảnh ấy, chúng ta cần một sức mạnh tinh thần để không tan biến, không lạc mất chính mình.
Và sức mạnh ấy đến từ âm nhạc Việt Nam.
⸻
2. Âm nhạc – trí nhớ tập thể của một dân tộc
Âm nhạc Miền Nam – hay còn gọi là nhạc vàng, nhạc Việt Nam Cộng Hoà – không phải chỉ là nghệ thuật giải trí.
Nó là mạch máu nuôi dưỡng tâm thức Việt lưu vong.
Trong những bài hát ấy, có:
 • tiếng ru của mẹ,
 • lời dạy của cha,
 • tình yêu đầu đời,
 • nỗi buồn chia ly,
 • sự mất mát của chiến tranh,
 • giấc mơ tự do,
 • và khát vọng làm người.
Âm nhạc là ký ức chung của một thế hệ – ký ức về một miền Nam trước 1975, tự do, nhân bản, đa nguyên, đa đảng, văn minh và giàu tình người.
Mỗi giai điệu vang lên như nhắc chúng ta rằng:
Đã có một Việt Nam như thế, một Việt Nam đẹp như thế, một Việt Nam tự do như thế.
Và đó chính là lý do khiến những bản nhạc ấy sống mãi trong lòng cộng đồng hải ngoại.
⸻
3. Những buổi văn nghệ cộng đồng – nơi hồn nước trở về
Bất cứ nơi nào có người Việt tỵ nạn, là nơi ấy có:
 • hội chợ Tết,
 • ngày Quốc Hận 30/4,
 • đêm văn nghệ gây quỹ,
 • chương trình từ thiện,
 • và những buổi họp mặt văn hoá.
Trong mỗi chương trình như vậy, âm nhạc giữ vai trò trung tâm.
Vì khi những bài hát vang lên – không ai còn xa lạ với ai.
Người Việt ở xứ người, dù đến từ miền Bắc, miền Trung hay miền Nam, chỉ cần nghe:
 • “Nối lại tình xưa”
 • “Sài Gòn đẹp lắm”
 • “Huyền thoại mẹ”
 • “Sầu lẻ bóng”
 • “Một mai giã từ vũ khí”
 • “Việt Nam, Việt Nam”
 • “Em tôi”
 • “Chiều vàng”
 • “Tôi đưa em sang sông”
là hồn nước trở về, hồn dân tộc trở về.
Những buổi văn nghệ ấy không chỉ để vui, để giải trí.
Đó là những buổi tưởng niệm văn hoá, để chúng ta không quên mình là ai, không quên mình đến từ đâu, và không quên trách nhiệm với quê hương.
⸻
4. Tại sao tôi gọi những bản nhạc ấy là KINH VIỆT NAM?
Kinh – theo nghĩa tôn giáo – là lời dạy giúp con người sống đẹp hơn, tỉnh thức hơn.
Nhưng trong đời sống của người Việt tỵ nạn, có những “bản kinh” khác không nằm trong kinh sách:
đó chính là những bản nhạc Việt Nam.
Vì sao?
Thứ nhất, âm nhạc chứa đựng lịch sử.
Mỗi bài hát nhắc ta nhớ lại:
 • một thời vàng son của miền Nam tự do,
 • một thời đầy hy vọng trước 1975,
 • và một thời cả một dân tộc bị đẩy vào bóng tối sau biến cố 30/4.
Thứ hai, âm nhạc nhắc nhở ta về nhân bản – điều cốt lõi của dân tộc.
Nhạc vàng không ca tụng đấu tranh giai cấp, không cổ vũ thù hận, không tuyên truyền đối lớp.
Nó chỉ nói về:
 • tình yêu,
 • nhân nghĩa,
 • trách nhiệm,
 • quê hương,
 • tình mẹ cha,
 • tình bạn bè,
 • và lòng người.
Thứ ba, âm nhạc giúp chúng ta giữ căn cước Việt Nam.
Con cháu sinh ra tại Mỹ, không biết nhiều về lịch sử, nhưng khi nghe những bài hát Việt Nam – tự nhiên trái tim chúng biết mình là người Việt.
Thứ tư, âm nhạc giúp phục dựng tự do.
Những bản nhạc ấy không chỉ là nghệ thuật – chúng là chứng nhân cho một nền văn hoá tự do bị đánh mất.
Và vì vậy, tôi gọi những bản nhạc ấy là:
KINH VIỆT NAM
Kinh của hồn dân tộc, kinh của tự do, kinh của tình người.**
⸻
5. Ca sĩ hát – là “TỤNG KINH VIỆT NAM”
Khi ca sĩ cất tiếng hát trước cộng đồng, họ không chỉ là người trình diễn.
Họ đang làm một việc thiêng liêng:
Họ đang tụng lên tiếng nói Việt Nam trong tâm hồn tập thể.
Họ biến những bài hát thành:
 • Lời kinh của ký ức
 • Lời kinh của hy vọng
 • Lời kinh của tự do
 • Lời kinh của dân tộc
Còn người nghe – chính là đại chúng cùng thọ trì, cùng gìn giữ.
Trong giây phút ấy:
 • Sân khấu trở thành điện thờ của văn hoá Việt
 • Khán giả trở thành cộng đồng hành giả
 • Bài hát trở thành bản kinh
 • Và tiếng hát trở thành nghi lễ
Không có tôn giáo nào kết nối rộng lớn như thế.
Âm nhạc vượt qua mọi tôn giáo, mọi niềm tin, mọi chia cách.
⸻
6. Âm nhạc đánh thức quyền làm người
Một câu hỏi thường được đặt ra:
“Tại sao những bài hát tình yêu lại có ý nghĩa chính trị? Tại sao lại trở thành ‘kinh’ dân tộc?”
Tình yêu là biểu hiện rõ nhất của tự do.
Không có tự do – tình yêu bị bóp nghẹt.
Không có quyền làm người – tình yêu chỉ còn là nỗi khắc khoải.
Nhạc vàng – cho dù nói về tình yêu nam nữ – cũng chính là tiếng nói đòi hỏi:
 • quyền được yêu,
 • quyền được buồn vui,
 • quyền được hạnh phúc,
 • quyền được sống đúng với chính mình.
Những quyền căn bản ấy – đáng tiếc thay – đang bị tước đoạt tại quê nhà.
Người dân muốn sống yên ổn thì phải:
 • “Nhất ù lì” – để khỏi bị chú ý
 • “Nhì nhất trí” – để khỏi bị làm khó
Đó không phải là đời sống của con người tự do.
Đó là đời sống của robot – được lập trình để tồn tại, không phải để sống.
Và chính vì vậy, âm nhạc trở thành tiếng chuông cảnh tỉnh, trở thành lời hiệu triệu:
 • Đừng quên mình là người Việt
 • Đừng quên văn hoá của mình
 • Đừng quên quyền sống trong tự do
 • Đừng quên trách nhiệm với dân tộc
⸻
7. Âm nhạc trong đời sống người Việt tỵ nạn – một phép màu văn hoá
Trong dòng chảy thời gian, rất nhiều cộng đồng di dân đã biến mất:
mất ngôn ngữ, mất văn hoá, mất căn cước.
Nhưng người Việt tỵ nạn – sau gần 50 năm – vẫn giữ được:
 • tiếng Việt,
 • văn hoá Việt,
 • nhạc Việt,
 • ẩm thực Việt,
 • tâm linh Việt,
 • và tình tự dân tộc.
Điều này không phải tự nhiên mà có.
Nó tồn tại được nhờ:
 • sự kiên trì của cha mẹ,
 • sự cố gắng của cộng đồng,
 • sự gắn kết của các hội đoàn,
 • và một phần rất lớn nhờ âm nhạc.
Âm nhạc giúp chúng ta không tan biến trong biển người của nước Mỹ.
Âm nhạc là phép màu níu giữ dân tộc Việt Nam trong trái tim chúng ta.
⸻
8. Kết luận – Kinh Việt Nam là lời cầu nguyện cho tự do và hồi sinh của dân tộc
Kinh Phật giúp con người tỉnh thức.
Kinh Thánh giúp con người vững niềm tin.
Nhưng Kinh Việt Nam – tức âm nhạc Việt Nam – giúp chúng ta giữ lại linh hồn dân tộc.
Khi ca sĩ hát, họ đang tụng Kinh Việt Nam.
Khi khán giả lắng nghe, họ đang thọ trì Kinh Việt Nam.
Và khi cộng đồng cùng hòa lòng vào tiếng hát ấy, chúng ta đang hồi sinh tinh thần Việt Nam.
Xin quý vị tiếp tục:
 • bảo tồn âm nhạc Miền Nam,
 • truyền lại cho thế hệ trẻ,
 • giữ cho tiếng Việt luôn sống trong từng gia đình,
 • và cùng nhau thắp lên hy vọng cho một ngày dân tộc Việt Nam được sống trong ánh sáng tự do.
Tụng Kinh Việt Nam là tụng cho mình, cho con cháu mình, cho tổ tiên mình,
và cho cả dân tộc Việt Nam.
“ VIETNAMESE SONGS ARE OUR VIETNAMESE SCRIPTURE –
AND SINGERS ARE CHANTING OUR NATIONAL SUTRA”
My name is Venerable Thích Huyền Việt.
I was born in 1947 in Central Vietnam, Quảng Nam.
My generation lived through war, division, loss of country, escape by sea, refugee camps, and the realities of exile. Each person of that generation carries a different story, but we share one common wound:
the wound of losing our homeland and losing our freedom.
In 1980, I escaped Vietnam by boat and arrived at the Songkhla Refugee Camp in Thailand.
In 1981, the government and people of the United States welcomed me and gave me the chance to rebuild my life.
For more than forty years, I have not returned to Vietnam.
But Vietnam has never left my heart. Every heartbeat, every breath, every drop of sweat I have shed on American soil still carries the imprint of my homeland.
I continue to follow the situation in Vietnam, especially the difficult struggle for survival of the Unified Buddhist Church of Vietnam (UBCV), of which I am a member.
For me, to live as a Vietnamese refugee is to carry a dual responsibility:
to preserve Vietnamese culture and to support the Vietnamese people and the Vietnamese spiritual heritage in their time of need.
⸻
1. Vietnamese Refugees – A Wound that Never Fully Heals
Exile is not merely geographical separation.
Exile is a psychological and spiritual wound.
It is:
 • the longing for one’s ancestral land,
 • the sorrow of leaving behind the graves of our forefathers,
 • the fear that Vietnamese heritage will fade with time,
 • and the ache of remembering a freedom once lost.
We remember home but cannot return.
We remember our parents but cannot stand before their altar.
We remember the fragrance of our rice fields but can access it only through memory.
Above all, we remember freedom—a freedom taken from the Vietnamese people.
In such a condition, we need a spiritual force strong enough to keep us from being dissolved, forgotten, and erased.
That force comes from Vietnamese music.
⸻
2. Music – The Collective Memory of a People
South Vietnamese music—known as nhạc vàng, the music of the former Republic of Vietnam—is not simply entertainment.
It is the lifeblood that nourishes our Vietnamese identity in exile.
Within these songs live:
 • a mother’s lullaby,
 • a father’s teaching,
 • the innocence of young love,
 • the sorrow of separation,
 • the wounds of war,
 • the dream of freedom,
 • and the deep Vietnamese sense of humanity.
Music is the shared memory of our generation.
It preserves the image of a South Vietnam before 1975—free, diverse, democratic, and full of human warmth.
Every melody, when played again, reminds us:
There once was a Vietnam like this—
a Vietnam of beauty, dignity, and freedom.
This is why these songs have endured with such power in the Vietnamese diaspora.
⸻
3. Community Cultural Events – Where the Soul of a Nation Returns
Wherever Vietnamese refugees gather, there you will find:
 • Lunar New Year festivals,
 • Black April commemorations,
 • fundraising concerts,
 • charity programs,
 • cultural celebrations.
And at the heart of all these gatherings is music.
Because when those beloved songs are sung, something miraculous happens:
every Vietnamese person feels connected again.
Whether from the North, Central, or South, when we hear:
 • “Nối Lại Tình Xưa” (Rekindling Old Love)
 • “Sài Gòn Đẹp Lắm” (Beautiful Saigon)
 • “Huyền Thoại Mẹ” (Mother’s Legend)
 • “Một Mai Giã Từ Vũ Khí” (One Day I Lay Down Arms)
 • “Việt Nam, Việt Nam”
 • “Tôi Đưa Em Sang Sông” (I Escort You Across the River)
the spirit of the nation returns to us, and we return to it.
These concerts are not merely entertainment.
They are cultural memorials, reminding us who we are, where we came from, and what responsibility we carry.
⸻
4. Why I Call These Songs “Vietnamese Scripture”
In religious traditions, scripture contains teachings that uplift and awaken the human heart.
In the life of the Vietnamese refugee community, we have additional “scriptures” not found in temples or churches:
our Vietnamese songs.
Why?
First, they contain history.
Every song reminds us of:
 • the golden age of South Vietnamese culture,
 • the hopefulness before 1975,
 • and the darkness our nation entered after April 30, 1975.
Second, these songs preserve our humanity.
Unlike revolutionary propaganda music, South Vietnamese music does not teach hatred or class struggle.
It speaks of:
 • love,
 • compassion,
 • responsibility,
 • family,
 • country,
 • and the human condition.
Third, music preserves our identity.
Children born in America may not know the full history, but when they hear these songs, something inside awakens:
they recognize their Vietnamese soul.
Fourth, music keeps alive the memory of freedom.
These songs are the last witnesses to a free Vietnamese culture—a culture silenced in its homeland.
For all these reasons, I call these songs:
The Vietnamese Scripture —
the scripture of our national soul, of freedom, and of human dignity.
⸻
5. When Singers Perform – They Are “Chanting Vietnamese Sutras”
When a singer steps onto the stage and sings these songs, they are not merely performing.
They are engaging in a sacred cultural ritual.
At that moment:
 • The composer is the scribe of scripture.
 • The singer is the chanting practitioner.
 • The audience is the assembly receiving and transmitting the teaching.
 • And the stage becomes a sanctuary of Vietnamese culture.
No religion unites people so broadly.
Music crosses every boundary—religion, belief, class, and background.
This is why I say:
Singers chanting these songs are chanting our Vietnamese Sutra.
⸻
6. Music Awakens Human Dignity and the Demand for Freedom
People often ask:
“How can romantic songs have political meaning? Why call them scripture?”
Because love itself is a pure expression of freedom.
Without freedom, love suffocates.
Without human rights, even happiness becomes impossible.
South Vietnamese music—though often about love—expresses:
 • the right to love,
 • the right to feel joy and sorrow,
 • the right to dream,
 • the right to be fully human.
Tragically, these basic rights are still suppressed in Vietnam.
Citizens must live by two survival rules:
 • “First: stay silent.”
 • “Second: always agree.”
This is not the life of a human being.
This is the life of a programmed machine.
Therefore, music becomes:
 • a warning bell,
 • a call to awareness,
 • a call to unity,
 • a call to preserve our culture,
 • and a reminder to seek a future of freedom for our nation.
⸻
7. Music in the Diaspora – A Cultural Miracle
Throughout history, many immigrant groups have disappeared into the melting pot—losing their language and identity.
But after nearly fifty years, the Vietnamese refugee community has preserved:
 • the Vietnamese language,
 • Vietnamese spirituality,
 • Vietnamese food,
 • Vietnamese arts,
 • Vietnamese cultural values,
 • and above all, Vietnamese music.
This endurance is not accidental.
It is made possible through:
 • the dedication of parents,
 • the work of community organizations,
 • and the unifying power of music.
Music prevents us from being erased.
Music is the miracle that keeps us Vietnamese.
⸻
8. Conclusion – Vietnamese Scripture Is a Prayer for Freedom and Renewal
Buddhist sutras help people awaken.
Christian scripture sustains faith.
But Vietnamese Scripture—our music—preserves the soul of our nation.
When singers perform, they are chanting the Vietnamese Sutra.
When the community listens, they are receiving and transmitting the Sutra.
And when we gather in large numbers to share these songs, we are reviving the Vietnamese spirit.
May we continue to:
 • protect Vietnamese music,
 • pass it on to future generations,
 • keep the Vietnamese language alive,
 • and nurture the hope of a future where the Vietnamese people can live in true freedom.
To chant the Vietnamese Sutra is to chant for ourselves,
for our children,
for our ancestors,
and for the future of Vietnam.

United Opposition: Politics Without Money Has No Future

The so-called united opposition has no future because it has no money. In politics, organization, loyalty, and sustainability are financed. Without resources, even the strongest political rhetoric collapses.

When Hon. Boni Khalwale joined the opposition, it is alleged that shortly thereafter he was informed it was his turn to pay for basic expenses such as food. His response, “Two term,” symbolized a deeper problem: an opposition struggling to sustain itself financially.

History clearly shows that successful political coalitions in Kenya are anchored on economic power.

In 2013, TNA won largely because it brought together powerful and wealthy individuals, including influential families such as that of Mama Ngina Kenyatta. Financial muscle enabled coordination, messaging, logistics, and elite bargaining.

In 2017, the NASA coalition was formidable and highly effective because it included individuals with immense financial capacity, such as Jimmy Wanjigi and Raila Odinga. The coalition had resources to mobilize supporters, sustain nationwide structures, and challenge electoral outcomes.

In 2022, Azimio la Umoja had heavyweight figures like Raila Odinga and Uhuru Kenyatta. However, they lost to William Ruto, who had quietly built strong financial networks over time. He mobilized resources through a broad team, including diaspora fundraisers, and successfully sold the “Hustler vs. Dynasty” narrative, which resonated emotionally while being backed by serious financial organization.

By contrast, the current united opposition appears largely composed of leaders without strong independent financial bases ordinary politicians like many of us (“walala hoi”). This makes the coalition vulnerable and unreliable.

When Rigathi Gachagua was impeached, reports emerged that his staff went unpaid within a short period. This illustrates a critical lesson: political power that depends entirely on state office is fragile.

Leaders such as Rigathi Gachagua, Kalonzo Musyoka, Eugene Wamalwa, and Martha Karua are not widely known to own large, diversified businesses that generate steady daily income, unlike Raila Odinga’s Spectre International, which manufactures LPG gas cylinders and provides consistent cash flow. Independent economic power cushions political uncertainty.

Rigathi Gachagua reportedly invested heavily in the hotel industry, much of which depended on government-linked business and tenders. This model is risky. Once one exits power through impeachment, loss, or realignment the income stream collapses.

The lesson is simple but powerful: when you get any opportunity that pays well, invest in businesses that generate daily or steady income. Financial cash flow is political power. Money sustains staff, allies, campaigns, and long-term influence.

Equally important, leaders must help their people secure jobs, contracts, and business opportunities. When fundraising is required, those people will respond because politics has already delivered tangible value to them.

This is where communities like the Kikuyu, Kalenjin, and Luo have historically outperformed others. Their politics is closely tied to economic networks, professional placement, and business ecosystems.

Politics without money is noise. Politics with economic organization is power.

"She was heir to a shipping fortune. Then she fell in love with a Black jazz musician—and her family disowned her. So she spent her fortune publishing the voices they wanted silenced.

This is the story of the heiress who chose justice over jewels.
In 1928, Nancy Cunard walked into a Venice jazz club and heard Henry Crowder play piano. She was 32, an aristocratic British poet, heiress to the Cunard shipping line, surrounded by Europe's artistic elite. He was a self-taught Black musician from Georgia, playing with Eddie South's Alabamians.

By the end of the night, Nancy's privileged world had cracked open.
Their relationship wasn't just scandalous—it was considered biological treason. Mixed-race couples were kicked out of hotels. Newspapers published racist cartoons depicting Crowder with grotesquely exaggerated features and Nancy as a race traitor. Her mother, Lady Maud Cunard, was horrified.

"Is it true that my daughter knows a Negro?" her mother asked, the question dripping with disgust.  Nancy's response was defiant: publish a pamphlet titled Black Man and White Ladyship, send it to all her mother's society friends, and publicly defend her relationship as a rebuke to racist Britain.

The consequence was swift: complete disinheritance. The Cunard fortune—gone. Her place in British society—revoked. Her family—done with her.  Nancy accepted it without hesitation. Because Henry Crowder had given her something more valuable than money: he'd introduced her to the realities of racism in ways her privileged upbringing never could.

Nancy Cunard decided to use what remained of her wealth and influence to fight back.  She'd already established Hours Press in 1928, a small publishing house operating from a renovated farmhouse in Normandy. Using a 200-year-old Belgian hand press, Nancy personally set type, inked plates, and printed works by modernist writers—Samuel Beckett's first published work came from Hours Press.

But after meeting Crowder, her focus shifted. She visited Harlem, immersing herself in the Renaissance happening there—the explosion of Black art, literature, music, and intellectual thought that white America was largely ignoring or actively suppressing.
She met Langston Hughes. Zora Neale Hurston. W.E.B. Du Bois. She listened to their stories of segregation, lynching, systemic oppression. She learned about the Scottsboro Boys—nine young Black men sentenced to death in Alabama on false rape charges.
And Nancy decided to do something unprecedented: create an anthology that would document Black culture, history, and struggle in a way no publication ever had.

Negro: An Anthology took three years to compile (1931-1934). Nancy worked herself to exhaustion, tracking down contributors across continents, translating works, setting 855 pages of type by hand. The book weighed eight pounds. It contained 250 articles from 150 contributors—Black and white, from Africa, the Caribbean, America, Europe.  Langston Hughes contributed poetry. Zora Neale Hurston provided cultural analysis. W.E.B. Du Bois wrote on civil rights. Arthur Schomburg documented Black history. The anthology included music scores by Henry Crowder, photographs documenting racism, essays on colonialism, reports on the Scottsboro case.

It was revolutionary—not just in content but in concept. A wealthy white British woman using her platform and remaining resources to amplify Black voices at a time when most of the world wanted those voices silent.  The book was dedicated "to Henry Crowder, my first Negro friend."

Publishing it nearly bankrupted her. No publisher would take the risk, so Nancy paid for everything herself—using what little money she had left after disinheritance and proceeds from libel suits against racist press coverage.  When Negro was published in February 1934, it was immediately banned in British colonies across Africa and the West Indies. Colonial authorities understood exactly how dangerous this book was—it gave colonized people a vision of their own worth, their own power, their own right to resist.

Sales were dismal in Britain and America. The book was too expensive, too controversial, too ahead of its time. Many copies were later destroyed during the London Blitz.  But in Black intellectual circles? It was received as groundbreaking. Alain Locke called it "the best anthology, in every sense of the word, ever made about Negroes." Mary McLeod Bethune thanked Nancy for highlighting Black women's contributions.

Nancy had created something that wouldn't be fully appreciated for decades: the first comprehensive documentation of the Black Atlantic—a transnational portrait of African diaspora culture that celebrated achievement while unflinchingly documenting oppression.

But Nancy didn't stop there.

In 1935, when Mussolini invaded Ethiopia, Nancy became one of the earliest and most vocal critics. She wrote articles exposing the brutality of Italian occupation, the use of chemical weapons, the systematic destruction of Ethiopian culture. She predicted—accurately—that fascism's expansion in Africa was a prelude to a larger European war.

When the Spanish Civil War erupted in 1936, Nancy threw herself into refugee relief work. She trudged twenty miles in rain to reach camps. She organized fundraising—parties, dances, film screenings. She wrote stories about refugees' suffering for the Manchester Guardian, using journalism to mobilize support.

She worked until physical exhaustion forced her back to Paris, where she stood on street corners collecting funds.
Throughout, she drank heavily. Took lovers indiscriminately. Burned through friendships. Henry Crowder had left her by 1935, fed up with her infidelities and volatile temperament. Nancy's behavior became increasingly erratic, self-destructive.  But her commitment to fighting fascism never wavered.

When World War II began, Nancy worked as a translator in London for the French Resistance. She worked to the point of collapse, translating intercepted communications, supporting the underground fight against Nazi occupation.  She had gone from heiress to outcast to activist to resistance worker—each transformation stripping away more privilege, more comfort, more of the life she'd been born into.

By the time Nancy Cunard died in 1965 at age 69, she was destitute, alcoholic, weighing only 57 pounds. She died alone in a Paris hospital, her health destroyed by decades of relentless activism and self-destruction.  History largely forgot her. The men she'd published—Beckett, Pound—became famous. The causes she'd championed eventually gained traction. But Nancy herself faded from memory, reduced to footnotes in other people's biographies or objectified in photographs as a "muse" to famous artists.

But here's what Nancy Cunard actually was: a woman who looked at the racist, colonialist, fascist world of the 1930s and refused to be complicit. Who used her privilege not to insulate herself but as a weapon against injustice. Who gave up wealth, family, reputation, and eventually her health for causes that mattered more than comfort.

She published Black writers when no one else would. She documented colonialism's brutality when Europe wanted to look away. She fought fascism before most people recognized the threat. She worked for the Resistance when the Nazis occupied France.

Nancy Cunard proved that privilege isn't destiny—it's a choice. You can use it to protect yourself, or you can burn it down fighting for people the world has decided don't matter.
She chose to burn."

Furthermore, he testified that UNMISS had started coordinating with IGAD and the Office of the President to obtain security guarantees.

Regarding the entities he coordinated with in Juba, Malakal, and Nasir, Gen. Abiem clarified that he worked with UNMISS at its headquarters adjacent to the airport in Juba, with a field officer in Malakal, and with the Nasir Commissioner, Hon. James Gatluak Lew, in Nasir.

When asked if the involved parties had prepared a comprehensive report following the failure of the evacuation, he stated that no such report was made.
Gen. Abiem also alleged that he coordinated with the head of the United Nations Field Office in Malakal, who was in contact with the fifth accused in the case, Dr. Riek Machar.

He affirmed that he had no information about an investigation conducted by the United Nations into the evacuation. The third witness in the case, an SSPDF Military Intelligence (M.I.) officer, Captain Joseph Malong Akot, one of the soldiers evacuated on March 6, testified before the court. He stated that clashes between the SSPDF and the opposition forces began in mid-February 2025.

He stressed that the late Major General David Majur Dak had issued orders to all defense forces to prepare following news of large-scale mobilization and deployment operations by the opposition in Nasir on February 28, 2025, indicating that the mobilization continued until March 1, 2025.

The witness added that the attack began on March 2, led by the late Tor Gile Thoan and his deputy, Kang Makana, at 11:00 p.m., and continued until dawn.

On the morning of March 3, Tor Gile returned to lead the attack and was killed during the battle. The witness stated that he personally saw Tor’s body, which was wearing an SPLA (IO) uniform with the rank of colonel.

At the end of the session, the defense asked Captain Joseph Malong Akot a question about whether he had seen any of the accused in the dock in Nasir on that day. The witness replied that he had not seen any of them.

Nasir town has long been an opposition stronghold, going back to the Nasir Declaration in 1991 (Johnson, 2012). During the South Sudanese civil war, the town was held by the SPLA-IO until 2016, when the SPLA captured it. From the beginning, the SPLA acted as an occupying army. The local community complained that the army looted goods, stole cattle, and restricted the collection of firewood. The SPLA was in a penurious situation. It received no wages, food, 
or support, and was forced into selling ammunition to hostile Nuer youth in the surrounding area. 

The relationship further soured in 2023, when Nhial Batoang—the current commissioner of Ulang county was replaced as the commander of the Nasir barracks by Majur Dak, a Dinka lieutenant general. In February 2025, tensions increased between the SSPDF and members of the white armies, partially due to tensions over local women. These tensions led to armed clashes on 14 and 15 February, after government soldiers opened fire on local youth who had gone fishing. In letters to the government, Nasir’s Nuer community demanded the removal of the SSPDF from the Wechyar-Adiw barracks that are near Nasir town, and the deployment of the Necessary Unified Forces (NUF). It was thought that the NUF would be less hostile to the local community. Such a plan had been formulated during several high-level government meetings in 2024. Its implementation, however, had lost ground after the dismissal of Santino Deng Wol as the Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) in December 2024 and the appointment of the more bellicose Paul Nang Majok.46 James Koang Chuol—a Jikany Nuer commander from Nasir tasked with overseeing operations in Nasir town alongside Paromi Angui and Koang Thou—gave a statement explaining that all the available NUF had deployed, and those left in the cantonment sites only had sticks, making them unsuitable for deployment. What followed was a violent farce. The soldiers initially tasked with replacing the beleaguered battalion in Nasir town were largely Equatorian and refused to go. The only forces willing to deploy were two communitarian militias, both of which had extremely hostile relations with the Nuer community: the Agwelek 
(Craze, 2019; 2022a) and the Abu Shoq, a Padang Dinka militia from the Ngok Lual Yak section of Baliet county. These forces are not neutral,’ one of the fighters from the white armies said, they are 
government militias that fought us during the war. 

On 22 February, two barges carrying these militias were sent to relieve the SSPDF near Nasir town, although the Sobat River’s water levels were too low for the boats to pass. Whether by intention or design, the movement of the barges antagonized the Nuer communities of Upper Nile and northern Jonglei. White army fighters explained that they thought the dispatch of the two barges was a clear declaration of war. All along the river, they mobilized, firing on the barges as they moved towards Nasir. Government-aligned forces further inflamed the situation by launching airstrikes on SPLA-IO positions on 25 February in Doma payam, Ulang county, and in Chuil payam, Nyirol county. The government created the enemy it would then attack. Despite the bellicose atmosphere, some voices argued for restraint. At the beginning of March, the white armies of Nasir and Ulang counties did not reach a consensus on whether to attack the SSPDF barracks near Nasir town. Two Ulang Nuersections refused to participate in the initial assault on 3 March, which was led by Tor Gile Thoan, the Nasir white army commander. Gile, like many white army commanders, had been given a rank within the SPLA-IO during the South Sudanese civil war. In the initial discussions over whether to attack the Nasir barracks, however, Gile participated as a white army commander rather than a member of the SPLA-IO. To the extent that the SPLM/A-IO participated in these discussions, it was to try and dissuade the white armies from attacking Nasir town. The SPLM/A-IO feared that such an assault would give the government what it was looking for an insurgency to justify its own counterinsurgency. Other voices, however, pushed for the assault ncluding hardline Nuer politicians in the diaspora and in Addis Ababa, such as Duer Tut Duer, the chair-person of the South Sudan Reform Movement/Fighters and the former SPLM/A-IO governor of Sobat state. After a decade of mistreatment at the hands of the SSPDF in Nasir town, and with barges of Agwelek militiamen coming along the river, it was easy to paint a picture of an all-out war. An attack on the barracks would enable the elimination of a force that had long oppressed the Nuer communities of Nasir. 

The initial assault on 3 March saw the white army overrun the north gate of the barracks, which faces Nasir town, leading to an SSPDF retreat to the southern gate. Gile was injured during the assault, and his five bodyguards were killed. After the initial attack, the white armies ran out of ammunition and staged a tactical retreat. The SSPDF then mounted a search, discovered Gile, and according to white army fighters beheaded him, leaving his head impaled on a spike next to an SSPDF flag.50 This story quickly circulated among the Nuer youth of Nasir and Ulang and proved to be the precipitating spark for the 4 March assault in which the Nuer white armies including those of Ulang—under the command of Kang Makana, Gile’s deputy, captured the barracks. Dak and some of his soldiers survived the assault by hiding in an armoured personnel carrier. Negotiations began to rescue the lieutenant general, with Machar and the government contacting UNMISS to see if it could assist with the evacuation. All sides conspired in the fiction that the SPLM/A-IO was in control of the white armies. For Machar, this was a moment to demonstrate his influence. Pal Mai Deng, the SPLM-IO spokesperson, announced on 5 March that an agreement had been made to airlift Dak from Nasir town. An unsuccessful attempt to evacuate the soldiers was made the following day. The government was only too eager to lay the blame on Machar for the assault on Nasir town, wanting to tie him to the white armies. UNMISS, which was coordinating its operations from Juba, and where the head of the Malakal field office happened to be, was in contact with the SPLM-IO and believed its assurances that the opposition had control of the white armies on the ground, a fact not consonant with reality. Machar and the SPLM/A-IO leadership had relied on contact with Hokdor Chuol, one of the most important Nasir white army leaders during the South Sudanese civil war. Like Gile and Makana, Chuol had also received a position in the SPLA-IO during the war. Although he intervened and asked the white armies to allow Dak to depart, his plea—like that of Machar was not heeded. Some white army members have stated that they intended to kill Dak, regardless of what Machar might have asked of them, in order to avenge Gile’s death. Dak was killed on 7 March during an attempted UNMISS airlift evacuation, along with 27 of his soldiers and a UN crew member. Once again, as during the South Sudanese civil war, the white armies acted autonomously from the SPLM/A-IO, whose goals were political and related to its standing in Juba, not to the situation in Nasir. ‘It is the IO,’ one white army fighter said, ‘that let the situation get to this point.

Tunis, December 17, 2025

On the 15th anniversary of the outbreak of the Tunisian Revolution: The slogans of the revolution live on despite the coup against its course.

Today, the Tunisian people commemorate the anniversary of the outbreak of the great revolution in Sidi Bouzid, and its spread throughout the country and the Arab world, thanks to the blood of the glorious martyrs, the steadfast wounded, and the roaring masses raising slogans that echoed across the world: "The people want" and "If the people one day desire life, then fate must respond."

Despite the achievements of the years of the faltering democratic transition in the areas of constitutional and institutional development, freedom of expression, media, organization, and free electoral competition, populist rhetoric infiltrated the collective consciousness. It exploited the errors, difficulties, disagreements, and setbacks in embodying the values ​​of the revolution and safeguarding them from the dangers of counter-revolution and coup attempts. Populists capitalized on the Tunisian people's resentment and anger stemming from the failure to meet their expectations for development and social justice, using it to denigrate politics, politicians, parties, civil society, its organizations, and activists. They exploited public media that have been completely subjugated, reverting to a stilted language that praises the authorities and shutting their doors to any free or critical voice. Private media have been further restricted by drying up funding sources and wielding the infamous Decree 54 against journalists and media professionals, thus reducing the media's role to rallying support for the existing regime and justifying its policies instead of engaging in political and economic dialogue.

Despite the use of a subservient judiciary—whose elected institutions have been dissolved and its independence undermined—in dozens of sham trials against dissidents, lawyers, activists, and bloggers, and the arrest of scores of dissidents and activists, segments of the elite and the general public continue to defy intimidation and threats, raising slogans demanding freedom and social justice.

Loyalty to the principles and values ​​of the glorious December 17th-January 14th Revolution inherently requires political elites to demonstrate courageous, peaceful civil resistance against autocratic rule and its tendency to dismantle the political and civil spheres, and to tirelessly strive for judicial independence and the release of political prisoners. Nevertheless it also demands the courage to acknowledge shortcomings and their share of responsibility, despite differing positions and stances, for the setbacks of the decade of democratic transition, despite its achievements and gains.

While we value the united struggle of the various components of the political spectrum and civil society in demanding freedoms and rejecting the authoritarian tendencies of the ruling power, this remains insufficient unless it transforms into a shared political action that transcends the remnants of disagreements and conflicts and unifies efforts and demands.

The reasons that led to the rebellion against - and coup against - the constitution, foremost among them the sterile political conflict at the expense of consolidating institutional building, the revolution, and development, remain. They constitute the most important reasons for the continuation of the coup, which is leading the country toward a deepening crisis, armed with a discourse of betrayal and division among Tunisians. It has succeeded only in the systematic destruction of all democratic gains and in producing a tense and crisis-ridden political, social, economic, and moral landscape that recalls a similar scene 15 years ago. 

All experiences throughout history have proven that the most important element of power for despotic rulers is the fragmentation and disunity of their opponents. Will anyone take heed?

Long live the Tunisian revolution, eternal and inspiring!

Long live Tunisia!

On behalf of the National Salvation Front

The growing humanitarian crisis in Cameroon must be understood within a wider global shift in priorities. For decades, aid has largely flowed from the Global North to the Global South, sustaining life-saving interventions in contexts like the North-West and South-West regions. Today, that flow is shrinking. Funding cuts, donor fatigue, and the diversion of public resources by governments toward military expenditure have left humanitarian actors overstretched, under-funded, and increasingly unable to reach people in need.

In Cameroon, the impact is visible and painful. Assistance for vulnerable populations — displaced families, persons with disabilities, injured civilians, and crisis-affected youth — has dropped drastically due to lack of funds. Programs have been scaled down, targeting reduced, and entire communities left without regular access to health care, protection, or education support. This is not because needs have reduced, but because resources have.

Globally, governments are spending more on defense than ever before. Yet the question remains: Has the world become safer? Or are we witnessing more conflicts, deeper suffering, and shrinking humanitarian space? From Ukraine to Sudan, from Gaza to Cameroon, the evidence suggests a more unsafe and unequal world, where humanitarians struggle to operate and civilians pay the price.

As international funding contracts, it is time to seriously reflect on the power of local philanthropy and community solidarity. During the Anglophone crisis, Cameroonians repeatedly showed that compassion does not wait for international approvals. Through Facebook and online platforms, local communities mobilized funds for medical bills, burial support, school fees, shelter, and emergency care. Families came together to support victims of stray bullets, injured children, displaced widows, and survivors of violence.

We remember how community-driven fundraising helped save lives — including cases like the child injured by a stray bullet, where online solidarity filled the gap left by delayed or absent aid. Similar efforts supported people needing urgent medical care, like Median and countless others, who would otherwise have suffered in silence. These were not large grants, but fast, dignified, people-centered responses.

Local fundraising challenges traditional aid infrastructure, but it also complements it. With strong local networks, transparency, and trust, Cameroonians can collectively finance at least one or two community-led projects — medical emergencies, disability support, education assistance, or livelihood recovery — through Facebook campaigns, WhatsApp networks, churches, youth groups, and diaspora contributions.

The words of the Emergency Relief Coordinator remind us of a hard truth: this is not a resource problem, it is a priority problem. If the world can spend trillions on defense, it can invest a fraction of that in saving lives. But until global priorities shift, local action must rise.

She was heir to a shipping fortune. Then she fell in love with a Black jazz musician—and her family disowned her. So she spent her fortune publishing the voices they wanted silenced.
This is the story of the heiress who chose justice over jewels.
In 1928, Nancy Cunard walked into a Venice jazz club and heard Henry Crowder play piano. She was 32, an aristocratic British poet, heiress to the Cunard shipping line, surrounded by Europe's artistic elite. He was a self-taught Black musician from Georgia, playing with Eddie South's Alabamians.
By the end of the night, Nancy's privileged world had cracked open.
Their relationship wasn't just scandalous—it was considered biological treason. Mixed-race couples were kicked out of hotels. Newspapers published racist cartoons depicting Crowder with grotesquely exaggerated features and Nancy as a race traitor. Her mother, Lady Maud Cunard, was horrified.
"Is it true that my daughter knows a Negro?" her mother asked, the question dripping with disgust.
Nancy's response was defiant: publish a pamphlet titled Black Man and White Ladyship, send it to all her mother's society friends, and publicly defend her relationship as a rebuke to racist Britain.
The consequence was swift: complete disinheritance. The Cunard fortune—gone. Her place in British society—revoked. Her family—done with her.
Nancy accepted it without hesitation. Because Henry Crowder had given her something more valuable than money: he'd introduced her to the realities of racism in ways her privileged upbringing never could.
And Nancy Cunard decided to use what remained of her wealth and influence to fight back.
She'd already established Hours Press in 1928, a small publishing house operating from a renovated farmhouse in Normandy. Using a 200-year-old Belgian hand press, Nancy personally set type, inked plates, and printed works by modernist writers—Samuel Beckett's first published work came from Hours Press.
But after meeting Crowder, her focus shifted. She visited Harlem, immersing herself in the Renaissance happening there—the explosion of Black art, literature, music, and intellectual thought that white America was largely ignoring or actively suppressing.
She met Langston Hughes. Zora Neale Hurston. W.E.B. Du Bois. She listened to their stories of segregation, lynching, systemic oppression. She learned about the Scottsboro Boys—nine young Black men sentenced to death in Alabama on false rape charges.
And Nancy decided to do something unprecedented: create an anthology that would document Black culture, history, and struggle in a way no publication ever had.
Negro: An Anthology took three years to compile (1931-1934). Nancy worked herself to exhaustion, tracking down contributors across continents, translating works, setting 855 pages of type by hand. The book weighed eight pounds. It contained 250 articles from 150 contributors—Black and white, from Africa, the Caribbean, America, Europe.
Langston Hughes contributed poetry. Zora Neale Hurston provided cultural analysis. W.E.B. Du Bois wrote on civil rights. Arthur Schomburg documented Black history. The anthology included music scores by Henry Crowder, photographs documenting racism, essays on colonialism, reports on the Scottsboro case.
It was revolutionary—not just in content but in concept. A wealthy white British woman using her platform and remaining resources to amplify Black voices at a time when most of the world wanted those voices silent.
The book was dedicated "to Henry Crowder, my first Negro friend."
Publishing it nearly bankrupted her. No publisher would take the risk, so Nancy paid for everything herself—using what little money she had left after disinheritance and proceeds from libel suits against racist press coverage.
When Negro was published in February 1934, it was immediately banned in British colonies across Africa and the West Indies. Colonial authorities understood exactly how dangerous this book was—it gave colonized people a vision of their own worth, their own power, their own right to resist.
Sales were dismal in Britain and America. The book was too expensive, too controversial, too ahead of its time. Many copies were later destroyed during the London Blitz.
But in Black intellectual circles? It was received as groundbreaking. Alain Locke called it "the best anthology, in every sense of the word, ever made about Negroes." Mary McLeod Bethune thanked Nancy for highlighting Black women's contributions.
Nancy had created something that wouldn't be fully appreciated for decades: the first comprehensive documentation of the Black Atlantic—a transnational portrait of African diaspora culture that celebrated achievement while unflinchingly documenting oppression.
But Nancy didn't stop there.
In 1935, when Mussolini invaded Ethiopia, Nancy became one of the earliest and most vocal critics. She wrote articles exposing the brutality of Italian occupation, the use of chemical weapons, the systematic destruction of Ethiopian culture. She predicted—accurately—that fascism's expansion in Africa was a prelude to a larger European war.
When the Spanish Civil War erupted in 1936, Nancy threw herself into refugee relief work. She trudged twenty miles in rain to reach camps. She organized fundraising—parties, dances, film screenings. She wrote stories about refugees' suffering for the Manchester Guardian, using journalism to mobilize support.
She worked until physical exhaustion forced her back to Paris, where she stood on street corners collecting funds.
Throughout, she drank heavily. Took lovers indiscriminately. Burned through friendships. Henry Crowder had left her by 1935, fed up with her infidelities and volatile temperament. Nancy's behavior became increasingly erratic, self-destructive.
But her commitment to fighting fascism never wavered.
When World War II began, Nancy worked as a translator in London for the French Resistance. She worked to the point of collapse, translating intercepted communications, supporting the underground fight against Nazi occupation.
She had gone from heiress to outcast to activist to resistance worker—each transformation stripping away more privilege, more comfort, more of the life she'd been born into.
By the time Nancy Cunard died in 1965 at age 69, she was destitute, alcoholic, weighing only 57 pounds. She died alone in a Paris hospital, her health destroyed by decades of relentless activism and self-destruction.
History largely forgot her. The men she'd published—Beckett, Pound—became famous. The causes she'd championed eventually gained traction. But Nancy herself faded from memory, reduced to footnotes in other people's biographies or objectified in photographs as a "muse" to famous artists.
But here's what Nancy Cunard actually was: a woman who looked at the racist, colonialist, fascist world of the 1930s and refused to be complicit. Who used her privilege not to insulate herself but as a weapon against injustice. Who gave up wealth, family, reputation, and eventually her health for causes that mattered more than comfort.
She published Black writers when no one else would. She documented colonialism's brutality when Europe wanted to look away. She fought fascism before most people recognized the threat. She worked for the Resistance when the Nazis occupied France.
Nancy Cunard proved that privilege isn't destiny—it's a choice. You can use it to protect yourself, or you can burn it down fighting for people the world has decided don't matter.
She chose to burn.

WHEN HOPE ANSWERED THE CALL: HOW GEOFFREY MOSIRIA HELPED TURN A MOTHER’S TEARS INTO A MIRACLE

Yesterday, Geoffrey Mosiria KE  walked into a home that once echoed with fear, tears, and silent prayers. Today, that same home is filled with smiles, laughter, and hope.

Not long ago, this mother was living every parent’s worst nightmare. Her innocent child lay helpless, dependent on oxygen, fighting for life each passing day. Instead of experiencing the joy of motherhood, she watched her baby struggle, knowing that without urgent surgery costing Kshs 1.5 million, her child would not survive. Broken and exhausted, she reached a point where she gave up choosing to leave everything to nature, preparing her heart for the worst.
It was at her lowest moment that Geoffrey Mosiria received her call.

Geoffrey did not have millions. He did not have answers. But he had a heart that listens and the courage to act. He responded immediately, standing with her when hope was almost gone. Through his intervention and relentless efforts, Kshs 750,000 half of the required amount was raised. That single act of faith reopened doors that had shut. It restored belief. It stirred compassion in others. Step by step, the remaining funds were raised, and the child was finally taken to India for the life-saving surgery.

Yesterday, Geoffrey returned not as a fundraiser, not as a public figure but as a witness to a miracle. The child is now healthy, off oxygen, and full of life. The mother, once drowning in despair, is now a happy woman holding her healthy baby, tears of gratitude replacing tears of pain.

This story is a reminder that sometimes God uses ordinary people to perform extraordinary acts. Not because they have enough, but because they are willing. Mosiria chose to answer a cry that many would have ignored, and in doing so, he became the bridge between despair and hope, between death and life. 
Some stories are not told to praise men, but to remind humanity that kindness still exists.

This year (editor's note; every year), we have been forced to think twice about philanthropy. A ripple effect, people are shying away from it, or thinking thrice. I am one of those people, and who could blame us? 
Yet, in the midst, there are people still willing to help. I am also those people, although with more caution but fully aware that one can never be cautious enough. 
Philanthropy is like having a toxic relationship. 
A few years ago I had sworn not to ever help anyone on SM after I posted about a lady whose hand had been disabled from an injury, yet it was the hand she needed to wash clothes for people, to feed her kids. She was a single mother. People helped, a lot. Enough for her surgery. I gave her all the money, posted here for accountability. 
Only for a few days later to wake up to accusations that I had been sent ten thousand dollars and pocketed it. 
"Niliambiwa ulitumiwa ten thousand dollars." She said, fuming on the phone. I was like, it was 100. Yaani mpaka I had to go back to my messages to confirm how much came through. It was 100, but because her number was public, a busybody here (shame on you) had told her I was 'eating her money'. I can bet this busybody did not send a single penny. Evil, monitoring spirit! May your ancestral spirits not favour you, daimono. 
Yoh! Anyway, I sent her the transaction message, sent it to someone else for accountability and then blocked her. I stopped that fundraiser. When I next saw her, I ignored her. Also, she never did go for the surgery, because according to her, she had other money priorities - this I was told by the lady who had introduced me to her. I don't know what happened after because I never asked about her and I refused to be told about her.
Years came and went, I excused myself to people who needed my help to raise money. I gave when I could, from my pocket. Then a lovely lady, I was her senior and head girl in secondary school, told me what she was going through. It was bad. Rough. I know a lot of us are going through hard times but hers? He added that the campaign also seeks to bring youth initiatives together under one umbrella. “We aim to unite youth programs to harness their skills and energy, replant hope in people’s hearts, and prove that Gaza is still alive,” he said.

The campaign began on Omar al-Mokhtar Street, one of Gaza City’s central streets, where groups of young volunteers cleaned the area using only basic tools—brooms, dustpans, and shovels. Al-Dremly noted that around 85 percent of the municipality’s heavy and medium machinery was damaged during the war. Still, he stressed that the lack of equipment would not halt the initiative. “Gaza will rise again through its people’s spirit and love of life and land,” he said.

In the short term, the Municipality of Gaza plans to continue the campaign on a weekly basis, moving each time to a new location across the city.

One of the partners in the Gaza Municipality’s “Let’s Rebuild” campaign is the Sameer Project, founded by six Gazans living in the diaspora.

“Living abroad does not mean sitting aside and waiting for the world to decide when to act and help our people in Gaza,” said Hala Sabbah, an official with the project. “We’ve waited for too long. We felt the necessity to act.”

“Gaza needs immediate support,” she added. “As civil society organizations, even simple efforts matter. No one understands Gaza’s pain better than its people. That’s why we initiated this project — because we are Gazans, and we know how Gazans suffer.”

Launched in April 2024, the Sameer Project has continuously adapted its work to meet changing needs. During the famine, the focus was on food aid. During mass displacement, it provided tents and temporary shelters. Following the ceasefire, priorities shifted toward reopening blocked roads and salvaging damaged homes.

Two weeks after the ceasefire began, Sabbah and her team launched the “Hand in Hand, Let’s Rebuild It” campaign, responding to residents’ inability to return to their homes in northern Gaza, where streets and entrances remain buried under the rubble.

“We knew this work required heavy machinery and proper equipment,” Sabbah said. “But that doesn’t mean we do nothing. Any step that relieves people’s pain matters.”

Using every available resource — shovels, wheelbarrows, a limited number of bulldozers, brooms, and above all, youthful determination — the project mobilized at least 100 volunteers, including engineers, journalists, and students. So far, three main streets in Gaza City, Khan Younis, and the Abu Eskandar area have been cleared and reopened, easing the movement of people and vehicles.

Priority was given to roads that allow access for water trucks and basic services. “Water is a basic need for everyone in Gaza,” Sabbah said. “When we open a road, we make sure water trucks can pass. This alone can ease people’s daily suffering.”

Despite these efforts, Sabbah stressed that what they are doing addresses only a fraction of Gaza’s needs. “It’s a drop in the ocean,” she said. “The level of destruction is beyond anything normal.”

According to the UN Development Programme, rebuilding Gaza would cost around $40 billion, generate 40 million tons of rubble, and take up to 80 years if current Israeli restrictions remain in place.

A major obstacle is the severe lack of equipment. “We can’t operate across the entire Strip,” Sabbah explained. “Most heavy machinery was destroyed during the war.”

Local estimates indicate that Israeli bombardment deliberately targeted bulldozers and other heavy equipment, leaving only a very limited number of functioning machines in Gaza, mostly owned by private companies. In 2025, Israel permitted a limited number of machines to enter the Strip under specific sponsorship arrangements. The Government Media Office estimates that at least 500 heavy and medium machines are needed to support reconstruction efforts.

Fuel shortages further complicate the work. Since the ceasefire, Israel has allowed only 5–6 fuel trucks per day, covering roughly 10% of Gaza’s actual needs, despite pledges to allow 50–60 trucks daily. As a result, fuel prices have soared, with gasoline reaching 120 ILS ($37) per liter and diesel nearly 60 ILS (almost $14).

Alongside road clearance, the Sameer Project works to salvage partially damaged homes and turn them into temporary shelters when possible. “The first step is always checking the foundations,” Sabbah said. “We work with field engineers to make sure homes are safe.”

“So far, at least 62 homes have been cleared of rubble and partially repaired using wooden poles and plastic sheets,” she added. “They’re not ideal, but they’re safer than tents.”

In cases where foundations are unsafe, repairs are refused. Families are instead provided with tents erected beside their homes and warned not to return inside. According to Gaza’s Interior Ministry, at least 12 previously damaged homes collapsed during recent storms, killing eight people, including children.

One volunteer with the Sameer Project lost five family members when their home collapsed during the storm.

Beyond physical reconstruction, the initiative also considers the psychological toll of displacement. “People feel safer when they are close to their homes, even if those homes are destroyed,” Sabbah said. “We want to help them stay connected to their land, neighbours, and communities.”

“So far, at least 35 sand trucks have been provided to stabilize makeshift camps and prevent water accumulation,” Sabbah told Mondoweiss.

Grassroots efforts extend beyond rubble removal. The youth-led “Ele Elna Elak” campaign recently established a desalination plant serving camps in northern Gaza. Commenting on the initiative, content creator Bissan Ouda said, “This achievement, accomplished with almost no resources, is like digging through rock.”

Freedom for Christmas: the extraordinary journey of an enslaved woman to Britain
A newly unveiled statue in North Shields is casting fresh light on the extraordinary life of Mary Ann Macham – a woman whose courage carried her from the brutality of slavery in the US state of Virginia to freedom on the banks of the River Tyne on Christmas Day, 1831.

With the help of a friend in Virginia who was enslaved to the harbour master, Macham (who was enslaved on a plantation) hid beneath a tree and in the forest for six weeks while men on horses and bloodhounds searched for her. She was then smuggled to the harbour, where the second mate of a ship stowed her away with the cargo.

After many weeks at sea, including a stop in the Netherlands, Macham reached Grimsby. There she was taken by road to North Shields and welcomed by two “Miss Spences” on Christmas Day.

The Spence family were Quakers and committed abolitionists who offered her refuge and support. Macham’s story, dictated to members of the Spence family, was later published in the Christmas 1950 issue of Tynemouth Parish. Her powerful account survives today, with the original text available through the African Lives in Northern England website.

Macham lived in freedom in North Shields for the next 62 years. She worked in the Spence household and married a local man, James Blyth. Though her story is little known nationally, exhibitions about her have been held at the Old Low Light Museum in North Shields and the Discovery Museum in Newcastle. Local newspapers have told her story with pride and affection.

Macham’s story is an early example of a pattern which continued for most of the century, of Black American fugitives from slavery or anti-slavery activists coming to Britain and Ireland to work, lecture, publish and live.

Other figures such as Frederick Douglass, whose legal freedom was paid for by Quakers in Newcastle, and Moses Roper, who lectured far and wide, eventually settling for a time in Wales, are fairly well known. There are several possible explanations for why Macham’s story hasn’t had the same recognition.

First, there is still a distinct lack of attention paid to Black British history in general, particularly anything before Windrush, the ship that brought the first large group of Caribbean migrants to the UK in 1948. Second, Macham was not, as far as the records show, an abolitionist or anti-slavery activist in the traditional way of public lecturing, as Douglass was. She told her story knowing it would be shared, but otherwise it seems she used her freedom in Britain as simply that – freedom.

Where she lived is another possible explanation for the relative ignorance of her story. Less attention is paid to diverse histories in north-east England compared with, for example, London.

Why people came to Britain

Several factors made Britain attractive as a place of freedom. There was no legal chattel slavery in Britain and Ireland (though much continued in the British colonies), and the landmark Somerset v Stewart case of 1772 ruled that an enslaved person must be held to be free by virtue of their presence on British soil.

Fugitive and formerly enslaved people came consistently to Britain and Ireland throughout the 19th century. Arguably, nowhere were they more warmly received and, to an extent, understood than in the most industrialised, and therefore often most deprived, areas of the country, where workers made up a large portion of the population.

In the 19th century, the north-east was a thriving hub of anti-slavery activity, playing host to many Black abolitionists and playing an active part in publishing Black literature and facilitating freedom. Examples of this include the local Quaker sisters-in-law Anna and Ellen Richardson, who raised funds for the freedom of Frederick Douglass, and the Spence family, who welcomed Macham in North Shields and helped her start her new life.

Work on Black histories in the north-east include research by the local African Lives in Northern England Project and by Northumbria University’s Brian Ward, who published a book about Martin Luther King’s visit to Newcastle in 1967 and the wider historical context.

Many workers in industrialised places in Britain in the Victorian era – such as Manchester, the coal fields of Wales and the north-east of England – also claimed to feel “enslaved”. They saw parallels between their condition and that of the American slave, an idea perpetuated in contemporary literature such as Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852).

Of course, the experience of a white, free workforce cannot realistically be compared with the life of those in chattel slavery. However, the feeling of oppression, capitalist exploitation, poverty and mutual support among struggling people meant that regions like the north-east were ideally placed to welcome those fleeing persecution and seeking refuge.

The sentiment that fostered a welcoming atmosphere in North Shields for Macham persists to this day. Following the exhibition about her at the Old Low Light Museum in 2019, £800 was raised through fundraising to lay a stone at her grave, which previously only held the name of her husband.

The stone was laid in 2020 by students from John Spence Community High School – named after the family who helped Macham. This and the statue stand as a lasting tribute to her courage, and the hearts of the community that welcomed her on Christmas Day in 1831 and continues to honour her.
