Are South Sudan’s Armed Groups Fighting an Ethnic Community—or the State?

By Madit Majak
Independent Political Analyst | South Sudan Eagle Media

South Sudan’s violence is increasingly explained—and inflamed—through an ethnic lens. Whenever clashes erupt in Jonglei, Upper Nile, or parts of Equatoria, a familiar and dangerous narrative resurfaces in public debate and on social media: that armed opposition groups are fighting the Jieng (Dinka) community rather than the state.

Some opposition supporters openly deploy tribal rhetoric to mobilize non-Dinka communities against the government, portraying the Kiir administration as a “Dinka kingdom.” This framing persists despite the fact that South Sudan officially recognizes 64 ethnic communities, all of which are—at least formally—represented within state institutions. Such rhetoric is less about political accuracy than emotional mobilization.

At the center of this distortion lies the persistent conflation of the Government of South Sudan. While it is true that governing elites and senior security leadership are disproportionately drawn from the different communities, the state itself is not an ethnic entity. Governments are institutions—defined by policies, command structures, and power relations—not collective expressions of an entire people.

When political conflict is reduced to ethnic identity, state violence becomes communal blame. In a country with a history of mass atrocities fueled by identity politics, this framing is not merely irresponsible—it is lethal.

The Sudan People’s Liberation Army–In Opposition (SPLA-IO) emerged from the 2013 political crisis as a challenge to governance failures, political exclusion, and the concentration of power in Juba. Its stated objectives have centered on reform, accountability, and power sharing.

In practice, however, ethnic narratives have increasingly been used by some of its supporters to mobilize fighters and justify violence. Critics argue that the SPLA-IO’s military strength has relied heavily on mobilization within a single community, reinforcing perceptions that the conflict is ethnic rather than political. Whether intentional or not, this perception has deepened mistrust and hardened communal divisions—allowing political leaders to evade accountability by shifting blame onto entire communities.

The National Salvation Front (NAS), operating largely in Equatoria, arose from grievances over land dispossession, militarization of civilian areas, and political exclusion. Its leadership frames the struggle as resistance to authoritarian governance and systemic marginalization.

Yet perception matters as much as intent. When government forces deployed in NAS-affected areas are viewed as ethnically homogenous, communities increasingly interpret state violence as ethnic aggression. This perception—accurate or not—feeds resentment, radicalization, and cycles of retaliation that extend far beyond the original political grievances.

Perhaps no actor illustrates the dangers of ethnic framing more clearly than the White Army. It is not a formal rebel movement but a loose mobilization of armed Nuer youth, historically organized around community defense in the absence of reliable state protection. At various moments, the White Army has fought alongside or in parallel with the SPLA-IO, further complicating perceptions of the conflict.

Its mobilization is often reactive—shaped by insecurity, revenge attacks, and political manipulation. Yet clashes involving the White Army are routinely reduced to “Nuer versus Dinka” violence, obscuring deeper causes: state collapse, militarization of society, and the failure of the government to provide impartial security.

This reductionist narrative benefits political hardliners and war profiteers while condemning ordinary citizens to perpetual fear.

The greatest threat facing South Sudan today is not only renewed fighting—it is the normalization of ethnic hatred as the primary explanation for political conflict. Once violence is framed as ethnic destiny rather than political failure, accountability disappears and reconciliation becomes impossible.

Ethnic communities do not declare wars. Political and military elites do. Across South Sudan, ordinary Jieng, Nuer, Equatorians, Shilluk, and others are overwhelmingly victims—not architects—of violence. They lose lives, livelihoods, and futures while elites mobilize identity to protect power.

The critical question, therefore, is not which ethnic group armed movements are fighting, but what they are fighting against politically. The answer lies in unresolved power struggles, broken peace agreements, stalled security-sector reform, and a governance system that concentrates authority while externalizing blame.

For regional actors and international partners, the lesson is clear: peace efforts that ignore the political roots of South Sudan’s conflict—and instead tolerate or reinforce ethnic narratives—will fail.

South Sudan’s war is fundamentally about power and governance. Turning it into a war between communities guarantees only one outcome: endless conflict, with devastating consequences far beyond the country’s borders.

"یقیناً وہ (خالق) اسے دوبارہ پیدا کرنے (واپس لانے) پر پوری قدرت رکھتا ہے۔"

اس سورہ کا مرکزی تھیم یہ ہے کہ انسان کسی "Unsupervised System" (لاوارث نظام) میں نہیں رہ رہا۔ کائنات (Universe) اور انسان کی اپنی بیالوجی (Biology) اس بات کا ثبوت ہے کہ ایک "Supreme Authority" موجود ہے جس نے نہ صرف ڈیٹا ریکارڈ کرنے کے لیے "Surveillance System" (نگرانی کا نظام) لگا رکھا ہے بلکہ وہ اس پورے سسٹم کو دوبارہ "Reboot" (قیامت) کرنے اور انسان کو "Data Recovery" (دوبارہ زندہ) کرنے پر بھی قادر ہے۔
لہٰذا، دین (Deen) صرف چند رسومات کا نام نہیں، بلکہ یہ یقین ہے کہ "Input" (دنیا کے اعمال) کا ایک حتمی "Output" (آخرت کا نتیجہ) ضرور نکلے گا، اور کوئی بھی انسانی چال (Strategy) اللہ کے اس "Master Plan" کو شکست نہیں دے سکتی۔

Phase 1: دی سرویلنس سسٹم (The Cosmic Surveillance)
(آیات 1 تا 4: ڈاٹس کا پہلا کنکشن)

آغاز (The Hook):
اللہ تعالیٰ کائنات کے سب سے بڑے "Contrast" (تضاد) کی قسم کھا کر بات شروع کرتا ہے۔
"وَالسَّمَاءِ وَالطَّارِقِ..." (قسم ہے آسمان کی اور رات کو نمودار ہونے والے کی)۔
یہاں ایک سوال اٹھتا ہے: "وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا الطَّارِقُ؟" (تمہیں کیا معلوم وہ رات کو آنے والا کیا ہے؟)

جواب ملتا ہے: "النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ" (وہ اندھیرے کو چھیدنے والا، گھورنے والا ستارہ ہے)

ربط (Connecting the Dot):
اللہ نے ستارے کی قسم کیوں کھائی؟ اس لیے کہ ستارہ رات کے پردے میں چھپی چیزوں کو "Expose" (بے نقاب) کرتا ہے۔ جس طرح ستارہ اندھیرے میں دیکھ رہا ہے، بالکل اسی طرح ایک اور "نگاہ" ہے جو انسان کو دیکھ رہی ہے۔

اگلی ہی آیت اس حقیقت سے پردہ اٹھاتی ہے:

"إِن كُلُّ نَفْسٍ لَّمَّا عَلَيْهَا حَافِظٌ" (کوئی نفس ایسا نہیں جس پر ایک "نگران" مقرر نہ ہو)۔

منطق (Logical Flow):

ڈاٹ یہاں کنیکٹ ہوا: "Star in the Sky = Guardian on the Soul."

اے انسان! تو سمجھتا ہے کہ تو اندھیرے میں چھپ کر گناہ کر سکتا ہے؟ ناممکن! جس طرح کائنات میں ستارہ گواہ ہے، تیرے اوپر ایک "Data Recorder" (حافظ) لگا ہوا ہے جو تیری ہر موومنٹ، ہر فائل اور ہر ایکشن کو کلاؤڈ پر محفوظ کر رہا ہے۔ تو Under Surveillance (زیرِ نگرانی) ہے۔

Phase 2: دی بائیولوجیکل آرگیومنٹ (The Argument from Origin)

(آیات 5 تا 8: منطقی دلیل اور مرکزی بلیک ہول)

منتقلی (Transition):

اگر نگرانی ہو رہی ہے، تو اس کا مقصد کیا ہے؟ کیا یہ ڈیٹا کبھی استعمال ہوگا؟ انسان اس بات پر شک کرتا ہے کہ مرنے کے بعد وہ دوبارہ کیسے زندہ ہوگا؟ یہاں سورہ  آسمان سے ہٹ کر انسان کے "DNA" پر فوکس کرتی ہے۔

"فَلْيَنظُرِ الْإِنسَانُ مِمَّ خُلِقَ" (انسان ذرا اپنا "Source Code" تو چیک کرے، وہ کس چیز سے بنا ہے؟)

"خُلِقَ مِن مَّاءٍ دَافِقٍ" (وہ ایک اچھلتے ہوئے پانی [Fluid] سے بنا ہے)۔

یہ پانی کہاں سے آیا؟ "يَخْرُجُ مِن بَيْنِ الصُّلْبِ وَالتَّرَائِبِ" (وہ ایسے اچھلنے والے مادّے سے پیدا ہوا جو پچھلے (ریڑھ کی ہڈی) اور اگلے (سامنے کے جسمانی ڈھانچے) کے درمیان موجود نظام سے ظہور میں آتا ہے۔”)

دی بلیک ہول (The Pivot Point):

اب یہاں وہ مرکزی آیت آتی ہے جو پوری سورہ کا Power House ہے:
"إِنَّهُ عَلَىٰ رَجْعِهِ لَقَادِرٌ"

(بے شک وہ جس نے نطفے سے ڈیزائن بنایا، وہ اسے واپس لانے [Reload/Restore] کرنے پر بھی قادر ہے)۔

ربط (Connecting the Dot):

یہاں منطق کا زبردست بہاؤ ہے:

اگر ایک حقیر بوند (Input) سے اتنا پیچیدہ انسان (Output) بن سکتا ہے، تو اسی انسان کو دوبارہ بنانا (Re-creation) کیسے ناممکن ہوسکتا ہے؟

یہ آیت پچھلی آیات (نگرانی) اور اگلی آیات (احتساب) کو جوڑتی ہے۔ نگرانی اس لیے ہو رہی تھی کیونکہ "واپسی" (Return) طے ہے۔

Phase 3: دی گرینڈ آڈٹ (The Day of Exposure)
(آیات 9 تا 10: واپسی کا نتیجہ)
منظر کشی (The Scene):

جب وہ "قادر" ذات انسان کو واپس لائے گی تو کیا ہوگا؟

"يَوْمَ تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ" (جس دن تمام خفیہ فائلیں، نیتیں، اور راز "Decode" کر دیے جائیں گے)۔

دنیا میں انسان اپنے چہرے پر ماسک چڑھا لیتا تھا، اندر کچھ اور باہر کچھ۔ لیکن اس دن "Operating System" سارا ہڈن ڈیٹا (Hidden Data) اسکرین پر لے آئے گا۔

نتیجہ (Result):

"فَمَا لَهُ مِن قُوَّةٍ وَلَا نَاصِرٍ" (پھر نہ اس کے پاس اپنا زور ہوگا [Self-Power] اور نہ کوئی مددگار [External Aid])۔

آج انسان اپنی "Power" (سیاسی طاقت، دولت) یا "Nasir" (وکلاء، لشکر، دوست) کے بل بوتے پر قانون سے بچ نکلتا ہے۔ لیکن اس دن یہ دونوں سسٹم کریش (Crash) کر جائیں گے۔

Phase 4: دی فزیکل ایویڈنس (Validation from Nature)
(آیات 11 تا 14: کائناتی سائیکل)
تصدیق (Validation):

اللہ تعالیٰ اپنے اس دعوے (قیامت) کی سچائی کے لیے دوبارہ کائنات کی طرف متوجہ کرتا ہے۔

"وَالسَّمَاءِ ذَاتِ الرَّجْعِ" (قسم ہے آسمان کی جو بار بار پلٹتا ہے [Water Cycle/Rain])۔
"وَالْأَرْضِ ذَاتِ الصَّدْعِ" (اور قسم ہے زمین کی جو پھٹتی ہے [Plant Growth])۔

ربط (Connecting the Dot):
یہاں ڈاٹ کیسے کنیکٹ ہوا؟
آسمان کا پانی واپس آنا = زندگی کا واپس آنا۔
مردہ زمین کا پھٹ کر پودا نکالنا = مردہ قبر کا پھٹ کر انسان کا نکلنا۔
اللہ کہہ رہا ہے: تم روز اپنی آنکھوں سے "Resurrection" (حیات بعد الموت) کے ٹریلر دیکھتے ہو، پھر بھی میری بات پر شک کرتے ہو؟

حتمی بیان (Verdict):

سن لو! "إِنَّهُ لَقَوْلٌ فَصْلٌ" (یہ قرآن ایک دو ٹوک فیصلہ ہے)۔

"وَمَا هُوَ بِالْهَزْلِ" (یہ کوئی ہنسی مذاق یا تھیوری نہیں ہے، یہ ایک Absolute Reality ہے)۔

Phase 5: دی اسٹریٹجک وار (The Clash of Plans)
(آیات 15 تا 17: سیاسی انجام)
کشمکش (Conflict):

اب جب یہ پیغام اتنا سچا اور منطقی ہے، تو مکہ کے سردار (اور آج کا جدید منکر) کیا کر رہا ہے؟

"إِنَّهُمْ يَكِيدُونَ كَيْدًا" (یہ لوگ اس حق کو نیچا دکھانے کے لیے سازشیں، پروپیگنڈا اور چالیں [Schemes] چل رہے ہیں)۔

وہ سمجھتے ہیں کہ وہ اپنی چالاکیوں سے اللہ کے اس "سرویلنس سسٹم" کو دھوکہ دے دیں گے یا اسلام کے پیغام کو روک دیں گے۔

دی ماسٹر اسٹروک (The Divine Counter-Plan):
اللہ مسکرا کر کہتا ہے:

"وَأَكِيدُ كَيْدًا" (اور میں اپنی خفیہ تدبیر [Strategy] کر رہا ہوں)۔
اللہ کی تدبیر کیا ہے؟ وہ انہیں ڈھیل دیتا ہے، انہیں اپنی رسی لمبی کرنے دیتا ہے تاکہ وہ پوری طرح ایکسپوز ہو جائیں۔

اختتام (Conclusion):

"فَمَهِّلِ الْكَافِرِينَ أَمْهِلْهُمْ رُوَيْدًا" (تو اے نبیﷺ! ان کافروں کو تھوڑی سی مہلت دے دیں، انہیں ان کے حال پر چھوڑ دیں)۔

یہ ڈاٹ واپس جا کر آیت نمبر 8 اور 9 سے مل جاتا ہے۔ یہ مہلت اس لیے ہے تاکہ "یوم تبلی السرائر" کو ان کا حساب پورا ہو سکے۔ ان کی شکست یقینی ہے کیونکہ وہ اس ذات سے لڑ رہے ہیں جو ستاروں، انسانوں اور ایٹموں کو کنٹرول کر رہی ہے۔

حاصلِ کلام: جدید دور کے لیے سبق
(The Ultimate Takeaway for the Modern Era)

اس سورہ کو اگر آج کے دور میں "Download" کریں تو ہمیں تین بڑے اسباق ملتے ہیں جو "دین بطور نظامِ زندگی" کو واضح کرتے ہیں:

پرائیویسی کا اختتام (The End of Privacy):
جدید انسان سمجھتا ہے کہ وہ VPN لگا کر، انکونیٹو موڈ (Incognito Mode) میں جا کر، یا بند کمرے میں کچھ بھی کر سکتا ہے۔ سورہ الطارق بتاتی ہے کہ "الہی کیمرے" اور "ڈی این اے ریکارڈرز" ہر وقت آن ہیں۔ آپ کا ذاتی احتساب (Self-Accountability) ہی آپ کا واحد نجات دہندہ ہے۔

سائنس اور مذہب کی یکجائی (Unified Truth):
یہ سورہ بتاتی ہے کہ مذہب کوئی غیر منطقی چیز نہیں۔ جو خدا "Embryology" (پیدائش) اور "Meteorology" (بارش کے نظام) کو چلا رہا ہے، وہی خدا "Eschatology" (آخرت) کا نظام بھی لائے گا۔ اگر آپ سائنس کو مانتے ہیں تو آپ کو آخرت کو بھی ماننا پڑے گا کیونکہ دونوں اسی ایک "سسٹم" کا حصہ ہیں۔

انقلابی امید (Hope for the Struggle):

باطل نظاموں (Corrupt Systems) کی بظاہر مضبوطی اور سازشوں سے گھبرانے کی ضرورت نہیں۔ وہ "پلاننگ" کر رہے ہیں، لیکن اللہ کی "پلاننگ" ان پر حاوی ہے۔ مومن کا کام صرف اس "قولِ فصل" (قرآن) پر جمے رہنا ہے؛ نتیجہ اللہ کا "الگورتھم" خود نکالے گا۔

ایک جملے میں خلاصہ:
"تم ایک ایسے کائناتی شیشے کے گھر میں رہتے ہو جہاں ستارے گواہ ہیں، تمہارا جسم خود ثبوت ہے، اور واپسی کا دروازہ کھلا ہے—لہٰذا اپنی خفیہ فائلوں (نیتوں) کو صاف رکھو کیونکہ سسٹم کا مالک تمہیں دوبارہ آن کرنے والا ہے۔"

Jammu and Kashmir’s armless archer and Paralympics medallist Sheetal Devi edged out quadruple amputee Payal Nag of Odisha to win the gold in a much-anticipated clash of the Khelo India Para Games on Sunday.
In the battle between two teenagers, defending champion Sheetal came from behind to successfully bag her second gold medal of the Games at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium.
Pitted against the 17-year-old Payal, Sheetal, 18, triumphed 109-103 in their compound open final match.
Current Issue:
Payal lost all four limbs due to electrocution when she was a child, and she now shoots with prosthetic legs.
The sunny conditions in the national capital did not deter the competitive spirit of the archers, as 40-year-old Rakesh Kumar and 30-year-old Jyoti Baliyan also won gold medals in their respective events.
Jharkhand’s Vijay Sundi beat Haryana’s Vikas Bhakar 6-4 in the men’s recurve open gold medal match, while Haryana’s Pooja won the women’s recurve open gold after defeating Maharashtra’s Rajshri Rathod 6-4.
All eyes were on the women’s compound gold medal match between Sheetal and Payal.
Sheetal started with scores of 8 and 7, while Payal began with double 10s. However, Payal lost the upper hand in the third round, shooting a 7 for the first time, while Sheetal returned to her consistent best of 9s.
and 10s. The deciding fifth round saw Sheetal clinching the gold.
"Firstly, Payal played very well in the final, and with her continuous hard work, she will definitely get a medal for India soon. Personally, I am grateful for all the blessings bestowed by Mata Rani that I won my second gold medal at the Khelo India Para Games," Sheetal told SAI Media.
The soft-spoken Payal spoke about the technical aspects of the sport in her first Khelo India Para Games.
"Earlier, I used to shoot arrows with two devices in my prosthetic legs, but now I’m shooting with just one leg. It was difficult to adjust, but I still reached the final despite the discomfort, and there were also a lot of windy conditions today. But I am happy to have competed in the final and to have won the silver," she said.

The White Army: A Civilian Vigilante Outside the SPLA-IO Command Structure

By: Hon. Juol Nhomngek Daniel, National MP

Introduction

The White Army, often misunderstood as part of the SPLA-IO (Sudan People’s Liberation Army-In Opposition), is in fact a civilian vigilante group that emerged from the instinctive survival mechanisms of the Nuer community. Its existence reflects broader patterns of self-defence organizations across South Sudan, formed in response to insecurity, ethnic polarization, and weak state institutions. To equate the White Army with a formal military command structure is misleading, as its roots lie in community protection rather than organized rebellion.

Community Vigilante Groups as General Phenomenon Across South Sudan 

The White Army is one among several ethnic-based vigilante groups that have arisen in South Sudan. Comparable examples include: Gelweng, Titweng, and Tit Bai of the Dinka in Bahr El Ghazal Region, Arrow Boys of the Azande, Monyomiji in Eastern Equatoria State, Murle Youth, largely members of the Cobra Faction in Greater Pibor Administrative Area (GPAA), whose leaders have transitioned into 30 Youth Protection Teams (YPTs) and Abushok of the Dinka Apadang, who have since aligned with the SSPDF (South Sudan People’s Defence Forces).  These groups share a common origin. They are community-based militias formed to defend against external threats, often organized along age-sets or tribal lines. Their rise is symptomatic of deeper structural problems within South Sudan.

Causes of Vigilante Mobilization

The proliferation of such groups is driven by: Political manipulation by elites seeking to consolidate power, ethnic polarization and mistrust among communities, weak and unprofessional state security institutions plagued by corruption, impunity and poor governance that fail to protect civilians, competition over scarce resources, which fuels inter-communal violence.  Observers widely agree that the fragility of state institutions, particularly security agencies, is the most critical factor. South Sudan is a failed state due to collapse of basic governance since the government loses control over vast territory, cannot provide security, and fails to deliver essential services. Hence, the failure of South Sudan to provide protection to the communities that make them resort to developing their self-defence mechanisms, giving rise to vigilante groups like the White Army.

Targeting of the White Army

The SPLM-IG (Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In-Government) and its military wing, the SSPDF, have often targeted the White Army. This is partly because of the Nuer community, like the Dinka, is numerically large and politically influential. Nuer leaders in government are seen as competitors by elites from other ethnic groups, and in particular, leaders from Dinka ethnic group. The SPLM-IG therefore seeks to weaken the Nuer political base by undermining its grassroots defense structures. The prime by the SPLM-IG is the White Army, which the SPLM-IG views as the power base of Nuer leaders in both government and in oppositions. 

Therefore, the policy of the government is directed towards how to neutralize the White Army and weaken the leaders from Nuer Community. Thus, by pushing the White Army toward alignment with the SPLA-IO, the armed wing of the SPLM-IO, the main opposition, the SPLM-IG creates a justification to treat them as combatants. This is because once associated with the SPLA-IO, the White Army is no longer viewed as a civilian vigilante group but as part of an armed opposition force, thereby legitimizing military action against them.

Humanitarian crisis caused by the actions of the SPLM-IG and Legal Concerns

The problem arises when the SPLM-IG through SSPDF treats the issue of the While Army as the Nuer Civilian issue and uses it as a pretext of destroying grassroots Nuer Communities through indiscriminate bombing. This has legal implications internationally. While combatants are legitimate military targets under International Humanitarian Law (IHL), the problem arises when government forces use this justification that the While Army is part of the SPLA-IO to indiscriminately attack and bomb civilians in the villages.  This is the violation of the key principles of IHL, which emphasize that: 

(1)  The armed forces must distinguish between combatants and civilians. 
(2) The attacks must not cause excessive harm to civilians relative to the anticipated military advantage. 
(3) The collective punishment is prohibited. It provides that the civilians cannot be punished for the actions of combatants within their community. 

Therefore, the principles of the IHL prohibit the SSPDF from indiscriminately carrying out the bombardment of civilian areas under the pretext of targeting the White Army, which is the violation of the above three IHL. The indiscriminative attacks or bombardments of civilians without an adequate notice amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, as they are deliberately intended to intimidate and punish as a way of spreading terror in the entire communities rather than focusing on legitimate military objectives.

The SSPDF Must Give Adequate Notice before bombing or attacking

In order to the SSPDF to avoid liability under the IHL, it must give adequate warning that must actually reach civilians at risk, not just be symbolic gestures. The notice must allow civilians enough time to evacuate or take protective measures. There must also be advance warning before the attack, not simultaneously or afterward. The timing should balance military necessity with civilian safety. The messages given by the notice must be understandable to the local population, which means that it must be in language, format and in cultural context. The military must avoid technical jargon or vague phrasing that could confuse civilians. 

The means of Communication can be through leaflets dropped from aircraft, radio or TV broadcasts, text messages or phone calls, loudspeakers or public announcements. Using diverse methods increases reach and reliability. The warnings should indicate the area, nature, and approximate timing of the attack as general or overly broad warnings may be ineffective or cause unnecessary panic. Notices are must because they are part of the precautions in attack obligation under International Humanitarian Law (IHL). They supplement the rules of distinction (separating civilians from combatants) and proportionality (avoiding excessive harm relative to military advantage).

Conclusion

Using the White Army as the pretext of destroying the Nuer Grassroots Communities in totality is against the principles of IHL. The White Army cannot be used as the justification of indiscriminately bombing and attacking the Nuer grassroots Communities. If the SSPDF believes that members of the White Army who were part of the SPLA-IO are in a given village, then the SSPDF must give an adequate notice as explained above to the village concern.  After all, the White Army is not part of the SPLA-IO command structure but a civilian vigilante group born out of survival instincts in the face of insecurity. Its existence mirrors similar ethnic-based defense groups across South Sudan. The continuing by the SSPDF to use them as justification of destroying all communities of the Nuer people is illegal.

Bomb Disposal Unit, CID Crime Scene Unit Inspect Site of Shariatpur Explosion That Left Two Dead, One Injured; Bomb-Making Materials Recovered

Ajman Ali Sorder

Following the bomb explosion in Bilashpur Union of Zajira upazila in Shariatpur early Thursday that left two people dead and one injured, a 16-member team from the Anti-Terrorism Unit’s Bom disposal Unit and the CID Crime Scene Unit inspected the site. During the inspection, they recovered various materials used to make bombs.

Shankar Kumar Ghosh of the Anti-Terrorism Unit’s Bomb Disposal Team confirmed the matter over the phone at 12:45 pm.
He said that from 10:30 am, a team comprising 10 members of the Anti-Terrorism Unit’s Bomb Disposal Team and six members of the CID Crime Scene Unit had been working at the site. “We inspected the scene and its surrounding areas. During the inspection, we collected various bomb-making materials as evidence.
The recovered materials included gunpowder, splinters, broken glass, barbed wire, cassette tape, zarda containers and marble stones. “Most of the materials commonly used to make bombs were found at the site. We are collecting the evidence and will hand it over to Zajira Police Station. The police will then take further legal steps,” he added.
Regarding the matter, Officer-in-Charge (OC) of Zajira Police Station Saleh Ahmed told  that a 16-member team from the Anti-Terrorism Unit’s Bomb Disposal Unit and the CID Crime Scene Unit had been working at the site since morning. “They are recovering different types of evidence. The Bomb Disposal Unit and the CID will submit separate reports. Based on the evidence and their reports, we will take further action,” he said.
He said that last Thursday, an explosion occurred while bombs were being made in the Beparikandi area of Bilashpur Union. The explosion blew away the roof of a house. Around half a kilometre away from the scene, the body of Sohan Bepari (32), son of Delwar Bepari of Beparikandi village, was found in a crop field (garlic field). In the incident, Arman Nayan Molla (25) and Md Nabi Hossain (22) were also seriously injured. They were first rescued and taken to Zajira Upazila Health Complex. As their condition was critical, they were later referred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
Later, Md Nabi Hossain (22), son of Rahim Sardar of the same village, died at Dhaka Medical College Hospital around 4:30 pm while undergoing treatment. The other injured person, Nayan, is still receiving treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
He further said that earlier, on January 4, clashes broke out between two rival groups at Budhairhat Bazar in Bilashpur Union of Zajira upazila over dominance, during which more than a hundred cocktail bombs were exploded. One person, Jabed Sheikh (20), was injured in the incident. On that day, Zajira police recovered four buckets of cocktail bombs in abandoned condition during a drive.
Locals said the tin-shed house where the incident occurred had been built two months ago by Sagar Bepari, son of Abu Siddique Bepari.
According to police sources, the clash took place between followers of local UP Chairman Kuddus Bepari and those of his rival Jalil Madbar. The two sides have long been engaged in a dispute over dominance in the area. As part of this ongoing rivalry, multiple clashes have occurred at different times, during which both sides detonated cocktail bombs.
The cocktail bomb explosions in Bilashpur on April 5 and November 2 last year caused widespread concern. In connection with those incidents, police filed cases under the Explosives Act against Kuddus Bepari, Jalil Madbar and several of their supporters. Both Jalil Madbar and Kuddus Bepari were sent to jail by the court. Later, UP Chairman Kuddus Bepari was released on bail, while Jalil Madbar remains in jail.
Locals said the deceased Sohan was a supporter of Kuddus Bepari. At present, supporters of Kuddus Bepari led by Mannan Bepari and followers of Jalil Madbar led by Nasir Bepari are attempting to establish dominance in the area.

Unmasking the libelous individuals behind Watchdog Press
By Santino Riak Maker
I am writing to address the public, including Gen. Paul Malong Awan and Pagan Amum Okiech. This article focuses on the defamatory writings published by Watchdog Press, a Facebook page that claims to promote liberation but instead engages in blackmail and extortion.
I chose to write this article because the Watchdog Press page has deviated from its original mission, now attempting to coerce and defame my teacher, Dr. Sunday de John. Dr. Sunday de John is a South Sudanese citizen who holds a special place in the hearts of many, including mine because of his numerous charitable deeds, sociable nature, capabilities, and love for his people. He has educated generations in various schools and has fought for this country in multiple ways. Notably, he was among those who traveled to Ethiopia to train with the Red Army in Dima. With both medical and political expertise, Dr. Sunday de John boasts a wealth of experience across different fields, particularly in the media industry since 2003, where he authored the popular column “Third Eye” in the Khartoum Monitor Newspaper. He has collaborated with veteran writers such as Alfred Taban Logune, Edward Ladu Terso, Nhial Bol Akeen, Albino Odeng, Albino Okeny, Tabani Joseph, Professor Adam Chollong, Professor Taban Lo Liyong, Michael Koma, and many others.
Dr. Sunday de John has mentored several youth in the media industry, including myself, Dengdit Ayok Deng Agoor, Akol Ayom Wek Ateny, and others. He played a significant role in establishing the Citizen Newspaper. Through his writing, Dr. Sunday de John has actively advocated for the independence of South Sudan.
He is the youngest South Sudanese to have engaged in intellectual battles for the interests of South Sudan against established Sudanese writers such as Teyep Mustafa and Qudbi Mahdi, who owned their own newspapers. Additionally, he challenged certain South Sudanese figures whom he considered sellouts, including Dr. Wani Tombe and Dr. David De Chan. Despite his age being one of the challenges facing him at the time, Dr. Sunday de John emerged victorious. He has authored over 3,000 articles in support of President Salva Kiir Mayardit and the SPLM/A, while also recalling the liberation efforts of Dr. John Garang de Mabior.
Dr. Sunday de John has demonstrated exceptional courage, professionalism, and patriotism, which are rooted in his outstanding communication skills, both verbal and written. As a result, he stands apart from those associated with the Watchdog Press. I am compelled to advocate for him as someone whose life he has positively influenced on personal, academic, and intellectual levels. He has nurtured capable intellectuals, and his contributions are undeniably significant.
The individuals behind the libelous activities of the Watchdog Press are Kanybil Noon and Garang Malong Awan. They also have additional associates, including a man from our hometown of Yirol, who assists in managing the page. Future articles will reveal his identity.
Kanybil Noon approached individuals in Europe, specifically in Estonia and Latvia, who created Watchdog Press. He requested their assistance in establishing a Facebook page designed to remain untraceable to any cities in Eastern Africa and to keep their Kenyan and Ugandan phone numbers safe from potential cybersecurity monitoring. The primary objective of this page is to defame highly esteemed South Sudanese politicians, government officials, and well-known personalities, as well as to extort money from them.
Mr. Kanybil Noon is a criminal and a former national security officer who deserted his responsibilities and fled the country after committing multiple crimes, violating several articles of the National Security Act, 2014, specifically articles 53 (4), (5), (7), 57 (1), (2), (3), (6), 59, and 65. After his departure, he aligned himself with a foreign-sponsored political movement known as the People’s Coalition for Civil Action (PCCA). His objective is to employ any means necessary to further his agenda for regime change while evading prosecution for his criminal activities.
He did not leave the country for personal safety. Instead, he fled due to his involvement in illegal activities, including espionage and corruption, as outlined in the previously mentioned articles of the National Security Act, 2014. Consequently, he had to escape to avoid arrest and prosecution. Once in a foreign country, he allied himself with rebels in a desparate attempt to overthrow the government and evade accountability.
Of the individuals he targeted for libel through the Watchdog page, some are government officials or members of the first family, including H.E. President Salva Kiir Mayardit, Hon. Adut Salva Kiir, Gen. Gregory Deng Kuach, Gen. Akol Koor Kuc, Gen. Manasa Machar Bol, Amb. Monica Achol Abel Aguek, Hon. Chol Thon Abel, and Hon. Emmanuel Athiei Ayual, among others. Others are those who have refused to participate in defaming others or engaging in his subversive activities. This latter category includes Dr. Sunday.
After many years of exile in a futile and unproductive opposition, Dr. Sunday has reflected on his experiences and chosen to advocate for peace and progress in the country. This shift in focus does not serve the interests of Kanybil and Garang Malong, along with their sponsors. The two individuals lack credibility in all areas of life; they have minimal impact on public communication and harbor jealousy toward Dr. Sunday de John.
They want Dr. Sunday de John to insult the president and other government officials. Dr. Sunday has emphasized that President Salva Kiir Mayardit is not only a head of state and government but also a symbol of national unity and an elder; thus, he cannot bring himself to insult him. He has clarified that insults do not lead to national liberation; instead, they only accentuate personal hostilities, and he sees no valid reason to insult other South Sudanese. Furthermore, he has stressed that political issues should not be viewed as personal grudges, and he will not engage in personal attacks against any politician. Additionally, he has reiterated that character assassination is not an appropriate method for achieving any political objectives.
In advancing their incrimination agenda, Mr. Kanybil Noon and Garang Malong have even proposed titles for articles they want Dr. Sunday de John to write. For instance, Kanybil Noon, through Watchdog, suggested the title, “Salva Kiir Mayardit must step down to pave the way for peace and reconciliation.” They threatened that if Dr. Sunday de John did not comply, they would metaphorically place him in a "political coffin." This threat and refusal to comply served as the basis for publishing two articles under Dr. Sunday de John's name. However, these articles are purely defamatory and lack any substantive message. They launched various insults at Dr. Sunday, but are these articles factual? They are lies. Dr. Sunday is the son of a veteran who served the nation during wartime and in the government of South Sudan, having contributed to some of the foundational structures that the country relies on today. He comes from a large family, and the prospect of hunger would not drive him into politics. A family filled with engineers, pilots, militants, and other achievers cannot have their older brother labeled as a "foodiologist," a term that Kanybil and his associates have coined without being meaningful.
They aim to portray Dr. Sunday de John as a sworn adversary of the state. However, Dr. Sunday de John is an honest individual whose political stance is rooted in truth and national discourse, rather than personal grievances. Although personal insecurities have driven him to rebel, he has never publicly insulted anyone. He has always written, spoken, and acted with objectivity.
Dr. Sunday de John has come under scrutiny due to a perception, based on speculation within the rebel camps, that Hon. Adut Salva Kiir Mayardit may recognize him, bring him back home, and collaborate with him. This perception instills fear and threatens the rebels, given Dr. Sunday de John’s capabilities. Kanybil and his associates claim that President Salva Kiir Mayardit is pleased with Dr. Sunday de John's integrity. Consequently, they believe Dr. Sunday must be discredited; either through coercion to insult the president or by questioning his morality; so that he remains in rebellion, where he is deemed essential to support Gen. Stephen Buoy Rolnyang.
The claim that Dr. Sunday de John has switched allegiances for food is false. Dr. Sunday de John is a founding member of the South Sudan United Front/Army (SSUF/A); he was the one who announced its formation. Later, he disagreed with Gen. Paul Malong Awan, leading to their separation in 2020. Since then, Dr. Sunday de John has remained with his faction, the SSUF-Progressive. He has steadfastly refused to be exploited and has rejected attempts to coerce him into insulting the president, which is something Gen. Paul Malong Awan sought him to do.
Now, the victims of the Watchdog press have identified the individuals responsible for their defamation through this deceptive entity known as Watchdog. While the team is large, Kanybil serves as the owner and CEO of this criminal enterprise, with the others merely acting as administrators. Let us bring Kanybil and his libelous watchdog press to their senses, they must account for their crimes.
I am determined to combat this group. As journalists, we are steadfast in our commitment to upholding and adhering to ethical standards in our practice. If Kanybil and his lieutenant are serious, they should step forward and engage in open dialogue, just like others do. Why do they attack citizens, especially leaders, in secret? Do they believe that operating an alias Facebook page grants them lasting power? Do they think that the words of those hiding behind the curtains can genuinely help the country? They are aware that their statements lack factual support and that there is no evidence to back their claims, yet they continue this behavior as it amounts to extorting money from vulnerable individuals.
Dr. Benjamin Bol Mel was a victim of their attacks before he was dismissed; afterwards, they received payment and reversed their criticism of him into praise. This phenomenon is what wise people refer to as moral decay.
Pagan Amum, Malong Awan, Deng Bol Aruai, and other ineffective politicians who identify as the opposition fund the fight against Dr. Sunday de John. Unlike Dr. Sunday de John, these individuals deeply entrench themselves in corruption and unethical behavior. Gen. Paul Malong Awan has held various positions within the government, both at the state and national levels, and has a history of corruption, including attempts to undermine the constitution by overthrowing the president. I urge him to tell his son to keep quiet. Nobody wants to fight with Malong, he is an elder but if he cannot restrain Garang Achol, then let him endure this fight.
Pagan Amum Okiech disrespectfully opposes the president, he undermines the president, claiming that President Salva Kiir Mayardit coerced him into leading the firing squad against Commander Lekurnyang. Pagan harbors a personal grudge because Lekurnyang, a man he conspired against, was not only his relative by marriage but also a friend and colleague. His resentment toward President Salva Kiir Mayardit is so intense that he wishes for the president's demise. President Salva didn’t punish him, he only asked him to complete his job on his relative. So if President Salva is not out of power, Pagan has vowed not to come home. Why must all people be tied to him?
The evidence indicates that such a person is untrustworthy, and no rational individual would willingly submit to his leadership. His failure is inevitable, and the alliance he is attempting to forge, which desperately seeks the services of Dr. Sunday de John, is destined to fail at its inception.  
As long as Watchdog continues to spread lies, rumors, and defamation, I will stand firm in defending those it targets. My fight will be directed at those who sponsor Watchdog Press, not the unseen criminals behind it. They may claim to uphold morality, but no one who inflicts harm while hiding in the shadows can truly be considered moral.

THE UPRIGHT MAN: The Sacrifice and Betrayal of Thomas Sankara

​History often forgets the names of those who sought to break the chains of neocolonialism, but the name Thomas Sankara is etched in the hearts of the people forever.
​When Sankara took office in 1983, he didn’t just change the name of "Upper Volta" to Burkina Faso—he changed the identity of a nation. He envisioned a "Land of Upright People." He was a leader who drove a small car, rejected luxury, championed women’s rights, and fought for African self-sufficiency.
​But his vision was a threat to the status quo.

​THE FINAL BETRAYAL
​The most painful part of Sankara’s story isn't just the foreign interference—it’s the betrayal of a brother. Blaise Compaoré was more than a deputy; he was a man Sankara met in Morocco and considered a lifelong friend.
​On October 15, 1987, that bond was shattered.
​"It is me they want"

​At 4:15 p.m., Sankara sat with 13 colleagues at the National Headquarters to discuss the country’s future. By 4:30 p.m., the sound of gunfire tore through the air. After his guards and driver were struck down, Sankara made a final, selfless choice.
​Hoping to spare the lives of his friends in the room, he stood up and told them: "Step aside, it is me they want."
​He walked out with his hands raised, unarmed. The assassins did not hesitate. They riddled his body with bullets until he was unrecognizable. Tragically, his sacrifice did not stop the massacre; the gunmen entered the room and executed everyone except Alouna Traoré.

​THE AFTERMATH
​While Compaoré claimed he was home sick during the coup, he immediately seized power, a position he held for 27 years. The shadow of his involvement never faded.
​Sankara was only 38 years old when he died, but his spirit was never silenced. A note left at his grave perhaps says it best:
​"Do not worry, Mama Sankara, we will avenge the death of your son. We are all Sankaras."
​Thomas Sankara proved that you can kill a revolutionary, but you cannot kill the revolution.

Wuol said years of failed governance, stalled peace implementation, ethnic targeting, and widespread civilian suffering have rendered obedience to the state morally indefensible. He described the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement as a “false peace” that protects entrenched power rather than citizens, citing continued violence, displacement, starvation, and the detention of key opposition figures, including Dr. Riek Machar.

According to Wuo, communities in Upper Nile, Jonglei, and Unity States continue to face systematic attacks and exclusion, while repeated peace processes and ceasefires have failed to deliver accountability or protection. He stressed that resistance by marginalized groups should not be dismissed as criminality but understood as a response to a system that has blocked reform and justice.

Wuol warned that stability built on fear, silence, and impunity is not peace, arguing that when a government becomes the source of insecurity, rebellion shifts from being disorder to a moral response to injustice. He emphasized that any resistance must remain disciplined and avoid targeting civilians to retain moral legitimacy.

The opinion has sparked debate as South Sudan grapples with renewed violence and political uncertainty ahead of the planned December 2026 elections.

Letter from Pibor Monitor to the Lou Nuer Youth.

PIBOR MONITOR:

Dear Lou Nuer Youth.

We write as intellectuals to acknowledge the receipt of your letters of calling for peace. May God guide and bless us all in our search for peace! 

May God change our hearts so that we could change the hearts of our brothers in the villages who still believe that war is still an option to achieve peace in 21st century when diplomacy is the most effective than war. 

Glory and honour be to God! 

It looks like we've accepted that, no matter how it started since 2009 and has been ending lately, it shouldn't end the same this year, next year or any other year again. Mabruk aleikum!

Indeed, it was heavy. It was beyond our might. It was unbearable to the children and women. It killed the men we knew. It widowed our strong and, resilient women. It left us with everlasting pain. It torn our heart. It left us homeless.  It left us destitute, in solitude and detached. And from your letters, we join you in our divine, and collective call: THIS YEAR MUST BE DIFFERENT. And we, the youth, must be that difference. We, the youth of the two communities must be the difference because everytime the bell of propaganda was rung in Juba and Bor, it has always been us bleeding. It have been our women dying. Our livelihoods destroyed. Our homes burnt and our populations displaced. 

The only tool our enemy had on hand to destroy us was, propaganda. The destruction of our sisterly communities was achieved through misinformation and wrong narratives that digged deep into our roots, divided us on those petty differences, little did we know that it was actually through these divisions that they manipulated our minds, asserted their control both on our resources, and broken our social fabrics, with which we were able to interact with, and even replaced it with what we should say and what we shouldn't say, what we should do and who to interrogate with, who to not. And surely they succeeded since 2009. 

We as Murle community bled, fought, and by God's grace, still have a place to call a home today, regardless of the plans by Juba to clear or exile us for eternity just because we were proud of who we are — the Murle People and chose our home before anything else. 

If only we'd have had time, as the two sisterly communities who are the powerhouses of this great country, to sat down earlier and think about why we always die, we'd have identified a trace and benchmarks to the endless suffering of our children, women and elderly since day one. We wouldn't have accepted as communities to loose more than 100 men in battle just because of an act 5-10 thieves. It's like the communities have accepted to sacrifice more 1000s lives not to end the act of the few thieves who are spoiling our peace, and are enemies to both communities but to take a revenge driven by generalisation. It's like we have been accepting to loose no matter how armed with knowledge we are, and choose not to win the battle of the few criminals in the expense of many.  

Congratulations for having woken up! It's true that, problems not only destroy men, but also make some strong men. We are now the products of the problems we faced for all this while and thank you for choosing peace over war! 

Lou Nuer and Murle communities have been brothers and sisters for years before South Sudan came to being. We have always been good people toward each other. Even today, Murle man can willing choose to sleep in Lou Nuer home intead of other South Sudanese communities. This is trust. This is a sign that we have fight as brothers not enemies. This is a dedication that, despite our differences, we still believe in who we are. The brave men who can at any time could effect to what they resolve. Lou Nuer have never been killers in cold blood. We as Murle and Lou Nuer have always had one thing in common: Fight as men live as brothers. This has always been our definition until SPLA came in with their curses in 2005. They introduced their ways of survival in bushes which included propaganda, deception, lies and division as tools to assert control. And from that point, our communities and lives changed. Sadly, we're here today, at crossroads. No country, no food, no schools, no hospitals, no peace, no nothing. The country we all bled for now belongs to few and their families. Those few do as they wish. It is longer for all of us.

Our differences played a significant role after CPA in 2005 when our political leaders, since they were just fresh from bushes of the country as militias, learnt the divide and rule tactic that was used by British, and to eliminate their 'enemies', they divided us, misinformed us, armed us and kept us fighting.
 
Today, all of us, both the Lou Nuer and Murle are crying about the deteriorating living conditions and abject poverty we've caused to our sisters and mothers while the other side of the world is watching us while laughing. Truly, we're and have always played bigger fools! 

What do we have in common? Blood? Muddy villages? It's been our prayer too, that, we shouldn't loose anyone of us because of the conflicts which at the end burn our homes, takes those we love and displace our families every year just because of the action of the few criminals or those few top elites who either want to stay in power or enrich their families. Enough is enough! We shouldn't bleed for anyone again this year. We should instead bleed to protect our homes, protect our peace, and our properties. We shouldn't allow anyone to use us for their personal or political benefits. 

As we lastly waking up to face the challenges facing our communities heads-on, we should think about what we could do to work together so that instead of finishing ourselves, work together to identify the culprits who want to spoil our peace. The peace is ours. The peace is yours. The peace is for us. The peace is for our families. We should appreciate why we shouldn't choose war over fragile peace. We should appreciate the small peace we have instead of waiting for the big peace Juba is promising us. It'll take us eternity to achieve the Juba's peace. 

At the end, it's us who have been suffering. If we misunderstood ourselves because of our differences in politics, Riek and Salva are good friends who, since 1980s have been partying and drinking together. They have been friends for all these while we've been barking at each other as hungry dogs! If at all they have become enemies to each other lately, because of their divergent political views and ambitions, let their families start fighting each other first. They should lead by example. 

For all these years we've been burning our homes, kidnapping our own children and killing our women because of action of 2 or 3 mens who couldn't work for themselves but chose stay awake at night while we sleep so that they forcefully steal, or achieve their political goal. Let's take up the responsibility, and act responsible enough in our capacities to figure out these criminals and those who use us, and hold them responsible instead of destroying our homes, and killing ourselves. No matter who looses or wins, it's our communities who pay the price for the suffering. 

Get this clear: our muddy villages are not cursed as we might have thought. We have been lost. We lacked moral direction. We were misled. We should therefore, develop our muddy villages to be like Juba, Wau, Aweil and Bor. Enough of being laughing stocks in the South Sudanese societies. Because, while we were busy waging wars and fighting one another, Bor and Juba are weighing to such a great height yet. Nimule and Kapoeta are doing great because of border like the one Akobo and Pibor share with Ethiopia. We should emulate! 

After all, we are brothers. We are neighbours. We'll be neighbours forever. There's no day we will gk away where we are or get those who will love us more than those we have lived together for long. We ate together. We danced together. We traded together. We intermarried. This is our history. We should be proud of it. 

We too, were heartbroken and torn for the last few days. Rumour started as simple as they've been in the last years. It has in Lou Nuer area that, Murle youth are mobilized, allegedly by CA to attack Lou Nuer. We STRONGLY believe it as a PROPAGANDA of its great kind and yet as another plan by anti-peace elements to put, the two communities who enjoyed the fruits of peace in the the last few years, at mess again. We as intellectuals DO NOT like it. Murle people DO NOT like it and we believe Lou Nuer communities DO NOT like it too. We DO NOT want to bleed anymore, and our children and women DO NOT want to suffer any more. It's OUR believe!

Regardless of the political differences of our leaders, we, the communities are one and same people with one goal of peaceful coexistence and brighter future for our children. We are not ready to die for anyone or any political conflicts. We are for peace. Our peace is important. 

This is our message. This is our ringing bell of truth. This is our assurance to you all our friends and families from Lou Nuer and our beloved communities right from Burmath, Nyandid, Akobo, Uror and Nyirol, that, there's no ongoing mobilization in Murle land to attack Lou Nuer areas based on our political differences. It is high time we shouldn't use our wounds of the past to propagate violence. It's our prayer that, the year 2026 is for peaceful coexistence between the two communities. We are proud of our beautiful heritage and coexistence. Murle people stand for peace and love. 

This message however, is not an assurance that the typical 2 or 3 thieves will not be there to disturb us but an assurance that there's no MOBILIZATION about going to attack Lou Nuer here in Pibor and our God, the most highest will, as He has been doing, stand with us till these clouds of suspicion and doubts are cleared. As we are talking about this, there might be some thieves and criminals who would disturb us. Let's all, without blame, without pointing fingers, work hard to prevent them from spoiling our peace. They're enemies to both of us. We should all work together to protect our peace. 

Let's ALL stand for peace, even if not for the whole of South Sudan as a country now but for the safety of our few alive men, children and the widows of the two communities who suffered due to senseless wars fueled by misinformation, wrong narratives and hate preached by the unethical politicians of our bleeding country. 

We traded in fear and suspicion for long, and it resulted to the wars which still, up to today, non of us is happy about. Let's all say enough is enough. Let's all choose our own peace. Let's protect our homes, children and women. We're tired of being used. We must stand for ourselves and our communities NOW or else we will not stand for ourselves again. There's no force formed against us shall prosper if we all stand united in our pursuit for peace. 

We shall overcome!  We shall overcome! We shall overcome! 

May peace be with us all, now, and forever more! 

Salam Allah, the Most High, aleikum wa aleina!

The steel barrel of the musket was cold against the humid Massachusetts air. It was 1774, and the village of Granville was buzzing with a dangerous new word. You could hear it in the tavern, see it in the tight jaws of the farmers, and feel it in the Sunday sermons. The word was "Liberty."

For most men in Granville, the word meant freedom from a tax on tea or a stamp on paper. It meant telling a King across the ocean that he could not rule their wallets. But for the young man holding the musket, the word was sharper. It was a physical ache.

His name was Lemuel Haynes. He was twenty-one years old. He was a patriot, a calm and pious soul, and a soldier ready to die for his country. He was also a servant, bound by law to a master, and the son of a black father and a white mother who had abandoned him at five months old.

He stood on the village green, drilling with the militia, preparing to fight a war for independence while living in a house where he could not legally decide his own bedtime.

The contradiction was invisible to almost everyone but him.

Lemuel had grown up in the home of David Rose. He was not a slave in the southern sense—he was an indentured servant. The Roses were kind people. They treated him like a son, not a tool. They taught him to read the Bible by the light of the fireplace when the chores were done. They let him absorb the Psalms and the Gospels until the rhythms of scripture became the rhythm of his own speech.

But kindness is not freedom.

An indenture is a contract of ownership. Until he turned twenty-one, his body belonged to the Rose family. His labor was theirs. His time was theirs. When the men of Granville gathered to talk about the "tyranny" of King George, Lemuel stood quietly in the background, listening to men who owned other men shout about the evils of being owned.

It was a strange, suffocating irony. He absorbed the rhetoric of revolution. He read the pamphlets that said all men were born with natural rights. He believed them, perhaps more deeply than the men who wrote them. To a white farmer, "tyranny" was a tax. To Lemuel Haynes, "tyranny" was the defining condition of his existence.

Then came April 1775.

The news arrived in Granville like a thunderclap. The British regulars had marched on Lexington and Concord. Shots had been fired. Men were dead. The time for talking about liberty was over; the time to bleed for it had begun.

The Granville militia did not hesitate. They grabbed their powder horns and their coats. Lemuel Haynes did not have to go. As a servant, his obligation was to the farm. As a man of color, the quarrel between white colonists and a white King could easily have been seen as none of his business.

He went anyway.

He marched with his neighbors. He carried his kit and his gun, stepping in time with men who, in a different context, might not have shaken his hand. He was not a mascot or a drummer boy; he was a Minuteman.

This is where the logic of the era twists.

The colonial system was built on a precise hierarchy. White landowning men stood at the top. Women, servants, and the enslaved stood below. The system relied on the belief that this order was natural, ordained by God, and necessary for survival. A Black man with a gun, demanding rights, broke the unspoken rules of the hierarchy.

But the colonies were desperate. They needed every finger that could pull a trigger. The militia accepted Lemuel because they needed a soldier. They did not stop to consider that by handing him a musket and asking him to fight for freedom, they were handing him the moral authority to demand it for himself.

The rule works only as long as the servant stays silent. It works until the servant steps onto the battlefield and proves his blood is the same color as the master’s.

The march to Roxbury was long. The adrenaline of the alarm faded into the dull ache of marching feet and heavy packs. Lemuel saw the chaos of the siege of Boston. He saw the raw, unpolished reality of the Continental Army.

There was no glory in the mud. There was only the waiting, the disease, and the constant, gnawing hunger. In the camps, the distinctions of the village often melted away. A British bullet did not check for a pedigree. Typhus did not care if you were a deacon or a servant.

In the quiet moments between drills, Lemuel watched. He saw men who claimed to love liberty treat others with contempt. He saw the friction between the northern farmers and the southern officers. He saw the fracture lines of a new nation that was screaming for justice while standing on the necks of half a million enslaved people.

He finished his service in 1775, then signed up again to join the expedition to Ticonderoga in 1776. He was there when the Declaration of Independence was read. He heard the words: "We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal."

He took those words literally.

Most men went home after the war and went back to their plows. Lemuel Haynes went home and picked up a pen.

He did not raise a sword against the hypocrisies of the new nation. He raised an argument. He began to write, pouring his intellect onto the page. He wrote a manuscript titled "Liberty Further Extended."

In it, he did something radical. He took the very words of the Founding Fathers—the arguments they used against Britain—and turned them around to face the Americans. He argued that if liberty was a natural right given by God, it could not be limited by skin color.

"Liberty is equally as precious to a black man," he wrote, "as it is to a white one, and bondage equally as intolerable to the one as it is to the other."

It was a devastatingly simple point. It stripped away the complex justifications for slavery and left only the naked truth: You cannot be a patriot and a slaveholder without being a liar.

He didn't stop there. Lemuel Haynes became a minister.

This was his second revolution. In 1785, he was ordained. For over thirty years, he served as the pastor of a church in Rutland, Vermont. It was a white congregation. Every Sunday, a Black man stood in the pulpit, looking down at rows of white faces, interpreting the word of God for them.

He baptized their babies. He buried their dead. He mediated their disputes.

In the early years of the American Republic, this was almost impossible to imagine. A Black man holding spiritual authority over a white community was a direct challenge to the racial caste system. Yet, they loved him. They called him "Father Haynes."

He had disarmed them. Not with a musket, but with a character so undeniable and an intellect so sharp that their prejudice could not survive in his presence.

He lived to be eighty years old. He saw the nation grow, and he saw the shadow of slavery grow with it. He never stopped preaching the full meaning of the Revolution. He never let his neighbors forget that the work of 1776 was unfinished.

Lemuel Haynes reminds us that the American Revolution was not just fought by men in powdered wigs signing parchments in Philadelphia. It was fought in the mud by men who had no guarantee that the "freedom" they were fighting for would ever include them.

He fought anyway. He fought because he believed in the promise of the country more than the country believed in him.

Today, we look back at the founding of the nation and we often see a static picture. We see marble statues and oil paintings. We forget the mess. We forget the contradictions. We forget the men like Lemuel Haynes who stood in the gap between what America was and what it said it wanted to be.

He did not burn the system down. He stepped inside it, mastered its texts, fought its wars, and then politely, firmly, demanded that it live up to its own rules.

His life poses a question that still hangs in the air, two hundred and fifty years later. When we talk about liberty, are we talking about a privilege for the few, or a right for the many?

Lemuel Haynes knew the answer. He carried it on his shoulder in 1775, and he preached it from the pulpit until his final breath. The question is, have we learned it yet?

Sources: "Black Preacher to White America" by John Saillant; PBS "Africans in America" Historical Documents; The Lemuel Haynes Society Records. Some details summarized for narrative flow.

The Fragile Foundations of Abiy Ahmed’s Power and the Road Ahead in 2026

(OLF-OLA Press Release)

As we enter the new year, Abiy Ahmed’s hold on power remains  anchored in three interlinked but increasingly fragile pillars for his day-to-day survival.

The first pillar rests on the irresponsible diversion of a grotesquely disproportionate share of national wealth toward military expenditure. An army apparatus that has been fundamentally  weakened now survives only because extraordinary levels of public resources and external assistance are being funnelled into it at  the  expense of the essential needs of the country and its people. Even then, the extravagance has produced little more than inflated army numbers and some technological acquisitions. But numbers alone do not constitute an effective force. They cannot substitute for professionalism, morale, or genuine commitment. Tactical military technology is also no longer monopolized by the regime; it is increasingly accessible to opposition forces as well.

The security sector is also growing more fractured. Significant  segments of Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), federal police, intelligence services, and regional forces are  increasingly  dissatisfied—whether over the inequitable distribution of resources within the ranks or disillusionment with the political direction in which Abiy Ahmed is steering the country.

Parts of these forces continue to function primarily as instruments of political coercion. Throughout the past year, they have been  deployed to suppress dissent, intimidate communities, and project an image of control. However, the loyalist core of the ENDF also continues to erode with: battle field losses, mass desertions, and collapsing morale. The regime now relies on forced conscription,  emergency recruitment drives, counterfeit militias, and irregular formations to fill its ranks. Overextension across multiple fronts has  laid bare fatal weaknesses in command, logistics, and strategic  coherence. OLA’sengagement with these forces over the past year stands as a testament.

Summary of Our Military Engagements with Abiy’s Forces in 2025

Geographic and temporal Scope

• Western: Western and Wollega zones: Repeated overruns of military camps, interdiction of supply routes, and ambushes on ENDF units and militia forces;

• Central: Shewa zones (North, West, Southwest, Special Zone/Shaggar): Frequent engagements near key logistical corridors and in proximity to the capital;

• East and South: Arsi, Hararge, Guji, Borana, Wollo, Matakal, Benishangul: Sustained operations reflecting the geographic  spread of resistance and the regime’s difficulty in stabilizing any single conflict.

• Operation Cichoomina Kaayyoo (Q1 2025): A nationwide offensive marking a shift to a coordinated multi-front offensive.

• Operation Thousand Fronts (April 2025): A 10-day campaign  across 50+ districts, validating deep operational reach and simultaneity.

• Sustained Campaign (Q2-Q4  2025): Continuous, high-tempo  operations across all Oromia zones and beyond, systematically targeting command structures, supply lines, and recruitment efforts.

Cumulative Impact (Jan-Dec 2025):

• Regime Personnel Losses: Conservatively, at over 7,500 killed in action and 8,000+ wounded across all major engagements.

• Material Gains: Capture of thousands of small arms, hundreds of  crew-served weapons (PKM, DShK, sniper rifles), and vast ammunition stocks.

• Other impacts: Hundreds of political prisoners have been liberated from prison raids, repeated interdiction of the critical Ethio-Djibouti supply corridor, and the forced embedding of civilian officials in military camps for their protection

The military pillar of Abiy’s survival remains in name, but it is increasingly stretched, reactive, and dependent on external financial and political support.

The second pillar of Abiy Ahmed’s rule is the systematic deployment of propaganda, information control, and narrative  manipulation. State media, affiliated proxies, and cyber units  orchestrate narratives aimed at manufacturing  legitimacy,  discrediting opposition forces, and masking abuses. Restrictions on independent international media, internet  shutdowns, platform  restrictions, and the harassment or criminalization of independent  journalists remain standard practice. Coordinated online campaigns attempt to portray military setbacks as isolated  incidents and to depict resistance movements as illegitimate or externally manipulated.

This tool has also been central to the previous regime’s survival. What distinguishes Abiy Ahmed is the unprecedented scale and  brazenness of the disinformation. The regimeblatantly fabricates figures on captured opposition fighters, deploys its own militia and stages fictitious surrender spectacles out of thin air. It has, for example, recently informed multiple diplomats that it has killed over 40,000 OLA fighters without any hint of irony. 

It also routinely falsifies economic data on growth, inflation, and general macroeconomic performance. This is partly enabled by the dismantling of institutional mechanisms for factual reporting,  including the removal of a semblance of professionalism from the Central Statistical Agency following the dismissal of non-cadre professionals.

For a time, these tactics helped sustain Abiy Ahmed. Today, however, they are approaching their natural limits. Independent  local media increasingly refuse to echo official narratives. Opposition voices are finding new platforms. Social media, diaspora outlets, and citizen reporting continue to expose contradictions in the regime’s claims. 

Leaks from within the security establishment and local administrations reveal internal fractures. Attempts to repackage repression as “reform”, mismanagement as “capital city face-lift” and impunity as “transitional justice” are now met with open disbelief at home and growing scepticism domestically and abroad.

A third pillar of Abiy Ahmed’s survival is a deliberate attempt to widen existing political, social, and ethnic faultlines to prevent solidarity among the opposition across the political divide. Local conflicts are fueled or instrumentalized. Ethnic and communal identities are selectively mobilized. Suspicion between communities is encouraged.

Abiy uses this primarily to make  cross-sectional solidarity difficult. It also allows the regime to present itself as the “guardian of unity” against alleged fragmentation, even as its “policies” deepen the very fractures it claims to manage. Over the year, this approach has  attempted to increase the risk of localized violence and revenge  cycles, and undermine prospects for cross-cultural political cooperation.

Despite these attempts by the regime, our internal efforts to  consolidate the Oromo Liberation Army with major Oromo opposition leaders and key supporters within the regime have continued to bear fruit and will be further strengthened.

Beyond the Oromo political sphere, our commitment to building  principled solidarity with all forces that share our democratic  aspirations remains unwavering. We will continue, with full determination, to work with all opposition forces toward empowering our peoples to freely and collectively determine their own destiny. 

The foundations of Abiy Ahmed’s rule—fear of repression, confusion through falsehood and fragmentation of opposition—are no longer in place. They are brittle, strained, andexposed. The year ahead will be decisive.

Unity as the Shield: Why the Nuer Must Stand Together Against Division

By: Hon. Juol Nhomngek Daniel, MP

Introduction

South Sudan’s fragile peace and political landscape remain deeply scarred by cycles of violence, mistrust, and manipulation. Among the communities most affected by this turmoil is the Nuer. Today, the Nuer face a deliberate campaign of division and destruction orchestrated by the state. To survive and thrive, unity must be their strongest weapon. Internal differences must be set aside, for disunity only weakens their collective strength and exposes them to calculated state policies designed to dismantle their identity and existence.

Misconceptions About the Dinka Agenda

Many Nuer perceive the state as implementing a “Dinka agenda.” In reality, the government pursues its own survival strategy, exploiting the Dinka majority as a shield. Ordinary Dinka citizens also suffer under the regime’s oppressive policies. The state has worked tirelessly to misinform the Dinka majority, convincing them that other communities seek to overthrow them. This manipulation fosters mistrust and division, while the regime consolidates power for its own benefit. The truth is clear: the government does not act on behalf of the Dinka people. It acts for itself, using ethnic divisions as a tool of control.

The Nuer as a Target of State Policy

The Nuer community has been systematically targeted by the government’s national security apparatus. Policies classify Nuer counties into “hostile” and “friendly” categories, not to protect citizens but to divide them. Hostile counties such as Nasir, Ulang, Akobo, Nyirol, Uror, Fangak, Ayod, Rubkona, and Panyijiar have faced relentless military campaigns, airstrikes, and ground assaults. Friendly counties, meanwhile, are spared temporarily but not out of compassion, but to buy time until the state can turn its machinery of violence against them as well.

This strategy reveals the government’s view of the Nuer not as citizens, but as a rival nation to be subdued. The indiscriminate use of cluster bombs and airstrikes against civilians demonstrates elements of genocide, as defined by international law, which include: killing members of the group, inflicting serious harm, and deliberately creating conditions of destruction.

Revenge vs. Justice

The brutal massacre of Nuer civilians in Juba in December 2013 remains a painful wound. Yet revenge against the Dinka community cannot serve justice. True justice lies in implementing Chapter V of the Revitalized Agreement, which establishes mechanisms for truth, reconciliation, and accountability. The mechanisms of Transitional justice, which can provide comprehensive justice needs are: 

(1) Commission for Truth, Reconciliation, and Healing (CTRH). This mechanism is tasked with uncovering past violations and fostering healing.
(2) Compensation and Reparation Authority (CRA). This mechanism ensures that victims receive acknowledgment and support.
(3) Hybrid Court for South Sudan (HCSS). This mechanism prosecutes serious crimes, blending international and domestic standards.

The above three institutions are essential for addressing legacies of conflict, holding perpetrators accountable, and ensuring lasting peace. Importantly, they also guarantee justice for Dinka victims of Nuer actions, proving that reconciliation benefits all communities.

The Danger of Division among Nuer and other Communities

The government thrives on division. By spreading narratives that some Nuer communities “colonize” others, it seeks to fracture unity and weaken resistance. Nuer leaders who unconditionally cooperate with the regime often do so out of survival, not conviction. Therefore, their advice, shaped by fear, risks leading the Nuer into destruction. If the Nuer accept division, they will be destroyed. This makes their unity not an optional but the previous and existential.

The Path Forward: Reform and Federalism

The only way to counter the destructive policies of the state is through reform. The Revitalized Agreement offers a roadmap for building strong institutions, empowering grassroots communities, and ensuring justice. Federalism, in particular, provides a framework for protecting communities by decentralizing power and preventing its abuse by a single group or regime.

The Nuer should understand that without the strong institutions that can create the strong system, what happened to Dr. Riek Machar Teny and other leaders who are facing political motivated criminal trial and those in exile will not end with them but it will continue to face other leaders that will fight for welfare of the communities. 

As a matter of fact, Dr. Riek Machar Teny and political detainees including those in exile are being persecuted because of fighting for equality and protection of all communities under the law. Their struggle underscores the importance of systemic reform over short-term survival.

Conclusion

The Nuer people stand at a crossroads. Their division can lead to destruction but their unity can lead to survival and reform. The state’s campaign of misinformation and violence is designed to weaken and eliminate them. But by remaining united, rejecting divisive narratives, and fighting for the implementation of the Revitalized Agreement, the Nuer can secure justice, reconciliation, and lasting peace not only for themselves, but for all South Sudanese communities. This shows that unity is the shield, reform is the path and federalism is the guarantee.

Charles Deslondes (1789 – January 11, 1811) was a revolutionary who was one of the leaders in the 1811 German Coast uprising, a slave revolt that began on January 8, 1811, in the Territory of Orleans. He led more than 500 rebels against the plantations along the Mississippi River toward New Orleans. White planters formed militias and ended up hunting down the rebels.
The enslaved insurgents killed one Free Man of Color, the “commandant”, “overseer”, or “slave driver” on the Andry Plantation which started the revolt, and one white man during their retreat from the outskirts of New Orleans. The militia and the Army killed 95 enslaved people, reflecting killings in the battle on Bernard Bernoudy’s plantation, some gratuitous “accidental” killings of innocent enslaved people by the Army on its march from New Orleans, and the executions that followed the tribunals after the revolt was put down.
He was born on the plantation of Jacques Deslondes. Deslondes’s plantation succession records have him described as being a “Creole mulatto slave” by the name of Charles, “about 16 years old”, listed as a “field laborer.” He was likely baptized a Catholic.
