🇸🇴🚫 Collective Punishment: The Administration Officially Targets the Somali Community…

The war on Minnesota has moved from the streets to the paperwork. In a move that legal experts describe as "collective punishment" and human rights groups are calling ethnic cleansing by bureaucracy, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced today that the Trump administration is ending Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for thousands of Somali nationals. The deadline is brutal and precise: they must leave the United States by March 17 or face forcible deportation.

The justification offered by Secretary Noem is a masterclass in guilt by association. Speaking on Fox News, she argued that "allowing Somali nationals to remain... is contrary to our national interest," citing alleged fraud within Somali-linked charities as the pretext. Let’s be clear about what this means: because a specific group of individuals is accused of defrauding pandemic relief programs (an investigation, notably, that began under President Biden), the administration has decided to punish thousands of innocent Somali refugees who had nothing to do with it. This isn't justice; it is the weaponization of a crime to justify a purge.

The cruelty was amplified by the official Department of Homeland Security social media channels, which posted a message that sounded less like a government agency and more like an anonymous troll account: "Our message is clear. Go back to your own country, or we’ll send you back ourselves." This is the new language of American diplomacy…threats issued via tweet, stripping away any veneer of humanitarian concern or professional decorum.

Noem also claimed that conditions in Somalia have "improved" enough to warrant the return of refugees. This is a dangerous fiction. Somalia remains plagued by Al-Shabaab terrorism and instability. Sending families back to Mogadishu isn't a policy decision based on safety; it is a deportation quota disguised as a status review. The "improvement" is a lie told to clear the books.

This move cannot be viewed in isolation; it is the latest escalation in the siege of Minnesota. The state, which is home to the largest Somali population in the U.S., is currently occupied by over 2,000 federal agents. Following the shooting of Renee Good and the defiant stance of Governor Walz and Mayor Jacob Frey…who famously told ICE to "get the fuck out"…the administration is now exacting retribution on the state's most vulnerable residents.

President Trump has made the subtext text, threatening "retribution" against Minnesota Democrats for "aiding and abetting" the alleged theft of federal funds. But his vengeance isn't limited to politicians. Federal officials are now threatening to pause Minnesota’s eligibility for massive entitlement programs, including SNAP (food stamps) and childcare funding. The President is effectively holding the food security of poor Minnesotans hostage to punish the political defiance of their leaders.

The targeting of the Somali community serves a dual purpose. It feeds the administration's "Americans First" nativist base while simultaneously destabilizing a state that has become the face of the resistance. He wore war paint under his Army uniform and rode into Nazi-occupied Germany to steal 50 horses—becoming the last War Chief in his tribe's 200-year history.
Montana, 1913. Joe Medicine Crow was born into the Crow Nation at a time when his people's traditional way of life was fading into memory. The buffalo were gone. The open plains were fenced. The warrior culture that had defined his ancestors for generations seemed destined to become nothing more than stories.

But his grandfather, White Man Runs Him, made sure the stories survived.

White Man Runs Him had been a scout for George Armstrong Custer at the Battle of Little Bighorn in 1876. He'd witnessed the last great victory of the Plains tribes. Now, as an old man, he sat by the fire with young Joe and passed down the ancient ways.

He taught Joe about the War Chiefs—the highest honor a Crow warrior could achieve. To earn that sacred title, a man had to complete four specific deeds in battle:

Lead a successful war party.

Touch an enemy without killing him (counting coup).

Take an enemy's weapon in combat.

Steal an enemy's horse.

Joe listened with a broken heart. He was born too late. The age of horses and hand-to-hand combat was over. He'd never ride into battle. He'd never become a War Chief.

The tradition, his grandfather told him sadly, would likely die with the elders.

Joe went to college instead. He studied anthropology, determined to at least preserve his culture's history even if he couldn't live it. He was working on his master's degree when Pearl Harbor was attacked.

December 1941. Joe Medicine Crow enlisted in the U.S. Army.

Before he left for war, his grandfather called him close one final time. The old man's hands shook as he painted traditional red war designs on Joe's arms.

"You will go to war," his grandfather said. "Remember who you are. Remember what I taught you."

Joe promised. He wore the war paint under his Army uniform. He tucked a sacred eagle feather inside his steel helmet, hidden from view.

He was a modern American soldier preparing to fight Nazis with rifles and grenades. But in his heart, he was a Crow warrior preparing for something far older.

Joe was assigned to the 103rd Infantry Division and shipped to Europe in 1944. The fighting in France and Germany was brutal—machine gun fire, artillery barrages, tanks rolling through devastated villages.

Joe wasn't thinking about ancient traditions. He was trying to survive.

But sometimes destiny finds you anyway.

The First Deed: Lead a War Party

Somewhere in France, Joe's commanding officer gave him an order: take seven men and scout through German-held territory. They had to gather intelligence and return alive.

Joe led his squad through enemy lines using skills his grandfather had taught him—moving silently, reading the landscape, sensing danger before it appeared. They avoided German patrols, dodged landmines, completed their mission.

Every single man returned safely.

His commanding officer called it excellent leadership. Joe realized he'd completed the first deed.

The Second and Third Deeds: Take a Weapon and Count Coup

In a bombed-out French village, Joe was scouting ahead when he turned a corner and collided directly with a German soldier.

Both men were knocked backward. Joe's rifle flew from his hands and skidded across the rubble. The German soldier still had his weapon.

For one frozen second, they stared at each other. Then the German raised his rifle.

Joe didn't reach for his knife. He didn't run.

He charged.

Joe slammed into the German soldier before the man could fire, knocking him to the ground. He grabbed the rifle barrel and wrenched it from the enemy's hands.

Now Joe stood over him, holding the German's own weapon. The man lay terrified on the ground, waiting to die.

Joe looked at him—young, scared, defeated. He could have killed him. Instead, he let him go.

In those chaotic seconds, Joe had completed two more deeds: he'd taken an enemy's weapon in hand-to-hand combat, and by knocking the man down and touching him, he'd counted coup.

Three deeds completed. One remained.

The Final Deed: Steal an Enemy's Horse

This was the impossible one. It was 1945. The German army used tanks, trucks, and motorcycles. Horses were relics of a previous century.

Joe figured the ancient tradition would end at three-quarters complete. Close, but not enough.

Then, as Allied forces pushed deeper into Germany, something unexpected happened. German fuel supplies ran desperately low. In some areas, Nazi officers began using horses again for transportation.

Early one morning, Joe's unit approached a farmhouse occupied by SS officers. Through the morning mist, Joe spotted something that made his pulse race.

Behind the farmhouse was a stable. Inside were at least fifty horses—prized animals belonging to the German officers sleeping inside.

Joe stared at those horses and heard his grandfather's voice: Remember who you are.

This was it. This was his moment. The war would end soon. He'd never get another chance.

He waited for darkness. German guards patrolled the perimeter. Joe moved like a shadow—silent, invisible, using every hunting skill he'd ever learned.

He slipped into the stable. The smell of hay and horses filled his lungs—it smelled like home, like Montana, like everything his grandfather had told him about.

He moved among the animals, calming them with soft words in the Crow language. He found the finest horse, fashioned a makeshift rope halter, and swung onto its bare back.

Then he gave a loud war cry—the same cry Crow warriors had used for centuries.

He kicked the horse into a gallop and burst through the stable doors, leading all fifty horses behind him in a thundering stampede.

German soldiers shouted and fired into the air, but it was too late. Joe was already riding hard toward American lines.

And as he rode—with bullets whizzing past, with fifty stolen horses thundering behind him, with the modern world exploding all around—Joe Medicine Crow began to sing.

He sang a traditional Crow war song, the same song his ancestors had sung two centuries earlier when they rode across the plains.

For that moment, the tanks and trenches disappeared. He wasn't fighting in Germany in 1945. He was riding for his people, carrying their honor forward through time.

He arrived at American lines with the captured horses. His commanding officer was stunned. His fellow soldiers cheered—they'd just captured valuable enemy transportation.

But Joe knew what he'd really done. He'd completed the four deeds. He'd honored his grandfather. He'd kept a tradition alive.

When the war ended, Joe returned to Montana. He went to the Crow elders and told them everything.

They listened in silence. They verified each deed. They consulted the ancient laws.

Then they held a ceremony that hadn't been performed in generations.

They painted his face with traditional designs. They placed the War Chief headdress upon his head. They danced and sang the old songs.

Joe Medicine Crow was named a War Chief of the Crow Nation.

He was the last man to ever earn that title.

Joe lived to be 102 years old. He became a renowned historian and author, writing extensively about Crow culture and Native American history. He earned a master's degree from USC. He advised presidents and spoke at the Smithsonian.

In 2009, President Barack Obama awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, saying: "An act of extraordinary valor speaks for itself. So does a life."

But Joe always said the medals and honors were secondary. What mattered was the continuity—that he'd kept his grandfather's traditions alive in the middle of the most modern war in history.

He proved something profound: heritage isn't about the past. It's about carrying meaning forward, even when the world around you has completely changed.

Joe Medicine Crow died in 2016 at age 102. He was buried with full military honors and traditional Crow ceremonies—a bridge between two worlds until the very end.

He was the last War Chief. But his story ensures that what a War Chief represents—courage, honor, cultural pride, connection to ancestors—will never die.

Because sometimes the most powerful act of resistance is simply remembering who you are.

I WORE A $12 DRESS TO MEET HIS BILLIONAIRE FAMILY. THEY CALLED ME "TRASH" UNTIL I BOUGHT THEIR COMPANY.

I never told Julian that my monthly "allowance" was actually a $52,000 paycheck. 💸

To him, I was just Elena. The girl with the messy bun, the girl who clipped coupons for oat milk, the girl who drove a 2011 Honda Civic that rattled when it went over 40 mph.

He loved being the "provider." He loved buying me dinner at Chili’s and watching my eyes light up.

He had no idea that while he was stressing about his credit card limits, I was the Lead Systems Architect for one of the largest fintech firms in Chicago.

I didn’t hide my money to be deceitful. I hid it because my Nana raised me right.

"Elena," she told me before she passed, "A man who loves you for your wallet is an employee, not a husband. Wear rags, and see if he treats you like a Queen." 👑

So, when Julian finally said the words, "My parents want to meet you this weekend at the estate in Lake Forest," I knew it was test time.

I didn’t pack my Prada. I didn’t pack the Louboutins.

I put on a faded navy dress from a thrift store. I scraped my hair back. I drove my rattling Honda Civic right up to the wrought-iron gates of the Sterling-Vance estate.

The house was a monster. A sprawling, limestone beast that screamed "Old Money." Or at least, desperate new money trying to look old.

Manicured hedges. A fountain that probably cost more than my college tuition. And a row of Range Rovers in the driveway.

When I parked my rusted Honda next to them, the front door opened immediately.

It wasn’t a warm welcome.

Julian’s mother, Patricia, stood there like an ice sculpture. She was draped in silk that probably cost $500 a yard.

She didn’t look at my face. She looked at my shoes. Then my car. Then my bare wrists. 🛑

Her lip curled. Just a millimeter. But I saw it. I’ve seen that same look in boardrooms when old men realize a twenty-something woman is about to audit their books.

"Julian," she said, her voice dripping with fake sweetness. "Is this the... friend you told us about?"

"Fiancée, Mom," Julian said. But his voice was weak. He didn't step forward to hold my hand. He stayed on the porch, safe in her shadow.

That was Red Flag Number One. 🚩

Inside, the house was suffocating. Portraits of ancestors who looked miserable. Crystal vases on every surface.

Julian’s sister, Bella, walked in ten minutes late. She was holding a glass of wine and looking at her phone.

"Oh," she said, glancing up at me. "You’re the one who works in... support? Like, a call center?"

"I work in tech," I said quietly.

"Right. Tech support. Cute." Bella laughed. It was a cruel, sharp sound. "Julian, did you tell her we have a dress code for dinner? Or does she not own anything else?"

I waited for Julian to defend me. I waited for him to say, "She’s brilliant. She builds the security systems that keep your trust fund safe."

But he didn’t.

He just laughed nervously. "She’s simple, Bella. She doesn’t care about fashion. It’s... charming."

Charming. Like a pet. Like a charity case.

Dinner was a nightmare. 🍽️

They sat me at the far end of the table, miles away from Julian.

Patricia grilled me like I was a criminal suspect.

"Who are your people, dear?"

"My father was a mechanic," I said. "My mother taught third grade."

Silence. Absolute, horrified silence. You would have thought I said they were serial killers.

"How... quaint," Patricia said, wiping her mouth with a linen napkin. "And you expect to fit into this family? Into this lifestyle?"

"I expect to be treated with respect," I said, my voice steady.

Bella snorted into her wine glass. "Respect is earned, sweetie. And frankly, you look like you’re here to steal the silverware."

I looked at Julian. He was staring at his plate. He was ashamed of me.

That hurt more than the insults. The man I loved was ashamed because I wasn’t draped in logos.

"Excuse me," I said, standing up. "I need to use the restroom."

I walked down the hallway, my heart pounding. I wasn't going to cry. I was furious. 🔥

I found the bathroom, splashed cold water on my face, and took a deep breath. I was about to walk out and leave them forever.

But then, I heard voices from the library next door.

The door was cracked open.

"She is an embarrassment, Julian," Patricia’s voice hissed. "A mechanic’s daughter? Driving that scrap metal heap?"

"I know, Mom," Julian said.

"You cannot marry her. The Sterling-Vance image is fragile right now. We need the merger with the Kensington family. You need to marry Vanessa Kensington."

"I know," Julian said again. And this time, his voice was clear. "I’m not going to marry Elena, Mom. Relax."

I froze. My hand hovered over the door handle.

"I’m just having fun," Julian continued. "She’s easy. She pays for everything, she cooks, she cleans. She’s a placeholder until the Kensington deal goes through next month. I’ll dump her once the merger is signed."

"Good boy," Patricia purred. "Just make sure she doesn't make a scene at the engagement party next week. We have investors coming. We can't have her looking like... that."

"Don't worry," Julian laughed. "I'll buy her something decent to wear. She'll be so grateful she won't say a word."

I stood there in the hallway, and the sadness evaporated.

It was replaced by something cold. Something hard. 🧊

They thought I was a poor, naive girl they could use and discard. They thought I was a "placeholder."

They didn't know that the "Kensington Merger" they were so desperate for?

My firm was overseeing the due diligence.

And they definitely didn't know that the Sterling-Vance company was technically insolvent, surviving only on a line of credit from a bank...

A bank where I sit on the Board of Directors. 📉

I walked back into that dining room. I didn't yell. I didn't throw wine.

I smiled. A big, bright, predatory smile.

"Everything okay?" Julian asked, looking relieved that I hadn't run away.

"Perfect," I said. "I can't wait for the engagement party, Julian. I have a feeling it’s going to be unforgettable."

Two weeks later. The Engagement Party. 💍

The backyard was transformed into a fairy tale. String lights, a jazz band, waiters passing champagne.

Julian had bought me a dress. It was pastel pink and hideous. I wore it anyway.

I watched Patricia and Bella schmoozing with the investors. I saw Vanessa Kensington there, looking bored, waiting for her turn to claim my fiancé.

They were all so confident. So arrogant.

At 8:00 PM, Patricia tapped a spoon against her glass.

"Everyone, attention please!" she beamed. "We are so happy to celebrate our son Julian tonight. And we have a very special announcement regarding the future of the Sterling-Vance corporation!"

She gestured for Julian to come up. He grabbed my hand and pulled me onto the stage.

"Smile," he whispered to me. "Don't embarrass me."

I smiled.

I waited until the applause died down. I waited until Patricia looked at me with that smug, victorious grin.

Then, I stepped up to the microphone.

"Thank you, Patricia," I said. My voice boomed across the silent lawn.

"Before we celebrate, I actually have a little presentation of my own."

Patricia frowned. "Elena, what are you doing? Sit down."

"No," I said. "I don't think I will."

I pulled a small remote out of my purse and pointed it at the giant projection screen behind us.

The screen flickered.

It wasn't a photo of Julian and me.

It was a spreadsheet. A forensic accounting spreadsheet.

"What is this?" Bella shrieked from the front row.

"This," I said calmly, "Is the Sterling-Vance financial audit I completed this morning. It shows that this family has been embezzling funds for five years to pay for their cars, this house, and this party." 😱

The crowd gasped.

"And this," I clicked the button again. A new document appeared. "Is the foreclosure notice on this estate. I bought the debt this morning."

I turned to Julian. His face was white as a sheet. He looked like he was going to vomit.

Jacobin recently invited me to give a broad overview of “the American Jewish left after Oct 7th.” A few things I tried to argue here: one, that there was a real expectation after Oct 7th that the American Jewish community would “rally around the flag” and defend both Israel and American nationalism, and instead we found a very public and visible civil war in the Jewish community over the war in Gaza. Two, Jewish Voice for Peace has emerged not only as an important Palestine solidarity organization, but as one of the more important organizations on the American left, both for the particular way in which it merged 90s NGO politics with a mass and community-organized base, and also, through perhaps an accident of history, Israel and Palestine has emerged at the center of a global struggle around race and empire, “first” and “third world,” white supremacy, and colonial violence. My final point was more speculative but I try to suggest that class divides globally and also w/in the Jewish community are, in an overdetermined way, expressed through splits on Zionism. Not that Zionism is explicable thru a class analysis or that the ethnic cleansing of Palestine is primarily a class conflict, but rather that identifications w the state and its empire - much like the Vietnam War - tend to break along class lines, and this suggests broader possibilities for solidarity and coalitions on war, empire, and social spending. In 1943, on the frozen battlefields of World War II, winter was as deadly as any weapon.
Snow erased footprints. Silence swallowed soldiers.
And somewhere in that white wilderness, German forces began to fear something unseen.
Not a tank.
Not an airstrike.
But a man who moved like the land itself.
His name in U.S. Army records was Private Samuel White — a young man born in 1921 on Navajo land in New Mexico. To the military, he was just another soldier.
But his upbringing made him different.
Samuel was raised learning patience, observation, and survival.
Before he ever held a uniform, he learned how to listen to the earth, track movement, and stay invisible — not by hiding, but by blending in.
When America entered the war, he volunteered without hesitation.
During training, his skills stood out immediately. While others struggled at short range, Samuel calmly hit targets from distances most soldiers couldn’t imagine.
On the battlefield, those skills became critical.
He protected his unit, gathered intelligence, and operated in conditions few could survive. His calm focus and precision saved lives and earned deep respect from those who fought beside him.
His story was never widely told.
But it deserves to be remembered.
Because history isn’t only shaped by generals and headlines —
Sometimes, it’s shaped by quiet warriors who became part of the landscape itself.

DIMASANGCAY ALANGADI PUNDATO
(kilala rin bilang “Kumander Dimas”)
(Desembre 21, 1947 – Agosto 13, 2020)

Si Dimasangcay Pundato ay isang Muslim Filipino na may lahing Maranao, na kinilala sa kasaysayan bilang dating Moro revolutionary leader, peace negotiator, at opisyal ng pamahalaan. Siya ay nagsilbi bilang Vice Chairman ng Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) at kalaunan ay naging Chairman ng MNLF Reformist Group, isang paksyon na nabuo bunsod ng panloob na tunggalian at panawagan para sa reporma sa loob ng kilusan.

Noong panahon ng diktadurya ni Pangulong Ferdinand Marcos, pinamunuan ni Pundato ang pwersang Maranao ng MNLF mula 1973 hanggang 1985, at naging Vice Chairman ng MNLF noong 1978. Sa panahong ito, siya ay kinilala bilang isa sa iilang lider na aktibong nasa larangan ng armadong pakikibaka, habang ang iba pang lider ay nasa labas ng bansa. Kasabay ng pakikibaka laban sa diktadurya, isinulong din ni Pundato ang panloob na reporma sa organisasyon, partikular sa usapin ng ideolohiya at istilo ng pamumuno.

Noong 1980, tuluyang naputol ang ugnayan ni Pundato kay MNLF Chairman Nur Misuari matapos tumanggi ang huli sa mga panukalang reporma. Ang hidwaang ito ay humantong sa pagkakatatag ng MNLF Reformist Group, na pinamunuan ni Pundato, at naging hiwalay na daluyan ng negosasyon sa pamahalaan.
Sa panahon ng self-exile, nakipag-ugnayan si Pundato at ang MNLF Reformist Group kay Senador Benigno “Ninoy” S. Aquino Jr. sa Kuala Lumpur. Matapos ang pagpaslang kay Aquino noong 1983, ipinagpatuloy ni Pundato ang suporta sa mga adhikaing demokratiko ng kilusang anti-diktadura. Noong 1985–1986, isang taon bago ang EDSA People Power Revolution, nagpahayag ang MNLF Reformist Group ng suporta at pampulitikang kooperasyon sa kilusang Aquino, kapwa sa Estados Unidos at sa Pilipinas.

Pagkatapos ng pagbabalik ng demokrasya noong 1986, hiniling ni Pangulong Corazon Aquino—sa pamamagitan ni Aquilino “Nene” Pimentel Jr.—ang pagbabalik ni Pundato upang maging bahagi ng bagong pamahalaan. Matapos ang serye ng back-channel negotiations na kinasangkutan nina Christopher at Ramon Carreon, pati nina Ambassador Emmanuel Pelaez at Ambassador Mauyag Tamano, bumalik si Pundato sa Pilipinas noong 1987 nang walang inilatag na kondisyon, bilang pagpapakita ng suporta sa pambansang rekonsilyasyon at demokratikong transisyon.
Mula 1988 hanggang 1998, nagsilbi si Pundato bilang Executive Director ng Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA) sa ilalim ng iba’t ibang administrasyon, simula kay Pangulong Corazon Aquino hanggang sa administrasyon ni Pangulong Fidel V. Ramos, at hanggang sa unang bahagi ng pamahalaan ni Joseph Estrada. Sa kanyang siyam na taong panunungkulan, siya ay nakilala sa loob ng pamahalaan dahil sa transparency, development-oriented governance, at resource mobilization programs para sa mga Muslim na komunidad.

Isa sa mga makabuluhang ambag ni Pundato sa OMA ay ang institusyonalisasyon ng sistema sa pamamahala ng Hajj pilgrimage ng mga Pilipinong Muslim. Kabilang sa kanyang mga inobasyon ang pagpapababa ng pamasahe, pagpapahusay ng akomodasyon sa Saudi Arabia, at ang pagpapalakas ng ugnayan ng pamahalaan ng Pilipinas sa Muasasa (Hajj Establishment), na nag-angat sa kredibilidad ng mga Pilipinong Muslim sa pandaigdigang antas.

Noong panahon ng administrasyon ni Pangulong Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, hinirang si Pundato bilang Assistant Secretary, at kalaunan ay Undersecretary ng Office of the Presidential Adviser on the Peace Process (OPAPP). Sa tungkuling ito, nakatuon siya sa peace-talk deliberations, conflict resolution, at mediation sa pagitan ng pamahalaan at iba’t ibang Moro revolutionary groups.

Si Dimasangcay Pundato ay pumanaw noong Agosto 13, 2020, sa kanyang tahanan sa Marawi City, sa edad na 72. Ang kanyang buhay at gawain ay patuloy na pinag-aaralan sa larangan ng Bangsamoro history, peace and conflict studies, at political transition, bilang halimbawa ng paglipat mula armadong pakikibaka tungo sa pampulitikang pakikilahok at serbisyo sa pamahalaan.

Geronimo was an Apache leader and medicine man best known for his fearlessness in resisting anyone–Mexican or American—who attempted to remove his people from their tribal lands. He repeatedly evaded capture and life on a reservation, and during his final escape, a full quarter of the U.S. standing army pursued him and his followers. Here are some interesting facts about Geronimo that you may not know:
1. The origins of his name are disputed. The man who would become the most feared Indian leader of the 19th century was born sometime in the 1820s into the Bedonkohe, the smallest band of the Chiricahua Apache tribe that inhabited what is now New Mexico and Arizona. His given name was Goyahkla (“The One Who Yawns”), but as a young man he earned the moniker “Geronimo” after distinguishing himself in Apache raids against the Mexicans. The source of the name remains the subject of debate. Some historians believed it arose from frightened Mexican soldiers invoking the Catholic St. Jerome when facing the warrior in battle, while others argue that it was simply a Mexican nickname or a mispronunciation of “Goyahkla.”
2. Geronimo’s wife and children were murdered when he was a young man. Geronimo came of age during a period of bitter conflict between the Chiricahua Apaches and the Mexicans. In response to the Apaches’ penchant for staging raids to gather horses and provisions, the Mexican government had begun ambushing Apache settlements and offering lucrative bounties for their scalps. In 1851, while Geronimo and several other warriors were in the town of Janos on a trading mission, Colonel Jose Maria Carrasco and a detachment of around 400 Mexican soldiers ransacked his Bedonkohe encampment and slaughtered many of its inhabitants. When Geronimo returned later that night, he found that his mother, his wife and his three young children had all been murdered.
3. He broke out of U.S. Indian reservations on three different occasions. In the 1840s and 1850s, the Mexican-American War and the Gadsden Purchase placed the Chiricahua Apaches’ domain within the boundaries of the expanding United States. Geronimo and the Apaches violently resisted the influx of white settlers, but following several years of war with the U.S. Army, they reluctantly negotiated a peace. By 1876, most of the Chiricahuas had been shipped to San Carlos, an arid and inhospitable reservation located in Arizona. Geronimo avoided the reservation until 1877, when he was captured by Indian agents and brought to San Carlos in chains.
4. He was an accomplished artist who sold paintings to tourists late in life.
5. He was also an accomplished horseman who could ride standing up on two horses at once.
6. He died at Fort Sill, Oklahoma on February 17th, 1909.

CONTEND: Justice for the Victims of the Mindoro Bombings! Free Chantal Anicoche! End State Terror and Bureaucrat Capitalism!

The Congress of Teachers/Educators for Nationalism and Democracy (CONTEND) strongly condemns the brutal and indiscriminate bombings carried out by the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) in Abra de Ilog, Occidental Mindoro. These attacks have left entire communities devastated, homes destroyed, livelihoods lost, and indigenous peoples displaced from their ancestral lands. The bombings were not acts of defense but deliberate acts of state terror designed to silence resistance and sow fear among the poor and powerless.

Among the victims of this fascist violence is Chantal Anicoche, a 24-year-old Filipino community worker and recent Psychology graduate from the United States, who has been illegally detained following the January 1, 2026 bombings in Barangay Cabacao. Reports indicate that Chantal is being held by the 203rd Infantry Brigade of the Philippine Army, and authorities continue to withhold information about her condition and location. Her detention, following the deaths of three Mangyan-Iraya children and youth researcher Jerlyn Rose Doydora, exposes the government’s systematic attacks against humanitarian workers, environmental defenders, and advocates of indigenous rights. We demand Chantal’s immediate and unconditional release, and justice for all victims of the Mindoro bombings.

We hold the Marcos Jr. regime fully accountable for these atrocities. Under his leadership, the Armed Forces have once again been used as an instrument of repression, protecting the interests of mining corporations, landlords, and bureaucrat-capitalists at the expense of the Filipino people. The blood spilled in Mindoro is a direct result of a government that prioritizes militarization, corruption, and plunder over the welfare of its citizens.

Let us remember why armed resistance exists in the first place. The New People’s Army did not rise out of mere ideology but from generations of exploitation, oppression, and landlessness. As history teaches us, revolutionaries can be killed, tortured, or imprisoned, but new ones will always rise so long as peasants remain landless, workers underpaid, and ordinary Filipinos deprived of education, healthcare, and dignity. The state’s bombs cannot destroy the just anger of a people driven to fight for survival and justice.

The bombings in Mindoro expose the true face of bureaucrat capitalism, a system that uses public funds not to build schools, hospitals, or homes, but to buy weapons that terrorize its own citizens. These atrocities coincide with the regime’s massive corruption scandals, from ghost flood control projects to the ₱281-billion pork barrel and confidential funds under Marcos Jr. While communities are bombed into silence, the true plunderers in government remain free.

CONTEND calls for justice for all victims of the Mindoro bombings, the immediate release of Chantal Anicoche, and accountability for all those responsible, from the generals who ordered the airstrikes to the highest officials who enabled them. We demand an independent investigation into these atrocities and humanitarian aid for all displaced communities.

We urge all educators, students, and workers to denounce these acts of terror and stand with the people of Mindoro in their struggle for land, justice, and peace. The violence will not end until we confront the root causes of conflict, including feudal exploitation, imperialist control, and bureaucrat capitalism that rob Filipinos of their future.

Justice for Mindoro! Free Chantal Anicoche! End State Terror!
Fund education and social services, not bombs and corruption!

SADDAM MOBUTU: A LIFE OF POWER, PRIVILEGE, AND COLLAPSE

Ndolo Mathieu Kongulu Mobutu, popularly known as Saddam Mobutu, was one of the sons of former Zairian president Mobutu Sese Seko and his first wife, Marie-Antoinette Gbiatibongu Yetene. He was born on 21 April 1970 during the era of Zairianisation and was the eighth child of his mother.

He grew up at Camp Tshatshi in Kinshasa, the military nerve center of the Mobutu regime. From an early age, Kongulu developed a reputation for aggression and fearlessness, earning nicknames such as “Gang” and “Mobali ya Ngenge.” As he matured, he became known as “the Vatican,” a term suggesting that he operated as a power within the state. Among Mobutu’s sons, he was widely regarded as the most feared due to his temperament and proximity to elite military authority.

At his father’s directive, Kongulu was sent to the École de Formation des Officiers (EFO) in Kananga for military training. He later became an officer in the Division Spéciale Présidentielle (DSP), the elite presidential guard. During this period, he acquired the nickname “Saddam Hussein,” reflecting perceptions of his authoritarian behavior and alleged brutality. Many accounts portray him as someone who relied on force rather than legal processes, though these claims were never formally tested in court.

Kongulu lived a life of extreme privilege. He was known for his love of luxury cars, nightlife, gambling, and women, and he wielded influence in social and entertainment circles. He was associated with several business interests, including transport and import-export companies, as well as Yoshad Entertainment Productions. He also maintained close ties with the popular music group Wenge Musica BCBG, which was highly influential in the 1990s.

According to an investigative report by the German broadcaster ZDF, Kongulu was allegedly involved in the embezzlement of state resources, including the organization of secret gold shipments to The Gambia in the 1990s. These allegations aligned with broader findings of corruption under the Mobutu regime, although Kongulu was never formally prosecuted.

In May 1997, as Laurent-Désiré Kabila’s AFDL forces advanced on Kinshasa, tensions within the military leadership intensified. General Donatien Mahele Lieko Bokungu, the army chief of staff who favored a peaceful transition, was assassinated under unclear circumstances. Kongulu has been mentioned in some accounts as possibly linked to the killing, but no conclusive evidence has ever emerged to support the claim.

As the regime collapsed, Kongulu attempted unsuccessfully to organize resistance with elements of the DSP. On 17 May 1997, he was among the last prominent figures of the Mobutu government to flee Kinshasa, escaping across the Congo River to Brazzaville. His residence in Kinshasa was later looted and vandalized by rebels and civilians.

He attended his father’s funeral in Morocco later in 1997 before living in exile in Europe. Kongulu died on 24 September 1998 in Monaco at the age of 28. The precise cause of death was never officially disclosed, though various unverified reports suggested illness.

Saddam Mobutu’s brief and turbulent life remains a reflection of the excess, impunity, and unchecked power that marked the final years of the Mobutu regime, offering a stark lesson on the dangers of wealth and authority when unrestrained by accountability.

He was said to be the last replaced official and obstacle to Ferdinand Marcos, and whose resignation made it possible for the ex-President to declare martial law in 1972. He holds the singular Philippine Government Record of continuous longest serving public Officer from April 1937 to January 2001 or a total 63 years and 9 months spanning twelve Philippine Presidents.

➡️Yan entered the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) after graduating in the Arellano High School in 1937 and became a part of the PMA Class of 1941.

➡️On graduation day, Manuel Yan received the Presidential Sabre. This is a symbol of superiority in both academic work and military training, from Vice President Sergio Osmeña, the commencement speaker. In finishing at the top of his class, Manuel Yan became one of the few to accomplish this feat as a high school graduate. Many young boys who join the PMA do so after one, two or even three years of college work.

➡️He joined the Armed Forces of the Philippines in 1941. In 1942, he survived the Pantingan River Massacre, which took place during the Bataan Death March.

➡️After serving as the Chief of the Philippine Constabulary, Yan was appointed by President Ferdinand Marcos as the Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines in May 1968. In the AFP's history, Yan (at the age of 48) was the youngest military member who had ever held this position.

➡️However, Yan resigned his post in 1972 because he did not want to be involved with the implementation of martial law. In 1971, Yan had prominently told media that the grounds for Marcos to either impose of martial law or suspend the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus did not exist.

➡️Yan served the foreign service from 1972 to 1992 in various capacities as first Ambassador to Thailand up to 1981, then Ambassador to Indonesia up to 1987. After the resignation of Secretary of Foreign Affairs Salvador Laurel, he was nominated as Secretary of Foreign Affairs from February to October 1987, after which he served as Undersecretary of Foreign Affairs up to 1990 and finally as Ambassador to the United Kingdom up to 1992.

➡️From 1992 – 1994, he was appointed GRP chairman negotiating with Moro rebels.

➡️In 1994, President Fidel V. Ramos appointed him as the Presidential Adviser on Peace Process, a position which he retained until the overthrow from the presidency of Ramos' successor, Joseph Estrada.

➡️Among his notable achievements as the Presidential Adviser on Peace Process was engineering a peace pact with the Moro National Liberation Front, which signed the agreement with government in 1996 known as the 1996 Final Peace Agreement.

➡️Yan was awarded (in February 2008) an honorary degree by De La Salle University, a degree of Doctor of Humanities honoris causa for being the longest serving government official, serving eleven presidents from Manuel Quezon to Joseph Estrada. He served 63 continuous years from 1937 to 2001, a record which has not been broken as of 2019.

➡️Yan was firstly married to Amelia Acab (deceased) and later married Eloisa Fernandez. His children are Manuel Jr., Bev, Roby, Sita, Egay, Mawie, Leo, Mina, Joy, Raul and Lou. Yan died on December 4, 2008, at The Medical City Ortigas in Pasig.

Officials in the Trump administration insist its surges of federal agents into Democratic-led cities are necessary to round up undocumented immigrants, but the agents’ mission increasingly looks as if it is to frighten opponents of the administration into submission. But instead of submission, they appear to be sparking deeper and deeper opposition.

Since agent Jonathan Ross shot and killed Renee Good in Minneapolis, protests against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have broken out across the nation. Federal agents in Minnesota have responded by increasing their violent attacks, many of which have involved U.S. citizens and have been captured on video: agents breaking into a home with weapons drawn, a teenager dragged away from his job, agents guarding a restroom at Target, engaging in door-to-door searches without warrants, using illegal chokeholds, dragging people out of their cars. 

Confronted with footage of officers using prohibited chokeholds, White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson told ProPublica reporters Nicole Foy and McKenzie Funk: “Officers act heroically to enforce the law and protect American communities.” On Air Force One Sunday evening, Trump cut to the heart of MAGA’s attacks on those resisting ICE when, speaking about Renee Good, he told reporters: “At a very minimum, that woman was very, very disrespectful to law enforcement.” 

Luke Broadwater and Katie Rogers of the New York Times noted the response of Representative Jamie Raskin (D-MD) to Trump’s comment. Raskin recalled that the insurrectionists who attacked the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021, “violently attacked police officers and called them everything from traitors to pigs to racial epithets, and ruthlessly taunted them and maligned them for hours,” and yet Trump pardoned them. 

Raskin concluded that “Donald Trump’s very dubious characterization of Renee Good as having been disrespectful is not only factually suspect, but it’s legally irrelevant. The police do not have the right to shoot people in the head because they consider them having acted in a disrespectful way. That legal standard would have led to a slaughter on January 6.”

In The Atlantic yesterday, David Frum explained that the administration’s attacks on Good are not at all a true defense of law and order. “For MAGA America,” he wrote, “ICE is an instrument for cleansing violence.” ICE’s social media accounts celebrate videos of armed agents hurting unarmed nonwhite men and women who are then shown weeping, pacing, or with their head in their hands in a jail cell. Most of the situations the videos show, Frum writes, could be managed “with a couple of plainclothes officers bearing holstered sidearms.” But the point is not to enforce the law; “[t]he point is to prove that the fearsome power of the American state is being wielded by righteous MAGA hands against despised MAGA targets.”

Frum notes that ICE has lowered its standards to fit the deportation targets White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller has announced, lower standards that have increased the numbers of untrained and violent agents on the streets, but Frum attributes much of the violence of ICE to the fact that “its main purpose has become theatrical…. ICE is less a law-enforcement agency than it is a content creator.” 

Frum argues that the violence shows MAGA that a government they control is demanding respect from those overeducated coastal elites they think get too much respect. By punishing Good rather than letting her drive away, Ross made sure she didn’t get away with disrespecting him. 

The scenes ICE is performing seem to be the logical outcome of the idea of cowboy individualism Republicans have pushed since the 1980s: white men reclaiming the government they insist has been corrupted by Black Americans, women, and people of color and using the power of that government to defend the “real” America. In that scheme, anyone resisting the government is not showing proper subservience and is anti-American by definition. 

But the protests against ICE have created a problem for the MAGA ideology. Key to the idea of the individualist man as a real American is that he will protect white women. And yet white women are among those standing in the front lines against Trump, and now an ICE agent has killed one. 

On Sunday, David Marcus of Fox News warned that “organized gangs of wine moms” are using “Antifa tactics to harass and impede Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.” He claimed that those people organizing to protect their neighborhoods from ICE may be “criminal conspiracies.” He complained of “self-important White women” protesting “with a weird and disturbing glee.” He seemed to threaten them by warning: “if we simply allow these cosplaying would-be revolutionaries to do whatever they want…, Renee Good will not be the last to needlessly die.”

On Monday, Will Cain of the Fox News Channel echoed Marcus, saying: “There's a weird kind of smugness...in the way that some of these liberal white women interact with authority.” 

That idea that anyone challenging MAGA government is anti-American—even, perhaps, white women—helps to explain the Department of Justice’s decision not to investigate the shooting as an attack on Good’s civil rights, but instead to consider it as an assault on a federal officer. It is investigating not the shooting but the ties of Good and her widow to local activists. They'll tell you Custer died at the hands of Lakota and Cheyenne warriors.
They won't tell you the name of the woman who knocked him from his horse.
Her name was Buffalo Calf Road Woman. Northern Cheyenne warrior. Mother. Sister. Legend.
And for over a hundred years, her people kept her story secret—afraid of what the U.S. government would do if they knew the truth.
June 17, 1876. The Battle of the Rosebud. Montana Territory.
The Cheyenne and Lakota were fighting General George Crook's forces. The warriors were retreating. And in the chaos, a young warrior named Comes in Sight—Buffalo Calf Road Woman's brother—had his horse shot out from under him.
He fell. Surrounded. Trapped on the battlefield with soldiers closing in.
From the ridge, his sister saw it happen.
She didn't hesitate. She wheeled her horse around and rode straight into the gunfire. Bullets tearing through the air around her. Soldiers aiming at her from every direction.
She reached her brother, pulled him onto her horse, and galloped to safety.
The Cheyenne warriors saw what she'd done. Her courage—her refusal to let her brother die—rallied them. They stopped retreating. They turned back. They fought harder.
And they won.
The U.S. Army called it the Battle of the Rosebud. The Cheyenne called it something else: "The Fight Where the Girl Saved Her Brother."
Nine days later, George Armstrong Custer led the 7th Cavalry to attack an encampment along the Little Bighorn River.
He expected a few hundred warriors at most. Maybe a quick fight. An easy victory.
Instead, there were over a thousand. Lakota. Cheyenne. Arapaho. All prepared. All ready.
Buffalo Calf Road Woman rode again. Not for glory. Not for honor. For survival. For her husband, Black Coyote, fighting beside her. For her brother. For her people.
Eyewitnesses said she fought "out in the open." She never took cover. She stayed on her horse the entire battle, firing a six-shooter, refusing to hide while her people fought for their lives.
And then, in the chaos, she saw him: Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer.
She raised a club. And charged.
According to Cheyenne oral history—passed down through generations, whispered through families, preserved for 129 years in absolute silence—Buffalo Calf Road Woman struck the blow that knocked Custer from his horse.
He fell. And he didn't get back up.
Whether her strike killed him or whether he died moments later from other wounds, the Cheyenne don't say for certain. But they know this: she was the one who knocked him down. She was the one who ended his fight.
And for over a century, they never told anyone outside the tribe.
Why?
Because they were terrified. The U.S. government had already destroyed their villages, massacred their people, forced them onto reservations, banned their traditions, stolen their children. If the army knew that a Cheyenne woman—not even a man, but a woman—had brought down their famous general?
What would they do?
So the Cheyenne stayed silent. They told the story among themselves. They honored her in their songs, their memories, their oral traditions. But publicly? Nothing.
It wasn't until June 2005—129 years after the battle—that tribal elders finally broke their silence.
They stood before the world and said: Buffalo Calf Road Woman knocked Custer from his horse. She struck the blow. She changed the course of that battle.
And still, most Americans have never heard her name.
Here's what American history books tell you: Custer underestimated the enemy. He attacked a superior force. He was defeated. The end.
Here's what they don't tell you: A Northern Cheyenne woman rode into two major battles in nine days. She saved her brother's life under fire. She rallied warriors to victory. And she knocked one of America's most famous soldiers from his horse with a club while he was trying to slaughter her people.
They don't tell you that because admitting it would mean acknowledging something uncomfortable: that women fought. That Native warriors weren't just defending themselves—they were winning. That the "savage" people the U.S. was trying to exterminate included women who were braver, more skilled, and more strategic than the men sent to kill them.
After the battles, the U.S. government didn't give up. They sent more troops. They hunted the tribes relentlessly. They attacked villages in winter. They burned food supplies. They forced surrender.
Buffalo Calf Road Woman and her family fled. They endured freezing nights, starvation, constant attacks. In one brutal assault on their village, over forty Cheyenne were killed. Eleven babies froze to death the first night after they escaped into a snowstorm.
They were eventually forced onto reservations. Their way of life destroyed. Their children taken to boarding schools where they were beaten for speaking their language.
And Buffalo Calf Road Woman? She contracted diphtheria—"the white man's coughing disease."
She died in May 1879. She was approximately thirty-five years old.
Her husband, Black Coyote, committed suicide after her death.
She was buried in the hills near what is now Miles City, Montana, following Cheyenne tradition. There is no monument. No marker. No official recognition of any kind.
But her people never forgot.
For 129 years, they kept her story alive. They passed it down. Mother to daughter. Elder to child. Warrior to warrior.
They remembered the day she rode into gunfire to save her brother. They remembered the battle where she knocked Custer from his horse. They remembered that she fought not because she wanted glory, but because her family and her people were under attack and she refused to stand by and watch them die.
In 2005, when the Northern Cheyenne finally spoke publicly, they weren't asking for permission to tell her story. They were reclaiming it.
Because here's the truth that makes people uncomfortable: Buffalo Calf Road Woman wasn't an exception. She wasn't the only Native woman who fought. Moving Robe, Pretty Nose, Kate Bighead, Minne Hollow Wood—there were others. Women who took up arms. Women who refused to be passive victims.
But American history erased them. Because acknowledging their existence would mean acknowledging that the people being massacred weren't helpless. That they fought back. That they won battles. That women—Native women, specifically—were warriors every bit as capable as men.
And for a country built on the mythology of Manifest Destiny and westward expansion, that's a story they couldn't allow.
So they buried it. They wrote Custer as a tragic hero. They framed Little Bighorn as a cautionary tale. They never mentioned the woman who knocked him from his horse.
But the Cheyenne remembered.
Buffalo Calf Road Woman lived in a time when everything was being taken from her people. Their land. Their freedom. Their children. Their future.
And she fought back. Not once, but twice. Not from a distance, but in the open, on horseback, refusing to hide.
She saved her brother's life. She rallied warriors to victory. She struck a blow that helped turn the tide of one of the most famous battles in American history.
And then she lived quietly. She raised her children. She survived as long as she could in a world that was determined to erase her people.
She died young. Forgotten by the country that tried to destroy her. Remembered only by the people who loved her.
But her story survived. Because the Cheyenne refused to let it die.
And now, more than 140 years later, we finally know the truth:
The woman who knocked Custer from his horse wasn't a footnote. She wasn't a myth. She wasn't a legend inflated by time.
She was real. Her name was Buffalo Calf Road Woman. And she fought like hell.

It is important to be competent, but even more important to be wise, measured, and politically aware.

He wore war paint under his Army uniform and rode into Nazi-occupied Germany to steal 50 horses—becoming the last War Chief in his tribe's 200-year history.
Montana, 1913. Joe Medicine Crow was born into the Crow Nation at a time when his people's traditional way of life was fading into memory. The buffalo were gone. The open plains were fenced. The warrior culture that had defined his ancestors for generations seemed destined to become nothing more than stories.

But his grandfather, White Man Runs Him, made sure the stories survived.

White Man Runs Him had been a scout for George Armstrong Custer at the Battle of Little Bighorn in 1876. He'd witnessed the last great victory of the Plains tribes. Now, as an old man, he sat by the fire with young Joe and passed down the ancient ways.

He taught Joe about the War Chiefs—the highest honor a Crow warrior could achieve. To earn that sacred title, a man had to complete four specific deeds in battle:

Lead a successful war party.

Touch an enemy without killing him (counting coup).

Take an enemy's weapon in combat.

Steal an enemy's horse.

Joe listened with a broken heart. He was born too late. The age of horses and hand-to-hand combat was over. He'd never ride into battle. He'd never become a War Chief.

The tradition, his grandfather told him sadly, would likely die with the elders.

Joe went to college instead. He studied anthropology, determined to at least preserve his culture's history even if he couldn't live it. He was working on his master's degree when Pearl Harbor was attacked.

December 1941. Joe Medicine Crow enlisted in the U.S. Army.

Before he left for war, his grandfather called him close one final time. The old man's hands shook as he painted traditional red war designs on Joe's arms.

"You will go to war," his grandfather said. "Remember who you are. Remember what I taught you."

Joe promised. He wore the war paint under his Army uniform. He tucked a sacred eagle feather inside his steel helmet, hidden from view.

He was a modern American soldier preparing to fight Nazis with rifles and grenades. But in his heart, he was a Crow warrior preparing for something far older.

Joe was assigned to the 103rd Infantry Division and shipped to Europe in 1944. The fighting in France and Germany was brutal—machine gun fire, artillery barrages, tanks rolling through devastated villages.

Joe wasn't thinking about ancient traditions. He was trying to survive.

But sometimes destiny finds you anyway.

The First Deed: Lead a War Party

Somewhere in France, Joe's commanding officer gave him an order: take seven men and scout through German-held territory. They had to gather intelligence and return alive.

Joe led his squad through enemy lines using skills his grandfather had taught him—moving silently, reading the landscape, sensing danger before it appeared. They avoided German patrols, dodged landmines, completed their mission.

Every single man returned safely.

His commanding officer called it excellent leadership. Joe realized he'd completed the first deed.

The Second and Third Deeds: Take a Weapon and Count Coup

In a bombed-out French village, Joe was scouting ahead when he turned a corner and collided directly with a German soldier.

Both men were knocked backward. Joe's rifle flew from his hands and skidded across the rubble. The German soldier still had his weapon.

For one frozen second, they stared at each other. Then the German raised his rifle.

Joe didn't reach for his knife. He didn't run.

He charged.

Joe slammed into the German soldier before the man could fire, knocking him to the ground. He grabbed the rifle barrel and wrenched it from the enemy's hands.

Now Joe stood over him, holding the German's own weapon. The man lay terrified on the ground, waiting to die.

Joe looked at him—young, scared, defeated. He could have killed him. Instead, he let him go.

In those chaotic seconds, Joe had completed two more deeds: he'd taken an enemy's weapon in hand-to-hand combat, and by knocking the man down and touching him, he'd counted coup.

Three deeds completed. One remained.

The Final Deed: Steal an Enemy's Horse

This was the impossible one. It was 1945. The German army used tanks, trucks, and motorcycles. Horses were relics of a previous century.

Joe figured the ancient tradition would end at three-quarters complete. Close, but not enough.

Then, as Allied forces pushed deeper into Germany, something unexpected happened. German fuel supplies ran desperately low. In some areas, Nazi officers began using horses again for transportation.

Early one morning, Joe's unit approached a farmhouse occupied by SS officers. Through the morning mist, Joe spotted something that made his pulse race.

Behind the farmhouse was a stable. Inside were at least fifty horses—prized animals belonging to the German officers sleeping inside.

Joe stared at those horses and heard his grandfather's voice: Remember who you are.

This was it. This was his moment. The war would end soon. He'd never get another chance.

He waited for darkness. German guards patrolled the perimeter. Joe moved like a shadow—silent, invisible, using every hunting skill he'd ever learned.

He slipped into the stable. The smell of hay and horses filled his lungs—it smelled like home, like Montana, like everything his grandfather had told him about.

He moved among the animals, calming them with soft words in the Crow language. He found the finest horse, fashioned a makeshift rope halter, and swung onto its bare back.

Then he gave a loud war cry—the same cry Crow warriors had used for centuries.

He kicked the horse into a gallop and burst through the stable doors, leading all fifty horses behind him in a thundering stampede.

German soldiers shouted and fired into the air, but it was too late. Joe was already riding hard toward American lines.

And as he rode—with bullets whizzing past, with fifty stolen horses thundering behind him, with the modern world exploding all around—Joe Medicine Crow began to sing.

He sang a traditional Crow war song, the same song his ancestors had sung two centuries earlier when they rode across the plains.

For that moment, the tanks and trenches disappeared. He wasn't fighting in Germany in 1945. He was riding for his people, carrying their honor forward through time.

He arrived at American lines with the captured horses. His commanding officer was stunned. His fellow soldiers cheered—they'd just captured valuable enemy transportation.

But Joe knew what he'd really done. He'd completed the four deeds. He'd honored his grandfather. He'd kept a tradition alive.

When the war ended, Joe returned to Montana. He went to the Crow elders and told them everything.

They listened in silence. They verified each deed. They consulted the ancient laws.

Then they held a ceremony that hadn't been performed in generations.

They painted his face with traditional designs. They placed the War Chief headdress upon his head. They danced and sang the old songs.

Joe Medicine Crow was named a War Chief of the Crow Nation.

He was the last man to ever earn that title.

Joe lived to be 102 years old. He became a renowned historian and author, writing extensively about Crow culture and Native American history. He earned a master's degree from USC. He advised presidents and spoke at the Smithsonian.

In 2009, President Barack Obama awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, saying: "An act of extraordinary valor speaks for itself. So does a life."

But Joe always said the medals and honors were secondary. What mattered was the continuity—that he'd kept his grandfather's traditions alive in the middle of the most modern war in history.

He proved something profound: heritage isn't about the past. It's about carrying meaning forward, even when the world around you has completely changed.

Joe Medicine Crow died in 2016 at age 102. He was buried with full military honors and traditional Crow ceremonies—a bridge between two worlds until the very end.

He was the last War Chief. But his story ensures that what a War Chief represents—courage, honor, cultural pride, connection to ancestors—will never die.

Because sometimes the most powerful act of resistance is simply remembering who you are.

In 1973, during a bank robbery in Stockholm, hostages were held for days. When they were freed, some surprised the world by defending their captors and speaking of them with sympathy. Psychologists later called this response Stockholm Syndrome: the way fear and dependence can make victims emotionally lean toward those who control their fate.

It sounds irrational, until you remember something simple. When people are trapped and afraid, the mind is not trying to be brave. It is trying to survive. It clings to small mercies and tells itself a story it can live inside.

Today, experts use words like trauma bonding or coercive control. But the old story still helps us recognize something about ourselves, not just in crime dramas, but in everyday life and, if we are honest, in our politics.

Because something very similar lives inside Ghana.

For many people, politics is not about manifestos or ideology. It is about who can help you get a job. Who can get your transfer approved. Who can make a call when your name is stuck somewhere on a list. In a hard economy, these things are not luxuries. They are lifelines. And when a party becomes your lifeline, you do not relate to it like an idea. You relate to it like air.

This is how loyalty slowly stops being a choice and starts becoming a habit of fear.

If you want to see why, go and stand at Ghana’s border and look sideways. Think of the economic reality of a primary school teacher in West Africa. It is a lesson in geographic destiny. Same tired feet. Yet completely different lives.

In much of Francophone West Africa, that teacher is paid in a currency tied to the euro. In Ghana, the teacher is paid in a currency that has turned daily life into a negotiation with uncertainty. Here, even a loaf of bread is no longer just food. It has become a barometer of the social contract.

In 2026, a simple comparison tells a painful story. Economists call it the “bread runway”, the number of days a single month’s salary can sustain a household on the most basic staple. An Ivorian teacher enjoys over 650 days of bread security on one month’s pay. A Ghanaian teacher manages about 115 days. The difference is not effort. It is structure.

Because the cedi does not have the same protection as the CFA, every meal in Ghana is quietly exposed to exchange rates swings, shipping costs, and global prices. Basic nutrition has been quietly financialized. The teacher is no longer just teaching. Every day, they are also gambling with forces they do not control.

Then the state takes its share. In Ghana, a teacher loses about 22.4 percent, nearly a fifth, of their pay to taxes and social security, far more than in places like Togo, where the burden is closer to 10.6 percent. So the person whose money buys the least is also asked to give up the most. And while other countries protect basic foods with legally enforced price controls, Ghana leaves it to the market. So the worker carries the full weight of global shocks, port inefficiencies, and currency weakness alone. Sovereignty here has quietly become a surcharge.

This is the pressure people have been living under through much of the 4th Republic. And this is the soil in which blind loyalty grows.

You hear it in everyday talk. Yes, things are hard, but at least our people fixed this road. Yes, money was stolen, but our side built a school. Yes, the system hurts, but it once helped me or someone I love. Small mercies become proof of virtue. Big wrong things become “not that bad.”

This is not because Ghanaians are foolish. It is because human beings remember who helped them breathe when they were drowning.

Slowly, partisan identity becomes personal identity. Criticism feels like an insult, evidence feels like an attack, and people end up defending what should trouble them and fighting institutions not because they are perfect, but because they threaten a fragile sense of safety.

In places where politics comes with intimidation and threats, people quickly learn which opinions are safe. Silence becomes wisdom, praise becomes insurance, and even those who try to walk the middle are soon assigned a side, depending on who their words unsettle. 

And when you only hear one side, your world slowly becomes that side. You do not just believe the story, you defend it, not always because it is true, but because it is familiar.

This is where the old Stockholm story fits.

Like hostages, people under constant pressure can start to emotionally side with the very systems that keep them anxious. Not because those systems are good, but because the idea of stepping outside them feels terrifying. The known pain starts to feel safer than the unknown freedom.

This is not a Ghanaian defect but a human one, and no democracy can flourish when people relate to political parties the way captives relate to captors, grateful for small favors and afraid of open doors.

The answer is not changing parties, but changing the relationship itself. When jobs become rights, food stops being a gamble, institutions matter more than colors, and people can say “my party is wrong” and still feel whole, the country finally exhales.

Until then, we will keep voting, but many of us will vote like hostages negotiate, quietly, carefully, and imprisoned by fear.

And no nation is truly free when its citizens must bargain with their own chains just to breathe.

Kay Codjoe

BREAKING | After over five years of detainment, peasant woman organizer, activist, and poet Amanda Echanis has been acquitted of all charges as announced today by the Cagayan Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 10. Echanis currently sits as a councilor in the UP Diliman University Student Council (UPD USC).

Behind bars, Echanis continued to contribute to progressive movements as a cultural worker and student leader. In 2023, she published Binhi ng Paglaya (Seeds of Liberation), a collection of poetry and essays written while imprisoned. In 2025, she made a historic bid for councilorship in the UP Diliman University Student Council. She was named the first political prisoner to be elected into the council after topping the race. 

On December 2, 2020, Echanis was illegally arrested with her then-month-old son following a raid of her residence by members of the Philippine National Police, the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, and the Armed Forces of the Philippines. Four months prior to her arrest, her father, Randall “Ka Randy” Echanis, an National Democratic Front (NDF) peace consultant and fellow peasant leader was slain in Quezon City. 

“Ang kaniyang paglaya ngayong araw ay nagsisilbing laban ng mga pesante, organisador, at ng mga kababaihan. Ang kahalagahan nito ay nagmumula sa pagtutol ng laganap na karahasan at pananamantala sa mga kababaihan at mamamayang sumusuporta sa kampanya ng mga magsasaka.,” stated the Free Amanda Echanis Movement in a statement following the acquittal.

(Her release today serves as a fight for all peasants, organizers, and women. Its importance is rooted in resistance against the violence and exploitation of women and citizens supporting the campaigns of farmers.)

The Story.
        Notre Dame's defensive line overhaul continues to be a major focus in the transfer portal, and they've zeroed in on a significant target: former Oregon defensive tackle Tionne Gray. After a successful stint as a key backup for the Ducks, the highly-rated prospect is exploring his options, with the Fighting Irish looking to land him for a crucial interior presence. 

●Tionne Grays Size. 6-foot-6, 336 pounds.

●2025 Season (Oregon).18 tackles (2 TFL), 1 blocked kick in 13 games.

●Recruitment. A four-star recruit in high school, he was a top-200 national prospect.

●Eligibility. Three years remaining. Strengths & What He Brings to Notre Dame

●Imposing Size & Strength. Gray's sheer size is a game-changer for the interior, allowing him to occupy blockers and create havoc.

●Disruptive Potential. He possesses strong hands and moments of power, showing flashes of being a dominant force.

●Versatility. While a pure nose tackle, he has the athleticism to move around the line, fitting odd or even fronts.

●High Ceiling. Despite his production at Oregon, he's still developing, with scouts noting he's "barely scratching the surface," making him a high-upside 

Power Five starter.
●Immediate Need.  Notre Dame aims to pair him with other top recruits like Keon Keeley, filling crucial gaps in their defensive front. 
Why Notre Dame?

     Gray seeks a program where he can translate his physical tools into a larger role and accelerate his development, a path Notre Dame's coaching staff, led by Marcus Freeman, offers for elite talent looking for opportunity.

Assassinat à Carthage de Salah Khalaf صلاح خلف dit Abou Iyad أبو إياد

Salah Khalaf صلاح خلف, plus connu sous son nom de guerre Abou Iyad أبو إياد, est né en 1933 à Jaffa يافا, en Palestine. Dirigeant historique du mouvement national palestinien, il est l’un des fondateurs du Fatah فتح et fut longtemps considéré comme le numéro deux de l’Organisation de libération de la Palestine منظمة التحرير الفلسطينية, juste derrière Yasser Arafat ياسر عرفات connu sous le nom d’Abou Ammar أبو عمار.

Après son exil, Salah Khalaf s’installe au Koweït الكويت en 1959 où il exerce le métier d’enseignant. C’est dans ce pays qu’il participe à la fondation du Fatah aux côtés de Yasser Arafat ياسر عرفات, de Farouk Kaddoumi فاروق القدومي connu sous le nom d’Abou Lotf أبو اللطف, et de Khalil al-Wazir خليل الوزير connu sous le nom d’Abou Jihad أبو جهاد. Il adopte alors le nom de guerre d’Abou Iyad أبو إياد.

De la fin de l’année 1967 jusqu’en octobre 1970, il dirige les services de renseignements et de contre-espionnage de l’Organisation de libération de la Palestine. Il entretient parallèlement des relations étroites avec les organisations palestiniennes de gauche, notamment le Front populaire de libération de la Palestine الجبهة الشعبية لتحرير فلسطين et le Front démocratique pour la libération de la Palestine الجبهة الديمقراطية لتحرير فلسطين. 

Il joue un rôle majeur dans l’élaboration du programme politique de 1968, qui proposait l’édification d’un État démocratique multiconfessionnel sur l’ensemble de la Palestine, ouvert aux Israéliens rompant avec le sionisme.

À la suite de la rupture entre l’Organisation de libération de la Palestine et le roi Hussein de Jordanie الحسين بن طلال lors des événements de 1970 et 1971, Salah Khalaf devient l’un des principaux responsables de l’organisation Septembre noir أيلول الأسود. 

Après la guerre du Kippour de 1973, il opère cependant un tournant stratégique en renonçant aux opérations extérieures et en engageant l’Organisation de libération de la Palestine dans la recherche d’une solution politique. Il accepte alors l’idée d’un État palestinien limité à la Cisjordanie الضفة الغربية et à la bande de Gaza قطاع غزة, avec Jérusalem القدس pour capitale.

Il reprend par la suite la direction des services de renseignements et de contre-espionnage de l’Organisation de libération de la Palestine, consolidant son statut de principal adjoint de Yasser Arafat et de stratège influent du mouvement palestinien.

Le 14 janvier 1991, Salah Khalaf est assassiné à Carthage قرطاج, dans la banlieue de Tunis en même temps qu’Abou Mohammed أبو محمد de son vrai nom Fakhri Al-Oumari فخري العمري, et qu’Aboul Hol أبو الهول de son vrai nom Hayel Abdul Hamid هائل عبد الحميد. 

Les trois dirigeants sont abattus par des rafales de kalachnikov tirées par Hamza Abou Zeïd حمزة أبو زيد, un garde palestinien infiltré, membre du groupe dirigé par Sabri al-Banna صبري البنا connu sous le nom d’Abou Nidal أبو نضال, chef du Fatah-Conseil révolutionnaire فتح المجلس الثوري, une faction dissidente radicale qui accusait le Fatah d’avoir trahi la cause palestinienne.

Salah Khalaf s’était montré extrêmement critique à l’égard de cette organisation, affirmant qu’elle servait consciemment ou inconsciemment les intérêts d’Israël, et qu’elle avait causé davantage de dommages à la cause palestinienne qu’aux ennemis qu’elle prétendait combattre.

Ilocos Norte is a province in the northernmost part of Luzon, Philippines, known for its rich history, dramatic landscapes, and vibrant culture. It is bordered by the mountains of the Cordillera to the east and the West Philippine Sea to the west, giving it a mix of rugged coastlines, rolling sand dunes, green valleys, and historic towns.
The capital city, Laoag, is called the Sunshine City because of its warm climate and bright skies. Nearby is Paoay, home to the famous Paoay Church, a UNESCO World Heritage Site known for its massive coral-stone walls and earthquake-baroque architecture.
Ilocos Norte is also famous for the Bangui Windmills, towering white turbines along the coastline that symbolize clean energy and scenic beauty. Adventurous visitors enjoy sandboarding and 4x4 rides on the La Paz sand dunes, while nature lovers explore Kapurpurawan Rock Formation and Cape Bojeador Lighthouse in Burgos.
The province is proud of its strong Ilocano culture—culture—marked by thrift, resilience, and close family ties. Local cuisine is a big highlight, featuring favorites like bagnet, pinakbet, dinengdeng, and empanada.

Per intelligent assessment of the Genocide stoppage, Self-defense and R-ARCSS Peace-keeping Operation of Jonglei-Equatoria Front under the Command of SPLA-IO Sector Three, 8th Infantry Division, armed youth from Pajut, Duk and Poktap have joined SSPDF against SPLA-IO Forces despite serious warning from from SPLM/SPLA-IO. 

This is a dangerous mistake that armed youth from those areas have made. The Operation has given them a 4-hour ultimatum from now onwards to abandon SSPDF bases. 

Abandoning SSPDF bases will not aggravate and increase the wrath of the forces of the Operation. Hence, it will not jeopardize civilians in the area. 
Finally the Operation is urging the civilians in the targeted areas to cooperate and establish SPLM-IO civilian based structures with SPLA-IO forces on the mission.

As a proud son of the Lou Nuer people, I write this with a heavy heart and deep love for my community. Our people have long been renowned as fierce fighters brave, resilient, and unyielding in the face of oppression. For generations, we have defended our pastoral way of life with unmatched strength and courage. We do not bow or worship politicians; our loyalty lies first with our spiritual leaders and the rhythms of our land, cattle, and kin.

Yet, this very strength has too often been exploited. Over the years, we have seen leaders from both the government and opposition seek to harness Lou Nuer warriors as the vanguard for their own ambitions. It is a painful, repeating cycle: our bravery is praised when it serves another's cause, but the costs like lives lost, families shattered, communities displaced are borne almost entirely by us alone.

The recent news that SPLM-IO forces from our Lou Nuer areas are marching toward Juba breaks my spirit. Why us? Out of all the territories under SPLM-IO influence, why choose Lou Nuer youth and fighters to lead this advance? The reason is painfully obvious: our reputation as naturally strong, brave, and loyal fighters makes us the preferred spearhead. But this is not honor it is manipulation. History shows how such "marches" have ended in devastation for our people, with little gain for the broader cause.

I am no supporter of the Kiir administration.
The government has failed every citizen of South Sudan failing to deliver security, development, or justice. That truth stands undeniable. But the keyword is citizen all citizens, not just Nuer or Lou Nuer alone. The suffering is national, not subtribal for Lou Nuer alone. Making it personal or ethnic blinds us to the bigger picture and plays into the hands of those who thrive on division.

We have already made our stance clear by expelling SSPDF forces from our territories. That was a legitimate assertion of our right to self-determination and security in our homeland no one disputes our rejection of unwanted military presence. From there, the path forward should be dialogue: sit with the government, demand terms for how Lou Nuer areas are governed. Do we want our own local forces? No SSPDF at all? A neutral arrangement? We are a large, formidable population a force to be reckoned with. The government would have to listen if we approached with unified, reasoned demands rather than escalation.

Marching on Juba solves nothing. It risks dragging our people into yet another round of brutal conflict, endangering civilians, and achieving little beyond more bloodshed. It won't even truly advance Dr. Riek Machar's position or SPLM-IO goals in any sustainable way. The SPLM-IO generals from our area must pause and rethink this strategy. Wait for ongoing political trials and processes to unfold. If confrontation becomes inevitable later, so be it—but let it be deliberate, not impulsive.

Some people call us "Foolish Majority" I refuse to believe my Lou Nuer people are foolish. We are wise, strategic, and capable of proving our doubters wrong by choosing dialogue and unity over being used as cannon fodder once more.
May God bless the Lou Nuer, the entire Nuer nation, all 64 tribes of South Sudan, and our beautiful but wounded country. May leaders who prefer war over peace face judgment. South Sudan belongs to no individual or factions, it belongs to all of us. Let us protect it by refusing to be pawns in endless cycles of violence. Peace through strength and wisdom, not endless sacrifice.
