WHY IRAN CAN'T BE DEFEATED

Iran Is Not Venezuela: The Regime-Change Crowd Has No Idea What They’re Asking For

Trump’s January 2026 Warnings and the Protest Crackdown

President Donald Trump issued a series of high-stakes warnings to the Iranian government as it carried out a violent crackdown on major anti-government protests across the country. As the unrest spread, Trump publicly positioned the United States as prepared to intervene if the Iranian state escalated its use of force.

Trump warned that if the Iranian regime “violently kills peaceful protesters,” the United States would come to their rescue, stating that the U.S. was “locked and loaded.” As protests expanded to more than 190 cities, he repeatedly posted that Iran was “looking at freedom” and that the United States stood ready to help.

By January 10, his warnings sharpened. Trump cautioned the Iranian leadership directly, saying that if they started shooting, the United States would start shooting too. A day later, speaking aboard Air Force One, he confirmed that the U.S. military was studying “very strong options,” including possible strikes, in response to reports that more than 500 people had been killed during the crackdown.

Around the same time, Trump stated that Iranian leaders had reached out seeking negotiations after his threats. That claim, combined with Iran’s aggressive internet shutdowns and internal security measures, signaled that the regime was attempting to manage both external pressure and internal instability at once.

This is where most analysis stops. And this is where it starts to go wrong.

What Iran Actually Wanted to Negotiate

The first question people avoid is the most important one: what did Iran actually want to negotiate?

– Did Iran want Trump to lift the economic sanctions that have strangled its economy?

– Did Iran want to renegotiate the nuclear deal under terms that acknowledge its leverage, rather than assuming surrender?

– Did Iran want to negotiate how to suppress those attacking police officers and destroying public buildings, businesses, and mosques during the unrest?

It is not even clear what Trump is talking about.

Iran is not a pushover.  Iran is not Venezuela.

Iran is not built on Ali Khamenei alone, even though he has final authority on national security and foreign policy. The Iranian system was deliberately constructed to prevent collapse around a single figure. It has a president elected by the people who governs within a broader framework of institutions designed to protect the state.

Iran also possesses the capability to strike U.S. forces across the region, including in Qatar, Iraq, Jordan, and Israel. This is not theoretical. It is built into Iran’s deterrence posture.

Most people do not understand how the regime was engineered, and because of that, they consistently underestimate its durability.

⸻

The Layered Security Architecture of the Iranian State

Iran does not rely on a single force to maintain order.

There is the regular army, the Artesh, many of whose members are not ideologically loyal to the revolution. There is a regular police force tasked with everyday law enforcement and public order.

But those are not the pillars that hold the system together when pressure escalates.

⸻

The Basij: The Regime’s Internal Backbone

The Basij is a volunteer paramilitary militia primarily used for internal security, suppressing domestic dissent, and enforcing Islamic moral codes. It exists precisely for moments like mass unrest.

The active core of the Basij consists of roughly ninety to one hundred thousand full-time uniformed personnel. In times of crisis, the force can mobilize up to one million individuals for internal security and logistics. Iranian officials often claim total membership figures ranging from ten to twelve million, sometimes even higher, but most of those are symbolic members who hold cards for benefits such as university placement or job preference and do not actively participate.

In recent months, the Basij has been heavily deployed due to escalating tensions. In late 2025, tens of thousands were mobilized in provinces such as Golestan for intelligence and surveillance operations. By January 2026, the Basij had become a central component of the combined security forces suppressing protests in more than 108 cities nationwide.

Membership within the Basij is structured in tiers. Some are regular members who receive basic training and are mobilized only during major crises. Others are active members who undergo intensive ideological and military training and participate in routine surveillance and social control. At the top are special members, full-time IRGC personnel who serve as the professional leadership within the Basij.
⸻

When Containment Fails: The IRGC Steps In

If unrest escalates beyond what the police and Basij can handle, the system does not collapse. It escalates.

At that point, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, known as the IRGC or Sepah-e Pasdaran, becomes the primary instrument of control. Established in May 1979 by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the IRGC was designed to protect the Islamic Republic from internal and external threats and to serve as a counterweight to the regular military.

Today, the IRGC fields between 125,000 and 190,000 active personnel, with an additional force multiplier through the Basij. It operates as a parallel military with its own land, sea, and air capabilities.

⸻

A Parallel Military With Regional Reach

The IRGC oversees multiple branches. 

The Quds Force: It handles external operations and unconventional warfare, managing Iran’s regional network of allies and proxies. The Quds Force (meaning "Jerusalem Force") is the elite clandestine wing of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), specializing in extraterritorial operations, unconventional warfare, and military intelligence. 

The IRGC is the force that operates Iran’s missile systems and uses them to deter threats against the regime. It wages war both externally and internally, targeting anyone it perceives as an existential threat to the regime, including firing missiles into Israel.

As of early 2026, the Quds Force remains the primary architect of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance,” though its regional footprint has been significantly altered. Following the June 2025 conflict with Israel and the United States, the decimation of Hezbollah’s leadership, and the overthrow of the Assad regime, U.S. and Israeli strikes in mid-2025 destroyed many Quds Force command centers in Tehran and killed several senior intelligence leaders.

Despite these setbacks, the Quds Force still retains influence in Lebanon, parts of northern Syria, Iraq, and Yemen. The Quds Force reports directly to Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and serves as Iran’s primary tool for projecting power while maintaining plausible deniability.

The Aerospace Force: controls Iran’s missile program and expanding drone capabilities. 

The IRGC Navy: specializes in asymmetric operations in the Persian Gulf, relying on speedboats and swarm tactics rather than conventional naval power.

Beyond the battlefield, the IRGC functions as an economic and political power center. It controls a significant portion of Iran’s economy through construction, energy, and telecommunications. It moves money through front companies and informal financial networks to evade sanctions. And it answers only to the Supreme Leader, routinely overriding civilian institutions on matters of security and foreign policy.

To bring down the Iranian regime, the Basij and the IRGC would have to defect from the revolution. They will not, because they are the revolution.

____

Why Bombing and Decapitation Do Not Work

Israel and the United States have already bombed Iranian military facilities, including during the twelve days of unprovoked attacks. The results were minimal.

Most of Iran’s military assets are buried under hardened bunkers and tunnel networks. Leadership decapitation efforts shocked the system briefly, but junior officers immediately stepped in and continued operations, including missile launches.

Killing top commanders did not stop the machine. It proved how redundant it is.

⸻

Why Killing Khamenei Would Make Everything Worse

The idea of killing or kidnapping Ali Khamenei is dangerously simplistic. It would not dismantle the system. It would radicalize it.

Khamenei as a Global Shia Authority

Khamenei is not only a political figure. He is a recognized Shia source of emulation for millions of followers worldwide in Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Lebanon, Yemen, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, United Arab Emirates, Oman, Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Turkey, Nigeria, Tanzania, Kenya, Somalia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Egypt, and Jordan.

His religious edicts carry weight far beyond Iran’s borders.

As of 2026, the majority of the world’s Shia population is concentrated in a handful of countries, with Iran holding the largest share. Any attack on Khamenei would not be seen as a national issue alone. It would be perceived as a religious assault.

⸻

The Fatwa Factor and the Rushdie Precedent

If the United States or Israel were to kill Khamenei, the response would not be limited to states. Clerics would issue decrees. Fatwas would circulate. Individuals would act on them globally.

The Salman Rushdie case is proof. A death sentence issued decades earlier was still followed by an attempted assassination in 2022. The decree survived the death of the man who issued it. The belief survived longer than the state.

There are fanatics who will act on religious rulings regardless of time, borders, or personal cost.

____

The Shia Divide: Khamenei and Sistani

Within the Shia world, authority is split between two poles. In Najaf, Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani represents a quietist tradition that avoids direct political rule while exerting immense moral influence. In Qom and Tehran, Khamenei represents political activism and state power.

Sistani stayed out of politics even during the U.S. occupation of Iraq, yet shaped the country’s political transition by insisting on direct elections and national sovereignty. He rejected the Iranian model of clerical rule while still guiding society.
_____

Iraq’s system, however, is not Iran’s system.

How Iran’s System Was Forged

Iran’s Islamic Republic was born through violent revolution. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini overthrew the Shah and established a new order based on the doctrine of Velayat-e Faqih.

Through referendums in 1979, the monarchy was abolished and a theocratic constitution approved. Khomeini then consolidated power by purging rivals, creating the IRGC, enforcing Islamic law, and centralizing authority in the office of the Supreme Leader.

That office was designed for life.

After Khomeini’s death in 1989, Ali Khamenei inherited the structure and systematically strengthened it, making the Supreme Leader the ultimate authority over the state, the military, and the system itself.

_____

The Limits of Force and the Reality of U.S. Power

There are people calling for the United States to intervene directly. But killing Ali Khamenei will not solve the problem. Iran has a president and an entire civilian government apparatus that manages the economy and day-to-day governance. Khamenei does not run the economy, and removing him would not end repression or stabilize the country.

The United States could bomb some Iranian military assets, but that raises a basic question: how does that stop the violent crackdown on protesters inside Iran? Airstrikes do not dismantle internal security systems. They do not neutralize the Basij. They do not prevent police, intelligence services, or the IRGC from enforcing control on the streets.

The reality is that Iran has significant retaliatory capacity. The United States maintains military bases across Iraq, Syria, Jordan, and Qatar. Iran can strike those locations directly or activate its proxy forces throughout the region to target U.S. personnel and infrastructure. Any escalation would not remain contained.

There is also no appetite in Washington to invade and occupy Iran to overthrow the regime. That is not going to happen. It could be done, but it would require well over 100,000 troops and a long-term occupation. The American public has no tolerance for another large-scale military adventure. The cost would exceed the occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, especially because U.S. forces would face a formidable adversary in the IRGC—a force with real combat experience from conflicts involving Israel, Lebanon, Iraq, and beyond.

Given current U.S. posture and doctrine, Iran is not Washington’s primary strategic focus. It may be Israel’s central concern, but the United States is not willing to go to war with Iran at the cost of being distracted from its long-term objective: preparing to confront China. That is the central strategic priority. Even the war in Ukraine is increasingly viewed by parts of the U.S. leadership as a drain on trillions of dollars and resources that could otherwise be used to prepare for competition with China.

The most realistic tool the United States has is continued economic pressure—sanctions designed to constrain the regime and test whether internal pressures can cause it to fracture from within.

But even then, the system is not fragile.

It is layered, institutionalized, and deliberately built to absorb shock, protect the state, and retaliate when challenged.

Dear Sons and Daughters of Tangale,

On January 12th, 2026, a so-called resolution of the Tangale Traditional Council was released and circulated widely on social media. It claims loyalty to Governor Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya of Gombe State and lavishes praise on his alleged development projects in Tangale land. Look closely, and the truth is clear: this communique is propaganda. It is a manufactured display of compliance, A deliberate attempt to conceal neglect, coercion, and imposed authority.

Half of the resolution is spent praising the Governor for infrastructural development that does not exist. The claims of progress in health, education, and cultural preservation are false. No tangible development has reached Tangale land under Governor Inuwa. The rebuilding of Kantoma Shopping Complex and the Shela to Tudu-Kwaya road came entirely from Billiri LGA funds, not the state government. The General Hospital Billiri, a state project, remains unrepaired, while the Governor has blocked the hospital from accepting community donations for reconstruction or supplies. The resolution’s praise is hollow, divorced from reality, and a crude attempt to manufacture approval for a leader who has delivered nothing to our people.

Equally alarming is the claim of authority in the resolution. It invokes the TCDA constitution and the title “Grand Patron,” both of which no longer exist. For the avoidance of doubt, the 2001 TCDA constitution currently in file at the Corporate Affairs Commission, Article X (we will circulate it), contains no such powers, and the 2025 amendment expressly abolished the concept of “Grand Patronage.” The 2001 constitution strictly provides that the role of Grand Patron is advisory, not executive. Yet, the resolution directs district heads—who have no role, nor mentioned in the 2001 TCDA constitution—to dissolve legally constituted body, and legally elected TCDA executives. This is not ignorance; it is deliberate interference. The TCDA was created by Tangale people, for Tangale people, to safeguard our collective interests. No outsider, no Mai Tangle, and no district head has authority to override it.

The illegitimacy of the so-called resolution is clear. The individual in Poshiya, presented as Mai Tangle, is not a Tangale man. Tangale tradition is clear: our Mais are elected by the kingmakers. He was never elected. Only two of the nine kingmakers voted for him, and those votes were induced for an agenda. He was smuggled into the contest, yet now seeks to wield authority over all Tangale people through coercion. We are aware, the District Heads were pressured to attend the council meeting and forced to sign. The so-called unanimity is entirely fabricated. The January 12th resolution is not a reflection of Tangale consensus—it is a tool of control.

The resolution’s claims of “cultural preservation” are equally false. Imposing a non-Tangale man by Governor Inuwa as Mai Tangle is not preserving Tangale culture—it is a violation of it. True cultural preservation respects communal processes, elections, and traditions. Replacing authentic Tangale leadership with an outsider threatens the social and cultural fabric of Tangale land.

This is part of a broader, historical pattern. Minority tribes in Nigeria’s middle-belt, including southern Gombe, have long faced suppression and administrative domination to force submission to Hausa-Fulani rule. The imposition of a non-Tangale Mai and interference with the TCDA confirm Governor Inuwa’s intent to marginalize our people. This is deliberate. It is a strategy to weaken minority voices, undermine communal institutions, and sow division. Security agencies must take note: this is an unprovoked act aimed at destabilizing Tangale land.

To all Tangale people: the occupant in Poshiya does not represent us. No government, no coerced council, can override our collective will. Tangale socio-cultural institutions remain lawful, intact, and fully operational. The TCDA leadership under Comrade Danladi Bako remains legitimate. The TCDA branches and Tul Mana Associations remain intact. The General Assembly of the TCDA remains the highest decision-making body. Engage only with lawful Tangale representatives. Reject any attempt to exploit our structures for political or personal gain.

Our identity, heritage, and rights are non-negotiable. Tangale people will not be silenced, divided, or intimidated. We stand united, peaceful, vigilant, and ready to defend our institutions, our communal interests, and our cultural heritage.

The January 12th resolution is a charade. The meeting was headed by a non-Tangale man. Its praise is hollow. Its authority is false. Its intent is dangerous. Its consequences, if ignored, threaten the unity and stability of Tangale land. We call on all Tangale sons and daughters to remain informed, united, and resolute. Any attempt to misrepresent our people, intimidate our leaders, or destabilize our community will be met with lawful, collective resistance.

For and on behalf of the Indigenous People of Tangale,

SIGNED

Eli Ibrahim Kerek, PhD
Public Relations Officer
Tangale Community Overseas (TCO)
January 14, 2025.

AA ဟာ နှစ်တွေကြာလာတာနဲ့အမျှ ရိုဟင်ဂျာရွာတွေမှာ လူသတ်မှု၊ မီးရှို့ဖျက်ဆီးမှု၊ အတင်းအကျပ် ထွက်ပြေးစေမှုတွေကို ဆက်တိုက်ကျူးလွန်လာခဲ့တယ်ဆိုတဲ့ အသံတွေ၊ သက်သေတွေ ပိုပြီး ထွက်ပေါ်လာနေပါတယ်။ ဒါတွေကို မြင်ရ၊ ကြားရတဲ့အခါ “ဒီအဖွဲ့က စစ်ကောင်စီနဲ့ ဘာကွာလဲ” ဆိုတဲ့ မေးခွန်းကို မေးမိလာပါတယ်။

ကိုယ်ကိုကိုယ် လူထုကိုယ်စားပြုတော်လှန်ရေးအဖွဲ့လို့ ပြောနေကြပေမယ့်၊ လက်တွေ့မှာတော့ လူမျိုးရေးအမုန်းတရားကို အသုံးချပြီး အပြစ်မဲ့ပြည်သူတွေကို ရန်သူအဖြစ် သတ်မှတ်နေတာဟာ စစ်ကောင်စီရဲ့ လမ်းစဉ်နဲ့ အတူတူပဲ ဖြစ်ပါတယ်။ လူတစ်မျိုးကို လူမဖြစ်အောင် ဆက်တိုက်ဖိနှိပ်နေရင် အဲဒါကို လွတ်မြောက်ရေးလို့ မခေါ်နိုင်ပါဘူး။

ရိုဟင်ဂျာတွေဟာ စစ်ကောင်စီရဲ့ အကြမ်းဖက်မှုကို ခံစားနေရသလို၊ တချို့ လက်နက်ကိုင်အဖွဲ့တွေရဲ့ အကြမ်းဖက်မှုကိုပါ တပြိုင်နက် ခံနေရပါတယ်။ ဒါဟာ လူသားအဖြစ် မလက်ခံနိုင်တဲ့ အခြေအနေပါ။

အမှန်တရားကို မကြည့်ရဲဘဲ မျက်စိပိတ်ထားရင် တရားမျှတမှု မရနိုင်ပါဘူး။ စစ်ကောင်စီတစ်ဖက်တည်းသာမက ရိုဟင်ဂျာတွေအပေါ် အကြမ်းဖက်မှု ကျူးလွန်နေတဲ့ အဖွဲ့အစည်းအားလုံးကို တာဝန်ယူစေရမယ်ဆိုတဲ့ အသံကို နိုင်ငံတကာက ကြားရပါလိမ့်မယ်။ လူသားတန်ဖိုးကို အခြေခံမထားတဲ့ မည်သည့်အာဏာမျိုးမဆို တရားမရှိပါဘူး။

AMELIL “RONNIE” MALAGUIOK
(kilala rin bilang “Commander Ronnie”)

Si Amelil Malaguiok, na mas kilala sa alyas na “Commander Ronnie,” ay isang mataas na ranggong komandante ng Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) at kinikilalang mahalagang pigura sa Bangsamoro struggle para sa awtonomiya, partikular sa Central Mindanao noong huling bahagi ng ika-20 siglo. Siya ay binabanggit sa mga historical at security accounts bilang Chairman ng Kutawatu Revolutionary Committee (KRC), ang yunit ng MNLF na may saklaw sa lalawigan ng Cotabato.

Bilang military commander ng MNLF, si Malaguiok ay may mahalagang papel sa mga operasyong armado, lokal na pamumuno, at organisasyon ng pwersang Moro sa rehiyon. Ang kanyang pangalan ay madalas lumitaw sa konteksto ng negosasyon, tactical maneuvers, at internal dynamics ng MNLF sa panahon ng aktibong armadong tunggalian laban sa pamahalaan ng Pilipinas.

Noong unang bahagi ng dekada 1980, humigit-kumulang Abril 1980, si Malaguiok ay sumuko sa pamahalaan ng Pilipinas, isang pangyayaring itinuturing ng mga mananaliksik bilang makabuluhang punto sa maagang yugto ng MNLF, dahil sa kanyang mataas na ranggo at impluwensiya. Ang kanyang pagsuko ay nagkaroon ng malaking epekto sa balanse ng pwersa at pampulitikang dinamika sa Central Mindanao at sa loob ng Bangsamoro movement.

Matapos ang kanyang pagtalikod sa armadong pakikibaka, si Malaguiok ay sumapi sa pamahalaan at kalauna’y naging bahagi ng Civil Relations Service ng Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP). Sa panahong ito, siya ay inilalarawan sa mga ulat bilang isang dating rebel commander na naging katuwang ng estado, isang landas na sumasalamin sa masalimuot na proseso ng rekonsilyasyon at conflict-to-peace transition sa Mindanao.

Sa konteksto ng pagbuo ng mga autonomous na istruktura noong dekada 1980, si Malaguiok ay naitalaga sa isang mataas na posisyon sa regional autonomous government ng Region XII (Central Mindanao). Siya ay nagsilbing Chairman ng panig ng pamahalaan sa Local Territorial Political entity (LTP 12), isang pansamantalang mekanismong administratibo na nilikha sa panahon ng transisyon patungo sa awtonomiya.

Noong panahon ng administrasyong Corazon Aquino, iniulat na si Malaguiok ay tumol sa pagsasanib ng LTP 9 at LTP 12 tungo sa isang pinag-isang autonomous government sa ilalim ng ibang pamumuno. Ang pagtutol na ito ay humantong sa isang panandaliang barricade incident sa Cotabato City, na binabanggit sa mga historical accounts bilang halimbawa ng patuloy na tensiyon at pampulitikang maneuvering sa yugto ng post-conflict transition.

Ang papel ni Amelil “Commander Ronnie” Malaguiok ay patuloy na sinusuri sa larangan ng Bangsamoro history, peace and conflict studies, at political transition, bilang representasyon ng komplikadong landas mula sa pagiging rebel commander tungo sa pakikilahok sa pamahalaan. Ang kanyang karanasan ay madalas ginagamit ng mga mananaliksik upang ilarawan ang nagbabagong katapatan, internal divisions, at hamon ng kapayapaan sa Mindanao.

Ang impormasyong ito ay inilalahad para sa layuning dokumentaryo at akademiko lamang.

Jon Stewart's Raw Fury: Breaks Silence on TV, Brands Trump a "Vicious Old Bastard Draining America's Soul" Over Born-in-America Act
The red light flickered on, and for once, Jon Stewart didn't crack a smile. On the January 13, 2026, episode of The Daily Show, the comedian-turned-commentator ditched his notes, his jokes, and any semblance of restraint. In a monologue that felt more like a primal scream than satire, Stewart unleashed a torrent of unfiltered rage against President Donald Trump, triggered by the newly signed Born-in-America Act—a controversial measure aimed at tightening birthright citizenship rules and expediting deportations for those deemed "non-essential" to American heritage.
Stewart, who has been unusually subdued since Trump's return to office, stared straight into the camera. "This man—this vicious old bastard—is draining America's soul," he declared, his voice steady but laced with venom. He didn't soften a single word, painting Trump as a "relentless parasite" feeding on division, fear, and the nation's foundational ideals. The act, Stewart argued, isn't about security or sovereignty; it's a "cynical ploy to erase the very diversity that built this country, all while lining the pockets of his cronies and stroking his ego."
The segment pulled no punches. Stewart dissected the bill's provisions: mandatory DNA testing for citizenship claims, retroactive reviews of naturalized families, and fast-tracked removals for anyone with "questionable" lineage—measures critics say disproportionately target immigrants and minorities. He rolled clips of Trump touting the act as "making America pure again," juxtaposed with historical footage of civil rights struggles. "This isn't policy," Stewart thundered. "This is ethnic cleansing wrapped in a flag. And if we let it stand, we're complicit in the death of the American dream."
The studio audience sat in stunned silence at first, then erupted in applause. Social media detonated instantly—#StewartUnleashed trending globally, with millions sharing clips and debating the monologue's raw power. Conservative outlets branded it "unhinged hysteria," while progressives hailed it as a rallying cry. Trump fired back on Truth Social, calling Stewart a "washed-up has-been desperate for relevance," but the damage was done.
For Stewart, this wasn't just commentary; it was a declaration of war. After months of health-related quiet, his return felt personal, urgent. As one viewer tweeted: "Jon didn't come to play—he came to wake us up." In a polarized 2026, his words may just spark the resistance fire that's been smoldering.

Before this moment, the Oburu–Wanga axis could plausibly argue:

“We are inside government to protect our people”

“Engagement delivers development”

“Opposition for its own sake is outdated”

That argument collapses once the presidency is publicly perceived as:

- Rewarding loyalty ethnically
- Punishing dissent politically
- Categorizing opposition voters as politically irrelevant or “foolish”

At that point, remaining inside government stops looking strategic and starts looking submissive.

ODM’s broad-based wing now appears unable—or unwilling—to defend the dignity of its core constituencies. That is fatal for a party born in resistance.

The Sifuna–Orengo–Osotsi Axis Becomes the Moral Centre

This is where the recalibration happens.

Sifuna, Orengo, Osotsi, Babu Owino—and by extension Winnie Odinga—are no longer just a “rebellious faction.” 

In the post-Mt Kenya statement context, they become:
- The voice of self-respect
- The custodians of ODM’s original protest DNA
- The counterweight to transactional politics

Their argument shifts from “ODM is losing its soul” to:

“Our people are being insulted while their leaders sit silently at the table.”

That is a powerful, emotionally resonant position—especially among youth, urban voters, and politically conscious professionals.

Should Mama Ida continue to support Sifuna it would:
- Legitimize a breakaway as continuity, not betrayal
- Anchor the reformist wing in Odinga legacy politics
- Frame the conflict as principle vs convenience, not ambition vs loyalty

This mirrors the Ford Kenya → NDP moment almost perfectly:

- Jaramogi chose accommodation
- Raila chose confrontation

The party stayed; 
- the movement left
- Ford Kenya survived institutionally—but lost ideological gravity and became regionalized. 

ODM risks the same fate.

If the Oburu–Wanga axis succeeds in purging or sidelining Sifuna, Orengo, Osotsi, and others:
- ODM retains party machinery
- ODM retains numbers
- ODM retains access

But it loses:
- Youth energy
- Protest credibility
- Urban legitimacy
- Moral authority

The haemorrhage won’t be dramatic. It will be silent:
- Young voters disengage
- Professionals stop defending the party
- Civil society sympathy evaporates
- Turnout drops, not necessarily defections

That kind of loss doesn’t show up in press conferences—but it shows up on election day.

Before the Mt Kenya remark, a Sifuna-led (or Sifuna-fronted) party would have looked premature, even reckless. After it? It looks necessary.

Such a movement would likely position itself as:
- Reformist, not radical
- National, not ethnic
- Anti-dynasty but pro-legacy
- Opposition rooted in dignity, not anger

With Mama Ida’s moral blessing, it wouldn’t be framed as abandoning Raila—but protecting what Raila once stood for.
Sifuna doesn’t even need to be the ultimate presidential flag bearer. 

Sifuna's role could mirror early Raila:
- clearing the ideological ground for a new alignment.

By leaning into a reward-your-base message in Mt Kenya—symbolized by selective empowerment optics —Ruto may have unintentionally:
- Re-ethnicized national politics
- Re-legitimized opposition politics
- Handed ODM reformists their strongest rallying point since 2022

In trying to consolidate Mt Kenya, he may have reawakened opposition consciousness elsewhere.

If the reformist wing breaks away, it may lose initially—but inherit the soul of opposition politics.
And in Kenya, souls outlast offices. Babu Owino NTV Kenya Zuku Official Edwin Sifuna James Orengo

أصحاب الفخامة والسعادة رؤساء الدول والحكومات لدى الحلفاء الدوليين
المفوض السامي لحقوق الإنسان
أعضاء مجلس الأمن الدولي

الموضوع:     
الجرائم المرتكبة بحق السكان الكورد في أحياء الشيخ مقصود والأشرفية – مدينة حلب، وضرورة إنشاء آلية دولية لحماية المدنيين، وضمان سلام مستدام، ومساءلة المسؤولين عن هذه الجرائم.
سعادة الأمين العام،
السادة أعضاء مجلس الأمن..
تودّ جهتنا لفت انتباهكم بصورة عاجلة إلى الوضع الإنساني الكارثي والمتدهور في الأحياء الكوردية، ولا سيما الشيخ مقصود والأشرفية في مدينة حلب، في ظل تصاعد أعمال العنف المنهجي والانتهاكات الجسيمة للقانون الدولي الإنساني والقانون الدولي لحقوق الإنسان، وما يترتب عليها من تهديد مباشر لحياة مئات الآلاف من المدنيين الأبرياء.

أولاً: الوقائع ذات الصلة (Facts):
تشهد الأحياء الكوردية في الشيخ مقصود والأشرفية بمدينة حلب، منذ عدة أيام، حصارًا عسكريًا محكمًا وقصفًا متكررًا، تنفذه جماعات مسلحة إسلامية غير حكومية، تعمل تحت الزي العسكري وبالغطاء المؤسسي للجيش السوري، وبمشاركة مباشرة أو غير مباشرة من أطراف خارجية.
تستهدف هذه الهجمات مناطق مدنية مكتظة بالسكان دون أي تمييز أو مراعاة لمبدأي التناسب والضرورة العسكرية، ما يعرّض نحو 400 ألف مدني لخطر جسيم ووشيك، غالبيتهم من النساء والأطفال وكبار السن، ومن النازحين داخليًا الذين سبق أن فرّوا من انتهاكات مشابهة ارتكبتها الجماعات ذاتها في مناطق أخرى من سوريا.
إن طبيعة هذه الأعمال، من حيث التكرار والتنظيم، تدل بوضوح على وجود نمط ممنهج يهدف إلى إخضاع السكان المدنيين عبر العنف، وبث الرعب، وتهيئة الأرضية لتهجيرهم القسري.

ثانياً: الأطراف المتورطة (Perpetrators):
تُنفّذ هذه الأعمال العسكرية من قبل الألوية المسلحة التالية:
لواء سليمان شاه (62)
لواء سلطان مراد (72)
فرقة الحمـزات (76)
حركة نور الدين زنكي (86)
وهي جماعات مسلحة موثّقة دوليًا لتورطها في:
جرائم حرب؛ التهجير القسري للسكان؛ ممارسات التطهير العرقي والتغيير الديمغرافي القسري؛
وذلك في المناطق الكوردية الواقعة تحت الاحتلال التركي، ولا سيما عفرين، وسري كانيه (رأس العين)، وكري سبي (تل أبيض).
إن اعتماد هذه الجماعات أسماء قادة تاريخيين ارتبطوا بمراحل التوسع الإمبراطوري العثماني لا يُعدّ مجرد تسمية رمزية أو صدفة تاريخية، بل يشكل قرينة سياقية ذات دلالة قانونية على تبنّي نزعة أيديولوجية قائمة على الهيمنة القومية والاضطهاد الممنهج، الأمر الذي يُسهم في إثبات القصد الجنائي (Mens Rea) في جرائم الاضطهاد والتطهير العرقي.

ثالثاً: التكييف القانوني (Legal Qualification)
1.⁠ ⁠الجرائم ضد الإنسانية
تشكل الأفعال الموصوفة أعلاه، من حيث المبدأ (Prima facie)، جرائم ضد الإنسانية وفقًا للمادة (7) من نظام روما الأساسي للمحكمة الجنائية الدولية، ولا سيما:
الهجوم الواسع أو المنهجي الموجّه ضد سكان مدنيين (المادة 7/1)؛
الاضطهاد على أساس قومي وعرقي (المادة 7/1/ح)؛
الإبعاد أو النقل القسري للسكان (المادة 7/1/د)؛
أفعال لا إنسانية أخرى تتسبب بمعاناة شديدة أو أذى جسيم (المادة 7/1/ك).
ويعزز هذا التكييف القانوني ما ثبت سابقًا في سري كانيه (رأس العين)، حيث انخفضت نسبة السكان الكورد من 85% إلى أقل من 1%، بما يشكل دليلًا صارخًا على وجود سياسة ممنهجة للتغيير الديمغرافي القسري.
2.⁠ ⁠جرائم الحرب
كما تشكل هذه الأفعال جرائم حرب بموجب المادة (8) من نظام روما الأساسي، ولا سيما:
تعمّد توجيه هجمات ضد السكان المدنيين (المادة 8/2/ب/1)؛
تعمّد توجيه هجمات ضد الأعيان المدنية (المادة 8/2/ب/2)؛
شن هجمات عشوائية أو غير متناسبة (المادة 8/2/ب/4).

رابعاً: المسؤولية الجنائية والدولية (Responsibility):
1.⁠ ⁠المسؤولية الجنائية الفردية
تنطبق أحكام:
المادة (25) من نظام روما الأساسي (المسؤولية الجنائية الفردية)؛
المادة (28) (مسؤولية القادة والرؤساء)؛
على المنفذين المباشرين، وقادة الجماعات المسلحة، وكل من أصدر الأوامر أو سهّل أو ساهم أو تغاضى عن ارتكاب هذه الجرائم.
2.⁠ ⁠مسؤولية الدول
إن تزويد هذه الجماعات بالدبابات والأسلحة الثقيلة والطائرات المسيّرة الهجومية، إلى جانب تقديم الدعم المالي واللوجستي والسياسي، يترتب عليه مسؤولية دولية مباشرة وفقًا لـ:
المادة (16) من مواد لجنة القانون الدولي بشأن مسؤولية الدول عن الأفعال غير المشروعة دوليًا (المساعدة أو الإعانة)؛
المادة (41) (عدم جواز الاعتراف أو تقديم العون في أوضاع ناشئة عن انتهاكات جسيمة للقانون الدولي).

خامساً: الالتزامات الدولية الواجبة (Obligations)
بموجب:
المادة المشتركة الأولى من اتفاقيات جنيف (الالتزام باحترام وضمان احترام القانون الدولي الإنساني)؛
مبدأ مسؤولية الحماية (R2P)؛ فإن على المجتمع الدولي واجبًا قانونيًا إيجابيًا لا يقبل التأجيل، يتمثل في اتخاذ تدابير فورية وفعالة لمنع استمرار هذه الجرائم، وحماية السكان المدنيين من الإبادة والتهجير والاضطهاد.

Legal Memorandum

Submitted to:
His Excellency António Guterres
Secretary-General of the United Nations
Subject:
Crimes Committed Against the Kurdish Population in Sheikh Maqsoud and Ashrafieh Districts – Aleppo City, and the Necessity of Establishing an International Mechanism for Civilian Protection, Ensuring Sustainable Peace, and Accountability of Perpetrators
Excellency, Secretary-General,
Honorable Members of the Security Council,
Our organization wishes to urgently draw your attention to the catastrophic and deteriorating humanitarian situation in the Kurdish neighborhoods, particularly Sheikh Maqsoud and Ashrafieh in Aleppo, amid escalating systematic violence and gross violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law, which pose a direct threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of innocent civilians.
I. Relevant Facts
The Kurdish neighborhoods of Sheikh Maqsoud and Ashrafieh in Aleppo have, for several days, been under a tight military siege and continuous bombardment conducted by non-state armed Islamist groups, operating under military uniforms and under the institutional cover of the Syrian army, with direct or indirect involvement from external parties.
These attacks deliberately target densely populated civilian areas, without any distinction or regard for the principles of proportionality and military necessity, placing approximately 400,000 civilians at grave and imminent risk, the majority of whom are women, children, the elderly, and internally displaced persons who had previously fled similar violations perpetrated by these same groups in other areas of Syria.
The nature of these acts, in terms of repetition and organization, clearly indicates a systematic pattern aimed at subjugating the civilian population through violence, spreading terror, and creating the conditions for forced displacement.
II. Perpetrators
These military acts are carried out by the following armed factions:
• Suleiman Shah Brigade (62)
• Sultan Murad Brigade (72)
• Hamzat Division (76)
• Nour al-Din al-Zenki Movement (86)
These groups are internationally documented as being involved in:
• War crimes;
• Forced displacement of populations;
• Practices of ethnic cleansing and enforced demographic change;
particularly in Kurdish areas under Turkish occupation, notably Afrin, Serekaniye (Ras al-Ain), and Tal Abyad (Ras al-Ain).
The use of the names of historical figures associated with the expansion phases of the Turks and the Ottoman Empire is not a mere symbolic choice or a historical coincidence,  but  a contextual indicator , demonstrating the adoption of an ideology based on ethnic domination and systematic persecution. This helps to establish the criminal intent (mens rea) behind the crimes of persecution and ethnic cleansing.
III. Legal Qualification
1. Crimes Against Humanity
The aforementioned acts constitute, prima facie, crimes against humanity under Article 7 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, specifically:
• Widespread or systematic attacks directed against civilian populations (Article 7(1));
• Persecution on ethnic and national grounds (Article 7(1)(h));
• Deportation or forcible transfer of populations (Article 7(1)(d));
• Other inhumane acts causing severe suffering or serious injury (Article 7(1)(k)).
This legal qualification is reinforced by previous evidence in Serekaniye (Ras al-Ain), where the proportion of Kurdish residents declined from 85% to less than 1%, providing compelling evidence of a systematic policy of forced demographic change.
2. War Crimes
These acts also constitute war crimes under Article 8 of the Rome Statute, specifically:
• Intentionally directing attacks against civilians (Article 8(2)(b)(i));
• Intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects (Article 8(2)(b)(ii));
• Launching indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks (Article 8(2)(b)(iv)).
IV. Criminal and International Responsibility
1. Individual Criminal Responsibility
Provisions of:
• Article 25 of the Rome Statute (Individual Criminal Responsibility);
• Article 28 (Command Responsibility);
apply to direct perpetrators, leaders of armed groups, and all those who ordered, facilitated, contributed to, or turned a blind eye to these crimes.
2. State Responsibility
The provision of tanks, heavy weapons, and attack drones to these groups, alongside financial, logistical, and political support, entails direct international responsibility under:
• Article 16 of the International Law Commission’s Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (aid or assistance);
• Article 41 (prohibition of recognition or assistance in situations arising from serious violations of international law).
V. Binding International Obligations
Pursuant to:
• Common Article 1 of the Geneva Conventions (obligation to respect and ensure respect for international humanitarian law);
• The Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principle;
the international community has a positive legal duty that admits no delay, consisting of immediate and effective measures to prevent the continuation of these crimes and protect civilians from extermination, displacement, and persecution.
VI. Existential Necessity and Required Measures
The following measures constitute an existential and immediate necessity for the Kurdish population, and failure to implement them entails serious legal and political international responsibility:
• Establishing an urgent international mechanism for civilian protection in the affected Aleppo neighborhoods;
• Imposing an immediate, comprehensive, and verifiable ceasefire;
• Activating independent international investigative mechanisms (IIIM / fact-finding missions);
• Referring perpetrators to the International Criminal Court or activating universal jurisdiction;
• Linking any future political process in Syria to ending impunity and ensuring transitional justice.
Legal Conclusion
The continuation of these crimes in the absence of effective international intervention represents a grave failure of the international system to protect civilians and undermines the credibility of international law itself.
A just and sustainable peace in Syria cannot be envisioned without international criminal justice and comprehensive accountability for all those responsible for gross violations. Justice is not a political option; it is an international legal obligation that does not lapse with time.

➡️Ariel Porfirio Oliva Querubin is a retired Philippine Marine Corps officer and a recipient of the Philippines' highest military award for courage, the Medal of Valor. He is highly decorated soldier in the Philippines and was placed in various positions in the military prior to his retirement in 2010.

➡️Querubin was born in Dagupan, Pangasinan. He grew up in La Union and studied in Manila.

➡️In his youth, Querubin found himself involved in various misadventures. These youthful indiscretions nearly prevented him from graduating from the Philippine Military Academy. However, this experience helped temper his exuberance, and by the time he graduated, his academic performance allowed him to choose which branch of the military he would serve in. Querubin met his wife, Pong Azcarraga, while still in service with the Marines. Pong had two young sons from a previous relationship: Martin Loon, now the CEO of Cocolife, and John Michael Loon, a highly decorated marine officer who graduated from the Philippine Military Academy and served in the Battle of Marawi in 2017. Together, Querubin and Pong have four children: Alfred, Faye, Jaq, and John.

➡️He was a member of the leftist student group Samahang Demokratiko ng Kabataan until he attended the Philippine Military Academy, graduating in 1979. He then opted to become an officer in the Philippine Marine Corps.

➡️Querubin is a highly decorated military officer renowned for his courageous career and combat exploits. He has 67 battle and artillery scars throughout his service. Querubin holds the distinction of being one of the most highly decorated officers in Philippine military history, having received a total of 49 medals. Notably, he is a recipient of the prestigious Medal of Valor, the highest honor bestowed upon those who have displayed extraordinary heroism and sacrifice in combat situations.

➡️He has actively participated in various military operations against the Communist insurgency in the Philippines and the Moro conflict. He is credited with neutralizing several rebel leaders from both the Communist Party of the Philippines - New People's Army and the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). This includes the elimination of a CPP-NPA provincial chairman in 1981, four MNLF commanders in 1983, an NPA commander known as "Ka Ninong" in 1988, and an MNLF commander named Racquel Carreon in the same year. Additionally, Querubin is said to have played a role in the rescue operation of Hans Kunzli, a Swiss national who was kidnapped by a group led by a former member of the Moro National Liberation Front.

➡️On August 28, 1987, Reform the Armed Forces Movement rebels led by Gregorio Honasan attempted to oust President Corazon Aquino. They attacked Malacañang Palace, Camp Aguinaldo and Villamor Air Base. Querubin, along with Red Kapunan and Juancho Sabban, attempted to bring Philippine Military Academy cadets from Baguio to Manila to provide support for Honasan.

➡️In 1989, then-Captain Querubin was a co-founder of the Young Officers' Union (YOU). The YOU, along with another group known as the "Soldiers of the Filipino People" (SFP) and the Reform the Armed Forces Movement (RAM) participated in the attempted ouster against Corazon Aquino's government. He almost died in clashes with troops loyal to the government. Some reports indicate that he suffered from a gunshot wound;[8] Querubin himself stated that he was wounded by a rocket blast during clashes in Camp Aguinaldo. The military exercise eventually failed and Querubin and his comrades were detained. They were granted amnesty during the administration of Fidel Ramos, who succeeded Corazon Aquino as president.

➡️On June 8, 1994, the Abu Sayyaf militant group, a breakaway faction from the MNLF, carried out a kidnapping operation. Their target was a group of 75 civilians, including men, women, children, and a parish priest named Fr. Cirilo Nacorda. The Abu Sayyaf, led by the notorious commander Barahama Sali, who was known for his expertise with weapons and extreme brutality, separated the captives based on their religious beliefs. They released all the Muslim hostages but killed 16 Christians and took the remaining individuals, mostly teachers and Fr. Nacorda, as hostages. After the kidnapping in Lantawan, the Abu Sayyaf group, pursued by Philippine marines from the 2nd Battalion, managed to escape to Sumisip. Additional military forces were dispatched to break up the pursuit. On June 12, Philippine Independence Day, the remaining hostages, except for Fr. Nacorda, were released. That evening, a journalist named Cesar Soriano, working for ABS-CBN and CNN, approached Querubin and his men, seeking to be taken to Zamboanga City. Querubin, believing Soriano had vital information about Sali, threatened to throw his camera into the sea if he did not divulge the information. According to Soriano, he had been blindfolded when taken to Sali's location and witnessed the release of the captives, but he managed to peek through the blindfold and note landmarks that proved useful to Querubin.

➡️Querubin was deemed resigned on 30 November 2009 but formally retired on 23 December 2021 when the Philippine Marine Corps tendered his long-awaited retirement and testimonial ceremony.

➡️Throughout his military career, Colonel Querubin played a significant role in several legendary exploits and political movements that helped shape the history of the military and its role in an emerging global society. He was not only an excellent warrior in the jungles, fighting terrorism and insurgency, but he also represented a class of thinking Filipino soldiers imbued with a sense of idealism, willing to take urgent measures to assert their beliefs about the country's future.

➡️Querubin worked as an internal security consultant for San Miguel Corporation after being granted amnesty. He resigned his commission from the Armed Forces of the Philippines when he ran for a Senate seat as a member of the Nacionalista Party during the 2010 elections. His candidacy was not successful, only garnering 6.5 million votes and landing him 19th place in the senatorial race. He supported Grace Poe's candidacy during the 2016 presidential election.

➡️Querubin once again ran for a Senate seat as a Nacionalista in the 2025 Philippine Senate election, endorsed by 1Sambayan, Senator JV Ejercito, Senator Grace Poe and former President Rodrigo Duterte. Querubin, however, did not succeed in his second attempt, landing in 36th place in the senatorial race.

A CONSCIENCE LEFT BEHIND: THE ABANDONMENT OF BITNONG AND THE SILENCE OF THOSE WHO SWORE TO PROTECT US

The heart of our province is bleeding. While the world moves forward and Benguet demands accountability, the people of Barangay Bitnong, Dupax del Norte, are standing on the front lines of a battle they never asked for. Our fellow Novo Vizcayanos are being forced off their own roads and away from the lands they have nurtured for generations.

As of this January 2026, the government has chosen its side. The Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 30 in Bambang, Nueva Vizcaya, upheld a preliminary injunction in favor of Woggle Corporation. The court ordered anti-mining protesters to immediately dismantle the barricades, the only thing standing between peaceful farmers and heavy mining machinery, along the Keon Barangay Road that block access to the company's exploration area. The court also authorized the Philippine National Police (PNP) to assist court sheriffs in implementing the order and warned that individuals defying the writ could face contempt charges or arrest simply for standing on their own roads to protect their homes.

By ordering the removal of the community barricades, they have handed over our sacred watersheds to Woggle Corporation. They have chosen a piece of paper—an exploration permit—over the living, breathing lives of the people.

Our brothers and sisters in Bitnong aren’t just protecting nature, they are protecting the water we drink, the air we breathe, and the future of our children. The mountains of Nueva Vizcaya are not for sale. They are the "Watershed Haven" of the Cagayan Valley. Once the soil is stripped and the trees are gone, no amount of "exploration permit" money can bring them back.

Today, the people of Dupax Del Norte were left to fight alone, abandoned at the very moment they needed protection the most. While they stood their ground to defend their land, their rights, and their future, those who swore to serve them chose silence, distance, and comfort over courage.

The Irony of "Public Service". We were told the government exists to protect the weak. Instead, we see the police and the courts being used to protect the powerful. We were told our voices matter, but when the people of Bitnong shouted "No," the government looked the other way to count the potential gold and copper profits.

This day will be remembered, not just for the struggle of the people, but for the absence of those who should have been beside them. History will ask who stood up, and who looked away.

DUPAX DEL NORTE DID NOT LOSE ITS COURAGE; IT WAS ABANDONED BY THOSE WITH NO CONSCIENCE.

To the brave people of Nueva Vizcaya: We see your courage. We hear your voices. We stand with you. We stand with the families who fear for their water. We stand with the future generations who will inherit the scars we allow today.

The barricades may fall, but our spirits won’t. Stand with Bitnong today—because once our watersheds are gone, they are gone forever.

Matthew 17 1-9 – After six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them; his face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, conversing with him. Then Peter said to Jesus in reply, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud cast a shadow over them, then from the cloud came a voice that said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” When the disciples heard this, they fell prostrate and were very much afraid. But Jesus came and touched them, saying, “Rise, and do not be afraid.” And when the disciples raised their eyes, they saw no one else but Jesus alone. As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus charged them, “Do not tell the vision to anyone until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”

Points for Meditation
-“Christ’s Transfiguration aims at strengthening the apostles’ faith in anticipation of his passion: The ascent on the high mountain prepares for the ascent to Calvary” (Catechism, 568).

-“For a moment Jesus discloses his divine glory, confirming Peter’s confession” (Catechism, 555).

-“Moses and Elijah had seen God’s glory on the mountain; the law and the prophets had announced the Messiah’s sufferings” (Catechism, 555).

-“The whole Trinity appeared: the Father in the voice, the Son in the man, the Spirit in the shining cloud” (Catechism, 555).

-“The Transfiguration gives us a foretaste of Christ’s glorious coming … But it also recalls that ‘it is through many persecutions that we must enter the kingdom of God’“ (Catechism, 556).

-“According to the senses, the light of the sun is the most intense ever known in nature. But according to the spirit, the disciples saw for a short time a brightness more intense: that of the divine glory of Jesus” (Pope Benedict XVI, Angelus, 2011).

-The three apostles were rewarded for 1)saying Yes to Christ’s invitation, 2) praying, and 3) staying close to him.

-They saw who Christ really was. I saw the beauty of who my spouse really is. Do I guard that “Tabor vision”? or do I focus on my spouse’s faults? (cf. von Hildebrand)

-Think of the Transfiguration when praying the Glory Be prayer.

-St. John wrote that if your love for God is cold you should recall to your mind a time when it was fresh and exciting so that your passion will return.

Verbatim Reconstruction: Preserving Hadi’s “Prophetic Voice” through meticulously translated speeches and interviews.

Media Framing Analysis: Exploring how Hadi dismantled decades of state-sponsored narratives to establish a sovereign cultural identity.

The Theology of Insaaf: Documenting the role of faith-based ethics in building a new era of justice for 180 million voices.

Dr. Mohammad Ali: An Assistant Professor in the Department of Communication at the University of North Dakota. He brings unparalleled academic rigor to this project, holding a Dual PhD, one from Syracuse University and another from the University of Maryland, College Park.

Connect With Us
Join us as we explore the praxis of a revolutionary and the language of cultural struggle. Whether you are a researcher, a student activist, or a human rights defender, this is the story of a sovereign idea that refuses to be silenced.

We strengthened ourselves and combined energy to see that Mr Johnson his wife and child lose their lives. WHO IS THE GENOCIDE CULPRIT?

A Critical Examination of the Claim That “Muslims Are Also Killed” as a Response to the Genocide of Christians and Indigenes/Natives of Nigeria

by
Barr. John Apollos Maton
20th December 2025

INTRODUCTION: THE DANGEROUS SIMPLICITY OF FALSE BALANCE

In every conflict marked by sustained violence against a particular group, there emerges a predictable rhetorical maneuver: false equivalence. When the subject of mass killings of Christians is raised, especially in locations plagued by sectarian violence, a familiar refrain is deployed; “Muslims are also killed.” This statement is often presented not as a call for universal justice, but as a rhetorical shield meant to dilute, deflect or delegitimize the claims of targeted persecution. The purpose is not to mourn all victims or empathise with survivors, but to suspend moral urgency, silence advocacy and neutralize accountability.

The unanswered questions by the protagonists of “Muslims are also killed” despite repeatedly asking is a simple but uncomfortable one: Who is the culprit of the gangster killing spree in Nigeria? 

When Christians are being killed systematically, and the response is that ‘Muslims are also killed’, then logic demands further inquiry; Who is killing whom? Under what circumstances? With what intent? And in whose name? These are not questions of sentiment but of truth, evidence and responsibility. To refuse to ask these questions is not neutrality, it is complicity in obscuring reality.

DEFINING GENOCIDE AND TARGETED VIOLENCE

Genocide is not defined merely by the existence of death inflicted by gangster and selective violence; it is defined by domestic cum international law based on observed pattern, intent and identity. The killing of members of a group because they belong to that group constitutes a crime of a fundamentally different moral and legal category than killings resulting from crime, collateral conflict or intra-group violence (eg. arising from boundary disputes).

When Christian communities are attacked and killed in their bedrooms while asleep, in their villages, churches, farmlands and market places, often without reprisal aggression, the issue is not about quantum numbers alone. It is targeting. It is the selection of victims based on ethnoreligious identity. It is the destruction of lives, livelihoods, properties, sacred spaces and communal continuity. To respond to such evidence with the vague assertion that “others are also killed” is to evade the definition of genocide entirely.

No serious moral framework allows the suffering of one group to be dismissed simply because suffering exists elsewhere.

THE “MUSLIMS ARE ALSO KILLED” ARGUMENT: A LOGICAL AUTOPSY

At first glance, the claim that “Muslims are also killed” appears humane. Who would deny that all lives matter? Yet when examined closely, the argument collapses under its own contradictions.
If Muslims are also killed, then by who and why? Are they killed by Christians acting collectively? Are Christian militias invading Muslim villages? Are churches mobilizing armed groups to attack mosques? What is the evidence, public declarations or ideological manifestos supporting such claims?

The answer, based on available historical records including data, is unequivocal: No. Christians, as a collective religious group, have not organized, celebrated, or justified mass attacks on Muslims in the territorial locations under discussion. There are no evidential records and data of Christian mobs chanting religious slogans while burning Muslims or their settlements, worship places, livelihoods and markets. Nor are there such records and data of sermons by Christian clerics calling for the extermination of Muslims. No coordinated religious campaigns encouraging violence or crime. This absence of evidence is not accidental. It reflects a fundamental asymmetry that the claims in “both sides” narrative refuses to confront.

THE QUESTION OF EVIDENCE: RECORDINGS, ADMISSIONS, AND PATTERNS

One of the most damning aspects of modern conflicts is that they are often documented by the perpetrators themselves. Videos, photographs, statements and social media posts have become tools of intimidation and ideological signaling.

In the cases under discussion on genocides against Christians, there exist repeated instances where attackers openly identify themselves, invoke religious language, and frame their violence as justified or divinely sanctioned. These are not anonymous accidents. They are ideological acts. When individuals proudly record and disseminate evidence of their crimes, they remove ambiguity about intent.
By contrast, there is no comparable archive of Christians collectively boasting about religiously motivated mass violence. This is not a claim of moral perfection, but of empirical reality. Individual crimes exist everywhere. Organized religious extermination by Christians in these contexts does not exist. Thus, when Muslims are killed, the crucial question remains unanswered by deflection: who killed them, and why?

COLLATERAL DEATH VERSUS TARGETED EXTERMINATION

Another deliberate confusion lies in the failure to distinguish between collateral deaths and targeted killing for extermination. In territorial locations affected by insurgency, banditry, and terrorism, civilians of all identities may tragically die. But not all deaths are equal in meaning.

When a Christian farmer is killed because his farmland is trespassed and crops ravaged, his homestead is seized, his church burned, and his village erased, the motive is clear. When worshippers are massacred during religious services, the symbolism is undeniable. When survivors are told to convert, flee, or die, the intent is explicit.
If Muslims are killed in clashes between armed groups, criminal networks, or internal disputes, those deaths are tragic and demand justice, but they do not negate evidence of a parallel, targeted campaign against Christians. Conflating the two is not analysis; it is obfuscation. Yet, the question remains; who killed the Muslims and why?

WHY THE FALSE BALANCE IS POLITICALLY USEFUL

The insistence on “both sides suffer” serves powerful political interests. It allows governments to avoid naming perpetrators. It enables international actors to maintain diplomatic comfort. It shields extremist ideologies from scrutiny by dissolving them into generalized chaos.

Most dangerously, it gaslights victims including survivors. It tells survivors that their suffering is exaggerated, their fear misplaced, and the death of their kinsfolk is a mere statistic in a symmetrical tragedy. This rhetorical strategy does not promote peace—it perpetuates silence. History shows that genocide is rarely denied outright in its early stages by the perpetrators and supporters of the evil. Instead, it is minimized, relativized, pacified and buried under calls for patience and restraint, so the voices of the victims are lost and the true agenda hidden. In Plateau State and many parts of Nigeria, the strategy denying cries against this Genocide is to have even the government misnormered it as being "Insecurity" or the infamous "Farmer-Herder Clash". 

THE MORAL FAILURE OF SILENCE AND DEFLECTION

There is a profound ethical failure in responding to cries of persecution with deflection. Moral seriousness requires specificity. Justice requires naming crimes accurately. Peace requires confronting uncomfortable truths. To acknowledge that Christians are targeted does not require hatred of Muslims. To demand accountability does not require collective blame. But to refuse acknowledgment because it disrupts a preferred narrative is to abandon both truth and humanity. The question is not whether Muslims are also killed. The question is whether Christian deaths are being used as a bargaining chip in a moral shell game designed to avoid responsibility.

WHY CONDEMN THE AID COMING FOR CHRISTIANS?

1. The Moral Contradiction at the Heart of the Objection

The first question that must be confronted honestly is this: why would any morally serious person oppose humanitarian aid to civilians facing mass violence, regardless of their faith? Aid is not a theological endorsement; it is a response to human suffering. Condemning assistance to Christian communities under attack does not reduce violence, save Muslim lives, or advance justice—it merely withholds relief from victims. When opposition to aid becomes louder than condemnation of the killings themselves, priorities are exposed. Humanitarian intervention should never be framed as a zero-sum competition between communities, especially in a context where civilians of multiple faiths are being brutalized by armed groups.

2. The Missed Opportunity for Collective Advocacy

Nigeria’s insecurity has attracted rare international attention, and this moment could have been used constructively to amplify all civilian suffering. Instead of rejecting the framing of Christian victimhood outright, critics could acknowledge it while simultaneously presenting evidence of Muslim civilian casualties and calling for inclusive protection. International actors are capable of responding to multiple crises at once. Denial does not broaden concern; it narrows it. By rejecting the language of “Christian genocide” rather than supplementing it with documented accounts of Muslim suffering, critics inadvertently weaken the overall case for international engagement against terrorism.

3. Denial as a Strategy—and Its Consequences

There is a profound difference between contextualizing violence and denying it. When denial becomes the dominant response, it signals that controlling the narrative matters more than protecting lives. If Christians are being targeted in identifiable patterns—through church attacks, village raids, forced displacement, or selective killings—then disputing terminology should never take precedence over stopping the violence. The insistence on denial, especially when paired with hostility toward aid, creates the impression that reputational defense of a group or ideology has eclipsed compassion for victims. This perception, whether intended or not, damages trust and deepens communal suspicion.

4. If the Culprit Is the Same, Why Resist Intervention?

If both Christians and Muslims are suffering at the hands of the same armed actors—terrorist groups, criminal militias, or transnational extremists—then logic demands a united civilian front. Aid, investigations, and security interventions aimed at dismantling those networks should be welcomed, not resisted. Shielding perpetrators indirectly—by downplaying their impact on one community—undermines the safety of all communities. Terrorist violence does not respect religious boundaries; it exploits them. Any response that fragments civilian solidarity only strengthens the attackers.

5. The Responsibility of Muslims in Indigenous Communities

Muslims who are of the Indigenous tribes of Nigeria, like indigenous Christians, have deep historical, cultural, and communal ties to their regions. Their interests are aligned with peace, stability, and the protection of ancestral lands—not with violent actors who destabilize societies and invite external chaos. Standing against terrorism does not mean standing against Islam; it means standing for life, dignity, and coexistence. When indigenous Muslim voices openly support interventions that protect all civilians, they reclaim moral leadership and make it harder for extremists to masquerade as defenders of faith.

6. Aid Is Not the Enemy—Violence Is

Ultimately, the question is not whose suffering counts more, but whether suffering is allowed to continue unchecked. Humanitarian aid for Christians under attack does not negate Muslim suffering; it establishes a precedent that civilian lives matter. The appropriate response to selective attention is not obstruction, but expansion—demanding broader protection, deeper investigations, and comprehensive aid for all affected communities. Condemning aid aimed at one group risks normalizing cruelty. Supporting aid, while insisting on inclusivity, affirms a shared commitment to justice and human life above sectarian rivalry.

WHO, THEN, IS THE CULPRIT?

If Christians are not attacking Muslims as a religious collective, yet Muslims are also among those killed, then the perpetrators must be clearly and explicitly identified: armed extremist groups, criminal militias, terrorist organizations, or ideological movements that exploit religion for power and violence. Historical and contemporary data suggests the Islamist Fulani jihadists as the only group that fits this narrative; immigrants whose pristine motive from their first incursion to some territories that are constituent parts of what comprise present-day Nigeria was an Islamic jihad aimed at conquest and displacement of native people and institutions.

The refusal to distinguish between Islam as a faith and the Fulani violent actors who profess Islam harms everyone. It allows the Fulani settler immigrants and extremists to hide behind populations of indigenous ethnic groups and critics to be accused of bigotry for asking legitimate questions. Precision is not prejudice; it is the foundation of justice.

CONCLUSION: TRUTH IS NOT HATRED

Asking “Who is the culprit?” is not an act of hostility. It is an act of moral responsibility. 

The lives of Christians lost to targeted violence cannot be erased by the rhetorical symmetry of the culprits. Nor can justice be achieved by pretending that all deaths arise from the same causes or carry the same intent.
If Muslims are killed, they deserve justice. If Christians are targeted for extermination, they also deserve justice, recognition and protection. These truths are not mutually exclusive. What is unacceptable is the weaponization of one tragedy to silence another. Truth demands clarity. Justice demands courage.

And, history will judge not only those who killed, but those who refused to ask who did it, and those who keep pretending not to know it's the continuation of the genocidal campaign of the immigrant Islamist Fulani jihadists against the Native Indigenous Ethnic People and Christians of Nigeria.

The history of the Tawi-Tawi Provincial Capitol is closely tied to the creation of the province itself. The initial provincial capital was briefly established in Batu-Batu, a location on the mainland. Public Statement on the Prerequisites for Genuine National Dialogue in South Sudan: Demands of the SPLM-IO
The concept of a National Political Dialogue is not a prerogative of any single party or leader. It is not the property of the SPLM-IG nor President Salva Kiir Mayardit. Rather, it is an inclusive, multi-stakeholder process where diverse groups such as political elites, civil society, ethnic leaders, women, and youth come together to build consensus and address deep-seated political crises, conflicts, and national challenges. 
The inclusive dialogue, which is participatory and agreed freely is known as genuine dialogue. Such dialogue often paves the way for constitutional reforms, power-sharing agreements, or peaceful transitions in fragile states. The purpose of genuine dialogue is to broaden participation beyond traditional elites, foster social cohesion, and tackle the root causes of instability through structured negotiation and agreement on governance, rights, and identity.
From the definition of what is meant by true national dialogue above, it is clear that National Dialogue is not mere political talk. It extends beyond conversation to include specific conditions concerning participants’ attitudes, the environment, and the purpose of the interaction. For dialogue to be deemed genuine, the following prerequisites are non-negotiable:
Key Prerequisites
(1) Equality and Mutual Respect. Participants must relate to each other as equal partners, with no hierarchical relationships. Respect for the human person and recognition of each individual’s unique contribution is fundamental to successful dialogue. 
(2) Active and Empathetic Listening. Dialogue requires genuine willingness to listen and understand, not simply to counterargue. Empathy, which is “shared suffering” is essential to build connection and trust.
(3) Open-Mindedness and Reflection. Participants must be willing to challenge their own assumptions, suspend personal beliefs temporarily, and consider alternative perspectives with humility.
(4) Trust in the Process. Dialogue must be approached with faith in its ability to produce shared solutions, not as a battlefield to “win” arguments.
(5) Beyond Information Exchange. The purpose of dialogue is deeper than sharing facts as it seeks mutual understanding, transformation, joint problem-solving, and social change.
(6) Safe and Supportive Environment. Genuine dialogue thrives in a protective environment where participants feel secure to speak honestly without fear of exploitation or belittlement.
(7) Finally, Free Civic and Political Space. Dialogue cannot exist without freedoms of expression, speech, and association. Civil society must be empowered to contribute meaningfully to political, economic, and social life.
Position of the SPLM-IO
The SPLM-IO under Dr. Riek Machar Teny does not reject dialogue. However, we insist that any dialogue falling short of these prerequisites is not dialogue but a mere political gathering. Therefore, the demands of the SPLM-IO for it to participate in the dialogue include:
(1) Political detainees, including Dr. Riek Machar Teny, must be released without any condition.
(2) Dialogue must be inclusive, involving all opposition groups inside and outside South Sudan and conducted in a neutral environment agreed upon by all parties. 
(3) The so-called SPLM-IO faction under Par Kuol (Delink group) is not recognized as part of SPLM-IO under His Excellency Dr. Riek Machar Teny and cannot represent us as it will make the dialogue void ab initio. Their inclusion is a deliberate sabotage by SPLM-IG, and we cannot be party to the dialogue where they are participating as factions of the SPLM-IO unless they come under different name independently or as part of the SPLM-IG. 
(4) We reject sham dialogues designed to entrench SPLM-IG’s dominance.
(5) The dialogue must accomplish permanent peace, and a verified ceasefire must be established once and for all, instead of returning to square one. 
Conclusion
The SPLM-IO under Dr. Riek Machar Teny reaffirms its commitment to peace and dialogue. But dialogue must be valid and genuine, which means that it must be a collaborative, open, and understanding process aimed at shared learning and transformation. We will not entertain political tricks or cosmetic gatherings. Our demand is simple: a dialogue we demand is that which respects the principles of equality, inclusivity, and freedom, and that leads to lasting peace for the people of South Sudan John Mangar Reechdit

There is now a strong likelihood Donald Trump will order his military option of choice on Iran

(By ABC North America bureau chief John Lyons)

There is now a strong likelihood that US President Donald Trump will order air strikes against Iran.

In some ways, Trump has backed himself into a corner, declaring defiantly that should the Iranian regime open fire on its own people, then the US would take action against the regime.

He's told protesters that help is on its way. What help? And when?

The regime has done exactly what Trump warned against. While an information blackout has made it difficult to assess the exact extent of the death toll, it is clear that hundreds, if not thousands, of Iranian protesters have been killed by the country's security forces.

So what are Trump's military options?

At this stage, the one that's most likely is air strikes on military bases and warehouses controlled by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its civilian enforcers, the Basij militia.

The Basij will be a possible target for the US as they are vital in trying to put down these protests. The Basij are volunteers who answer to the IRGC. Many workplaces have Basij members — often their colleagues may not even know for sure that they are Basij, even if they have suspicions.

A member of the Basij receives many benefits — such as prized jobs or places in universities for which they would not otherwise have qualified.

But there is one condition: the IRGC can call upon them at any point to do whatever is required to "protect the Islamic Revolution".

Now is when the IRGC will be calling in those debts. They will be instructing the Basij to work their way through the various crowds and then to try to disperse them.

In 2009, I saw members of the Basij trying to break up crowds. They ride around on motorbikes, usually dressed in black and often with their faces covered by scarves to protect their identities.

I saw some with clubs who, without warning, would start bashing members of the crowd. Others carried machetes. They roam the streets like gangs, often 15 or 20 in one group.

Many of those protesting will know the fear that 15 or 20 Basij arriving at a scene can instil. The Basij can — and do — kill with impunity.

What the Basij will be worried about at the moment is whether the size of the crowds could mean that when they try to break up a protest there is a chance they'll be overpowered, despite being armed with bike chains, knives and machetes.

If this were to happen across the country, it would become a tipping point for the protesters.

This would be the point at which the regime may start to lose the streets.

Iran weakest it's been in years 

The reason air strikes are the most likely option for the US is because at present, there is no US naval battle group near Iran — which means the US cannot, for the moment at least, use naval-based weapons. But it can quickly marshal significant air power from its various bases through the Middle East.

The Saudis and Emiratis, among others in the region, are nervous about the US launching a new attack on Iran — they fear the response that Iran may engage in.

But a major calculation of the Trump White House is that Iran is the weakest it has been for many years. Air strikes last year by Israel and later by the US have weakened the country.

Added to this is the fact that Iran's major proxy militia, Hezbollah, has been largely degraded by Israel. This means that Iran's ability to respond is limited. Israel and the US have made sure that Israel is largely protected against incoming missile attacks from Iran, as was shown last year.

Very few missiles fired by Iran were able to penetrate Israeli airspace, with many intercepted by Jordanian and other jets as they crossed the Middle East.

In the year since his return to the White House, Trump has settled upon his military option of choice: short, surgical operations that raise minimum danger for US forces.

Trump is eschewing the military strategies used by so many of his predecessors — so far, at least. He's decided not to deploy large numbers of US forces into foreign conflicts it may then take years to extract them from.

Under the Trump military doctrine, the quagmires of Iraq, Afghanistan and Vietnam are a thing of the past. As an instinctive politician with an extraordinarily sharp sense of the public mood, Trump knows Americans are fatigued from these sorts of conflicts.

Trump boosted by Maduro operation 

The Trump White House, and Trump himself, are clearly pumped by the recent successful extraction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

History will judge it as one of the most extraordinary military operations of modern times. US intelligence had spent months studying the daily habits of Maduro and his family. As US defence officials have said, the Pentagon in Washington knew Maduro's daily routines, what he liked to eat and even the behaviour of his pets.

While they obviously will not reveal their sources, clearly the US had either human intelligence inside the Maduro inner circle or electronic surveillance, including video, inside the highly fortified presidential compound.

That operation has been popular with his Make America Great Again base. His supporters liked the imagery of US soldiers bringing in a foreign leader, who they believe has been responsible for allowing drug cartels to supply the United States, to be "brought to justice." Not a single US soldier lost their life.

Likewise, the US air attacks last year on Iran's nuclear facilities were popular. While the extent of the damage to those facilities is disputed, what is not disputed is that the US caused damage to Iran's nuclear program without losing a single US soldier.

Iranian state television reported no civilian deaths. But in his operation in Venezuela, civilians and security forces lost their lives.    

Trump's language in recent days has been strong. He's promised protesters in Iran that "help is on the way." He's also said the US is "locked and loaded" when it comes to its military.

But he's also giving himself room to back down. "It looks like they're killing a lot of people, but that hasn't been confirmed," he told reporters. "I'll know very soon."

The intelligence briefings the president will be receiving in coming days are almost certain to confirm these killings.

Based on that, there is a strong possibility that the US will launch air strikes on Iran.

15 November 2025 – Borderless Africa Forum: The Undoing of Those Borders
Last week in Addis Ababa, we gathered to mark 141 years since the Berlin Conference, held in Germany, where the process of partitioning Africa among European powers formally began.
On 15 November 1884, thirteen men—no women, no Africans—sat to redraw Africa’s destiny. They created artificial borders, fragmented civilizations, and laid the foundation for division, domination, and exploitation.
Exactly 141 years later, on 15 November, we gathered again—not to divide, but to undo.
Not to conquer, but to unite.
Not to exploit, but to build.
While they met to divide Africa, we met to reunite it.
This history is our heritage. We cannot deny it, and we cannot erase it. But we must not allow it to imprison our future. Africa can no longer live within the imagination of those thirteen men. We must imagine our own future—one shaped by our people.
A future where we are united by shared culture, common economic interests, geostrategic cooperation, and collective defence against the existential threats we face.
That future begins with free movement.
It begins by removing visas imposed on Africans by Africans.
It continues with the African passport, reclaiming and reshaping our identity.
Then an African currency, strengthening our economic sovereignty.
And beyond that, deeper political, security, and institutional integration.
Without these steps, how do we defend ourselves against those determined to dominate, divide, and exploit us?
How do we rise if we remain trapped within borders we did not draw?
The era of division must give way to the era of unity.
The time to build a borderless continent is now.
