THE GUARD REQUESTED OUR IDS. MY DAD PRESENTED HIS RETIREMENT CARD. "SHE'S JUST WITH ME," HE TOLD HIM. I SLIDED FORWARD A CARD STAMPED WITH THE PRESIDENTIAL CREST. THE SCANNER LIT UP: "YANKEE WHITE TOP PRIORITY." THE GUARD GRABBED THE RED HOTLINE. "CLEAR THE VIP PASSAGE. NOW." MY DAD COULDN'T BELIEVE IT 
The line stalled beneath the steel awning at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, rain ticking like a countdown on the concrete. The guard’s boots stopped in front of us. His eyes moved from my face to my father’s hands—steady, older, proud.
“IDs,” he said.
My dad passed his retirement card with a soft smile. “She’s just with me,” he added, the way parents do when they think proximity still protects. The guard nodded politely, already turning the card back.
I didn’t rush. I didn’t explain. I slid my card forward.
It was matte, unassuming, stamped with a crest most people only see on TV. The scanner chirped once—then glowed. The words appeared like a whisper made official: YANKEE WHITE — TOP PRIORITY. The guard froze. Not dramatic. Professional. Different.
He reached for the red hotline.
“Clear the VIP passage,” he said, voice clipped. “Now.”
My father’s mouth opened, then closed. I felt it—the moment when a lifetime of assumptions rearranges itself. Around us, radios crackled. A door we hadn’t noticed opened. The rain stopped mattering.
No one asked questions out loud. That’s how real authority moves—quiet, decisive, allergic to spectacle. A supervisor arrived who knew my name without asking. Another who avoided it entirely. My dad tried to laugh it off. “She’s family,” he said again, softer this time.
I kept my eyes forward. Some things don’t need defending.
We walked through a corridor that smelled like ozone and coffee, past badges that didn’t match, past faces that didn’t linger. The passage closed behind us with a sound like punctuation.
Later, in the car, my dad finally spoke. “Since when?” he asked. Not accusing. Just… recalibrating.
I didn’t answer then. Not because I couldn’t—but because timing matters. And because the part he saw was only the front of the card.
What he didn’t see was the date it activated—or why it had limits placed after my name.
He didn’t hear the second call that came once we cleared the gate.
And he definitely didn’t know what I’d already agreed to do… before I ever slid that card forward. TO BE CONTINUE IN COMMENTS

🫣😱 Karácsony Gergely és az ő tangás sörhasú, meg magassarkúban vonagló követői lennének a modern szabadságharcosok?

A következő sorokban tárgyalt hír hallatán még nem tudjuk eldönteni, hogy sírni szeretnénk, vagy inkább egy jót kacagunk rajta. Mindenesetre elgondolkozató az, hogyan jutottunk el oda, hogy Karácsony Gergely bekerült ugyanabba a sorba, ahol Tőkés László is szerepel. A főpridemester ugyanis megkapta ugyanazt az emberi jogokért járó díjat, mint Tőkés 1991-ben. Nagyot fordult a világ, alig több mint harminc évvel ezelőtt még az állampolgárokat a kommunista elnyomástól megmentő, az IGAZI szabadságért kiálló emberek érdemelték ki az emberi jogi díjat, ma pedig azok, akik tangás férfiakat szeretnek látni vonaglani Budapest utcáin. 

Szóval 2026-ban ott tartunk, hogy a kommunista elnyomás ellen harcolni egyenlő lett - sokak szerint - azzal, ha valaki abban a tévképzetben él Európában, hogy őt bárki elnyomja azért, mert azonos nemű embert szeret, se ezért azzal “harcol”, hogy kis tangában, csillogós sminkkel Lady Gagára vonulgat a város utcáin át, majd lő néhány szelfit az Instagramra és a TikTokra. Ez ma, a hollandok szerint a szabadságharc. Nem az mondjuk, hogy minden fórumon, minden nap és minden órában kiáll valaki például egy értelmetlen háború lezárása mellett. Ez nem szabadságharc ma a hollandok szerint. De csillámos sminkben meg kisbugyiban rúdtáncolni egy kamionon az az. Te jó Isten.

A PLACE FOR SANCTUARY. DAILY DOSE.
Regardless of where you live, we’ve all had our share of extreme weather events these past few months.
And this we know, storms upend days. And lives.
And most storms, in our life and world, are not even weather related, though the effect feels the same. Times when relationships unravel. Health deteriorates. Beliefs crumble. Hope evaporates.
And this much is undeniable: sometime in our life, every single one of us needs a storm-home. A place for sanctuary. A place for restoration. A place for healing.

Which brings me to one of my favorite stories—which I wish had been our go-to textbook for my seminary’s class on pastoral care.
"Today was a Difficult Day," said Pooh.
There was a pause.
"Do you want to talk about it?" asked Piglet.
"No," said Pooh after a bit. "No, I don't think I do."
"That's okay," said Piglet, and he came and sat beside his friend.
"What are you doing?" asked Pooh.
"Nothing, really," said Piglet. "Only, I know what Difficult Days are like. I quite often don't feel like talking about it on my Difficult Days either...
"But goodness," continued Piglet, "Difficult Days are so much easier when you know you've got someone there for you. And I'll always be here for you, Pooh."
And as Pooh sat there, working through in his head his Difficult Day, while the solid, reliable Piglet sat next to him quietly, swinging his little legs... he thought that his best friend had never been more right."
(Thank you A.A. Milne)

Can we stop and embrace this gift? The gift of the power of presence.
Yes, the healing gift of “storm homes.” A place where we need no restrictor plate in our soul.
Storms, mental and emotional, take a toll. And you never know when reaching out makes a difference. A kind gesture or word. A gentle tone. Or just, being there.
And I love Piglet’s skill set necessary for being a “storm home” (safe place) for someone having a “difficult day”: Sitting together, quietly, swinging your legs.
Gratefully, at some time, we come face to face with the reality that no one of us is on this human, or faith journey, alone.
Life is fragile and therefore, we are connected.
This week we will remember that it is in our DNA to be, and to need, storm homes.
To offer storm homes to others.
To ask for a storm home when we struggle.
And we hope for places where healing can begin.

“For spiritually alive people, for people of deep and genuine faith, we don’t want to surrender to despair and cynicism, reactivity and fragmentation. We want to be healed and empowered, so we can participate in healing and empowering other people.” Thank you, Brian McLaren.

#ATENCION Petro llama de nuevo al pueblo a las calles porque quieren tumbar el salario mínimo.

El presidente Gustavo Petro llamó a la movilización ciudadana para defender el decreto del salario mínimo vital y familiar, ante lo que calificó como un intento de la “oligarquía y los oligopolios” de acudir al poder judicial para derribarlo. A través de un extenso mensaje, el mandatario advirtió que sectores económicos buscarán frenar tanto el salario vital como el decreto que obliga a grandes conglomerados a pagar más impuestos.

Petro sostuvo que no existen fundamentos científicos para afirmar que el salario vital generará inflación y aseguró que la ciencia económica desmiente esos argumentos. Recordó que el salario vital está ordenado por la Constitución de 1991, en su artículo 53, y cuestionó por qué en más de tres décadas no se ha cumplido ese mandato constitucional.

Según explicó, el cálculo del salario vital parte de datos oficiales del DANE sobre el costo de la canasta mínima vital de las familias colombianas en 2025, dividido por el promedio de trabajadores por hogar, lo que arroja un ingreso cercano a los dos millones de pesos mensuales. Afirmó que esta propuesta desató la reacción de los grandes grupos económicos.

El presidente también criticó al Congreso por no legislar en favor de los trabajadores y señaló la compra de votos como una de las raíces de la corrupción política. En ese contexto, llamó a los ciudadanos a no vender su voto y a no respaldar a quienes, según dijo, legislan para los “megarricos y las mafias”.

Finalmente, Petro anunció que el salario vital será presentado como proyecto de ley y planteó que su discusión deberá darse en un nuevo Congreso o incluso en una Asamblea Nacional Constituyente, con el objetivo de garantizar de manera permanente los derechos laborales y el mínimo vital de las familias trabajadoras.

The Story Behind the Music. 

The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, mobilized the nation against racial injustice by making sure almost everyone in the United States and across the world, saw America’s Neanderthal, perceived supremacy horrors – on the nightly news, while watching peaceful Black people getting clubbed and arrested for exercising their rights.
“Americans are waking up. A grand reckoning awaits us.”

The making of my song Role Model, Tribute To Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Purposely placed as the first track to my new album, The Songbook of Life. 

Civil Rights icon Martin Luther King Jr., to many at home and abroad, is still best known for his “I Have A Dream” speech at the 1963 March on Washington. Emory University’s political science professor Andra Gillespie’s recent work, shows us why Dr. King’s legacy is more complex and significant than those inspirational words. Throughout which, she talks about the uncomfortable conversations Americans still need to have about race and justice in order to truly honor his legacy.

Dr. Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. spent two summers working on the tobacco farms along Firetown Road in Simsbury, Connecticut. Today many historians would agree argue such time spent in Connecticut, picking tobacco as a teenager, was rather influential to his life throughout. And here is where my song picks up. 

On Martin Luther King Jr. Day, the Simsbury Free Library honored the civil rights leader who has inspired millions of people around the world and unveiled the MLK in CT Memorial. Students completed the researched we’d started years earlier about Dr. King’s time in Connecticut, they created a documentary, raised $150,000 and designed the outdoor memorial on the grounds of the Simsbury Free Library.

Since around age 7, I pondered in awe and shared admiration, made bets with my older cousins brothers and sisters, got sent to my room by my grandparents and away from the table by my mom, when the argument got too heated and I’d slammed my fist down on the table at them… as if in a living courtroom drama.

I’d always felt that the world would be forever indebted to the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., a man who’ve put his life and that of his families on the line, as he fought and died valiantly in a peaceful struggle in the name of equality, and social justice. 

Many of my families friends thought that I’d go into school and study laws, for I was such a fierce debater. Of course, I had to be, since I was the 4 child among 8 siblings. One just had to be quick thinking in order to not get ran over, railroaded nor left behind. I did not yet live in the United States of America, and perhaps I certainly would have if I did. But I lived in Honduras, where I grew up as a child. Besides our family economic situation took a downward spiral long before my high school or college age. Reason for my heading out to sea at 15 to navigate.

This great nation, the United States of America, honors the late civil leader every year with a national holiday scheduled around his birthday on January 15th. Given the importance of his work, much of which continues to ring true today, it’s no surprise that Dr. King has inspired music from a wide range of artists throughout the world, from Prince, to Steve Wonder, U2, Paul Simon, Queen, to Elvis Presley, etc. I did the research and to realized there were actually 12 songs written by these artists about, Dr. King, as I sat out to write, compose and produced one about his legacy.

While Stevie Wonder’s iconic song served as the chief architect and his piece of music help to usher in and champion the MLK Day, as an official, federal holiday. This year, I’m honored to join a little side of that list, as I followed some of the greatest musicians on the planet, I proudly introduced a song track that offers reverence, respect, honor and appreciation for a man who’s battled for equality, gave up his life for such struggle, as he was brutally assassinated. The song track, My Role Model (tribute to Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King), is the first on my album, The Songbook of Life. 

Engineered and recorded at Playbach Studios, produced by Guillermo Torres,en Hatorey, Puerto Rico.

The following, is a selection of some of the most notable songs inspired by the late civil rights leader. In their own way, these tracks have undoubtedly help to keep the dream alive. My hopes and prayers, is that My Role Model, might do the same for the generations that follows. Coming soon.

The teachings of Dr. king
While being a part Garinagu kid, growing up as a boy, in an English speaking, expat-Caymanian, Roatanian, West Indian household in Honduras. We were required to first learn to speak, read and write English, prior to entering the school system, which was all taught in Spanish. 
We were each required to focus on important historic or current events, subject matter to ask questions, research, read and write about in English. I focused on the Bible, Genesis, the story of Joseph in Egypt,  the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., Civil Rights Movements and the events occurring in the United States of America. 

Nearly 60 years later,  I could still recite psalm 23 in both, English and Spanish, still remember and often return to Joseph story as a key point to reference, while advocating for equality and justice during debates. 

I believe it was during an interview in 1957, when the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. first said, “It is appalling that the most segregated hour of Christian America, is between 11:00 am and 12:00 P.M, as he rejected former President Eisenhower’s justifications issued to White American business owners, as a mandated right to exclude Black people from being able to shop and sit at the Sears and Roebuck’s and other businesses lunch counters.
While at the same time, advocating thus teaching about the benefits and right to integration, an end to segregation for a better America. That same year in December, he was awarded the the Nobel peace price.

Dr. King, again repeated this very significant phrase during another NBC interview on Meet the Press on Sunday morning in 1963. Although according to experts, that assertion remains true even today. About eight-in-10 American congregants still attend services at a place where a single racial or ethnic group comprises at least 80 percent of the congregation, according to findings from the most recent (2012) National Congregations Study, as cited by the Pew Research Center.

Three years after he initially agreed to be a guest on the show, Dr. King made his first appearance on the National Broadcasting Company television program, NBC’s “Meet the Press,” where he addressed the legal and moral justifications for the student sit-ins and the federal governments “responsibility of protecting all of the citizens of this nation.” Meanwhile, down in Honduras and throughout the Caribbean island, including Puertoricans, whom spoke English, hang on to every word he said. There were no English broadcast news anywhere in Central America during such times and no translation available. Except for Radio Belize that came clear across the ocean and was picked up live in Puerto Cortes. Of course Belize, was still under British rule and many West Indians, such as my mother and grandmother got their news from there, which they followed play by play. 

A few years prior to Dr. King being assassinated, mother had obtained a great job, with Don Manuel Cano and Doña Julita De Cano, owners of Cafe Campana in San Pedro Sula. Job was in another city, and she’d had to leave us behind and being cared for by my grandmother and aunt. Of course initially, the job entailed domestic work, while mother further prepared herself in English that would enable her to work as a live in tutor for their daughter, Doña Araceli, whom was about to marry Dr. Alberto Downing. During such time English was very limited throughout most of Honduras, except for the Bay Islands, which was then over 99% English speaking, and less than 1% Spanish speaking and bad Spanish at that.

As the months and perhaps year drew by, mother was able to relocate us to the city of San Pedro Sula, as she always said, “without leaving anyone of my 8 children behind.” She was indeed also transferred to work with the newlywed couple. As their first set of children arrived, mother received an assistant, who’d help with the house chores, while mother concentrated on tutoring the children in English. However, she’d convinced the dawning’s, they needed to order American books and magazines by which she could best tutor American history. 
Of course, many of these books were based on the civil rights movement, Ebony and Jet’s magazines. So every week, they be a fresh turn over and the dawnings home, and I had a fresh batch of reading materials at age 6, 7, 8 years old.  I would read, and studied about the civil rights movement as if I was studying for a test. Mostly impressed, since in Honduras, we did not see any black people dressed in such high fashion if clothes, shoes, homes, styles, etc.
However, though sad, as the tears went by, it was how we would would also followed, the play by play of Dr. King and Senator Robert Kennedys asesination. 

I remain interested in African American history, long before writing and publishing books about history. Gave lectures during black history month, at churches, schools and universities following the publication of Africans in the Americas. Around 2005, as conclusive research emerged that a 15 year old young, Martin Luther King had spent 2 semesters as he worked picking tobacco at farms in Simsbury Connecticut, a committee was formed out of First Church Simsbury UCC, the Then Christian Activities Council and several other churches, with the intent of creating a memorial and erecting a  statue of Dr. King, thus honoring his legacy, to which I was invited to participate by Rev. Edwin Ayala, (RIP), respectable honorable mentor and the associate director of the Christian Activities Council, (CAC).

We met regularly and fought vigorously to win the battle to present a case that would honor his legacy and keep his dream alive. Of course, it wasn’t until someone suggested that such statue might be built and erected outside, behind the library and not at the front of the library as we previously agreed. And it was then, we all grew frustrated and against the inept system of entrenched prejudice and walk away to fight another day. Back surgery rob my quest for fight, and I believed it wasn’t until around 2010, when the local Central High School, wrote and received Grants to researched Dr. King’s time in Connecticut, they also created a documentary that helped them raised $150,000 and designed the outdoor memorial on the grounds of the Simsbury Free Library.
These young people took it to task to complete what the adults had started, but couldn’t fully push to finally get that mighty important tasks up the hill of challenges. 

The following is a brief history and completion of The MLK Memorial in Simsbury, Connecticut outside of the library… unveiled amidst mid global pandemic, January 18/2021.

The memorial includes five glass panels focused on different aspects of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr’s life.

Duelul legitimităților: Frica lui Iliescu de Rege și împăcarea târzie

Relația dintre Ion Iliescu și Regele Mihai I nu a fost doar o animozitate între două persoane, ci ciocnirea violentă dintre două lumi: România comunistă, care refuza să moară, și România istorică, care încerca să renască. În primii ani de după Revoluția din 1989, pentru Ion Iliescu, fostul ministru al tineretului comunist ajuns președinte, Regele nu reprezenta un simplu cetățean, ci „Pericolul Suprem”. Iliescu știa că legitimitatea sa provenea din haosul revoluției, în timp ce legitimitatea lui Mihai venea din istorie și Constituția din 1923. Această insecuritate politică a generat una dintre cele mai rușinoase campanii de manipulare din istoria recentă.

Momentul de panică totală pentru puterea de la București a fost Paștele anului 1992. Crezând că popularitatea monarhiei este neglijabilă, Iliescu a permis vizita Regelui. Calculul său s-a dovedit a fi o eroare colosală. Peste 1 milion de oameni au ieșit pe străzile Bucureștiului, scandând „Majestate, nu pleca, asta este țara ta!”. Imaginea Regelui la balconul hotelului Continental, aclamat de o mare de oameni, l-a îngrozit pe Iliescu. Frica de a pierde puterea l-a determinat să ia măsuri extreme: timp de 5 ani, Regelui i s-a interzis accesul în țară, sub pretexte penibile, fiind acuzat că vrea să destabilizeze statul.

Punctul culminant al umilinței a avut loc în 1994, pe aeroportul Otopeni. Regele, sosit cu avionul, a fost ținut prizonier pe pistă, înconjurat de trupe speciale, și trimis înapoi în exil, fiind tratat ca un infractor internațional, nu ca un fost șef de stat care întorsese armele împotriva nazismului. Propagandiștii FSN-ului au lansat zvonuri otrăvite la televiziune, spunând că Regele vine „să ia pământurile țăranilor” și să plece cu „vagoane de aur”, minciuni care au prins rădăcini adânci în populația dezinformată.

Însă, istoria are un simț al ironiei deosebit. Împăcarea dintre cei doi, survenită după anul 2000, nu a fost una emoțională, ci pur pragmatică. Revenit la putere în 2001, Ion Iliescu avea nevoie disperată de sprijin pentru intrarea României în NATO și UE. Avea nevoie de un ambasador regal pe lângă curțile europene, acolo unde trecutul său comunist nu era bine văzut. Așa s-a produs „strângerea de mână istorică”. Iliescu i-a restituit Regelui proprietățile (Castelul Peleș, Săvârșin) și cetățenia, iar Regele a acceptat să facă lobby pentru țară, trecând peste uriașul său orgoliu rănit. A fost un pact de neagresiune: Iliescu a primit validare externă, iar Regele a primit dreptul de a muri acasă.

Amb. Cde. James Mawich Bichiok is a prominent politician and a member of the SPLM National Liberation Council, representing Fangak County in Jonglei State, South Sudan. He is a dedicated supporter of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) whose efforts have consistently focused on fostering peace, unity, and community development in Fangak County. His political career is deeply intertwined with his commitment to uplifting the voices and aspirations of the Fangak people.

Promotion of Peace and Harmony
Amb. James has worked tirelessly to promote peace and harmony among the people of Fangak. His dedication to dialogue and collaboration has been pivotal in bridging divides within the community. He has reached out to bomas and payams affected by floods and conflict, demonstrating a remarkable commitment to the welfare of vulnerable populations. By engaging closely with local leaders, Amb. James has emphasized unity and mutual respect among diverse groups, regardless of political or logistical challenges. This approach has contributed to creating a cohesive community atmosphere conducive to development and stability.

Role in SPLM Initiatives
In 2026, Amb. James personally visited civilians in Fangak County to reconnect the SPLM with the local community under the theme of restoring trust in peacebuilding. He paid special attention to vulnerable populations affected by flooding.

In 2024, Amb. James led an SPLM mission to Fangak County, organizing a major rally to mobilize support for the party and its leadership under H.E. Gen. Salva Kiir Mayardit, President of the Republic of South Sudan. This rally provided a platform for the Fangak community to express their commitment to SPLM and articulate their vision for the county’s future.

The overwhelming support for Amb. James from the people of Fangak is a testament to his character and dedication. Residents publicly declared their 100% endorsement of SPLM leadership, emphasizing their desire to see the movement thrive and their commitment to the principles of development, governance, and enduring peace.

Conclusion .
Amb. Cde. James Mawich Bichiok has become a symbol of hope and leadership in Fangak County and South Sudan. The support he receives from his community underscores the power of local voices in shaping broader national dialogues.

The Armed Forces of Malta (AFM) has welcomed Intake 261, consisting of eighty eight new recruits, including seven females.

On their first day, the recruits reported to Luqa Barracks at 0700hrs after successfully completing a rigorous selection process, which included:

•⁠  ⁠A physical fitness test
•⁠  ⁠Military and written assessments
•⁠  ⁠An interview
•⁠  ⁠A full medical examination

During the day, the recruits took the Oath of Allegiance to the People and the Republic of Malta and its Constitution.

This intake also includes 12 Officer Cadets, among them three female candidates, who will commence their training in the coming weeks. The full recruitment process will span between four and five months and will guide participants through the transition from civilian to military life. Training will include a combination of academic and practical modules, covering military drill, fieldcraft, skill at arms, physical fitness, and other essential competencies required to begin a military career.

This journey is a demanding one. Only those who achieve the required standards, demonstrate adequate levels of fitness, and display the right attitude will succeed and earn their place in the Passing Out Parade, which marks the culmination of this recruitment phase.

The Minister for Home Affairs, Security and Employment, Byron Camilleri, conveyed his encouragement to the new recruits as they embark on this training, which leads to service in the interest of our country. He noted positively that once again more young people have come forward to pursue a career in a Disciplined Corps, stating that this also reflects the strengthened conditions of those who serve our country on a daily basis in recent years. This, in turn, helps attract more talent to the Armed Forces of Malta, ultimately benefiting our citizens through an ever-improving service.

The Commander of the Armed Forces of Malta, Brigadier Clinton J. O’Neill, expressed the AFM’s commitment to providing the best possible training opportunities for the recruits. He wished them every success and encouraged them to listen to the advice of their directing staff, work together as a team with their squad mates, never give up, and approach every task with a positive attitude and a strong will to succeed.

He also expressed his hope to see all recruits and officer cadets who have begun this journey successfully form up and pass out during the final parade of this intake.

The PNP has always prioritized the mental health and well-being of its personnel. “Marami tayong mga programa para sa internal cleansing at preventive intervention, at mas paiigtingin pa natin ito upang maiwasan ang mga insidente habang sinusuportahan ang ating mga opisyal sa kanilang tungkulin,” dagdag ni PLTGEN Nartatez.

The Bantay Kaisapan Program of the PNP Health Service provides a holistic mental health framework to support officers in managing stress, preventing burnout, and maintaining well-being. In 2025, Bantay Kaisapan conducted 61,906 psychological exams, 74,672 stress management sessions, 67,895 anger management interventions, and 809 stress debriefings. 

Psychoeducational initiatives included 61,371 mental health materials distributed, 18,049 psychological monitoring sessions, 932 counseling sessions, 591 tele-counseling activities, as well as individual psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy services. Personnel undergoing promotion, recruitment, schooling, or restoration also received regular psychological and psychiatric evaluations to ensure readiness and fitness for duty.

Leadership and mentorship are reinforced through initiatives such as the One-Day Squad Leaders’ Summit and True Leader’s Heart (TLH), equipping squad leaders to guide with empathy, foster accountability, and build cohesive teams. “A good leader doesn’t just command—he guides, mentors, and inspires. Our squad leaders are being trained to connect authentically with their personnel, strengthening both morale and discipline,” said PLTGEN Nartatez.

Operational accountability is also emphasized through the Monthly Comparative Report of Squad Weekly Interactive Meeting (SWIM), where PNP units exceeded the annual target of 849,984 reports, achieving 1,100,204 reports, or 129% of the target. Complementing this, the Chaplain Service conducted 24,868 counseling activities nationwide, providing spiritual support and holistic care.

Discipline is enforced through the Integrity Monitoring and Enforcement Group (IMEG), which filed 664 administrative cases involving 1,035 officers and 138 criminal cases against 201 respondents in 2025. Cases ranged from preliminary investigations to hearings and resolutions, resulting in reprimands, suspensions, dismissals, and service sentences, reflecting a firm yet fair approach.

Restorative programs such as FORMPOLICE (Focused Reformation/Reorientation for Police Officers’ Internal Cleansing) provide officers with training to restore discipline and professional values. In 2025, 48 officers underwent 30-day FORMPOLICE programs for grave offenses, while 543 officers participated in 7-day programs, strengthening ethical standards and professional responsibility.

PLTGEN Nartatez added, “Through preventive care, fair enforcement, and reformation, we are shaping a PNP that responds effectively to challenges while embodying integrity, resilience, and accountability.”

He further emphasized, “Ang bawat hakbang na ginagawa natin—mula sa mental health programs hanggang sa leadership training—ay nakatuon hindi lamang sa pagpapatupad ng batas, kundi sa paghubog ng mga opisyal na may puso at prinsipyo. Ipinapakita nito na ang PNP ay tunay na serbisyong tapat at nararamdaman.”

Highlighting accountability, he added, “We will continue to enforce discipline firmly but fairly. Walang sinuman sa ating hanay ang exempted sa pamantayan ng integridad. Sa 2026, mas tutukan natin ang pagpapaigting ng mga programang ito upang mas mapalakas at mapanatili ang integridad, disiplina, at kagalingan ng bawat opisyal. This is how we ensure public trust and a stronger police force.”

These initiatives reflect the PNP’s commitment to safeguarding personnel welfare, preventing misconduct, and fostering professional growth, advancing the vision of a Bagong PNP para sa Bagong Pilipinas: Serbisyong Mabilis, Tapat, at Nararamdaman.

In 1950, when Frank E. Petersen Jr. walked into the Marine Corps recruiting office, America was a different place. The military had only been integrated for two years. Many still believed that African Americans couldn't be fighter pilots—that they didn't have what it took to handle the speed, the pressure, the split-second decisions that meant the difference between life and death at 30,000 feet.

Frank Petersen was about to prove them spectacularly wrong.

Born in Topeka, Kansas, in 1932, young Frank had always looked up at the sky with wonder. While other kids dreamed of being baseball players or cowboys, Frank dreamed of flying. Not just flying—but pushing machines to their absolute limits, mastering the most dangerous job in the most elite fighting force in the world.

When the Korean War erupted, Petersen earned his wings and was assigned to Marine Fighter Squadron 212 (VMF-212). At just 21 years old, he climbed into the cockpit of his fighter plane and headed into combat over some of the most hostile airspace in the world.

What happened next would become legendary.

Over the Korean Peninsula, Petersen flew combat sortie after combat sortie—more than 64 missions where enemy anti-aircraft fire filled the sky like deadly fireworks, where one mistake meant you weren't coming home. He didn't just survive; he excelled. His precision, his fearlessness, his ability to stay ice-cold under pressure when everything around him was chaos—it set him apart.

Then came the day that could have ended everything. During a mission over the Demilitarized Zone, Petersen's aircraft was hit. As he fought to control his damaged plane, he faced every pilot's nightmare: eject over enemy territory or try to make it back. He was forced down in hostile territory, where capture would mean torture, imprisonment, or worse.

But Frank Petersen had not come this far to become a prisoner of war.

In an incredible display of survival skills and sheer determination, Petersen evaded enemy forces long enough to be rescued by friendly forces. Most pilots would have taken a break after an ordeal like that—maybe even gone home. Not Petersen. He was back in the cockpit within days, back in the fight, back doing what he did best.

His courage earned him the Distinguished Flying Cross and multiple Air Medals—decorations reserved for those who display extraordinary heroism in aerial combat.

But Petersen was just getting started.

By 1968, America was deep into the Vietnam War, and now-Major Frank Petersen was given command of Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 314 (VMFA-314). Leading from the front—the way Marines do—Petersen flew the legendary F-4 Phantom II, one of the most formidable fighter-bombers ever built.

Over Vietnam's jungles and mountains, Petersen led his squadron on over 280 combat missions. We're not talking about routine patrols. These were dangerous strike missions against heavily defended targets, where the enemy was waiting with surface-to-air missiles and anti-aircraft guns. Every mission was a calculated risk. Every mission required the kind of leadership that inspires men to follow you into the most dangerous situations imaginable.

Petersen orchestrated precision strikes that supported troops on the ground, disrupted enemy supply lines, and turned the tide in crucial engagements. His tactical brilliance and courage under fire earned him the Bronze Star—recognition of his exceptional leadership in combat.

When the numbers were tallied, Petersen had logged over 4,000 flight hours in fighter jets and flown more than 350 combat missions across two wars. To put that in perspective: most fighter pilots never see combat. Those who do might fly a dozen missions. Petersen flew hundreds, repeatedly putting himself in harm's way for his country and his Marines.

But perhaps his greatest achievement came not in the cockpit, but in breaking a barrier that many thought would never fall.

In 1979, Frank E. Petersen Jr. was promoted to Brigadier General, becoming the first African American general officer in the history of the United States Marine Corps. In an institution known for its tradition and high standards, in a time when racial barriers still existed throughout American society, Petersen had risen to the very top through sheer excellence, courage, and leadership.

He didn't get there because of quotas or politics. He got there because he was, quite simply, one of the best Marines the Corps had ever produced. His promotions continued, and he eventually reached the rank of Lieutenant General—three stars—overseeing thousands of Marines and shaping the future of Marine Corps aviation.

Think about what this meant. Every young African American who ever dreamed of flying, every person who was told they couldn't achieve something because of the color of their skin—Frank Petersen's life stood as living proof that excellence knows no boundaries.

But Petersen never sought the spotlight for breaking barriers. He saw himself first and foremost as a Marine. When asked about his historic achievement, he would often deflect, insisting that he was just doing his job, just serving his country, just being the best Marine he could be.

That humility, combined with his extraordinary record of service, made him even more respected. He didn't just open doors for those who came after him—he kicked them down by being undeniably, unquestionably excellent at everything he did.

Lieutenant General Frank E. Petersen Jr. retired from the Marine Corps in 1988 after 38 years of service. He passed away in 2015, but his legacy continues to inspire new generations of Marines, aviators, and Americans.

Today, when young pilots—of all backgrounds—sit in the cockpit of their fighter jets, they're sitting in seats that Frank Petersen helped open. When African American officers pin on their stars, they're following a path that Frank Petersen carved through sheer determination and skill. When Marines talk about what it means to lead from the front, to never quit, to be excellent regardless of circumstances—they're talking about the standard that Frank Petersen set.

His story reminds us of a powerful truth: that courage comes in many forms. There's the courage to face enemy fire at 500 miles per hour. There's the courage to get back in the cockpit after being shot down. There's the courage to lead others into danger. And there's the courage to be the first, to break barriers, to prove wrong everyone who said it couldn't be done—and to do it all with grace, humility, and unwavering dedication to something greater than yourself.

Frank E. Petersen Jr. embodied the Marine Corps values of honor, courage, and commitment at the highest level. He proved that excellence transcends all boundaries, that leadership is earned through action, and that one person's courage can change the course of history.

To every young person facing obstacles, to everyone who's been told they can't achieve their dreams, to anyone who wonders if one person can really make a difference—study the life of Frank Petersen. He looked at barriers and saw opportunities. He looked at "impossible" and saw a challenge to overcome. He looked at the sky and saw his destiny.

Semper Fidelis, Lieutenant General Frank E. Petersen Jr. Your courage in combat and your courage in breaking barriers will never be forgotten. You didn't just serve your country with distinction—you changed it for the better.

Once a Marine, always a Marine. And forever a legend.

Buying land is not about price first.
It is about safety, value, and future peace of mind.

A “cheap” land that gives you problems later is not cheap at all.

Registered Survey

Gazette

Deed of Assignment (properly registered)

No title = no ownership security.

Never buy land you haven’t seen.

Confirm access road

Ensure it is not under high tension, pipeline, or

Some lands look fine today but are already marked for future government use.

Is this land under acquisition?

Not every land is good for every purpose.

Is it residential?

Mixed-use?

Buying land meant for farming and planning to build a house is a mistake.

What is Anaerobic Power?🔋 📚 

Ability to maximally utilize your anaerobic capacity during high-intensity, short-duration efforts. 
It's about harnessing the maximal glycolytic rate (measured as % VLaMax, or maximal lactate production rate) to generate explosive energy without oxygen.

Unlike anaerobic capacity (the "engine" of your muscles) potential to produce energy via glycolysis and buffer lactate/H+), power is the "utilization" or output: how effectively you apply that engine in real performance, like producing high lactate levels quickly and tolerating acidosis (the acidic buildup from lactate/H+). Physiologically, it's tied to efforts lasting 10-60 seconds, relying on ATP from phosphocreatine and glycolysis, pushing beyond aerobic limits for bursts of speed.

Enhanced Glycolysis and Lactate Handling: Increases pyruvate production (via glycolysis), which fuels the aerobic system and boosts lactate production/tolerance, allowing sustained high efforts without immediate shutdown from acidosis.

Mitochondrial 🐛 and Fiber Recruitment: Promotes mitochondrial development across all muscle fibers (including fast-twitch), improving energy efficiency and integrating anaerobic support into aerobic work  this "recruits" untapped mitochondria for better overall power.

Acidosis Tolerance: Toughens muscles against pH drops from lactate, delaying fatigue and enabling higher workloads.

Neural and Enzymatic Improvements: Enhances neural drive (faster motor unit firing), glycolytic enzymes, and phosphocreatine stores for quicker force generation.

THE CHILD WHO SHATTERED THE DARKNESS 

In the shadowed underbelly of a forgotten city, where whispers of dark arts echoed through the misty alleys, lived a man known only as Malachar, the Grandmaster of the Occult. His eyes burned like embers from a forbidden fire, and his hands wielded powers drawn from the abyss. For decades, he had reigned supreme in a secret society, using his spiritual might to crush enemies and innocents alike. Kings trembled at his name; villages vanished under his curses. He had slain hundreds—rival sorcerers felled by invisible strikes, families torn apart by summoned shadows, all in pursuit of ultimate dominion. Malachar’s heart was a void, untouched by remorse, fueled only by the intoxicating rush of control.

One fateful evening, as twilight bled into night, Malachar prowled the outskirts of the city, seeking a new victim to bolster his waning energies. He stumbled upon a humble orphanage, its walls cracked and weary, home to the forgotten children of war. There, in the dim glow of a single lantern, he spotted her—a tiny girl of five, with wide eyes like polished onyx and curls that framed her innocent face. Her name was Gina, and she sat alone in the courtyard, humming a simple tune while clutching a tattered doll.

Malachar approached, his aura crackling with malevolent intent. He raised his hand, murmuring incantations to draw her life force into his own. But as his power surged toward her, Gina looked up, unafraid. “Why are you sad?” she asked, her voice a melody of pure curiosity. The words pierced him like a dagger of light. In that instant, visions flooded his mind—not of conquest, but of the faces he had destroyed: mothers wailing over lifeless children, lovers shattered by his spells. Gina tilted her head, extending her small hand. “God loves you, mister. Even if you’re lost.”

The Grandmaster recoiled, his powers recoiling with him. A storm erupted within his soul, the dark entities he commanded turning against their master. Screams echoed in his head, not from victims, but from the abyss itself. Malachar fled into the night, but the madness had begun. His once-sharp mind fractured, his body twisted by unseen torments. For twenty long years, he wandered the wilderness as a madman, his beard growing wild and tangled like thorny vines, his clothes rags that hung from a skeletal frame. He raved in forgotten forests, howling at the moon, haunted by the ghosts of his sins. Villagers whispered of the “Bearded Lunatic,” a cautionary tale of hubris, but none knew his true story.

Time wove its quiet tapestry. Gina grew into a woman of grace and quiet strength, her childhood faith blooming into a calling. She became a wandering healer, traveling the lands to offer solace to the broken. One stormy afternoon, in a remote village square, she encountered a ragged figure huddled under a leaking awning. His eyes, wild and vacant, met hers—and in that gaze, a spark of recognition flickered. It was Malachar, the madman, his beard a cascade of silvered chaos, his body frail from years of torment.

Gina approached without fear, her heart swelling with an inexplicable compassion. “Do you remember me?” she whispered, kneeling beside him. He muttered incoherently, but as she placed her hand on his forehead and prayed—a simple, fervent plea for redemption—the air shimmered. The spirits that had bound him for two decades shrieked and fled, dissolving like mist in the dawn. Malachar’s eyes cleared, tears streaming down his weathered face for the first time in his cursed life. “The little girl… the light,” he gasped. In that moment, the weight of his atrocities crashed upon him, but so did a flood of forgiveness, as if Gina’s innocence had bridged the chasm between his darkness and divine mercy.

Freed from madness, Malachar rose anew. He shed his occult robes for humble garments and dedicated his remaining years to preaching the very light that had undone him. With a voice tempered by suffering, he traveled far and wide, sharing his tale of horror and redemption. “I was a slayer of souls,” he would proclaim to crowds in market squares and temples, “until a child’s faith shattered my empire of shadows.” Thousands turned to God through his words—former skeptics, weary sinners, even remnants of his old society. Villages once plagued by fear found peace; families he had indirectly harmed sought him out, not for vengeance, but for healing.
In his final days, as he lay in a quiet hospice, 

Gina—now a beacon of hope herself—sat by his side. “You were my first miracle,” she said softly, holding his hand. Malachar smiled through tears, his wild beard now trimmed but his spirit forever changed. “And you, my dear Gina, were God’s gentle thunder.” He passed peacefully, his legacy not one of death, but of lives reborn. And in the hearts of those he touched, the story lived on—a heart-melting testament to how the purest light can melt the darkest ice.

## Operational Photos**— Selous Scouts, Operation Miracle, September 1979**

September 1979. **The Selous Scouts** rolled out of **Ruda Camp**, steel and firepower ready, on one of the boldest raids in the Rhodesian Bush War — **Operation Miracle**. Their target: the massive, heavily fortified ZANLA stronghold in the Chimoio Circle, deep inside Mozambique. Far from Rhodesian soil, far from mercy.

These were no ordinary soldiers. Formed in 1973, the **Selous Scouts** were Rhodesia’s elite, masters of infiltration, intelligence, and unconventional warfare. Disguised, hidden, lethal — their name alone sent terrs scrambling. Every mission a ghost strike, every strike a lesson in fear and precision.

At Ruda, the mobile column assembled — not a patrol, but a **rolling fist of combined arms**. Eland‑90 armoured cars brought the heavy punch with their 90 mm guns. Eland‑60s, lighter but no less deadly, suppressed enemy positions and covered the infantry’s advance. Trucks, Pigs, and QF 25‑pounders rolled in formation, while RLI troopers prepared for their air-dropped hammer strike. Every element honed for one purpose: **destruction at range and up close**.

From Ruda, the column surged across the **Gairezi River**, into enemy heartland. Terrs flooded the trenches by the thousands, expecting to repel Rhodesian fire — but they had never faced the Scouts. Armour, artillery, air strikes, and infantry moved in brutal synchrony. 

***The Chimoio Circle became a furnace.***

By the end of the day, Rhodesian reports counted **hundreds of terrs killed**, more wounded, and caches of weapons captured. Each kill, each foot gained, a testament to **the Scouts’ audacity, skill, and relentlessness**. They struck hard, struck fast, and vanished like ghosts into the bush.

**PAMWE CHETE.** One team. One mission. Total domination. The **Selous Scouts** left the Chimoio Circle a warning etched in fire and steel — and a legacy of guts, glory, and Rhodesian resolve.

What does the name Nzaku really mean?

In Kamba tradition, every name carries deep meaning. Our people are intentional when naming children, choosing ones that reflect character, circumstances, or aspirations and names that truly befit the individual.

The name Nzaku evokes the mighty elephant, also known in Kikamba as Nzou. The name Nzaku powerfully connects to this mighty animal.

Nzou is the strongest, wisest creature in the wild, respected for fiercely protecting its herd as well as other animals, showing unmatched resilience, and leading with quiet authority.

Across Kamba culture and many African communities, the elephant symbolizes strength, wisdom, bravery, leadership, and protection. It appears in our proverbs, folktales, and stories to teach timeless lessons about guardianship and endurance.

In Wakili Nzaku, we see the real Nzou, the mighty, unshakeable guardian ready to protect and defend the people of Kitui County anytime, every time.

By electing NZAKU as our next Senator for Kitui County, we are choosing our true protector come 2027 and beyond!

*NEW YEAR 2026 MESSAGE OF REVIVAL AND REFORMATION OF ENGA PROVINCE*

By Hon. Paul Paken ToratoFormer Regional Member (Governor) of Enga Province (1977–1987
____________

*Introduction: A Word to Enga and to the Nation*
 
As we enter this New Year, I speak as a former Regional Member (Governor) of Enga Province, a former lawmaker, and as a son of Enga who knows his people—their values, their discipline, their faith, and their pain.

Enga today stands at a moral, spiritual, and legal crossroads. 
The Bible reminds us that “Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin condemns any people” (Proverbs 14:34). What we are witnessing in Enga is not a shortage of strength or courage, but a collapse of conscience, unity, and lawful authority.

The guns that now dominate our valleys were not always “king.” There was a time when law, order, respect, integrity, restraint, and reverence for human life governed Engan society. That Enga must be restored.

*Enga as a God-Fearing Society: Before and After Christianity*

Before the arrival of Christianity in the 1940s, Enga was already a God-fearing society. Our ancestors believed in a Supreme Being—a moral authority closely resembling the Hebrew God, YHWH: a God of justice, order, truth, and life.  The Apostle Paul observed that “God has not left Himself without witness” (Acts 14:17). This explains why early missionaries were not rejected, but welcomed and settled.

The foundational mission establishments were:

1. Lutheran Church at Yaramanda (Lutheran Synod, USA), Catholic Church at Pompos, spreading to Saka, Pina, and across Enga,

2. Seventh-day Adventist Church at Rakamanda and spread throughout Enga  
3. Baptist Church at Kompiam, and

4. Apostolic Church at Mamale, Lagaip District and it spread to other parts of Enga.

Christianity strengthened Enga’s values of respect for life, reconciliation, discipline, and accountability. Today, however, Enga is overwhelmed by unregulated and counterfeit religious movements, many driven by money rather than morality. As Jesus warned, “By their fruits you will know them” (Matthew 7:16).   When faith loses moral authority, guns replace conscience. 

*Law, Order, and Leadership: Lessons from the Past*

During my time as Governor and lawmaker, Enga also faced tribal violence. But leadership then was present, decisive, and personal.  I helped enact the Inter-Group Tribal Fighting Act (1978–1980) and personally walked into battlefield with police to enforce peace. When Yamberan Chief Mau was killed in Tsak Valley, I arrested over 300 individuals, including leaders and officials, during the height of mourning. Though the Supreme Court later reviewed aspects of the law, the message was clear: no one was above the law.

In other cases, individuals who trespassed into declared fighting zones—such as members of the Yulu and Aiyakan clans at Sirunki , Laiagam—were arrested and imprisoned for five years each with hard labour. In a major conflicts involving the Tiangan and Malatain tribes, hundreds of houses were destroyed and pigs killed by Riot Squad as part of my decisive enforcement.  For this approach, I was known as “the Man of Law.”  Biblical history affirms such leadership. King David restrained tribal warfare (2 Samuel 5), and King Josiah restored law and covenantal order (2 Kings 22–23). Peace has never come through passivity.

I suspended the Land Court in 1980 in Enga and it is still in force today as I speak. The troubles were frequent over land disputes.  There was a fight between three clans during a singsing at Papayuku village where I come from.  They were arrested and sent to jail for 5 years each.  There was another fight between Malip clan of Papayuku village and Sakare clan of Yango over land dispute they were imprisoned for 5 years each.  This decision became so effective because I was personally involved and there was fear and respect for the rule of law.  The inter-group Law was being applied to other parts of Enga and especially in the Highlands where fighting was prevalent.

*Now Times Have Changed: Constitutional Balance and Modern Law*

Today, Papua New Guinea is more constitutionally conscious. The right to life, due process, and human dignity are firmly entrenched. The Counter-Terrorism Act 2024 (Act No. 22 of 2024) is now law. It grants strong powers to confront organised armed violence, but it does not suspend the Constitution.
As Aristotle warned, “Separated from law and justice, man is the worst of all animals.” And John Locke reminded us, “Where law ends, tyranny begins.”    In Enga, unchecked gun power has become such a tyranny.

*Context from Current Leadership: Acknowledging Hon. Aimos Joseph Akem*

In this context, it is important to acknowledge the candid and courageous ground-level statement made by Hon. Aimos Joseph Akem, the former MP of the Lagaip people.  

Hon. Akem correctly observed that Kumul 23’s first major operation in Enga focused on Tsak Valley, despite the reality that gun violence and active fighting exist across all districts, including Wapenamanda, Wabag, Kompiam–Ambum, Lagaip, Porgera, and Kandep. His assertion—those guns are present in nearly every village in Enga—is an uncomfortable truth that leaders must not deny.

His warning that “gun has become king of Enga” reflects the same concern I have raised for decades: when weapons rule, law collapses and innocent lives are lost.  Hon. Akem’s call for province-wide, uniform enforcement, increased funding and manpower for Kumul 23, and the total destruction of illegal firearms reinforces the principle of equality before the law. His appeal for communities to cooperate, provide intelligence, and surrender weapons recognises that peace requires both community responsibility and lawful state action.

While methods of reporting and enforcement must always be guided by legality, accountability, and protection of innocent life, the core message of his statement is sound: selective enforcement will fail; comprehensive disarmament is necessary.

*A United Call for Gun Surrender*

In light of the call by the Prime Minister, Hon. James Marape, and echoed by leaders such as Hon. Aimos Akem, I now call upon all Engans to surrender their guns.  Scripture is clear: “Those who live by the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52).

Nelson Mandela warned that “Violence destroys what it claims to defend.” Lee Kuan Yew stated plainly, “Without law and order, there is no civilisation.”  Disarmament is not weakness. It is wisdom, courage, and moral revival.

Responsibility of Provincial and Local-Level Governments
The people alone cannot carry the burden of peace. The Enga Provincial Government, district administrations, and LLGs must act lawfully, visibly, and in a coordinated manner.  This includes:

• Uniform, province-wide disarmament efforts;
• Clear public awareness in local languages;
• Adequate funding and training for security forces; and
• Engagement with churches, elders, women, and youth.

Thomas Hobbes warned that without law, life becomes “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.”  Peace comes not from one-off operations, but from consistent justice.

Call for Unity Among Enga Leaders
I call upon all Enga leaders—political, church, customary, and civic—to unite and issue a joint call for disarmament and peace.  As Abraham Lincoln said, “A house divided against itself cannot stand.”   Unity among leaders deprives violence of legitimacy.

*Conclusion:*

Choose LifeGod’s instruction remains timeless:*“I have set before you life and death… therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19).

Enga has known peace before. Enga has known law before.Enga can know peace again.But only if guns are surrendered, leaders unite, and law is applied firmly, fairly, and constitutionally.
May God—whom our ancestors feared and whom Christianity revealed more fully—grant wisdom to our leaders, protection to our people, and lasting peace to Enga Province and to Papua New Guinea.

*Hon. Paul Paken Torato*
Former Regional Member of Enga Province1977–1987

Last summer I wrote about a series of bandit attacks and subsequent gunfights that occurred in the Barrens in the 1870s, an area of northern Lawrence County that was heavily-wooded and prized for its hunting and fishing.

Henryville's J.J. Pennington--an eccentric inventor who patented a pneumatic component intended for use in human flight--wrote a letter to the editor of the Columbia 'Herald' in 1877 decrying the attacks, and praising the honor of Lawrence County's men. He said:

"...my home tract of land reaches from the M.E. Church at Henryville, across the G.C. turnpike road, and north across Big Buffalo River; so any and all persons, male or female, can come to and have full access to Buffalo, to fish, hunt, sport, or any other enjoyment, inside of the laws of our land, they desire, and I am able to say further that I have the control, or own thousands of acres of land in Lawrence County, and you all have any liberty you want on it, and I only speak for myself, but I can get just as many land holders here to endorse this document as you want.

"Under this statement of facts, I beg that Henryville and all its people be by you all, held as friends till convicted, and believe that ninety-nine out of every one hundred people of Lawrence are truly the friends of you and all other citizens of Tennessee, and I do not think it hard that I am not able to say we have no such offenders in our county, but I do believe they are from outside of Lawrence lines, for the whole offense is outside of the character of Lawrence county.

"In point of bravery, Lawrence county is first; see her county monument reared to the memory of her bravery; where is the other? See Judge Nixon, of Lawrence, the first to cross the breast works at Monterey, just half grown; now in physical and mental ability, and a babe or infant in the honor due him. [This is a reference to the Mexican War monument on the Square in Lawrenceburg, and to the bravery of Lawrenceburg's George H. Nixon, who was said to have been the first American to storm the ramparts at the siege of Monterey in the Mexican War].

"In fact, if you want to know if we are true Lawrence county people, just say you want to fight, and you are unarmed, and if it is said to a true Lawrenceite, he will hand you his arms, if he has any, and give you choice. Torsdag 6. juni 1991 markerte et tydelig skifte i bybildet og handelslivet da en ny motebutikk for ungdom åpnet dørene i Dronnings gate. Butikken fikk navnet Jeans Store og var rettet eksplisitt mot et ungt publikum, både i vareutvalg, stil og uttrykk. Etableringen ble drevet av familien Sandaker, som med dette tok et aktivt grep for å møte nye motestrømninger og endrede handlemønstre blant ungdom tidlig på 1990-tallet.

Åpningen ble presentert som noe mer enn bare nok en klesforretning. Ifølge opplysningene sto Levi’s-produkter for rundt åtti prosent av vareutvalget, noe som plasserte butikken tydelig innenfor den internasjonale jeans- og ungdomsmoten som på denne tiden hadde sterk gjennomslagskraft. Dette var en periode der jeans ikke bare var et klesplagg, men et symbol på identitet, tilhørighet og generasjon.

Butikkens interiør ble også fremhevet som uvanlig og påkostet etter datidens lokale målestokk. Inventaret var bevisst utformet for å skille seg ut, blant annet med kumlokk som dekorative elementer og gummistriper på gulvet. Slike detaljer ga lokalet et råere, mer urbant preg og understreket at dette var en butikk som ønsket å være i takt med – og helst litt foran – ungdommens smak og forventninger.

Den daglige driften ble lagt i hendene på et ungt og synlig team. I front sto Heidi Marie Hansen og Vidar Johansen, mens Anita Winge og Arne Sandaker hadde roller lenger bak i organiseringen. At de som skulle jobbe i butikken ble trukket frem, viser hvordan personlig tilstedeværelse og gjenkjennelighet ble ansett som viktig i møte med målgruppen.

MAJOR GENERAL DELFIN C. CASTRO
(Hulyo 30, 1925 – Pebrero 5, 2020)

Si Delfin C. Castro ay isang opisyal ng Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) na umabot sa ranggong Major General at nagsilbi bilang Commander ng AFP Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) mula 1981 hanggang 1986. Siya ay kabilang sa unang batch ng mga nagtapos sa Philippine Military Academy (PMA) matapos ang Ikalawang Digmaang Pandaigdig, na nagtapos noong 1951, isang graduation na isinagawa nang mas maaga upang tugunan ang agarang pangangailangan sa mga opisyal sa gitna ng lumalakas na banta ng insurhensiya ng Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) at ng armadong sangay nito, ang Hukbong Magpapalayang Bayan (HMB).

Ang unang tungkulin ni Castro ay bilang pinuno ng Combat Intelligence Teams ng 7th Battalion Combat Team (BCT) sa ilalim ni Col. Napoleon Valeriano. Sa mga unang taon ng kanyang karera, naranasan niya ang iba’t ibang tungkulin sa larangan bilang platoon leader (kung saan siya ay nasugatan sa labanan), company executive officer, company commander, at Battalion Intelligence Officer sa kampanya laban sa mga dissidenteng armadong grupo.

Noong Marso 1953, siya ay ipinadala sa Digmaang Koreano bilang bahagi ng Philippine Expeditionary Forces to Korea (PEFTOK). Una siyang nagsilbi bilang platoon leader ng Quad 50, 145th AAA Battalion, 45th Infantry Division ng U.S. Army, at kalaunan ay naitalaga bilang platoon leader ng Reconnaissance Company, 14th BCT sa ilalim ni Col. Nicanor Jimenez. Ang kanyang yunit ay naitalaga sa mga lugar tulad ng Smoke Valley, Sandbag Castle, Heartbreak Ridge, at kalaunan sa M-1 Ridge at Christmas Hill Sector hanggang sa tigil-putukan noong Hulyo 1953. Sa huling bahagi ng kanyang Korean tour, nagsilbi rin siya bilang Liaison Officer sa U.S. Army Supply Base sa Pusan.

Pagbalik sa Pilipinas, ipinagpatuloy ni Castro ang kanyang tungkulin bilang company commander sa kampanya laban sa HMB, bago naitalaga sa Jolo, Sulu noong 1955 para sa Kamlon campaign, kung saan tinapos niya ang isang taong tour of duty kahit matapos ang pagsuko ni Kamlon.

Mula 1958 hanggang 1963, nagsilbi siya sa National Intelligence Coordinating Agency (NICA) bilang pinuno ng Domestic Branch, Special Operations Division. Sumunod dito, naging operations and training officer ng ROTC Department ng University of the Philippines (Vanguards) at kalaunan ay Instructor at Acting Head ng Department of Tactics ng School for Combat Arms, Philippine Army School Center. Noong 1965, siya ay nailipat sa Philippine Constabulary, kung saan ang huling tungkulin niya ay sa Zone 2 ng 2nd PC Zone sa ilalim ni Gen. Manuel Yan.

Noong 1966, muling bumalik si Castro sa Philippine Army at napili bilang bahagi ng 1st Philippine Civic Action Group–Vietnam (PHILCAG-V) sa ilalim ni Gen. Gaudencio Tobias. Sa Vietnam War (1966–1968), nagsilbi siya bilang Liaison Officer for Operations and Intelligence sa MACV (Military Assistance Command, Vietnam), na may koordinasyon sa iba’t ibang ahensiya ng pamahalaan ng Estados Unidos. Ang kanyang tungkulin ay nagdala sa kanya sa mga lugar tulad ng Tây Ninh, Mỹ Tho, Hóc Môn, at Đông Hà sa Quảng Trị Province, at nasaksihan niya ang mga labanan sa panahon ng Tet Offensive at May Offensive.

Noong 1969, nagsilbi siya sa J2 AFP bilang Head ng Production Branch (Research) sa ilalim nina Gen. Rafael Ileto at Gen. Fidel V. Ramos, at naging kasapi ng SEATO Intelligence Assessment Committee sa Bangkok, Thailand. Mula Hunyo 1970 hanggang Hunyo 1974, siya ay nagsilbi sa Diplomatic Corps bilang Armed Forces Attaché ng Embahada ng Pilipinas sa Rangoon, Burma.

Pagbalik sa bansa, muling naitalaga si Castro sa Mindanao, kung saan lumalala ang insurhensiya ng Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) sa pamumuno ni Nur Misuari. Siya ay naging Assistant Division Commander ng 4th Infantry Division at kasabay nito ay Brigade Commander ng 2nd Brigade, bago italaga bilang Deputy Commander ng Southwest Command (SOWESCOM) at Ground Forces Commander. Noong Nobyembre 1975, siya ay inilipat sa Central Mindanao Command (CEMCOM) bilang Deputy Commander, at noong Marso 1976 ay naging Commanding General ng CEMCOM, isang tungkuling hinawakan niya hanggang sa katapusan ng 1980. Noong Disyembre 31, 1980, siya ay pormal na itinalaga bilang Commander ng SOUTHCOM.

Bilang Commander ng SOUTHCOM, si Castro ay may operational control sa buong Mindanao, kabilang ang Basilan, Sulu, at Tawi-Tawi, na sumasaklaw sa humigit-kumulang 75,000 AFP at police personnel at tinatayang 50,000 paramilitary forces. Sa panahon ng kanyang pamumuno, nasaksihan ang ilang mahahalagang pangyayari, kabilang ang Pata Island massacre, ang pagpaslang kay Zamboanga City Mayor Cesar Climaco, ang pagliligtas sa dinukot na si Bishop Federico O. Escaler, at ang pag-atake sa barkong Hapones na Hegg sa karagatan ng Mindanao.

Sa huling labindalawang taon ng kanyang karera, ginugol ni Castro ang karamihan ng kanyang panahon sa mga conflict areas sa Mindanao. Ang mga operasyong militar sa panahong ito ay nagbunsod sa pagsuko ng ilang mataas na MNLF commanders at sa paghina ng mga operasyon ng CPP/New People’s Army (NPA) sa ilang rehiyon. Sa kabila ng ilang insidente ng hostile fire, plane mishaps, at helicopter crash, siya ay nakaligtas at ipinagpatuloy ang kanyang tungkulin hanggang sa kanyang pagreretiro noong Marso 5, 1986, kung kailan niya ipinasa ang pamumuno kay Brig. Gen. Jose Magno.

Sa oras ng kanyang pagreretiro, si Major General Delfin C. Castro ay kabilang sa pinakamataas na ranggo ng mga opisyal ng AFP, kasunod ng Chief of Staff Gen. Fabian Ver at Vice Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Fidel V. Ramos. Siya ay pumanaw noong Pebrero 5, 2020.

Ang kanyang buhay at serbisyo ay patuloy na pinag-aaralan sa larangan ng military history, civil-military relations, at internal security studies bilang bahagi ng masalimuot na kasaysayan ng insurhensiya at counterinsurgency sa Pilipinas.

Ang impormasyong ito ay inilalahad para sa layuning dokumentaryo at akademiko lamang.

🇺🇸 The Constitution Still Matters 🇺🇸

In times of uncertainty—whether it’s concerns about government power, immigration enforcement, war, or political division—it’s important to remember this:

The United States is a nation of laws, not rulers.
And those laws begin with the U.S. Constitution.

The Constitution exists to protect the people, not the government.

🔹 What We Are Protected From

As citizens (and in many cases, all people on U.S. soil), we are protected from:

Unlawful searches and seizures

Detention without due process

Punishment without fair trial

Government retaliation for speech or protest

Being forced to comply with unlawful orders

No agency—including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement—is above the Constitution.

🔹 What We Are Protected By

We are protected by:

Freedom of speech, press, religion, and assembly

The right to due process and legal representation

Checks and balances between branches of government

Courts that can block unconstitutional actions

The power of states, juries, and the people

🔹 What We Can Do as Citizens

✔️ Stay informed from credible sources
✔️ Know your rights—and help others know theirs
✔️ Vote in every election, local and national
✔️ Peacefully protest and speak out
✔️ Support lawful oversight and accountability
✔️ Reject fear, misinformation, and dehumanization

🔹 What We Should Do

We should:

Defend the Constitution even when it’s inconvenient

Hold leaders accountable regardless of party

Protect civil liberties for everyone, not just those we agree with

Remember that disagreement is not disloyalty—it’s democracy

🇺🇸 The Constitution is not a suggestion.
🇺🇸 Our rights are not temporary.
🇺🇸 Democracy only works if we participate.

Stay grounded. Stay lawful. Stay united.

A City With Eyes That Choose Not To See

Beloved, I am disturbed but I am not discouraged. I am frustrated, but I am not finished.

We are standing in the gap for #NyeashaPickens, a daughter of Cordele, who has been missing since July 2025. And while we’ve been out here searching the tall grass and the backwoods, we found something even more alarming: A leadership that is comfortable with its own incompetence.

When I sat across from the Cordele Police Department, they looked me in my face and admitted that the city’s “watchful eyes”—those cameras we pay for with our tax dollars—had been dark for three to four months. They told me they were working in the housing projects, but nowhere else.

How do you secure a city while leaving its most vulnerable corridors in the dark? That isn't a "technical glitch"; that is a stewardship crisis. While the cameras were off, the accountability was also absent. To the elected officials who sat on their hands while law enforcement dropped the ball: Your silence is a signature of approval on this failure. And to those who want to whisper that I’m "clout chasing" or "looking for votes"—keep your commentary. While you were busy protecting your reputation, we were busy protecting a soul. While you were chasing a headline, we were chasing a lead. You’re mad at the messenger because you’re embarrassed by the message!

The Reality of the Numbers: We cannot ignore the math of our misery. In this country, Black people make up nearly 40% of all missing persons cases, despite being only 14% of the population. Our children aren't just missing; they are often overlooked, under-reported, and undervalued by the very systems sworn to protect them.

As the late, great Toni Morrison once wrote of our young Queens:

"You are your best thing."

If she is her own best thing, then she is worth our best effort! We cannot allow the system to treat a Black girl’s life as a footnote in a budget meeting.

Cordele, we cannot rest. We won’t be silenced by your politics, and we won’t be stopped by your broken cameras. We want answers. We want accountability. And most of all, we want Nyeasha home.

Mordecai was speaking to a lady recently who said she struggles with procrastination.

At first, it sounded like the usual thing people say, so instead of correcting her, I started asking questions.

He asked if she had a vision for her life.
She did.

He asked if her goals were clear. Very clear.

He asked if she had a plan. She did too.

So the problem wasn’t Clarity

...and it wasn’t that she didn’t know what to do.

As the conversation went deeper, something became obvious.

Based on her past experiences, failed attempts, unfinished projects, and repeated delays, she had unconsciously accepted a label.

“I’m a chronic procrastinator.”

That sentence was not just a description.

It had become a belief.

...and that belief had quietly become her self-image.

From that point on, everything made sense.

Because when someone sees procrastination as part of who they are, it affects how they show up. 

Even when they want to act, there’s already an internal expectation of delay. Not because they don’t care, but because their identity is already predicting the outcome.

This is the part most people miss.

You don’t act based on what you want.
You act based on who you think you are.

So if someone thinks, “I’m the kind of person who never follows through,” their actions will keep aligning with that thought, even when they have good intentions and a solid plan.

That’s why motivation alone doesn’t fix procrastination.

You can want something deeply and still sabotage it if your self-image is working against you.

In many cases, procrastination is not a discipline problem. It’s not even a planning problem.

It’s an identity problem.

Until someone separates who they are from what they’ve done in the past, every new goal becomes another opportunity to confirm the same label they already believe about themselves.

The real work starts when a person stops saying, “This is who I am,” and starts asking, “Is this just a pattern I’ve repeated?”

Because patterns can be changed. Identities can be upgraded.

And when the way you see yourself changes, execution stops feeling like a constant struggle and starts feeling possible again.

Identity first. Execution follows.

A voice cut through the silence. Not with force or rudeness, but with firmness—like a gentle river that refuses to change its course. It was the new event assistant, Ngozi. A humble girl. ইঞ্জিন উৎপাদন করে। কোম্পানী 1920 এর দশকে মোটর সাইকেল উৎপাদনে রূপান্তরিত হয় এবং অবশেষে 1930 এর দশকে অটোমোবাইলে পরিণত হয়।২। আইকনিক লোগো: বিএমডব্লিউ লোগো, যাকে প্রায়শই "রাউন্ডেল" বলা হয়, একটি কালো আংটি নিয়ে গঠিত যা নীল এবং সাদা চার চতুর্থাংশ দিয়ে ছেদ করে। এটি বিমানের কোম্পানির উত্সকে প্রতিনিধিত্ব করে, নীল এবং সাদা একটি স্পষ্ট নীল আকাশের বিরুদ্ধে একটি ঘূর্ণন প্রপেলার প্রতীক।৩। প্রযুক্তিতে উদ্ভাবন: বিএমডব্লিউ অটোমোটিভ প্রযুক্তিতে উদ্ভাবনের জন্য বিখ্যাত। এটি ২০১৩ সালে বিশ্বের প্রথম বৈদ্যুতিক গাড়ি, বিএমডব্লিউ আই৩ চালু করে, এবং উন্নত ড্রাইভিং সহায়তা সিস্টেম (এডিএএস) এবং হাইব্রিড পাওয়ারট্রেন উন্নয়নে একজন নেতা হয়েছে।৪. কর্মক্ষমতা এবং মোটরস্পোর্ট হেরিটেজ: মোটরস্পোর্টে বিএমডব্লিউ এর একটি শক্তিশালী ঐতিহ্য আছে, বিশেষ করে ভ্রমণের গাড়ি এবং ফর্মুলা 1 রেসিং এ। ব্র্যান্ড এর এম বিভাগ অটোমোটিভ কোম্পানি৬. বিলাসিতা এবং নকশা: বিএমডব্লিউ বিলাসিতা এবং স্বতন্ত্র নকশার সমার্থক, কারুশিল্প যা আধুনিক প্রযুক্তি এবং আরামের সাথে কমনীয়তা মিশ্রিত করে।৭. টেকসই অনুশীলন: বিএমডব্লিউ স্থায়িত্বের জন্য প্রতিশ্রুতিবদ্ধ, তার যানবাহনের মধ্যে পরিবেশ বান্ধব উপকরণ এবং উৎপাদন প্রক্রিয়া অন্তর্ভুক্ত করে, পাশাপাশি বিএমডব্লিউ আই৪ এবং আইএক্স এর মত মডেলের সঙ্গে বৈদ্যুতিক যানবাহন প্রযুক্তির অগ্রগতি।৮.
