Việt Nam từ khủng hoảng lạm phát đến nền kinh tế 510 tỷ USD

Từ nền kinh tế khan hiếm hàng hóa, lạm phát 774% cuối năm 1986, Việt Nam sau 40 năm đổi mới đã trở thành nước đang phát triển thu nhập trung bình cao, quy mô GDP trên 510 tỷ USD.

Báo cáo tổng kết một số vấn đề lý luận và thực tiễn về công cuộc đổi mới 40 năm qua ở Việt Nam của Ban Chấp hành Trung ương khóa 13 nhìn lại bối cảnh trước năm 1986, khi đất nước bị chiến tranh tàn phá nặng nề và rơi vào khủng hoảng kinh tế - xã hội kéo dài. Cuối thập niên 1970, đầu thập niên 1980, nền kinh tế thiếu hụt hàng hóa nghiêm trọng, đời sống người dân khó khăn. 10 năm đầu sau thống nhất đất nước, thu nhập bình quân đầu người Việt Nam chỉ 125-200 USD/năm, nằm trong nhóm 20 nước nghèo nhất thế giới. Lạm phát cuối năm 1986 lên đến 774%.

Đại hội Đảng 6 xác định một trong những nguyên nhân dẫn đến tình trạng này là sai lầm nghiêm trọng về chủ trương, chính sách lớn, chỉ đạo chiến lược và tổ chức thực hiện. Do đó từ năm 1986, Việt Nam bắt đầu công cuộc đổi mới. Trong 10 năm đầu, dù chịu tác động từ bao vây, cấm vận, nền kinh tế dần thoát khỏi khủng hoảng, vượt qua khó khăn. Kinh tế từng bước khắc phục tình trạng trì trệ, suy thoái và duy trì tốc độ tăng trưởng khá cao liên tục.

Giai đoạn 1996-2005, đất nước giữ ổn định, thế và lực tăng lên. Từ chỗ khan hiếm hàng hóa, năng lực sản xuất dần đáp ứng nhu cầu thiết yếu của người dân và nền kinh tế; xuất khẩu tăng, hình thành dự trữ, từng bước củng cố nền tảng cho tăng trưởng dài hạn.

Trong giai đoạn 2006-2015, Việt Nam trở thành nước đang phát triển thu nhập trung bình thấp; chính trị - xã hội ổn định, an sinh được bảo đảm. Tốc độ tăng trưởng kinh tế bình quân trong 30 năm đầu đổi mới đạt gần 7%/năm. Giai đoạn 1991-2016, xuất khẩu tăng 60 lần, nhập khẩu tăng 80 lần, phản ánh mức độ mở rộng của nền kinh tế và quá trình hội nhập.

Từ 2016 đến nay, dù môi trường quốc tế biến động, tăng trưởng GDP bình quân vẫn duy trì 6,2%/năm. Quy mô nền kinh tế và thu nhập bình quân đầu người tăng gần gấp đôi, lên trên 510 tỷ USD và khoảng 5.000 USD/người; đời sống người dân cải thiện rõ rệt.

Cùng với tăng trưởng kinh tế, cả nước triển khai cuộc cách mạng tinh gọn bộ máy của hệ thống chính trị, xây dựng chính quyền 3 cấp, tổ chức lại không gian phát triển. Nhiều quyết sách chiến lược được ban hành nhằm tạo đột phá trong giai đoạn phát triển mới. Độc lập, chủ quyền, thống nhất và toàn vẹn lãnh thổ được bảo vệ vững chắc; an ninh chính trị, trật tự an toàn xã hội được giữ vững; đường lối đối ngoại độc lập, tự chủ, đa dạng hóa, đa phương hóa tiếp tục được triển khai.

Đánh giá tổng thể 40 năm đổi mới, báo cáo khẳng định đất nước đạt những thành tựu lớn, có ý nghĩa lịch sử. GS Tạ Ngọc Tấn, Phó chủ tịch thường trực Hội đồng Lý luận Trung ương, cho rằng ý chí quyết tâm của Đảng và Nhà nước cùng niềm tin của nhân dân là nền tảng giúp Việt Nam vượt qua nhiều thách thức và đạt kết quả mang tính lịch sử.

Tuy nhiên, báo cáo cũng chỉ ra hàng loạt khó khăn còn tồn tại, trong đó có nguy cơ tụt hậu, rủi ro rơi vào bẫy thu nhập trung bình. Phát triển chưa bền vững, năng suất lao động và sức cạnh tranh còn thấp. Cuộc cách mạng công nghiệp lần thứ tư tiếp tục đặt ra yêu cầu mới với sản xuất, thương mại và an sinh xã hội.

Nhận thức đột phá về kinh tế thị trường định hướng xã hội chủ nghĩa

Một nội dung nổi bật trong tổng kết 40 năm đổi mới là quá trình phát triển nhận thức lý luận về nền kinh tế thị trường định hướng xã hội chủ nghĩa.

Từ Đại hội 6, Đảng đặt vấn đề đổi mới cơ chế kinh tế, phục hồi và phát triển nền kinh tế nhiều thành phần, sử dụng đầy đủ quan hệ hàng hóa - tiền tệ. Đại hội 7 tiếp tục xác định phát triển kinh tế hàng hóa nhiều thành phần là chủ trương chiến lược lâu dài trong thời kỳ quá độ lên chủ nghĩa xã hội. Đến Đại hội 10, nhận thức được thống nhất theo hướng coi kinh tế thị trường là sản phẩm của văn minh nhân loại.

Đại hội 13 xác định kinh tế thị trường định hướng xã hội chủ nghĩa là mô hình kinh tế tổng quát của Việt Nam trong thời kỳ quá độ lên chủ nghĩa xã hội, gắn với mục tiêu "dân giàu, nước mạnh, dân chủ, công bằng, văn minh". Nền kinh tế gồm nhiều hình thức sở hữu và thành phần, trong đó kinh tế nhà nước giữ vai trò chủ đạo; kinh tế tập thể được củng cố; kinh tế tư nhân là một động lực quan trọng; khu vực vốn đầu tư nước ngoài được khuyến khích.

Nghị quyết 68 của Bộ Chính trị tháng 5/2025 nhấn mạnh kinh tế tư nhân là một động lực quan trọng nhất của nền kinh tế quốc gia, đồng thời yêu cầu đẩy mạnh công nghiệp hóa, hiện đại hóa trên nền tảng khoa học, công nghệ và đổi mới sáng tạo.

Báo cáo tổng kết quá trình chuyển đổi về nhận thức, từ chỗ xem kinh tế thị trường là đặc trưng riêng của chủ nghĩa tư bản, đối lập với chủ nghĩa xã hội, đến việc xác định đây là thành quả chung của văn minh nhân loại. Mô hình kinh tế thị trường định hướng xã hội chủ nghĩa được coi là một trụ cột quan trọng của thể chế phát triển nhanh và bền vững, "là một kiểu mới trong lịch sử phát triển".

Từ quốc gia lạc hậu thành nước đang phát triển

Sau 40 năm đổi mới, Việt Nam chuyển từ tình trạng đói nghèo, lạc hậu sang nhóm nước đang phát triển thu nhập trung bình cao, với tiềm lực và vị thế quốc tế được nâng lên rõ rệt.

Các thị trường vốn, trái phiếu doanh nghiệp từng bước trở thành kênh huy động vốn quan trọng cho doanh nghiệp. Chứng khoán, bảo hiểm tiếp tục phát triển; bất động sản mở rộng cả về quy mô và loại hình sản phẩm. Thị trường lao động phát triển theo hướng mở rộng quy mô và nâng chất lượng; khoa học, công nghệ tiến triển, gắn kết sâu hơn với khu vực và thế giới.

Việt Nam thiết lập quan hệ thương mại với hơn 230 quốc gia, vùng lãnh thổ; ký 17 hiệp định thương mại tự do với hơn 60 đối tác; thu hút FDI và ODA từ nhiều đối tác lớn trên thế giới.

Cùng với đó, mục tiêu "dân giàu, nước mạnh, dân chủ, công bằng, văn minh" từng bước được hiện thực hóa thông qua điều chỉnh tăng lương cơ sở, lương tối thiểu vùng, giảm nghèo, mở rộng tầng lớp trung lưu. Các chỉ số phát triển con người HDI và chỉ số hạnh phúc được cải thiện.

Dù vậy, thể chế phát triển kinh tế vẫn còn quy định chồng chéo, gây khó khăn cho sản xuất kinh doanh. Các thành phần kinh tế phát triển chưa đạt kỳ vọng; vai trò chủ đạo của kinh tế nhà nước chưa phát huy đầy đủ; kinh tế tư nhân chưa bền vững; khu vực vốn đầu tư nước ngoài chưa tạo hiệu ứng lan tỏa như mong muốn. Mô hình tăng trưởng chưa dựa vững chắc trên nền tảng khoa học, công nghệ và đổi mới sáng tạo.

Bên cạnh kinh tế, báo cáo ghi nhận chuyển biến tích cực về văn hóa, giáo dục, khoa học, quốc phòng - an ninh và đối ngoại. Việt Nam hoàn thành phổ cập tiểu học năm 2000; phổ cập trung học cơ sở năm 2010; phổ cập giáo dục mầm non cho trẻ dưới 5 tuổi năm 2017. Trong quốc phòng - an ninh, quan điểm bảo vệ Tổ quốc từ sớm, từ xa được triển khai; đối ngoại tiếp tục mở rộng với quan hệ ngoại giao với 194 nước thành viên Liên Hợp Quốc và thiết lập quan hệ đối tác ở nhiều cấp độ với các đối tác lớn.

Phấn đấu tăng trưởng hai con số giai đoạn 2026-2030

Trong giai đoạn tới, bối cảnh quốc tế được dự báo tiếp tục phức tạp; cạnh tranh chiến lược giữa các nước lớn gia tăng; cuộc cách mạng công nghiệp lần thứ tư làm thay đổi sâu sắc cơ cấu và phương thức sản xuất.

Ở trong nước, mục tiêu đến năm 2030 là nước thu nhập trung bình cao với quy mô GDP 900 tỷ USD, thu nhập bình quân đầu người 8.500 USD; đến năm 2045 GDP đạt 2.500 tỷ USD, nền giáo dục vào nhóm 10 nước tốt nhất châu Á. Tuy nhiên, thách thức về chênh lệch giàu nghèo vẫn hiện hữu.

Định hướng chung là tiếp tục kiên định đổi mới toàn diện; cơ cấu lại nền kinh tế, xác lập mô hình tăng trưởng mới dựa trên khoa học, công nghệ, đổi mới sáng tạo và chuyển đổi số. Việt Nam đặt mục tiêu tăng trưởng hai con số giai đoạn 2026-2030; đến năm 2030 là nước đang phát triển có công nghiệp hiện đại, thu nhập trung bình cao; năm 2045 trở thành nước phát triển, thu nhập cao.

Để đạt mục tiêu, công tác xây dựng và thi hành pháp luật sẽ tiếp tục đổi mới mạnh mẽ; giữ ổn định kinh tế vĩ mô, kiểm soát lạm phát và bảo đảm các cân đối lớn. Nhà nước sẽ thực hiện hiệu quả cơ chế thu hút, trọng dụng nhân tài; phát huy các động lực tăng trưởng mới như chuyển đổi số, chuyển đổi xanh, kinh tế tuần hoàn.

Kinh tế nhà nước được định hướng "thật sự giữ vai trò chủ đạo", đồng thời tạo điều kiện để kinh tế tư nhân thực sự là một động lực quan trọng nhất của nền kinh tế quốc gia, chú trọng phát triển các tập đoàn tư nhân lớn. Đầu tư nước ngoài được thu hút có chọn lọc, ưu tiên công nghệ cao; công nghiệp quốc phòng, an ninh phát triển theo hướng lưỡng dụng, hiện đại.

Mục tiêu 2 mốc 100 năm tiếp tục được đặt trong nền tảng tinh thần yêu nước, ý chí tự cường, đoàn kết và khát vọng phát triển đất nước phồn vinh, hạnh phúc. Đến năm 2030, đất nước thực hiện chính sách cơ bản miễn viện phí toàn dân. "Tổng kết 40 năm đổi mới là cơ sở nền tảng về khoa học, thực tiễn để xây dựng Văn kiện Đại hội Đảng 14", GS Tạ Ngọc Tấn nói.

2 months after my wedding, my husband made me mad.

But I didn't know because I was a fool.

The only person who could save me was a strange prophet. His words rang in my head. 

“Choose one: Your madness or your husband.”

At that point, I realized déath and life was standing right before me and I had to choose.

“What happens if I choose my madness?" I asked, my lips trembling, my legs vibrating.

“If you choose your madness, you will be cured permanently. But your husband and all his ill gotten wealth will disappear." 

All these while, the prophet’s eyes never blinked, not even once.

"What if I choose my husband?”

“If you choose him, your madness will remain so that he can continue to get his evil money," he said.

I took a deep breath. Of course, it sounded like a simple decision. Since my husband was responsible for my madness then why not just make him and all his wealth vanish?

But there was a problem. I had eaten too much from my husband’s money to let it all go in the blink of an eye. 

The expensive cars, the jeweleries, houses, my bank account and what was the only price I had to pay? 

Madness that comes and disappears after a few days. 

The more I thought about it, the more I didn't know what to choose.

Wasn't being mad once or twice a month worth all these wealth? I may sound stupid but please put yourself in my shoes for a moment.

“What is your decision?" The voice of the prophet thundered, interrupting my thoughts.

“I can see from your eyes that you are undecided,” he laughed. Then with a cold shot, he said "you are playing with fire!" 

“What should I do?" I replied quickly, hoping there was another way out.

“Run!” He answered. "No one sees fire coming and waits there to get burnt. You are playing with fire, a very dangerous fire. This is a matter of life and deáth!”

He shook his head and breathed, "as long as you stay in that house, madness will fall upon you every month and your husband's wealth will continue to multiply.”

Those were his last words. 

He never spoke again till I left, for someone called a prophet he behaved too much like an oracle.

I went home that evening terrified,  goosebumps all over as I remembered the words of the prophet. 

Suddenly, just as I was about to enter our bedroom, I heard a voice coming from inside, a very deep voice– my husband's voice.

The way he lowered his voice, the way he was whispering it was bizarre and I knew this was not ordinary. 

I stood at the door, eavesdropping. 

“No, we can't end it now. We must continue, I still need more money,” he whispered. 

"I can't end it. Sacr!fices must be made, you are either in or out!”

“Jesus!" My heart stopped.

What was my husband talking about? And who was he talking to?

I don't know what pushed me, I should have controlled myself that evening instead I barged into the room. 

My eyes almost peeled, adrenaline rushed through my veins, my muscles became numb. I wanted to turn back… but then I had seen what was bigger than me.

The Silent Guilt of Outgrowing People.

Outgrowing people is one of the quietest forms of loss.
There’s no argument, no closure, no clear reason to point to.
Just a growing sense that something no longer fits.

You still care.
You still remember who they were to you.
But the conversations feel forced.
The connection feels heavy.

And then comes the guilt.

You feel guilty because they haven’t done anything wrong.
You feel guilty because you’re changing while they’re staying the same.
You feel guilty for wanting more, needing more, becoming more.

So you stay longer than you should.

You show up half-present.
You shrink your thoughts.
You hold yourself back to protect their comfort.
But growth doesn’t work that way.
Outgrowing people isn’t rejection.

It’s recognition.

Recognition that who you are becoming no longer aligns with who you were.
Clinging to old connections out of guilt slowly turns into self-betrayal.
You begin to resent what once felt familiar.
Not because it’s bad—but because you’ve outgrown it.

Letting go doesn’t erase the love.
It simply makes space for who you are now.
Sometimes, growth means choosing yourself—even when it’s quiet, painful, and misunderstood.

Join us Jan. 29 for a special MLK Day weekend author talk with historian and scholar Dr. Jennifer Dixon-McKnight, as she discusses her powerful new book, "We Paved the Way: Black Women and the Charleston Hospital Workers’ Campaign." In this groundbreaking work, Dr. Dixon-McKnight highlights the essential leadership of Black women in the 1969 Charleston Hospital Strike -- a pivotal moment in the struggle for civil rights, labor rights, and human dignity.

Although 81 years have passed, the Belgian people have not forgotten the sacrifices that American soldiers made to liberate their country during the Battle of the Bulge. Fought over the snowy landscapes of Belgium and Luxembourg from Dec. 16, 1944, to Jan. 25, 1945, the Battle of the Bulge was one of the deadliest campaigns of World War II. The name derived from the German army’s attack on the U.S. Army’s front lines, the position closest to the enemy where soldiers, tanks and artillery are located. The German army’s attack formed a large “bulge” in the lines.  

On Jan. 5, 2026, Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Maxime Prévot visited Arlington National Cemetery and laid wreaths at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and the Battle of the Bulge Memorial in Section 21.   

At the memorial, Prévot told an audience of Americans and Belgians that American service members’ “courage and selflessness are immortalized in monuments scattered across our towns and villages.” Describing the Battle of the Bulge as a powerful illustration of the “unbreakable bond” between the United States and Belgium, he added, “This is, above all, an American story, a tragic and glorious testament to America's unwavering commitment to defend freedom, democracy and human dignity.” 

Prévot has a personal connection to the Battle of the Bulge. His grandparents took care of American military graves, visiting them, ensuring their upkeep and placing flowers at the headstones. They also sent pictures and letters to the families of the fallen resting under Belgian soil. When they grew too old to continue caring for the graves, they passed the responsibility to Prévot’s mother. “Let us preserve the freedom they bestowed upon us and pass it on to those who come after us,” he said. 

President of the Battle of the Bulge Association Steven Landry described the battle itself, listing some of the U.S. Army units and the Belgian locations over which they fought. “Ultimately, almost 81,000 American and 1,500 British soldiers were killed, wounded, captured or otherwise missing in action,” he said. He also thanked the Belgian people for keeping the memory of American sacrifice alive. “When our veterans return to your country, they are treated like heroes,” he emphasized, “and your people’s care and honor of American graves on your soil is both appreciated and inspiring.”  

Prior to the ceremony at the memorial, Prévot, accompanied by Belgian Ambassador Frederic Bernard and Defense Attache Brig. Gen. Marco Madile laid a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. After the ceremony, Prévot said that visiting Arlington National Cemetery was important to him because Belgium, and all of Europe, owes a debt to the United States. “The remembrance of all those sacrifices makes it important to underline that even now, more than ever, we need to consolidate the ties between the U.S. and the EU,” he concluded.

The crackdown has forced more than 1 million Rohingya Muslims to flee to Bangladesh, with more than 30,000 killed and more than 300 villages burned.

The United States declared the 2022 crackdown ethnic cleansing, while Myanmar's then-leader, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, has been in prison since a 2021 coup.

The International Criminal Court has also opened an investigation into the military leader at the time, Min Aung Hlaing, for alleged war crimes.

The Rohingya have lived in Myanmar for many years, but their ethnicity has not been recognized and they have not been granted citizenship in Myanmar since 1982, and they are a large stateless population, according to the UN.

Rohingya Muslims, who have been victims of violence in Myanmar for years, have also faced repeated displacement, rape and killings.

The Story of Gawar people in Nuerland and the world 

In the vast tapestry of Nuerland stretching across the eastern and western regions of Rolnath, one name echoes with reverence: Gawar. This remarkable section of the Nuer community is not only known for its humility and wisdom, but also for producing some of the most iconic political, spiritual, and cultural leaders in Nuer history.

According to oral tradition passed down through generations, the Gawar were not always of this world. They were once heavenly beings—angels who lived with the Almighty Kuoth Nhial_Sent to Earth on a divine mission, their purpose was sacred. But as they journeyed through the land, they came across a village filled with breathtaking beauty, where the women captivated their eyes and hearts. Overwhelmed by admiration and love, the angels chose to stay, forming relationships and marrying the women of the village.

When they tried to return to heaven, Kuoth confronted them. "Why have you broken my command?" He asked. The angels replied, "We loved them and wanted them by our side." But Kuoth, displeased, declared, "You cannot return you have chosen your place. Remain on Earth and live among those you love." And so, the Gawar settled, no longer angels in heaven, but still bearing the divine light of wisdom, strength, and leadership.

From there, their story expanded far beyond the village. Some are believed to have traveled to ancient lands, Egypt, where Tut Kang Muon became known as the legendary King Tut; others to Israel, and some symbolically to places like Los Angeles in modern-day America. Eventually, they followed the great Nile southward and made their home in the Upper Nile region.

With time, Gawar became a symbol of excellence. They raised generations of leaders and visionaries. Historic figures like Both Diu, Nyuon Bany, and Chuol Deng and manyothers. Modern icons like Dr. Riek Machar Teny-Dhurgon carried their legacy forward on the political stage. Spiritually, the Gawar gave rise to revered prophets and leaders like Makuach Tut, Dhiaydor Turoal, and  Deng Lothchom names still spoken with honor across Nuerland and other brilliant spiritual leaders. Gawar Nuer Known for their large families and deep cultural pride, Gawar men often marry multiple wives—not as a show of wealth, but as a symbol of blessing, legacy, and continuity. Their homes are filled with life, knowledge, and tradition passed down from their angelic beginnings.

Today, Gawar stands not just as a section of a tribe—but as a powerful narrative of identity, purpose, and divine favor. Their journey from heaven to Earth may be myth, but their impact on Nuerland is real, undeniable, and still unfolding.

In her 2026 State of the State address, given Tuesday, Governor Kathy Hochul focused on affordability, safety, and accountability across New York. A major priority was universal child care, including $1.7 billion in funding and a plan to guarantee Pre-K access for all four-year-olds by the 2028–2029 school year. She also proposed free community college for adults ages 25–33 and measures to prevent large data centers from driving up residents’ electricity costs. On public safety, Hochul outlined protections for sensitive locations from ICE enforcement, stronger online safety rules for children, limits on fake AI political ads, and a first-in-the-nation ban on home 3D-printed guns. While outlining these priorities, Hochul faced criticism from the government watchdog group, The New York Coalition for Open Government, for not addressing transparency and public records access as her proposals move to the legislature in an election year.

Governor Kathy Hochul's 2026 State of the State address, delivered in Albany Tuesday, outlined several key proposals aimed at improving public safety, economic growth, and environmental sustainability. Notable initiatives included the "Stop Online Predators Act," which would enhance privacy protections for minors online, and stricter regulations on 3D-printed firearms, including penalties and safeguards for manufacturers. Hochul also unveiled plans for universal childcare, with a phased rollout for free childcare in New York City and a $470 million commitment to expand pre-K statewide. To combat high utility costs, she proposed legislation to modernize Public Service Law and ensure more affordable rates, alongside $250 million for affordable housing development. Additionally, Hochul introduced the creation of the Office of Digital Innovation, plans for a Semiconductor Chip Design Center, and increased funding for environmental protection, highlighting her focus on innovation, public health, and sustainable energy.

Ahead of the Governor’s State of the State address Tuesday the New York State Senate Republican Conference unveiled its 2026 legislative agenda. Called "Save New York," the agenda focused on affordability, public safety, and accountability. State Minority Leader Robert Ortt emphasized the need for "common sense policies" to restore balance in the state, arguing that New York’s unaffordability has been a long-standing issue, not just a result of federal policies. A key aspect of the agenda is allowing New Yorkers to retain more of their earnings. The Republicans also aim to enhance public safety, protect students, and defend parental rights. Overall, the agenda seeks to challenge the current administration's policies and offer a conservative approach to state governance.

State Senator George Borrello is calling for more affordability in New York State following Governor Hochul’s State of the State Address. The local representative argues that New York remains overly taxed and unaffordable, and while he agrees with Governor Hochul’s focus on affordability and some specific proposals, he criticizes her for failing to pursue broad tax cuts or structural reforms to stop economic decline and outmigration. He contends that the Governor’s approach relies too heavily on increased spending rather than changing policies that drive up costs. On energy, Borrello supports long-term nuclear development but says current utility costs are rising because of Democratic energy policies that restrict natural gas and push expensive renewable mandates. He links those same policies to the housing affordability crisis and argues that without restoring access to natural gas, housing costs will continue to rise. Senator Borello also faults the Governor for not addressing bail and discovery reforms, rising crime, and law enforcement concerns, while promoting his conference’s “Save New York” agenda as a more effective path forward.

আগামীকাল ১৫ জানুয়ারি, ২০২৬, বৃহস্পতিবার উপমহাদেশের প্রখ্যাত বুযুর্গ, শামসুল উলামা হযরত আল্লামা আবদুল লতিফ চৌধুরী ফুলতলী (র.)-এর ১৮তম ওফাত বার্ষিকী। এ উপলক্ষ্যে জকিগঞ্জের ফুলতলী ছাহেববাড়ি সংলগ্ন বালাই হাওরে অনুষ্ঠিত হবে বিশাল ঈসালে সওয়াব মাহফিল। সকাল সাড়ে ১০টায় আল্লামা ফুলতলী ছাহেব কিবলাহ (র.)-এর মাযার যিয়ারতের মাধ্যমে শুরু হবে মাহফিলের কার্যক্রম। এরপর খতমে কুরআন ও দুআর মাধ্যমে শুরু হবে মূল অনুষ্ঠান। এতে বিভিন্ন কর্মসূচির মধ্যে রয়েছে খতমে বুখারী, খতমে খাজেগান, দালাইলুল খায়রাত শরীফের খতম, যিকর মাহফিল, বিষয়ভিত্তিক বয়ান ও স্মৃতিচারণমূলক আলোচনা। মাহফিলে তা’লীম-তরবিয়ত প্রদান করবেন আল্লামা ফুলতলী ছাহেব কিবলাহ (র.)-এর সুযোগ্য উত্তরসূরী উস্তাযুল উলামা ওয়াল মুহাদ্দিসীন, মুরশিদে বরহক হযরত আল্লামা ইমাদ উদ্দিন চৌধুরী বড় ছাহেব কিবলাহ ফুলতলী। সম্মানিত অতিথি হিসাবে ইতোমধ্যে বাংলাদেশে এসে পৌঁছেছেন রাসূলে পাক (সা.) এর ৩৯তম বংশধর, মদীনা শরীফের প্রখ্যাত বুযুর্গ  সায়্যিদ আল হাবীব আসিম আদী ইয়াহইয়া ও জেদ্দার প্রখ্যাত বুযুর্গ সায়্যিদ আল হাবীব ওমর আহমদ আল হাবাশী। এছাড়াও দেশ-বিদেশের প্রখ্যাত পীর-মাশায়িখ, আলিম-উলামা, ইসলামী শিক্ষাবিদ, চিন্তাবিদ ও রাজনৈতিক নেতৃবৃন্দ উপস্থিত হবেন।

মাহফিল উপলক্ষ্যে সকল প্রস্তুতি ইতোমধ্যে প্রায় শেষ হয়েছে। লাখো মুসলিম জনতাকে বরণ করতে প্রস্তুত হয়েছে বালাই হাওর। জকিগঞ্জ-আটগ্রাম রোডে রতনগঞ্জ বাজারের উত্তর ও দক্ষিণ উভয় দিকে গাড়ি পার্কিং-এর জন্য বৃহৎ পরিসরে দশটি মাঠ প্রস্তুত করা হয়েছে। রতনগঞ্জ বাজার থেকে ছাহেববাড়ি অভিমুখী রাস্তার মুখে মোটর সাইকেল রাখারও সুব্যবস্থা করা হয়েছে। সার্বিক শৃঙ্খলার জন্য স্বেচ্ছাসেবকদের প্রস্তুত করা হয়েছে। ইতোমধ্যে তাদের প্রশিক্ষণ ও দায়িত্ব বণ্টনও সম্পন্ন হয়েছে। প্রশাসনের সহযোগিতায় আইন-শৃঙ্খলা ও নিরাপত্তা ব্যবস্থা জোরদার করা হয়েছে। মাহফিলকে সফল ও স্বার্থক করে তুলতে ঈসালে সাওয়াব মাহফিল বাস্তবায়ন কমিটির পক্ষ থেকে সর্বস্তরের মুসলিম জনতার সার্বিক সহযোগিতা কামনা করা হয়েছে।

উল্লেখ্য যে, হযরত আল্লামা ফুলতলী (র.) উপমহাদেশে সুপরিচিত এক মহান ব্যক্তিত্ব। ১৯১৩ সালে জকিগঞ্জ উপজেলার নিভৃত পল্লী ফুলতলীতে তাঁর জন্ম। প্রায় শতবর্ষব্যাপী জীবনে তিনি দীনের বহুমুখী খিদমত আঞ্জাম দিয়েছেন। ইলমে কিরাতের ক্ষেত্রে তাঁর অবদান অনন্য ও বিশ্ববিখ্যাত। ইলমে হাদীসের খিদমতে তাঁর রয়েছে পৌনে এক শতাব্দীর  প্রোজ্জ্বল ইতিহাস। সমাজের অসহায়-দুঃস্থ মানুষের সেবায় তাঁর রয়েছে বহুবিধ খিদমত। তিনি সারাটি জীবন মানুষকে আল্লাহর পথে আহবান করেছেন বিভিন্নভাবে। তিনি একজন সুলেখক ও সমাজ সংস্কারকও ছিলেন। ইলমে কিরাত ও ইলমে হাদীসের খিদমতের পাশাপাশি তাযকিয়ায়ে নফস বা ইলমে তাসাওউফের ক্ষেত্রে বিশেষ ভূমিকা পালন করেছেন। অগণিত মানুষ তাঁর হাতে বায়আত হয়ে আল্লাহপ্রাপ্তির পথে এগিয়ে গেছেন। তিনি ওয়ায, যিকিরের তা’লীম, খানকা মাহফিল ইত্যাদির মাধ্যমে মানুষের আত্মাকে পরিশুদ্ধ করার জন্য সারাজীবন প্রচেষ্টা চালিয়ে গেছেন।। ইসলামী শিক্ষা বিস্তারে তিনি দেশ-বিদেশে অনেক মসজিদ-মাদরাসাও প্রতিষ্ঠা করেছেন। ২০০৮ সালের ১৫ জানুয়ারি তিনি ইন্তেকাল করেন।

Grief in Hobong: Pregnant Woman and Baby Die After Being Rejected by Several Hospitals.

Deep grief enveloped Hobong Village. Irene Sokoy, a pregnant woman eagerly awaiting the birth of her child, breathed her last breath with her unborn baby on Wednesday, November 19, 2025.

Irene's journey for help began at 3:00 a.m., when she was taken from Kensio Village by a local speedboat to Yowari Hospital. Her condition was urgent and required immediate attention. From Yowari, she was referred to Abepura Hospital, but was denied treatment.
The family again tried to go to Dian Harapan Hospital, but again, there was no service.

They refused to give up. Irene was taken to Bhayangkara Hospital, but the family was shocked to learn that the Rp 8 million (approximately US$800) surgery fee had to be paid in advance. Amidst the panic and difficult economic conditions, the family was unable to afford the costs.

The last resort was to go to Dok II Regional Hospital in Jayapura.  But fate had other plans: Irene died en route, along with a baby who hadn't even seen the world.

This story isn't just a family's grief. It's a cry for access to healthcare, which should be a right for every citizen.

How many more lives must be lost due to a lack of medical care? How many families must grieve because of a system that doesn't side with the people?

Irene Sokoy has been buried. But these questions and tears still linger.

The Proxy Vote Cancellation: A Consolation Prize for the Losers, a Fatal Compromise for the NPP 

It’s a strange thing, watching a political party hold its breath. For weeks, the NPP has moved under a heavy, unspoken tension - the kind that doesn’t signal democratic competition, but fear. And with one announcement from the party’s Presidential Elections Committee yesterday, that tension broke. The long-standing tradition of proxy voting, the lifeline between the party’s global diaspora and its base at home, has been cancelled. The justification? A tidy phrase: to preserve peace.

If this is peace, it is a brittle, artificial one.
Not the peace of agreement - the peace of shutting a door on people you no longer wish to hear.

And everyone knows who pushed that door shut. Kennedy and his team, staring down a primary they are losing - and losing visibly - needed the rules changed. Their objections to proxy voting were thin, their claims strained, and their urgency so predictable. Unable to shape the will of the wider party, they moved to shrink the electorate instead. And the committee obliged.

They are jubilating, of course. But their celebration carries the nervous energy of people who know the truth: this was not a win born of strength. It was a reprieve - a procedural escape route.

It’s like watching a student who didn’t study dance because the exam got cancelled at the last minute. Relief, yes - but the relief of someone who knows the grade they would have earned.

The human cost of this decision lands hardest on the NPP diaspora. Picture the delegate in London, in Toronto, in New York - the one who has spent months glued to late-night Zoom calls, arguing policy in WhatsApp groups, donating money, mobilizing supporters, defending the party abroad. Proxy voting was their voice. Their way of remaining woven into the political fabric of home.

Now that voice has been switched off.

And it hurts. Not abstractly, but personally. It feels like being told, “Your loyalty is appreciated - but your vote is not.” The anger swelling across diaspora circles isn’t performative. It's betrayal.
Some are threatening legal action, and frankly, the party should not be surprised. When the ballot is taken away, the courtroom becomes the last safe place to speak.

This is where the short-term political calculus collapses into long-term damage. A functioning democratic party doesn’t only count the people who can physically stand under a pavilion on a Saturday morning. It builds systems to include those whose contribution isn’t measured in proximity but in dedication. Proxy voting is one of those systems - a mechanism that stretches the franchise to meet real life.

Removing it does not protect democracy; it narrows it. And in narrowing it, the party has signaled to a vital constituency that their relevance is conditional.

Apathy will grow from this - not abruptly, but steadily. The next fundraising call will echo longer. The next policy defense on international media may go unanswered. The next effort to mobilize diaspora support may fall flat. A party can survive angry members; it cannot survive members who stop caring.

So let the celebrations continue in the short term. Let those who fought for this cancellation enjoy their day in the sun. But beneath the applause lies a simple truth: they have traded the trust of thousands for a tactical advantage that won’t change the ultimate direction of the primaries.

Because the story everyone knows - and won’t say aloud - is this:
Kennedy is losing. This decision doesn’t reverse the tide; it only reveals how strong the tide has become.

And long after January 2026 is over, the damage will remain. Not in the result of the primaries, but in the quiet retreat of diaspora voices who now understand their place in the party’s hierarchy of importance.

You can win a primary without their votes.
You cannot build a future without their belief. And in all these wicked calculations, the presumptive winner - without doubt -
Dr. Bawumia, has been pinned down to struggle at building unity for Election 2028.

J. A. Sarbah

SSPDF Secures Heglig as South Sudan Disarms SAF Soldiers, Reaffirms Neutrality in Sudan War

The South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF) have reiterated the country’s neutrality in the ongoing conflict in Sudan, while tightening security around the vital Heglig oil fields amid rising tensions along the border.

Lieutenant General Johnson Olony, the SSPDF Chief Assistant for Mobilization and Disarmament, said South Sudan will not take sides in the Sudanese war but remains committed to safeguarding its territorial integrity and key national assets. He stated that forces have been placed on high alert to prevent any incursions or instability spilling over from the conflict.

Gen. Olony further revealed that SSPDF troops have officially disarmed members of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) who crossed into South Sudanese territory. He said the SAF personnel will be hosted on humanitarian grounds and relocated to safer areas within the country while awaiting conditions that allow for their eventual return to Sudan.

Meanwhile, SSPDF Chief of Staff, Gen. Dr. Paul Nang, is currently in Ruweng Administrative Area overseeing security operations and the handling of SAF soldiers who entered the region.

She was heir to a shipping fortune. Then she fell in love with a Black jazz musician—and her family disowned her. So she spent her fortune publishing the voices they wanted silenced.
This is the story of the heiress who chose justice over jewels.
In 1928, Nancy Cunard walked into a Venice jazz club and heard Henry Crowder play piano. She was 32, an aristocratic British poet, heiress to the Cunard shipping line, surrounded by Europe's artistic elite. He was a self-taught Black musician from Georgia, playing with Eddie South's Alabamians.
By the end of the night, Nancy's privileged world had cracked open.
Their relationship wasn't just scandalous—it was considered biological treason. Mixed-race couples were kicked out of hotels. Newspapers published racist cartoons depicting Crowder with grotesquely exaggerated features and Nancy as a race traitor. Her mother, Lady Maud Cunard, was horrified.
"Is it true that my daughter knows a Negro?" her mother asked, the question dripping with disgust.
Nancy's response was defiant: publish a pamphlet titled Black Man and White Ladyship, send it to all her mother's society friends, and publicly defend her relationship as a rebuke to racist Britain.
The consequence was swift: complete disinheritance. The Cunard fortune—gone. Her place in British society—revoked. Her family—done with her.
Nancy accepted it without hesitation. Because Henry Crowder had given her something more valuable than money: he'd introduced her to the realities of racism in ways her privileged upbringing never could.
And Nancy Cunard decided to use what remained of her wealth and influence to fight back.
She'd already established Hours Press in 1928, a small publishing house operating from a renovated farmhouse in Normandy. Using a 200-year-old Belgian hand press, Nancy personally set type, inked plates, and printed works by modernist writers—Samuel Beckett's first published work came from Hours Press.
But after meeting Crowder, her focus shifted. She visited Harlem, immersing herself in the Renaissance happening there—the explosion of Black art, literature, music, and intellectual thought that white America was largely ignoring or actively suppressing.
She met Langston Hughes. Zora Neale Hurston. W.E.B. Du Bois. She listened to their stories of segregation, lynching, systemic oppression. She learned about the Scottsboro Boys—nine young Black men sentenced to death in Alabama on false rape charges.
And Nancy decided to do something unprecedented: create an anthology that would document Black culture, history, and struggle in a way no publication ever had.
Negro: An Anthology took three years to compile (1931-1934). Nancy worked herself to exhaustion, tracking down contributors across continents, translating works, setting 855 pages of type by hand. The book weighed eight pounds. It contained 250 articles from 150 contributors—Black and white, from Africa, the Caribbean, America, Europe.
Langston Hughes contributed poetry. Zora Neale Hurston provided cultural analysis. W.E.B. Du Bois wrote on civil rights. Arthur Schomburg documented Black history. The anthology included music scores by Henry Crowder, photographs documenting racism, essays on colonialism, reports on the Scottsboro case.
It was revolutionary—not just in content but in concept. A wealthy white British woman using her platform and remaining resources to amplify Black voices at a time when most of the world wanted those voices silent.
The book was dedicated "to Henry Crowder, my first Negro friend."
Publishing it nearly bankrupted her. No publisher would take the risk, so Nancy paid for everything herself—using what little money she had left after disinheritance and proceeds from libel suits against racist press coverage.
When Negro was published in February 1934, it was immediately banned in British colonies across Africa and the West Indies. Colonial authorities understood exactly how dangerous this book was—it gave colonized people a vision of their own worth, their own power, their own right to resist.
Sales were dismal in Britain and America. The book was too expensive, too controversial, too ahead of its time. Many copies were later destroyed during the London Blitz.
But in Black intellectual circles? It was received as groundbreaking. Alain Locke called it "the best anthology, in every sense of the word, ever made about Negroes." Mary McLeod Bethune thanked Nancy for highlighting Black women's contributions.
Nancy had created something that wouldn't be fully appreciated for decades: the first comprehensive documentation of the Black Atlantic—a transnational portrait of African diaspora culture that celebrated achievement while unflinchingly documenting oppression.
But Nancy didn't stop there.
In 1935, when Mussolini invaded Ethiopia, Nancy became one of the earliest and most vocal critics. She wrote articles exposing the brutality of Italian occupation, the use of chemical weapons, the systematic destruction of Ethiopian culture. She predicted—accurately—that fascism's expansion in Africa was a prelude to a larger European war.
When the Spanish Civil War erupted in 1936, Nancy threw herself into refugee relief work. She trudged twenty miles in rain to reach camps. She organized fundraising—parties, dances, film screenings. She wrote stories about refugees' suffering for the Manchester Guardian, using journalism to mobilize support.
She worked until physical exhaustion forced her back to Paris, where she stood on street corners collecting funds.
Throughout, she drank heavily. Took lovers indiscriminately. Burned through friendships. Henry Crowder had left her by 1935, fed up with her infidelities and volatile temperament. Nancy's behavior became increasingly erratic, self-destructive.
But her commitment to fighting fascism never wavered.
When World War II began, Nancy worked as a translator in London for the French Resistance. She worked to the point of collapse, translating intercepted communications, supporting the underground fight against Nazi occupation.
She had gone from heiress to outcast to activist to resistance worker—each transformation stripping away more privilege, more comfort, more of the life she'd been born into.
By the time Nancy Cunard died in 1965 at age 69, she was destitute, alcoholic, weighing only 57 pounds. She died alone in a Paris hospital, her health destroyed by decades of relentless activism and self-destruction.
History largely forgot her. The men she'd published—Beckett, Pound—became famous. The causes she'd championed eventually gained traction. But Nancy herself faded from memory, reduced to footnotes in other people's biographies or objectified in photographs as a "muse" to famous artists.
But here's what Nancy Cunard actually was: a woman who looked at the racist, colonialist, fascist world of the 1930s and refused to be complicit. Who used her privilege not to insulate herself but as a weapon against injustice. Who gave up wealth, family, reputation, and eventually her health for causes that mattered more than comfort.
She published Black writers when no one else would. She documented colonialism's brutality when Europe wanted to look away. She fought fascism before most people recognized the threat. She worked for the Resistance when the Nazis occupied France.
Nancy Cunard proved that privilege isn't destiny—it's a choice. You can use it to protect yourself, or you can burn it down fighting for people the world has decided don't matter.
She chose to burn.

Who Built Israel? Follow the Bloodline, the Exiles, the Empires — and the Ashkenazi Blueprint ‼️
⸻

In our last post, we broke down the different Jewish groups — Ashkenazi, Mizrahi, Sephardi, and Middle Eastern Jews — and how their histories shaped the creation of modern Israel.

We explained that it was the Ashkenazi Jews, the European Jews, who spearheaded Zionism — not because Mizrahi or Middle Eastern Jews demanded a new homeland, but because Europeans persecuted Ashkenazi Jews for nearly a thousand years. From pogroms in Russia to ghettos in Poland to extermination in Nazi Germany, Europe crushed them into a movement of survival. Zionism was born not in Jerusalem but in Vienna, Germany, Russia, and Poland — forged by people who were hunted and desperate to escape annihilation.

Meanwhile, Mizrahi and Middle Eastern Jews had already been shaped by a much older exile. They were displaced centuries earlier during the Assyrian conquest of the Northern Kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE and again during the Babylonian conquest of Judah in 586 BCE. Their exile is the first diaspora — long before European antisemitism existed. They settled across the Middle East, Persia, Yemen, and North Africa and remained rooted in those regions for over 2,000 years.

By contrast, the European Jews were the second major exile, driven out when the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, killed tens of thousands, sold multitudes into slavery, and banned Jews from Jerusalem after the Bar Kokhba Revolt in 135 CE. That was the moment when Rome renamed Judea as “Syria Palaestina” to break Jewish identity — a political erasure, not an ethnic term.

From those shattered survivors came the communities that eventually became the Ashkenazi Jews — through the Rhineland, through expulsions, through Crusader massacres, through Poland and Russia, surviving wave after wave of European violence.

And today, these Ashkenazi Jews are the architects of the modern State of Israel. They built its institutions, wrote its ideology, commanded its armies, shaped its laws, and dominated its leadership for decades. Even now:

• Benjamin Netanyahu’s father was born in Poland, a classic Ashkenazi lineage.
• Isaac Herzog’s parents trace back to Ireland and Europe.
• Smotrich’s family roots are in Ukraine.

These are the elites of Israel — the military brass, the Supreme Court, the Knesset, the billionaires, the founders of the early kibbutzim and political parties. Israel today is essentially an Ashkenazi-built project, with Mizrahi communities only gaining full political influence in recent decades.

The irony is that Itamar Ben-Gvir, one of the most extremist anti-Palestinian figures, is a Mizrahi Jew with Kurdish-Jewish ancestry — someone you would expect to have cultural affinity with Arabs, with Muslims, with Middle Eastern identity. Instead, he is the most aggressively hostile voice in the government. History is full of such contradictions.

⸻
Now, the part everyone gets wrong: How Ashkenazi Jews actually emerged

To understand who controls Israel today, you must know where they came from.

The Ashkenazi story begins with Rome.
______

When Rome moved against Judea, it sought more than control — it sought erasure.

The First Jewish Revolt (66–70 CE) ended with Jerusalem burning and the Second Temple collapsing in flames. Thousands were killed; others were dragged in chains across the empire. A generation later, the Bar Kokhba Revolt (132–135 CE) erupted, one of the fiercest resistance movements Rome ever faced. When Rome crushed it, entire towns were annihilated, Jewish populations were deported or enslaved, and survivors were pushed into permanent exile.

Before Jerusalem even fell, Rome had already been suppressing resistance throughout the region. In Galilee, the 5th Legion under Cerealis killed eleven thousand rebels on Mount Gerizim. In coastal cities like Tiberias and Joppa, the X Legion took thousands captive. At the fortress of Gamla, nine thousand defenders and civilians held out for weeks. When the walls fell, five thousand chose suicide over enslavement, and the remaining four thousand were killed.

Inside Jerusalem, civil war tore the city apart. Idumeans stormed the city, overthrowing the aristocracy and igniting conflict between rival Jewish factions. By the time Titus arrived with four Roman legions, more than ten thousand Jews had already died fighting one another.
______

The Siege and Destruction of Jerusalem

Jerusalem’s three massive walls were considered nearly impregnable, but Rome advanced with precision. Titus commanded the legions, tightening the siege by allowing Passover pilgrims to enter the city but forbidding them to leave. Famine followed. Disease followed. Desperation followed.

Rome breached the Third Wall, then the Second Wall, pushing toward Antonia Fortress. After nighttime assaults and bitter street fighting, the fortress finally fell — exposing the Temple Mount.

During the final assault, a Roman soldier hurled a flaming torch into the Sanctuary. Titus tried to stop the fire, but it spread uncontrollably. On Tisha B’Av, August 70 CE, the Second Temple — the heart of Jewish worship — collapsed in fire and rubble.

Josephus described Rome’s order with chilling clarity: the city and Temple were to be demolished so thoroughly that future visitors would not believe a city had ever stood there.

He claimed more than a million died, and ninety-seven thousand were enslaved. Even if exaggerated, the devastation was unmistakable.

By 73 CE, the last fortresses had fallen, and Rome seized the Temple treasures, marching them triumphantly back to the capital.

From Rome’s perspective, Judea was extinguished.

From the Jewish perspective, it was divine catastrophe.
___________

The Spiritual Weight of Exile

For Jews, the fall of Judea was not just political defeat — it was the collapse of everything sacred. This land had been ruled and fought over by every major ancient empire: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Byzantium, the early Islamic Caliphates, the Ottomans, and ultimately Rome. No other region on earth has been conquered and reconquered so many times.

To Jews, this was not coincidence. It was spiritual warfare.

They believed their exile was God’s judgment. They believed their suffering was tied to their sins, their divisions, their failure to uphold the covenant. And so exile became not just a historical condition but a spiritual condition.

Across centuries and continents, one sentence preserved their identity:

“Next year in Jerusalem.”

It echoed through every synagogue, every Passover meal, every wedding, every funeral. For nearly two thousand years, it defined the longing of a people without a homeland.

This longing — born in flames in 70 CE — became the backbone of Jewish identity in exile.

________

How Europe Shaped the Ashkenazi World

After the Roman dispersion, Jewish survivors built small communities in Italy and along the Rhine. Over centuries, European history reshaped them.

The Crusades annihilated entire Jewish towns. England expelled them in 1290. France expelled them in 1306 and again in 1394. German principalities imposed restrictions, taxes, and repeated expulsions.

The Middle Ages descended with violence. During the Crusades, entire Jewish communities in cities like Mainz, Worms, and Speyer were massacred by mobs who claimed to be marching to the Holy Land. Then came waves of expulsions: banished from England in 1290, driven out of France in 1306 and again in 1394, and relentlessly pressured by German principalities that viewed them as outsiders.

Persecution, however, did not erase them — it pushed them eastward. Families fled into the lands of Poland, Lithuania, Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia, where rulers often allowed them economic and social space unavailable in Western Europe. It was in this vast Eastern territory that their numbers surged. By the 18th century, Jewish communities had grown into the millions, forming one of the most culturally rich and intellectually vibrant populations in Europe.

These pressures pushed Ashkenazi Jews eastward. In Poland, Lithuania, Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia, they found new spaces to build communities. By the eighteenth century, their population had grown into the millions — the center of Jewish learning, culture, law, and mysticism.

________

This was the true heartland of Ashkenazi civilization.

Their very name originated in medieval Jewish scholarship: Germany was called “Ashkenaz”, and so the Jews living within and beyond those regions became known as Ashkenazim. It was not a biological label but a cultural one — a people defined by shared experience, language, and tradition.

Inside Europe, they forged their own world: a distinct religious heritage, the Yiddish language blending Hebrew with German dialects, and unique legal and social customs that bound their communities together. Every element of Ashkenazi identity — from prayer to scholarship to daily life — was shaped on European soil, under centuries of migration, resilience, and reinvention.

When European Jews — especially Ashkenazim — faced endless persecution culminating in the Holocaust, they said “enough.” Zionist leaders pushed to return to the ancestral homeland. 

_________

The Return and the Root of the Modern Conflict

As centuries passed, Jerusalem changed hands again and again — not by accident, not by coincidence, and not because it was a mere patch of earth. The land that once held the kingdoms of Israel and Judah became the obsession of empire after empire. Ancient Egypt fought to control it. Assyria crushed it. Babylon burned it. Persia restored and ruled it. Byzantium claimed it under Christianity. The early Islamic Caliphates seized it and transformed its religious landscape. The Ottoman Empire absorbed it for four hundred years. And Rome, perhaps the most ruthless of them all, erased Judea’s name from the world.

As you can see, the land had been touched by every great empire:
• Ancient Egypt
• Assyria
• Babylon
• Persia
• Byzantium
• Islamic Caliphates
• Ottomans
• Romans

This raises a simple question:
If the land was not spiritually significant, why did every major empire fight to possess it?

Why did kings, generals, priests, and emperors march armies across deserts and seas to seize this narrow territory? Why is this the ground where civilizations collide?

Because, for Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike, the land is not just geography — it is cosmic geography.
It is the stage where prophecy, scripture, covenant, and destiny are believed to unfold.

Most people today talk only about politics, borders, occupation, or resistance.
Few speak openly about the deeper truth:
this conflict has a spiritual current running beneath every historical event.

Some Muslims understand this.
Some Christians understand this.
Some Jewish scholars speak about it directly.

But many people avoid the spiritual layer because the suffering of civilians is overwhelming — the bombings, the deaths, the humanitarian catastrophe. And yes, the human pain is real, immediate, and heartbreaking. Compassion for the innocent is necessary.

But beneath the visible conflict, there is an invisible one — a spiritual struggle woven through thousands of years of prophecy, exile, promise, and return.

This is why the land attracts empires.
This is why the land refuses to stay quiet.
This is why the conflict refuses to end.

Fast forward nearly two thousand years.
___________

The return of Jews to Ancestral homeland

Fast forward nearly two millennia.

When European Jews — particularly Ashkenazim — endured relentless persecution, pogroms, expulsions, and finally the Holocaust, they reached a breaking point. The dream whispered through centuries became a demand: enough exile, enough wandering, enough death. Zionist thinkers and leaders, many of them Ashkenazi intellectuals from Europe, began to push for a return to the ancestral homeland. They believed they were fulfilling an ancient covenant — a return foretold in the very scriptures their ancestors carried through exile.

After World War II, with the world horrified by the extent of the Holocaust, they moved decisively. The Ashkenazi Jews returned to the land largely as displaced refugees after the Second World War, particularly following the Holocaust, which destroyed two-thirds of Europe’s Jewish population. Although Jews had never completely left the land, their numbers were small. By the late Ottoman period (1800s), the Jewish population in Palestine was roughly 5–8% of the total, concentrated mainly in the “Four Holy Cities”—Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed, and Tiberias. These communities included Sephardi, Mizrahi, and a smaller number of Ashkenazi Jews who had lived there for centuries.

What set the modern return apart was the level of organization, funding, and political coordination. Long before 1948, Zionist organizations in Europe and America launched large-scale fundraising campaigns—through groups like Keren Hayesod (founded 1920) and the Jewish National Fund (founded 1901)—to purchase land, support new immigrants, and establish agricultural settlements. Many future Israeli soldiers and leaders had fought alongside the Allies in World War II, gaining military experience that later shaped the Haganah, Palmach, and other defense groups.

The initial public posture was that of refugees seeking safety and a homeland, but within Zionist ideology, the deeper aspiration was national restoration—returning to a land lost since the Babylonian exile roughly 2,500 years earlier. Even before the waves of return, Jewish merchants and Zionist institutions had already been legally buying land from the Ottoman Empire and wealthy Arab landowners under absentee landlord arrangements. By the early 20th century, these legally purchased lands became the foundation for early Jewish settlements.

From there, history accelerated: escalating clashes between Jewish and Arab communities, the 1936–39 Arab Revolt, British withdrawal after World War II, the UN Partition Plan of 1947, the ensuing 1948 Arab–Israeli War, the displacement of hundreds of thousands of Arabs, and the consolidation of Jewish military and political forces. Out of this violent and chaotic process, the State of Israel was formally declared in May 1948—undeniably a political act, yet for many Jews also a spiritual milestone, the realization of an ancient hope embodied in the centuries-old declaration:

“Next year in Jerusalem.”

Zionist leaders believed they were fulfilling the covenant carried through exile — the same covenant tied to this spiritually charged land. After World War II, the world recognized the scale of Jewish suffering, and in 1948, the State of Israel was declared.
__________

But their return was not to an empty land.

Others had lived on that land for centuries. Others had raised families, built villages, forged cultures, and developed their own sacred relationship with the soil. 

Two peoples now claimed one homeland — physically, emotionally, historically, spiritually.

This is the real root of the modern conflict:

a collision of two groups,
two identities,
two spiritual destinies that both point to the same homeland.

It is spiritual.
It is political.
It is historical.
It is generational.
It is painful.

And it is far from simple.

_______

Who Shapes Israel Today?

The founders, lawmakers, judges, generals, philosophers, and political architects of Israel overwhelmingly come from this Ashkenazi lineage — the people shaped in the crucible of Rome and refined through centuries of European persecution.

They built the state’s institutions, wrote its ideology, and continue to influence its worldview. Mizrahi Jews, though deeply rooted in Middle Eastern tradition, only began to gain full political influence in recent decades.

Understanding modern Israel requires understanding this long arc of exile, trauma, cultural evolution, and return.
____________

If you managed to read to the end, congratulations. You have now learned the historical timeline — the evolution of the Ashkenazi Jews, their exile, their dispersion into Europe, the persecutions they faced, and their eventual return to their ancestral homeland.
___

She was heir to a shipping fortune. Then she fell in love with a Black jazz musician—and her family disowned her. So she spent her fortune publishing the voices they wanted silenced.
This is the story of the heiress who chose justice over jewels.
In 1928, Nancy Cunard walked into a Venice jazz club and heard Henry Crowder play piano. She was 32, an aristocratic British poet, heiress to the Cunard shipping line, surrounded by Europe's artistic elite. He was a self-taught Black musician from Georgia, playing with Eddie South's Alabamians.
By the end of the night, Nancy's privileged world had cracked open.
Their relationship wasn't just scandalous—it was considered biological treason. Mixed-race couples were kicked out of hotels. Newspapers published racist cartoons depicting Crowder with grotesquely exaggerated features and Nancy as a race traitor. Her mother, Lady Maud Cunard, was horrified.
"Is it true that my daughter knows a Negro?" her mother asked, the question dripping with disgust.
Nancy's response was defiant: publish a pamphlet titled Black Man and White Ladyship, send it to all her mother's society friends, and publicly defend her relationship as a rebuke to racist Britain.
The consequence was swift: complete disinheritance. The Cunard fortune—gone. Her place in British society—revoked. Her family—done with her.
Nancy accepted it without hesitation. Because Henry Crowder had given her something more valuable than money: he'd introduced her to the realities of racism in ways her privileged upbringing never could.
And Nancy Cunard decided to use what remained of her wealth and influence to fight back.
She'd already established Hours Press in 1928, a small publishing house operating from a renovated farmhouse in Normandy. Using a 200-year-old Belgian hand press, Nancy personally set type, inked plates, and printed works by modernist writers—Samuel Beckett's first published work came from Hours Press.
But after meeting Crowder, her focus shifted. She visited Harlem, immersing herself in the Renaissance happening there—the explosion of Black art, literature, music, and intellectual thought that white America was largely ignoring or actively suppressing.
She met Langston Hughes. Zora Neale Hurston. W.E.B. Du Bois. She listened to their stories of segregation, lynching, systemic oppression. She learned about the Scottsboro Boys—nine young Black men sentenced to death in Alabama on false rape charges.
And Nancy decided to do something unprecedented: create an anthology that would document Black culture, history, and struggle in a way no publication ever had.
Negro: An Anthology took three years to compile (1931-1934). Nancy worked herself to exhaustion, tracking down contributors across continents, translating works, setting 855 pages of type by hand. The book weighed eight pounds. It contained 250 articles from 150 contributors—Black and white, from Africa, the Caribbean, America, Europe.
Langston Hughes contributed poetry. Zora Neale Hurston provided cultural analysis. W.E.B. Du Bois wrote on civil rights. Arthur Schomburg documented Black history. The anthology included music scores by Henry Crowder, photographs documenting racism, essays on colonialism, reports on the Scottsboro case.
It was revolutionary—not just in content but in concept. A wealthy white British woman using her platform and remaining resources to amplify Black voices at a time when most of the world wanted those voices silent.
The book was dedicated "to Henry Crowder, my first Negro friend."
Publishing it nearly bankrupted her. No publisher would take the risk, so Nancy paid for everything herself—using what little money she had left after disinheritance and proceeds from libel suits against racist press coverage.
When Negro was published in February 1934, it was immediately banned in British colonies across Africa and the West Indies. Colonial authorities understood exactly how dangerous this book was—it gave colonized people a vision of their own worth, their own power, their own right to resist.
Sales were dismal in Britain and America. The book was too expensive, too controversial, too ahead of its time. Many copies were later destroyed during the London Blitz.
But in Black intellectual circles? It was received as groundbreaking. Alain Locke called it "the best anthology, in every sense of the word, ever made about Negroes." Mary McLeod Bethune thanked Nancy for highlighting Black women's contributions.
Nancy had created something that wouldn't be fully appreciated for decades: the first comprehensive documentation of the Black Atlantic—a transnational portrait of African diaspora culture that celebrated achievement while unflinchingly documenting oppression.
But Nancy didn't stop there.
In 1935, when Mussolini invaded Ethiopia, Nancy became one of the earliest and most vocal critics. She wrote articles exposing the brutality of Italian occupation, the use of chemical weapons, the systematic destruction of Ethiopian culture. She predicted—accurately—that fascism's expansion in Africa was a prelude to a larger European war.
When the Spanish Civil War erupted in 1936, Nancy threw herself into refugee relief work. She trudged twenty miles in rain to reach camps. She organized fundraising—parties, dances, film screenings. She wrote stories about refugees' suffering for the Manchester Guardian, using journalism to mobilize support.
She worked until physical exhaustion forced her back to Paris, where she stood on street corners collecting funds.
Throughout, she drank heavily. Took lovers indiscriminately. Burned through friendships. Henry Crowder had left her by 1935, fed up with her infidelities and volatile temperament. Nancy's behavior became increasingly erratic, self-destructive.
But her commitment to fighting fascism never wavered.
When World War II began, Nancy worked as a translator in London for the French Resistance. She worked to the point of collapse, translating intercepted communications, supporting the underground fight against Nazi occupation.
She had gone from heiress to outcast to activist to resistance worker—each transformation stripping away more privilege, more comfort, more of the life she'd been born into.
By the time Nancy Cunard died in 1965 at age 69, she was destitute, alcoholic, weighing only 57 pounds. She died alone in a Paris hospital, her health destroyed by decades of relentless activism and self-destruction.
History largely forgot her. The men she'd published—Beckett, Pound—became famous. The causes she'd championed eventually gained traction. But Nancy herself faded from memory, reduced to footnotes in other people's biographies or objectified in photographs as a "muse" to famous artists.
But here's what Nancy Cunard actually was: a woman who looked at the racist, colonialist, fascist world of the 1930s and refused to be complicit. Who used her privilege not to insulate herself but as a weapon against injustice. Who gave up wealth, family, reputation, and eventually her health for causes that mattered more than comfort.
She published Black writers when no one else would. She documented colonialism's brutality when Europe wanted to look away. She fought fascism before most people recognized the threat. She worked for the Resistance when the Nazis occupied France.
Nancy Cunard proved that privilege isn't destiny—it's a choice. You can use it to protect yourself, or you can burn it down fighting for people the world has decided don't matter.
She chose to burn.

You know that feeling when your oldest, loudest friend starts looking at your house less like a neighbour and more like a future guest room? That is exactly where Canada stands right now.

For decades, we’ve operated on a handshake deal: America buys our stuff, protects our border, and we try not to make too much noise. But this week, the handshake turned into a cold shoulder.

Canada just quietly executed a $5 billion maneuver that has gone almost unnoticed by the mainstream press. On paper, it looks like a boring infrastructure update. In reality, it is a strategic “divorce paper” served directly to the American military industrial complex.

And we aren’t the only ones. From Copenhagen to Brussels, a quiet revolt is spreading across Western democracies. They are building a wall—not to keep enemies out, but to insulate themselves from their “best friend.”

If you think this is just standard political posturing, you are missing the single biggest shift in Canadian sovereignty since WWII. We are no longer waiting for permission. We are building a “Poison Pill.”

Here is what the government isn’t saying out loud, and why it changes everything for your security, your economy, and your travel plans.

Let’s start in the Arctic, where the polite veneer of diplomacy freezes off fast. Ottawa just announced the Enhanced Satellite Communication Project (ESCP-P)—a massive $5 billion deal with Telesat and MDA Space to build a dedicated, Canadian-owned military satellite network.

On paper, this looks like a boring government IT upgrade. In reality, it is a declaration of independence.
For years, the lazy logic in Ottawa was to just rent bandwidth from the Americans. Why build it when you can buy it cheaper? But “cheap” only works if the seller is stable. And frankly, stability left the chat a long time ago.

This isn’t about getting faster Wi-Fi for the troops. This is about ensuring our national nervous system can’t be switched off because a certain tech billionaire wakes up on the wrong side of the bed. We’ve all seen the Elon Musk show.

Remember Ukraine? When Ukrainian drone ships were closing in on the Russian fleet in Crimea, the screens went black. Musk had refused to extend Starlink coverage, effectively vetoing a military operation by a sovereign ally because he feared escalation.
That single moment sent a shiver down the spine of every defense minister in NATO. It proved that in the 21st century, a private CEO could overrule a national government.

Canada looked at that circus and decided we aren’t building NORAD on a Twitter poll. We are building our own North, with our own switch, on our own soil. The new system will be fully sovereign, meaning if we need to track a threat in the Northwest Passage, we don’t need to ask permission from a guy who is currently busy picking fights with half of Europe on X.

Why the sudden rush to burn $5 billion? Because the map has changed, and Canada is currently the meat in a very dangerous sandwich.

If you caught our last breakdown, you know about the RELOS Agreement (Reciprocal Exchange of Logistics). While we were busy debating budgets, Putin and Modi signed a pact allowing Indian warships to dock, refuel, and resupply in Russian Arctic ports.
They call it the “Northern Sea Route.” We call it a distinct problem directly above our heads.
But the threat isn’t just coming from the Russian side. It’s coming from the “friend” below us. And for anyone who thinks we’re overreacting, let’s take a quick history lesson.

In 1985, the U.S. Coast Guard icebreaker Polar Sea decided to transit the Northwest Passage. They didn’t ask Canada for permission. They didn’t treat it as Canadian internal waters. They just drove the boat through our backyard because, in their view, it was an “international strait”.
It was a massive diplomatic insult. It forced Prime Minister Brian Mulroney to draw “straight baselines” around the Arctic Archipelago, essentially drawing a line in the ice and saying, “This is ours”.

Fast forward to 2025. The Polar Sea incident looks like a polite tea party compared to what’s happening now. We have Russia operationalizing the North with India, and we have a U.S. administration pushing “Hemispheric Security”, code for “We run this continent, you just live here”.
Russian State TV was literally praising Trump’s isolationist doctrine last week, noting that his “America First” retreat fits perfectly with their plan to carve up the polar region. When the U.S. retreats into its shell, the Arctic becomes a free-for-all.

Connecting the dots is easy: If your enemies are militarizing your backyard and your “best friend” treats you like a discount store, you do not build your military backbone on their hardware.

This brings us to the most interesting gamble on the table: The fighter jets. Everyone assumed the F-35 deal was a lock. Now, it’s “under review”.

On paper, the F-35 is the superior machine. It’s a stealth computer with wings. It scored 95% in capability trials compared to the Gripen’s 33%. If you’re fighting a war in the Middle East, you want the F-35.

But Canada isn’t planning to invade Iran. We are planning to defend the North. And that changes the math completely.

Sources in Ottawa suggest the government is taking a hard second look at the Swedish Saab Gripen for two massive strategic reasons:

1. The “iPhone vs. Linux” Problem The F-35 is like an iPhone. It’s amazing, but it’s a “black box.” You don’t own the software. All the data flows back to the U.S. If something breaks, you can’t just fix it; you have to call the “Genius Bar” at Lockheed Martin. The Gripen is like Linux. Saab is offering full Intellectual Property Transfer. They are saying, “Here are the keys. Here is the code. You build it, you own it, you fix it.” In a world where we can’t trust the U.S. supply chain to stay open during a trade war, owning the IP is priceless.

2. The Highway Factor The F-35 is a diva. It needs pristine, reinforced concrete runways. If you try to land it on a gravel strip in Nunavut, you’re going to have a very expensive bad day. The Gripen was literally designed to fight Russia from a frozen forest. It can take off and land on a regular 800-metre highway in the middle of winter. It can be refueled and rearmed by a team of conscripts in 10 minutes on a snowy road. That is an Arctic fighter.

3. The Poison Pill Saab is offering to build a manufacturing hub in Canada, creating 10,000 jobs. This isn’t just about jobs; it’s a geopolitical “Poison Pill.” By building Gripens here, Canada becomes a manufacturing powerhouse for Ukraine and other European allies. We become essential to them, not just dependent on the U.S.

It’s a risky move. The U.S. will hate it. Lockheed Martin is already lobbying hard. But if the goal is “Don’t be a Vassal State,” building your own jets is a pretty good way to start.

Naturally, the comments section exploded this week over the “Defence Mobilization Plan” documents obtained by the CBC. The headline number was 300,000 “citizen soldiers,” which caused immediate panic about conscription.

Stop. It’s not a draft. It’s a reality check.

The military is finally admitting they are broken. They cannot handle a war, a BC forest fire, a Quebec ice storm, and a banking cyber-attack simultaneously. The new plan is a “Whole of Society” approach, a Supplementary Reserve similar to the National Guard or the Scandinavian model.

These are civilians, teachers, coders, truckers, who keep their day jobs but get basic training to handle logistics and disaster response so the Regular Force can actually fight.

For the first time in forever, the government is treating us like adults. They are saying, “The world is dangerous. We need help. Who’s in?”. Judging by our inbox, Canadians aren’t pacifists; we just hate wasting our time. Give us a real mission, and we’ll show up.

If you think this is just Canadian paranoia, look at Denmark.
Usually the most polite, pro-American ally in the room, Danish Intelligence just released a 2025 Outlook that effectively lists “American pressure” as a security risk.They explicitly warned that the U.S. is pivoting to a “Hemispheric Security” model—code for “America First, everyone else is a vassal”, and looking at Greenland like it’s real estate.

White Man Runs Him (Mahr-Itah-Thee-Dah-Ka-Roosh; c. 1858 – June 2, 1929) was a Crow scout serving with George Armstrong Custer’s 1876 expedition against the Sioux and Northern Cheyenne that culminated in the Battle of the Little Bighorn.
Early life
Also known as White Buffalo That Turns Around, he was born into the Big Lodge Clan of the Crow Nation, the son of Bull Chief and Offers Her Red Cloth. At the age of about 18, he volunteered to serve as a scout with the United States Army on April 10, 1876, in its campaign against the Sioux and Northern Cheyenne, traditional enemies of the Crow.
Service as a scout
White Man Runs Him "enlisted on April 10, 1876 at the Crow Agency, Montana Territory, for six months in the 7th United States Infantry." On June 21, 1876, he was transferred to Custer’s Seventh U.S. Cavalry as part of a contingent of six Crow warrior/scouts, including Goes Ahead, Curly, Hairy Moccasin, White Swan, and Half Yellow Face, the leader of the scouts. He scouted for Lt. Charles Varnum’s column in the days preceding the battle. In the early morning hours of June 25, 1876, he and other Crow scouts accompanied Varnum and Custer to the Crow’s Nest, a high point on the Little Bighorn/Rosebud Creek divide, from which the Little Bighorn valley could be viewed at a distance of about seventeen air miles. The scouts could see indications of a large horse herd and the smoke of many morning fires, though the encampment itself was hidden from view on the valley floor. The Crow scouts advised Custer that the encampment was very large. Custer prepared to attack, however. Custer was concerned that during the morning of June 25, Sioux/Cheyenne warriors had detected the presence of his 650-man force, and if he did not promptly attack, the villagers would scatter, thus denying the army the confrontation it sought with the Sioux/Cheyenne forces.
White Man Runs Him White Man Runs Him 1858 1929 Find A Grave Memorial
Convinced they were about to die in battle, the scouts took off their uniforms and donned Crow war clothing. When Custer demanded to know why, they responded that they wished to die as warriors rather than soldiers. Custer was angered by what he perceived as fatalism and relieved them from further service about an hour before engaging in the final battle. White Man Runs Him retired to a ridge along with Goes Ahead, Hairy Moccasin, and Strikes That Bear (an Arikara scout) to join Major Marcus Reno. They were engaged briefly in battle, but would survive the engagement. He then joined Colonel John Gibbon's column.
Later life
After the battle, he lived on the Crow reservation near Lodge Grass, Montana. He was the stepgrandfather of Joe Medicine Crow, a Crow tribal historian who used his grandfather’s stories as a basis for his later histories of the battle, and grandfather to Pauline Small, the first woman elected to office in the Crow Tribe of Indians. His status as a Little Big Horn survivor made him a minor celebrity late in life, and he even made a cameo appearance in the 1927 Hollywood movie Red Raiders.
White Man Runs Him lived the remainder of his life on the Crow Reservation in the Big Horn Valley region of Montana, just a few miles from the site of the famous battle. He died there in 1929.
Legacy
White Man Runs Him was buried in the cemetery at the Little Big Horn Battlefield. His account of the battle is told in the work "The Custer Myth" by C. Graham, on pages 20 to 24," and also in It Is a Good Day to Die: Indian Eyewitnesses Tell the Story of the Battle of the Little Bighorn.
A slough near Lodge Grass, Montana, is known as Baaishtashíilinkuluush Alaaxúa ("Where Whiteman Runs Him Hid"). A coulee, Baaishtashíilinkuluush Isalasáh te, which is named after him, is also known as "Whiteman's Creek."

In 1790, President George Washington tasked General Josiah Harmar with leading the first major military expedition of the new United States Army. Harmar, a Revolutionary War veteran from Pennsylvania, commanded roughly 1,450 men—320 regulars and 1,130 militia—with orders to destroy Native American villages along the Maumee River in present-day Ohio. The Western Confederacy, a coalition of tribes including the Miami, Shawnee, and Delaware, had resisted American settlement in the Northwest Territory. Washington's administration viewed military force as necessary to secure lands promised to Revolutionary War veterans and open the region to white settlement.

Harmar's expedition departed Fort Washington (modern Cincinnati) in September 1790, marching north into hostile territory. His force suffered from poor training, inadequate supplies, and low morale among the militia. The troops burned several abandoned villages but found few Native warriors willing to engage in open battle. Harmar divided his force multiple times to pursue fleeing inhabitants—a tactical error that would prove catastrophic. The Western Confederacy, led by war chiefs including Little Turtle of the Miami and Blue Jacket of the Shawnee, recognized the weakness in Harmar's scattered formations.

On October 19 and 22, Native warriors ambushed Harmar's detached units near the Maumee villages. In fierce fighting, they killed approximately 183 American soldiers and wounded 31 others—roughly one-eighth of Harmar's entire force. The militia units broke and fled under attack, leaving regular army soldiers to fight desperate rearguard actions. Harmar retreated to Fort Washington, having destroyed villages but suffering humiliating tactical defeats. He claimed success based on the burned towns, but military analysts recognized the expedition as a failure.

The disaster triggered a court of inquiry that officially exonerated Harmar, though he resigned his commission in 1792. His defeat emboldened the Western Confederacy and demonstrated that Native forces could defeat American armies using woodland warfare tactics. The expedition exposed critical weaknesses in the young nation's military system: untrained militia, poor logistics, and officers inexperienced in frontier combat. Harmar's failure forced Washington and Congress to confront the reality that westward expansion would require a professional standing army, not just citizen-soldiers.

Harmar's defeat set the stage for two more disasters—St. Clair's catastrophic loss in 1791 and continuing frontier warfare until Anthony Wayne's victory at Fallen Timbers in 1794. His campaign revealed that the Revolutionary War's success against British regulars had not prepared American commanders for unconventional warfare against Native coalitions. The losses forced a fundamental rethinking of military strategy and organization in the early republic.
