In fencing, guards and parries are related but not the same thing—think position vs. action.

🛡️ Guards (the position)

A guard is how you hold your weapon and body to be ready to defend or attack. It’s basically your default stance.

Examples:
 • En garde – the basic ready position
 • High guard / low guard
 • Inside guard / outside guard

Guards are:
 • Mostly static or semi-static
 • About coverage (what line you’re protecting)
 • Your starting point before an attack or defense

⸻

✋ Parries (the movement)

A parry is an active defensive action—you move your blade to deflect or block an incoming attack.

Examples:
 • Parry 4 (inside high line)
 • Parry 6 (outside high line)
 • Parry 7 & 8 (low lines)

Parries are:
 • Quick, intentional movements
 • A reaction to an opponent’s attack
 • Usually followed by a riposte (counterattack)

⸻

🧠 Simple way to remember it
 • Guard = where your blade is
 • Parry = how your blade moves

Or:

You wait in a guard; you survive with a parry.

How Dr. Marie Grace Pascua Is Failing the Indigenous Peoples She Claims to Represent

Five days ago, on January 23, 2026, Dr. Marie Grace T. Pascua turned another year older. Her colleagues at the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) posted warm birthday messages online, calling her a leader and a daughter of the Cordillera. She smiled for the photos and accepted the praise.
But while she celebrated, thousands of indigenous families across the Philippines were still fighting to keep their lands from being taken away. 

These are the same people, farmers, elders, mothers, fathers—whose ancestors have lived on those mountains, rivers, and forests for generations. They are asking for one simple thing: to be heard. To be asked before anyone starts digging, building, or cutting down trees in their sacred places.

Instead, under Chairperson Pascua’s leadership, NCIP is giving companies the green light even when communities say a clear “NO.”
Here are the hard facts in simple words:

Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) is being ignored
The law (RA 8371, the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act) says no project—especially mining or big energy projects—can go forward without the honest agreement of the affected indigenous community.

If even one person or family strongly objects, the project must stop. That is what the Supreme Court said in a 2022 decision (Cosalan vs. Lepanto).

But in places like Mankayan and Itogon in Benguet, people are blocking roads and risking arrest, without real consultation. Some say their signatures were faked. Others say they were never even invited to meetings.  

This is happening right now in the same Cordillera region where Pascua was born and raised.
The same story repeats everywhere

In Nueva Vizcaya, NCIP gave a company a “Certificate of Non-Overlap,” saying “no indigenous people or ancestral land here.”
But families who have lived there for generations know that is not true. 

Their homes, farms, and burial grounds are on that land.
Similar things are happening to Lumad in Mindanao, Aeta in Central Luzon, and Pala’wan in Palawan. When they try to protect their land, they are often called “troublemakers” or worse.

The biggest contradiction of all
Dr. Pascua is not only the head of NCIP.
She is also a top official in NTF-ELCAC—the government’s task force against communist insurgency.

That same task force frequently labels indigenous people who defend their land as “rebels” or “supporters of terrorists.”
Schools get closed. Leaders get red-tagged. Families get visited by soldiers. Some disappear or are killed.
So on one hand, Pascua says she protects indigenous rights. On the other hand, she helps run a system that punishes the very people who are trying to use those rights.

How can she do both? Many indigenous groups say she cannot—and that she is choosing the wrong side.
Billions of pesos, but where are the results?
The government gives NCIP around ₱1.8 billion to ₱2.2 billion every year. That is a lot of money.

But after 27 years working in PUBLIC SERVICE (including many years before she became chair), Pascua still has not fixed the biggest problems:
Slow issuance of ancestral domain titles
Fake or forced FPIC processes
Communities left without real help when companies arrive

After all these years and all that money, indigenous peoples are still marching in the streets, sleeping on roads, and going to court just to be treated like human beings with rights.
Dr. Pascua, you are from Ifugao. You know what it feels like when outsiders come and take what is not theirs. You know the pain, the fear, the anger.

You were supposed to be different. You were supposed to be the shield.
Instead, too many see you as part of the problem.
The birthday messages have stopped.

 The real messages from the communities are loud and clear:
Listen.
Respect the “no.”
Stop helping the companies that destroy homes and sacred places.
Choose your own people over your position.
If you cannot or will not do that, then the honest thing is to step down.

Because the land does not forget.
The ancestors do not forget.
And the children who are growing up watching this betrayal will not forget either.
The struggle is the same in Cordillera, Mindanao, Palawan, and everywhere else.

It is time for real protection—not photo opportunities, not dual roles that cancel each other out, not more empty promises.
Justice is not complicated.

It starts with listening when indigenous peoples say NO.
Anything less is failure.
And right now, that failure has a name.

Ministarstvo vanjskih poslova BiH naglašava da je međunarodna zajednica obilježavala godišnjicu i dan sjećanja na Holokaust, dok je Milorad Dodik prepoznat kao negator genocida koji je, kako se navodi, lično djelovao u medijima u smislu relativizacije genocida počinjenog u Srebrenici 1995. godine.

When Jane Muthoni received her diagnosis. Stage III breast cancer. Her first thought wasn’t about survival rates or treatment options. It was about money. “How will I pay for this?” she whispered to the empty consultation room after her doctor stepped out.

Her salary as a primary school teacher in Nakuru barely covered rent and her children’s school fees. There was nothing left for catastrophic illness.

Three days later, her sister launched a harambee through M-PESA. Within a week, they had raised 670,000 Kenyan shillings from colleagues, church members, distant relatives and strangers who had seen her story shared on WhatsApp groups.

The psychology behind this outpouring reveals something profound about Kenyan philanthropy. We give differently than the West, but no less powerfully.

Needing comes with a nakedness and vulnerability. A visceral, morning-alarm nakedness of waking up and knowing that your life depends on the mercy of people who may or may not check their M-Pesa notifications today. I have lived this nakedness for fifteen years now, since my first cancer diagnosis.

The psychology of giving, I’ve understood, is never really about giving at all. It’s about everything else; power, optics, guilt, grace and the stories we tell ourselves to sleep at night when other people’s children are counting pills instead of sheep.

                                 Worthiness

My cousin Otis called me last Tuesday, didn’t ask how I was doing, we’d long ago exhausted that particular social nicety, to tell me about a WhatsApp group he’d been added to. Another fundraiser. This one for a young woman in Kisumu with cervical cancer, stage IV, needing 2.3 million shillings for treatment in India. He wanted to know if I thought she was genuine.

“What makes someone genuine?” I asked him.

There was a pause that had entire philosophical treatises.

“You know,” he finally said. “Like, is the story real? Have you seen these scammers nowadays?”

There it was. The fundamental calculation of contemporary giving in Kenya is not “Does this person need help?” but “Does this person deserve my belief?” We have mathematized mercy, created algorithms of authenticity and turned suffering into a competitive sport where only the most convincing performances of pain secure funding. Understandably because of the growing number of conning and dubious people using very sensitive cases of illness, funeral or school fees to extort money from unsuspecting or simply genuinely caring Kenyans.

I told James I didn’t know if she was genuine. How could I? I knew she was scared, because everyone with cancer is somewhat scared, even the scammers; perhaps especially the scammers, who have metabolized their desperation into survival strategy. Fraud exists. Of course it does. What do we sacrifice when we let the possibility of fraud injure our capacity for response?

              Harambee and the Hijacking of Hope

Harambee appears on Kenya’s coat of arms, loosely meaning “all for one” in Swahili. It was supposed to be our post-independence rallying cry and social technology that would lift us collectively from poverty, disease and illiteracy. Jomo Kenyatta wielded it as a nation-building spell, and for a while, it worked. Schools materialized in villages. Hospitals rose from red soil. Communities built themselves from the ground up.

Something happened along the way. Politicians discovered that harambee events could be channels to launder ill-gotten money and posturing generosity in public could purchase political capital more efficiently than actual governance. The Gen Z protesters who flooded Nairobi’s streets in 2024 understood this intuitively. They demanded an end to political harambees outside of collective giving because they recognized that what was being offered was no longer giving at all. It was money laundering with a moral veneer.

I’ve been on the receiving end of this spectacle. I remember a particular fundraiser in 2017, when my cancer had metastasized and I needed 4.37 million shillings for emergency treatment in India. A local politician showed up uninvited, carrying a stack of cash. The cameras loved it. He gave a speech about the importance of supporting our youth while his bodyguards stood around looking bored. He handed over 10,000 shillings and left before the event was over.

Later, someone did the math. The MP had recently been implicated in a corruption scandal involving 80 million shillings of county funds. His 10,000 shilling donation represented 0.125% of what he’d allegedly stolen. He bought redemption at a 99.9875% discount.

I received the money. They said that cancer doesn’t care about the political optics of the donors but I understood that giving, at scale, has very little to do with need and almost everything to do with the giver’s self-image. That MP didn’t come to save my life. He came to save his reputation. I was simply the prop in his moral theater.

                                Illness Economics

Because our public hospitals are stretched thin and private care is a privilege, every cancer patient is quickly thrust into the ugly waters of desperation and survival. You learn quickly that your illness is not just a medical condition but a narrative product that must be packaged, marketed and sold to an increasingly skeptical audience.

The market demands certain conventions. Your story must be tragic but not depressing. Hopeful but not naive. You must be fighting, always fighting, never surrendering or admitting that sometimes you’re just profoundly tired of being alive. You must post updates frequently enough to prove the money isn’t being misused but not so frequently that donors experience compassion fatigue. You must show gratitude constantly, effusively, even when you’re so exhausted from treatment that the thought of typing “Thank you so much, God bless” one more time makes you want to throw your phone into the nearest ditch.

I have written extensively about my cancer journey on Substack, Medium, in newspapers, on social media. I have appeared on podcasts, television and radio. I have shared photographs of my hospital room,

medication schedules and surgical scars. The terrible truth is that the more I exhibited my illness, the less funding I received. However, the more I transformed my suffering into consumable content, the more people felt comfortable engaging with it.

This creates a perverse incentive structure. The sickest, most desperate patients become content creators, churning out illness narratives on social media the same way productivity influencers churn out morning routine videos. We optimize for engagement. We A/B test our suffering. We learn which photographs of thin and ugly hospital days generate the most sympathy shares.

People who can’t or won’t perform their illness this way die quietly, off-camera, without ever going viral.

                            Our Stories

A man sees a fundraiser for a child’s cancer treatment. He feels something. A tug. A hesitation. His mind starts working. Is my contribution enough to matter? Is this real? What if I donate and nothing changes?

Most giving decisions happen in seconds, driven by emotion before logic steps in. A compelling story moves us but doubts can also just as much halt us mid-click. The difference between giving and scrolling past? Often, it’s not wealth, but the mind.

                          Empathy Threshold/Gap

Humans are wired to care but that instinct has limits. We respond more to one suffering person than to many. The “identifiable victim effect.” A child in need with a face moves us more than statistics on a crisis affecting thousands. This is why effective fundraising focuses on individuals and not abstract problems. A single, vivid story is more powerful than numbers alone.

For all our generosity in crisis, preventative health initiatives struggle to attract the same support. Cancer screening programs, diabetes prevention and mental health services face chronic funding shortages.

Empathy gap for acute and chronic needs isn’t unique to us but takes on particular urgency in our context. We respond powerfully to immediate suffering we can see and relate with but struggle to mobilize around statistical lives and future risks.

When Jane Muthoni’s story circulated on WhatsApp, it included her photograph in a hospital bed, her children beside her. The image generated 40% more donations than text-only appeals.

We’re wired to respond to identifiable victims. This is why personalized storytelling remains the most effective fundraising strategy across cultures.

                                   Guilt Paradox

Guilt can drive generosity but too much of it backfires. When people feel overwhelmed by suffering, they disengage. This is called “compassion fatigue.” We shut down, not because we don’t care, but because caring too much is exhausting. The best appeals don’t dwell in despair. They offer a bridge between need and action. “Here’s the problem. Here’s how you can help. Here’s the impact.” People give when they believe their contribution will do something tangible.

                          Trust is Everything

On charitable behavior, people are far more likely to give when they trust the recipient. This is why transparency matters. Clear goals, real updates and proof that donations reach their purpose. Crowdfunding succeeds when people believe in who is asking, not just what they are asking for. The most successful campaigns are personal, direct and human.

The thing everyone thinks about but few say directly is that medical fundraising fraud exists in Kenya. It’s probably more common than we want to admit. There are people who fabricate diagnoses, Photoshop hospital bills and run multiple fundraisers under different names. The internet has made this easier and more profitable than ever.

A lady named Betty infiltrated our unsuspecting community of young cancer survivors, Kisumu Cancer Society, then led by Jadudi and postured as one of us. She ran a fundraising appeal for three weeks until the internet caught up with her. I was two months fresh off India, still in isolation and sensitive to infections. We were bullied for two weeks on Twitter and Facebook until a phone call from Betty’s cousin came to vindicate us. Apparently, she started defrauding family with threats of suicide and treatment which, yes, she was sick and on treatment for HIV but mot cancer as earlier claimed by her. Story for another day.

What the fraud panic misses is the vast majority of fraudulent fundraisers exist because legitimate medical care is inaccessible. Scammers aren’t exploiting our generosity than they’re exploiting the same broken healthcare system that’s killing the rest of us. They’ve simply chosen a different survival strategy.

I’m not defending fraud. I’m saying that when life becomes a crowd-sourced campaign, the social contract is broken. When a government builds a healthcare system so inadequate that citizens must constantly beg each other for survival, and healthcare or education becomes a privilege determined by thinning resources, we have already accepted a collective fraud. We have agreed to pretend that this is normal and acceptable and asking a person to raise millions of shillings on WhatsApp while undergoing chemotherapy is a reasonable way to organize a society.

The proposed Public Fundraising Appeals Bill of 2024 seeks to license and regulate harambees, imposing fines of up to 5 million shillings for violations. The government’s solution to fraud is bureaucracy, paperwork and licensing yet no one is talking about public pilferage at SHA or billions of tender fraud and stupid trips abroad wasting our money. Regulation doesn’t address the root cause that we’ve privatized survival in a public crisis.

                               Proximity Principle

People give when others give. This is the principle of social proof. Seeing donations pour in creates urgency or collective-persuasion. If so many people believe in this, maybe I should too. This is why early support in fundraising is critical. The first few donors set the momentum. It’s also why public pledges work by identifying donors who encourage others to follow.

Kenyans are more likely to donate to someone in their extended social network than to an anonymous cause. Proximity principle explains why harambees remain our most effective fundraising mechanism because they leverage existing social bonds and community obligations.

In other contexts, charitable giving happens at arm’s length. Donors give to organizations, rarely meeting recipients. In our case, the relationship is direct, personal and reciprocal.

Reciprocity is both a cultural tradition and a practical insurance in a country where formal safety nets remain fragile. Today I give to your medical fund; tomorrow you might contribute to my child’s education.

I’ve noticed something curious about who gives to medical fundraisers in Kenya. It’s rarely the very rich. Oh, they might make a token contribution if a fundraiser goes viral and their brand needs the positive PR. The real money comes from the ordinary people who are themselves one medical emergency away from needing a fundraiser.

This makes psychological sense. The very rich can maintain the illusion of invulnerability. They have health insurance that actually works, access to private hospitals where doctors don’t go on strike, enough money to fly to India or South Africa or Germany if things get serious. They can afford the luxury of viewing illness as something that happens to other people.

Ordinary people know better. They see themselves in every cancer patient’s story. They know that their own health insurance has a fine print labyrinth designed to deny coverage. Their savings could be wiped out by a single catastrophic diagnosis. They give because they understand, viscerally, that next time it could be them posting their M-Pesa number on Twitter.

There’s also the diaspora factor. Kenyans abroad often give more generously than local donors but their giving comes with a peculiar emotional economics. Guilt mixed in with the generosity; guilt about having escaped to countries with functioning health systems, earning in currencies that make Kenyan medical bills seem manageable and not being present for family emergencies. Their donation is a way to purchase proximity.

                           Visibility Factor

Public donations in Kenya are, on average, 2.7 times larger than anonymous ones. We are social beings, motivated by community standing and reputation. The public nature of giving in our communities serves an important accountability function. It ensures resources reach intended recipients and creates social pressure that increases participation rates.

The most successful fundraising campaigns in Kenya now blend emotional storytelling with transparency and accountability. Digital M-CHANGA platform, which has facilitated over 100,000 fundraisers, provides real-time updates on contributions and withdrawals, addressing trust concerns that sometimes limit giving.

Meanwhile, larger foundations such as the Africa Cancer Foundation have learned to connect abstract preventative work to human stories showing not just statistics but faces and action areas of those affected by early cancer detection programs.

With Kenya developing its philanthropic ecosystem, the challenge isn’t changing our giving nature but expanding it and leveraging our powerful cultural traditions of mutual aid while building sustainable systems that address root causes alongside immediate needs.

Jane Muthoni completed her treatment last year. This January, she organized a thanksgiving ceremony for her donors. “Now I give what I can, when I can,” she says. “Even if it’s just 200 shillings. I now understand it was never about the amount. It was about being seen in your darkest hour.”

We give because under different circumstances, it could be us on the receiving end. In this view of our shared vulnerability lies the truest psychology of Kenyan giving.

                  Accountability and Integrity

Te contradiction at the heart of medical fundraising is that donors have a right to know their money is being used appropriately but the level of surveillance they often demand is dehumanizing.

I’ve had donors ask for my complete medical records. Itemized hospital bills. Photographs of medications. Receipts for every expense. They want to see the tumor scans, chemotherapy schedules and doctor’s notes. Some of this is reasonable accountability. Some of it crosses into medical voyeurism.

The line is difficult to draw because the stakes are genuinely high. Fraudulent fundraisers have made many Kenyans skeptical of appeals for financial help, making it harder for genuine cases to get urgently needed assistance. However, the response cannot be to treat every sick person as a potential scammer who must prove their legitimacy through invasive disclosure.

What would accountability look like if it centered dignity?
Having a trusted third party such as a hospital, community organization or religious institution verify the medical need without broadcasting every intimate detail to the internet. M-Changa has, in response, made it mandatory for medical records to be uploaded to the platform and verified by their team before fundraiser is approved. We can’t eliminate all risk of fraud without also eliminating the possibility of helping people who need privacy to maintain their humanity.

I think about the young woman my cousin asked about, the one with cervical cancer needing 2.3 million shillings. I don’t know if her story is genuine but I know that cervical cancer mortality in Kenya is catastrophically high because most cases are diagnosed late, screening is inadequate and treatment is expensive. Asking a stranger to prove the authenticity of her suffering before we consider helping her says something devastating about what we’ve become.

                                 Social Media

WhatsApp groups are now the infrastructure of Kenyan medical fundraising. You wake up to find you’ve been added to three new groups overnight. Each has the same format. A paragraph about someone’s medical emergency, an M-Pesa/Paybill number and desperate appeal. In the best cases, there are hospital documents attached. In the worst cases, just a name and a sob story.

The group dynamics are fascinating from a psychological standpoint. There’s always someone who immediately sends 1,000 shillings and announces it publicly, setting the social expectation. There’s always someone who asks probing questions about accountability. There’s always someone who shares a testimony about how they once organized a fundraiser that turned out to be fake, so everyone should be careful. There’s always someone who forwards the message to ten other groups without contributing anything themselves.

And then there’s the silence. Majority of people in these groups never say anything. They read the appeal, maybe they feel something or don’t and then they scroll on. The silence is not necessarily callousness. Often it’s simply overwhelm.

When you’re in forty WhatsApp fundraising groups and every week brings three new medical emergencies, four new funeral appeals, two new education fundraisers, at what point do you just tune out?

Social media has democratized fundraising in some ways. Mobile-money apps and social media platforms have provided a conducive environment for quick and efficient fundraising in Kenya that thrives on the harambee spirit. You don’t need a celebrity endorsement or a fancy event. You just need a phone, a story and the willingness to make your suffering public.

However, this democratization has a dark side. It creates an attention economy where the most dramatic, most shareable and most emotionally manipulative stories win. Cancer patients are content marketers. We learn the vocabulary of virality. We understand that a photograph of a child fucked up sick and thin to the bomes in a hospital bed performs better than a paragraph about medical bills. We know that stories with clear villains (corrupt politicians who won’t help) and clear heroes (generous strangers who might) generate more engagement than complex, ambiguous narratives about systemic failure.

I’ve tried to refuse this game. I’ve crafted my illness narratives with an eye toward shareability. I’ve timed my appeals to coincide with salary days when people have money in their M-Pesa accounts. I’ve used the right hashtags, tagged the right influencers and written the right hooks. Sometimes it worked. My fundraisers succeeded not because my cancer was worse than anyone else’s but largely because my story was also generally known, having talked about it publicly. Me being a writer who knows how to tell a compelling story has not helped much. This should disturb us. This should make us question what we’ve built.

                   Cancer and Class

There are cancer patients who fly to South Africa or India for treatment. Some access clinical trials at Aga Khan or Nairobi Hospital. Others rely on the overwhelmed public system at Kenyatta National Hospital or MTRH. Many moerebdie at home because they can’t afford to even begin treatment.

I’ve existed in all these tiers at different points. When my family still had money, before cancer consumed our land titles and savings and dignity, I went to India. When the money ran out but I was working and could still fundraise effectively, I accessed private care in Nairobi. When even that became unsustainable, I joined the long queues at KNH, the place where barely a handful of operational bone marrow transplant centers exist and most patients with aggressive leukemias either perish early or must seek expensive treatment abroad.

The psychology of giving is shaped by this stratification. People are more willing to donate to ‘aspirational’ patients seeking cutting-edge treatment in foreign hospitals, whose stories suggest that with enough money, survival is possible. They’re less willing to fund the grinding mundane reality of chronic illness management in the public system.

This creates a macabre hierarchy. The patient trying to raise 5 million shillings for CAR-T cell therapy in India gets more attention than the patient trying to raise 50,000 shillings for basic chemotherapy at KNH. Never mind that the second patient’s need might be more urgent, easily met and likely to result in actual survival. The first patient has a better story. More hope. More shine.

                      Power Dynamics of Aid

I lost a friendship because of money. A close friend had contributed significantly to my fundraisers over the years. Then came a point where she started making decisions about my life. What treatments I should pursue. Which doctors I should see. How I should spend the funds that had been raised. When I pushed back and asserted that I was still the author of my own medical decisions, she withdrew her support.

“I’ve invested so much in keeping you alive,” she told me. “The least you could do is listen to my advice.”

Invested. That word caught me. She wasn’t wrong, exactly. She had invested financially in my survival though investment implies return and ownership. The investor gets a say in how their asset is managed.

This is the shadow side of medical fundraising that nobody wants to talk about. Money creates power imbalances, generosity can easily become a tool of control and donors sometimes act like they’ve purchased equity in your body and dignity.

I’ve had donors try to dictate my treatment plans based on things they read on the internet. They become angry when I chose management care over aggressive treatment, as if my medical decisions were betraying their investment. Some tell me I was being ungrateful when I set boundaries around their involvement in my life.

The psychology here is complex. From the donor’s perspective, they’ve given sacrificially, foregone their own needs to help you survive and emotionally invested in your recovery, and they want to see their investment succeed. From this angle, their desire for input seems reasonable but from the recipient’s perspective, you’re already drowning in loss of health, independence, privacy and agency. The last thing you can afford to lose is the ability to make decisions about your own body, treatment or life.

                                      Enough

How much suffering is enough to warrant help?
This is the question that haunts medical fundraising in Kenya. If you need 100,000 shillings, people might help. If you need 10 million, they might decide you’re asking for too much, your life isn’t worth that much and at some point we have to accept limits.

Who decides those limits? On what basis?
I’ve needed both amounts at different times. The 100,000 shilling fundraiser was easier. People could conceptualize that number. It felt manageable, achievable. The 4.37 million shilling fundraiser for treatment in India was harder. I questioned whether it was really necessary to further impoverish my family and burden my friends. After all, we had tried our best with what we had and the cancer still metastasized. Could I find cheaper treatment? Should I make do with what’s available locally? Am I being unrealistic?

The unspoken subtext is maybe my life isn’t worth 4.37 million shillings. This is where the psychology of giving intersects with the philosophy of value. What is a life worth? In economic terms, there are metrics of disability-adjusted life years, quality-adjusted life years and cost-benefit analyses but in human terms, the question is obscene. My life is worth everything to me. Is it worth 4.37 million shillings to you? Should it have to be?

              Religious Narratives and the Spiritualization of Suffering

Religious narratives frame illness as a test of faith, divine will or even as a form of spiritual communication, adding layers of meaning to the experience of suffering. In our deeply religious society, this shapes both how sick people present themselves and how potential donors respond.

Patients speak fluent prayer warrior, post Bible verses on fundraising appeals even though they are agnostic and thank God for every donation even though. They do this because they understand that for many potential donors, seeing that “keeping faith” makes them more willing to give. They want to support someone who’s fighting both medically and spiritually. Doubt is bad for fundraising.

The spiritualization of illness cuts both ways. Sometimes donors tell me my cancer is a blessing,

divine assignment or platform for testimony. They find meaning in my suffering that I don’t necessarily feel and tell me about people who were healed through faith, implying that if I just believed harder, I wouldn’t need all these expensive medical interventions.

What happens when fundraisers fail? When the money doesn’t come through? That gets spiritualized too. “It wasn’t God’s will.” “God has a plan.” “He’ll make a way.” These phrases offer comfort to the person saying them but feel hollow to the person dying for lack of funds.

I don’t mean to mock people’s faith. Faith has sustained many Kenyans through impossible circumstances. However, I’ve noticed that the people who most loudly proclaim that “God will provide” are often not the ones actually providing. It’s easier to outsource responsibility to the divine than to confront your own capacity to help or not help.

                   Why People Give

After years of receiving donations and being a beneficiary of people’s generosity during my time of need for treatment, I’ve developed some theories about why people give or don’t give. Most of them are uncomfortable.

People give when giving makes them feel good about themselves. This sounds cynical but it’s not necessarily bad. The dopamine hit of helping another person is real and valid. The problem is when the need to feel good overwhelms the actual impact of the gift and donors become more invested in their own emotional experience than in the recipient’s dignity and wellbeing.

People don’t give when giving confronts them with their own vulnerability. Every cancer patient is a mirror showing you your own mortality. Some people can look into that mirror and feel moved to action. Others turn away, reflexively, almost violently. I don’t blame them. Many people have turned away from my suffering even before cancer made that turning away impossible.

People give to people who remind them of themselves or their loved ones. This is why certain fundraisers go viral while others languish in obscurity. A young mother with small children gets funded faster than the elderly man with no family. The articulate and educated patient who writes beautifully about their experience might not get funded faster than the patient who can barely operate a smartphone but has bared their physical wounds and utter sickness in public or has been assisted by a social media big wig. We fund the suffering that we can imagine ourselves experiencing.

People give less when they’re asked too often. Compassion fatigue is real. Out medical fundraisers have become ubiquitous, with thousands of small-scale fundraisers happening daily via mobile-money apps and social media, many people exist in a state of permanent philanthropic overwhelm. They’ve joined too many WhatsApp groups, seen too many desperate appeals and contributed to too many causes. Eventually, they become numb.

People give more when there’s social accountability. This is why harambees work better in tight-knit communities where people know each other. The psychology shifts from “Am I helping a stranger?” to “What will my neighbors think if I don’t help?” It’s not pure altruism but it’s effective.

                       Tyrannical Gratitude

We sort of have an unspoken contract in medical fundraising. You may receive help but you must be grateful. Endlessly, performatively and abjectly grateful. You must never complain about donors who attach conditions to their giving, demand regular updates and treat your medical crisis as a spectator sport. You must never admit that sometimes their help comes with so many strings attached that it feels more like entanglement than liberation.

I have sat in hospital beds, so sick I could barely lift my head, begging and composing thank-you messages because someone donated and expected acknowledgment within the hour. I have smiled through video calls with donors who wanted to “see how I was doing,” showing my most worn out self to reassure them their money wasn’t wasted. I have written tribute posts to people who donated substantial sums but whose actual presence in my life was toxic and draining.

The tyranny of gratitude is that you cannot afford to have boundaries or dignity when you need people’s money to survive. You cannot tell a donor that their advice is unwelcome, their religious counsel unhelpful or their constant checking-in intrusive. You cannot say, “Thank you for the money but please leave me some dignity while I recover.”

Although I tell myself I’ve been open about my illness, I know I’ve carefully avoided dwelling on its darkest moments because the darker moments don’t help much, ultimately. They only generate discomfort, distance, pity and the subtle withdrawal of support. People want to fund your recovery and not your despair.

                               Body Politic

Luo people say “tuo donjone yot to wuokne tek (entering sickness is easy, but leaving is difficult). Many Kenyan communities have similar expressions reflecting the fragile nature of the human body and the uncertain path to recovery. These proverbs recognize something we modernity-drunk Kenyans often forget. Illness is biological, social, medical and political.

Being sick in Kenya means encountering every failure of the state in concentrated form of understaffed hospitals, absent medicines, doctors fleeing to the diaspora, insurance schemes that promise universal coverage but deliver bureaucratic nightmares and politicians who cut ribbons at dilapidated cancer centers while secretly traveling to India and South Africa for their own treatment.

I’ve spent fifteen years navigating this landscape. I’ve come of age in the era of Kenya’s Social Health Insurance Fund Act of 2023, a framework meant to establish protections for people with chronic and critical illnesses, yet even with SHIF, private insurance and regular fundraisers, the thought of losing access to life-saving medication fills me with dread.

We have privatized survival in a public health crisis. We survive by networks, mercy and luck. Are you sick in the right networks? Can you mobilize the right mercy? Do you have the right luck?

                           Quiet Givers

I want to talk about the donors you don’t see. They never comment publicly, attend fundraising events or even demand acknowledgment. They just send money, visit you at home or help with chores. Often not much. Sometimes 500 shillings. Sometimes 2,000. They send it regularly, monthly, like clockwork, for years.

I have several donors like this. I don’t know most of their stories. One is a teacher in Kakamega who used to send me 100 shillings every month on the 5th. Another is someone who identified themselves only as ‘a parent who lost a child to cancer’ and sends varying amounts whenever they can. Another is a former classmate who never responds to my thank you messages but hasn’t missed a month in three years.

These donors have kept me alive more surely than any single large donation. They’ve given me the psychological security of knowing that even if a fundraiser fails, even if the WhatsApp groups go quiet, there will be something. Not enough to solve everything but something.

The psychology of this kind of giving is different from the idea of harambees. It’s private and consistent. It’s not about the giver’s image or social standing. It’s just… human. Person to person. Need to response.

These are my heroes. Not the politicians with their sacks of cash or cancer organizations with their branded donations or even the kind strangers who contribute once to a viral appeal. People who have integrated my story and treat my life as worth protecting even when I’m not trending.

                Systemic Failure and Personal Response

Even if every Kenyan donated to every medical fundraiser they encountered or we perfected the harambee system and eliminated all fraud, we would still have a healthcare crisis. Our social contract is broken when life becomes a crowd-sourced campaign.

Individual giving, no matter how generous, cannot substitute for functional public health infrastructure. It cannot replace the hematologists Kenya doesn’t have, bone marrow transplant facilities that barely exist or cancer medications that aren’t available in public hospitals. It cannot address the fundamental injustice of a system that treats diseases but not the structural injustice around them.

Thousands of WhatsApp groups. Millions of shillings raised person by person, 50 shillings at a time. We’ve built a jerry-rigged social safety net out of M-Pesa transfers and collective goodwill because the official safety net has too many holes to catch anyone. The terrible thing is that this jerry-rigged system sometimes works. People do get funded. Lives do get saved. I am alive partly because of this system but its success obscures the deeper failure. We’ve gotten so good at crowdfunding survival that we’ve almost stopped demanding that survival shouldn’t need to be crowdfunded.

                              Solidarity Ethics

If I’ve learned anything from fifteen years of giving, needing and receiving help, it’s that the psychology of giving is less important than the politics of need. We spend so much energy analyzing donor motivations, optimizing fundraising strategies, detecting fraud and performing gratitude but these are all downstream responses to an upstream problem. We’ve organized society in a way that makes continuous, desperate fundraising necessary for basic survival.

What would change if we reframed medical fundraising not as charity but as mutual aid as a community ensuring all its members have what they need to survive?
This is actually closer to the original harambee spirit before it got colonized by politics and skepticism.

Mutual aid assumes interdependence. We all take turns being the person who needs help and the person who gives it. There’s no fundamental difference between donor and recipient, just different moments in the same human experience of vulnerability.

I think about the teacher in Kakamega sending her 100 shillings every month. Maybe she does this because she remembers when she needed help. Maybe she does it because she knows she might need help again. Maybe she does it because she understands that we’re all just one diagnosis away from being on the other side of a fundraising appeal.

This is solidarity. Your survival matters because we’re in this together.

                     The Dignity of the Ask

The hardest lesson cancer has taught me is that asking for help is not weakness. It’s truth-telling. It’s being honest with the reality that we are not self-sufficient creatures. We need each other. Individualism is a luxury afforded only to the healthy and wealthy.

Asking for help should not require debasement, demand that you perform your suffering for an audience or mean surrendering your privacy, dignity and agency. It should not transform you into content, or a moral lesson for people who donate to feel good about themselves.

I want to live in a Kenya where illness does not isolate, cancer patients can be cancer patients and not fundraising entrepreneurs. We give to each other not because someone’s story went viral but because we’ve built systems that recognize health as a right and not a privilege to be crowdfunded.

Aappeals, posting my M-Pesa number. Gratitude and hope and faith. None of this is normal or acceptable. We deserve better than this.

The psychology of giving matters but the politics of need matters more. Until we address the latter, we’ll keep analyzing the former while people die waiting for their fundraiser to go viral.

Tuo donjone yot to wuokne tek. For fifteen years, I’ve been trying to find the exit. Sometimes I think the way out isn’t medical at all. Maybe it’s political. Building a society where life doesn’t have to be constantly negotiated or fundraised for.

Might the real healing start when we stop asking “Why do people give or not give?” and start asking “Why must they give at all?”

                  How to Encourage Giving

Make it personal → A single person’s story over abstract need.
Keep it transparent → Show where money goes. Updates matter.
Reduce doubt → Small contributions do make a difference. Every bit counts.
Create urgency → Immediate needs get faster responses.
Show impact → “Here’s what your help changed.”

At least 170 civilians killed in Myanmar air strikes during election: UN

January 30, 2026 (AFP)

At least 170 civilians were killed in more than 400 military air strikes in Myanmar in the weeks surrounding its widely-criticised elections, the United Nations said Friday.
Myanmar's month-long, three-phase vote, which wrapped up on Sunday, was imposed by the military in what democracy watchdogs dismissed as an attempt to rebrand army rule.

The UN rights office, which has been harshly critical of the elections, warned Friday that they had failed to respect fundamental human rights and that military attacks on the population had continued unabated.

"These elections did not prevent violence from continuing throughout 2025," James Rodehaver, head of the rights office's Myanmar team, told reporters in Geneva.

Speaking from Bangkok, he highlighted that 2025 was "the year in which more civilians died from airstrikes than any other since 2021", and that "air strikes continued even through election days".

The UN said "credible sources" had verified that at least "170 civilians were killed in some 408 military aerial attacks reported by open sources during the voting period", the nearly two months from early December.

Rodehaver warned though that the numbers could rise, pointing out that their verification was complicated since communications are cut off and due to "the fear of individuals in some of these locations to speak to us".

- 'Forcing people to the ballot box' -

The UN rights office pointed to initial reports of a military air strike "on a populated area with no reported presence of combatants" that killed up to 50 civilians in Bhamo Township, in Kachin State on January 22.

To curb any dissent, the military had also arrested 324 men and 80 women under its unilaterally-adopted election protection law, including for minor online activity, the office said, decrying the "grossly disproportionate penalties" doled out.

In one case, it said a 49-year sentence was handed down for posting anti-election materials.

Five years after the coup that swept Myanmar's junta to power, UN rights chief Volker Turk warned that "the profound and widespread despair inflicted on the people of Myanmar has only deepened with the recent election staged by the military".

He pointed out that "many people chose either to vote or not to vote purely out of fear, flatly at odds with their internationally guaranteed civil and political rights -- and with ripple effects on their enjoyment of economic, social and cultural rights".

"The conflict and insecurity continued unabated in large parts of the country. Opposition candidates and some ethnic groups were excluded," he said.

His office pointed out that the elections were held in only 263 of 330 townships, often exclusively in urban centres under military control, and limited in conflict areas.

"As a result, large segments of the population, especially the displaced and minorities, such as the ethnic Rohingya, were excluded," it pointed out.

Voter coercion was also reported nationwide.

In one incident on January 6, more than 100 villagers in the Sagaing region were arbitrarily detained and compelled to cast advance ballots, the rights office said.

Turk decried that five years of military rule in Myanmar had been "characterised by repression of political dissent, mass arbitrary arrests, arbitrary conscription, widespread surveillance and limitation of civic space".

"Now, the military is seeking to entrench its rule-by-violence after forcing people to the ballot box," he said.

Republika Bugarska je Bosnu i Hercegovinu priznala na današnji dan 31. januara 1992. godine, mjesec prije održavanja referenduma o nezavisnosti. Prva priznanja neke države uslijede nakon referenduma, ili odluke parlamenta. Dešavalo se kroz historiju da pojedine države u znak podrške narodima koji se bore za slobodu priznaju njihovu nezavisnost prije službenog akta same države koja biva priznata. Riek Machar Urges Peace Amid House Arrest Following 2025 Nasir Clashes
January 31, 2026 – Juba, South Sudan

South Sudan’s First Vice President and SPLM-IO leader, Dr. Riek Machar Teny Dhurgon, has renewed his call for peace and national unity while remaining under house arrest in Juba, following deadly clashes in Nasir County, Upper Nile State, in March 2025.

Authorities and independent media confirm Machar was placed under house arrest after intense fighting erupted between the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF) and armed youth militias, commonly known as the White Army. The government has alleged these forces were aligned with Machar’s SPLM-IO, an accusation his party denies.

The Nasir clashes were among the deadliest since the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement, claiming the lives of hundreds of SSPDF soldiers, including senior commanders. The violence prompted a sweeping security crackdown in Juba, with several SPLM-IO officials detained and security tightened around Machar’s residence.

Machar: “I Came for Peace”

Addressing the people of South Sudan, Machar reflected on his 2020 return to Juba, emphasizing his commitment to peace, reconciliation, and the implementation of the power-sharing agreement that ended years of civil war.

“When I came to Juba in 2020, I came for peace,” Machar said. “I came because I believe in South Sudan—a nation that has suffered too much, bled too deeply, and endured more than any people should ever have to.”

He underscored his concern for ordinary civilians: “I have never feared for my own life. But I have always feared for the lives of the innocent—the mothers struggling to feed their children, the youth searching for opportunities, and the elders who have seen too much destruction.”

Political Crisis and Fragile Peace

Machar’s detention has heightened fears of a political breakdown. International observers, including the United Nations and regional bodies, warn that his continued house arrest threatens the fragile unity government and risks renewed conflict.

The government has accused Machar of command responsibility for the Nasir violence, filing charges including treason and crimes against humanity. His party dismisses the allegations as politically motivated, calling the detention a violation of the peace agreement.

Despite the tension, Machar maintained a conciliatory tone, urging South Sudanese to reject division and fear. “Do not let fear or division consume us. We are one nation, and we must stand together,” he said.

Warning Against “Spoilers of Peace”

Machar also addressed political and military actors fueling instability. “To those who bring mercenaries and weapons instead of solutions, know this: South Sudan does not belong to the few who benefit from war. It belongs to the millions who dream of peace,” he said.

A Call to History

Concluding his message, Machar appealed to South Sudanese resilience and the international community: “Let history remember that in our darkest moments, we did not give up. No amount of power is worth the suffering of a nation.”

As South Sudan prepares for long-delayed elections and continues to face insecurity, Machar’s house arrest remains a focal point of political tension—one that could determine whether the nation moves toward stability or slides back into conflict.

Renk County, Upper Nile State — (Sat Jan 31st 2026 ) 

H.E. Jacob Dollar Ruot, the Governor of Upper Nile State, today officially opened the newly constructed statue of the late Dr. John Garang De Mabior in Renk County, marking a significant moment of remembrance and national pride.

The ceremony was attended by government officials, community leaders, and members of the public who gathered to honor the legacy of the late Dr. John Garang De Mabior, the founding leader of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement/Army (SPLM/A) and a symbol of the struggle for freedom, unity, and justice.

Governor Jacob Dollar Ruot was accompanied by the Commissioner of Renk County, Hon. Diing Deng Lueth, alongside other high-ranking government officials. The event underscored the commitment of the Government of Upper Nile State to preserving the history of the liberation struggle and inspiring future generations with the values and vision championed by Dr. John Garang.

In his remarks, H.E. the Governor emphasized that the statue stands as a reminder of sacrifice, resilience, and the enduring quest for peace and development in South Sudan. He called on citizens, particularly the youth, to uphold the principles of unity, patriotism, and nation-building embodied by the late leader.

Hon. Diing Deng Lueth welcomed the Governor and expressed appreciation for the choice of Renk County as the site of this important monument, noting that the statue will serve as a source of inspiration and historical education for the community.

Today, Assam pays tribute to one of its greatest warriors on the occasion of Bir Chilaray Diwas, observed every year on Maghi Purnima.

Among the legendary heroes who shaped Assam’s glorious history, Chilaray shines as a golden name. He was the younger brother of Maharaja Naranarayan, the ruler of the Koch Kingdom, and served as its most brilliant commander.

Born to Maharaja Biswa Singha, the founder of the Koch dynasty, and Queen Padmavati, Chilaray was named Shukladhwaj at birth, as he was born on a full moon day. Legends say he led battles dressed in white, riding a white horse and carrying a white flag—earning him the name Shukladhwaj. His lightning-fast attacks in war made him famous as Chilaray, meaning the one who strikes like a kite. British historian Edward Gait called him the “Kite King.”

A master of warfare from childhood, Chilaray was also highly learned, with deep knowledge of Sanskrit, literature, grammar, law, astrology, music, and art. He was a great patron of culture and spirituality and, along with Maharaja Naranarayan, played a crucial role in supporting Srimanta Sankardeva in establishing and spreading Eka Saran Naam Dharma. Chilaray himself authored the valuable Sanskrit text Sarawati Tika and had mastery over 24 musical ragas, with a special love for Borgeet.

Under his leadership, the Koch army defeated the Bhutia, Kachari, and Ahom forces in several battles, leading to a vast expansion of the Koch Empire across present-day Assam, North Bengal, and parts of today’s Bangladesh.

In recognition of his unparalleled bravery and contribution, the Government of Assam has been observing Bir Chilaray Diwas as a state holiday since 2005.

Was this not a chapter of pure glory?

On this sacred birth anniversary of Bir Chilaray, we bow our heads in deep respect and heartfelt remembrance to this timeless hero of Assam.

New warrior statues, whose original paints have been preserved, were discovered during ongoing excavations at the site of the Terracotta Army in Xian, one of China's mind-blowing archaeological discoveries. The presence of purple and green pigments sheds light on China's early dynasty dye technology.

The presence of purple pigment particularly surprised archaeologists because purple dye was rare and expensive in ancient times.

Dr. Zhang Wei from Shaanxi Archaeological Institute said, "These warriors must belong to the emperor's special guard unit. Purple is the imperial color in China.” 

Another riddle is where the purple paint comes from. Was it obtained from seashells or was it imported through pre-Silk Road trade?

Most Terracotta soldiers lose their color while underground. However, the reason for the preservation of the paints in these statues is:

🎨Clay layers: The statues are covered with a layer of moisture-proof clay.

🎨Minerals: Mercury (red), malachite (green) and hematite (purple) were used in the pigments.

🎨Sudden burial: fire and flood of 206 BC "sealed" the paints, leaving some of the statues airless.

The Qin terracotta warriors wore a variety of colors. Upper garments included shades of light green, vermilion, maroon, pink, light purple, sky blue, white, and ochre, while trousers were generally light green, though red, sky blue, light purple, and white were also common. In short, the terracotta warriors' clothing was brightly colored, but without a unified color scheme. Among the many colors, light green, vermilion, light purple, and sky blue were the most frequently used, suggesting these were the primary colors of the terracotta warriors' clothing.

The Qin terracotta warriors' painting technique also had many unique features. Observation of cross-sections of terracotta fragments proves that before firing, the surface of the terracotta warriors was coated with fine mud, and also with a thin layer of a glue-like substance (lacquer).  Unfortunately, due to the passage of time and exposure to air, the surface moisture of the terracotta warriors evaporated quickly, causing the lacquer to peel and flake off. What we see now are only the original color of the terracotta body.

One of the surprises was a green-faced terracotta warrior. This is the only terracotta warrior discovered to date whose face is entirely painted green with malachite green pigment, except for its black hair, beard, and pupils. The reason for this remains a mystery. Because of its immense value, this green-faced terracotta warrior (the last image) is the only one prohibited from being exhibited abroad.

In February 1836, Seminole war parties executed a devastating coordinated assault on Florida's Atlantic coast sugar plantations, destroying at least 21 estates south of St. Augustine in a single sweeping campaign. These attacks represented strategic warfare, not random violence—the Seminoles targeted the economic infrastructure sustaining white settlement while liberating enslaved people who had knowledge, skills, and motivation to join their cause. The raiders burned cane fields, demolished sugar works, and torched plantation houses, erasing months of labor and investment in flames. Many enslaved Blacks abandoned their masters during the chaos, swelling Seminole ranks with people who understood both Southern agriculture and the brutality that awaited recapture.

The plantation raids demonstrated sophisticated military planning. Rather than scattered, opportunistic strikes, the attacks rolled down the coast in systematic waves. The Seminoles understood these plantations as military targets—they fed settlers, generated wealth for removal campaigns, and symbolized the expansion that threatened Seminole survival. By destroying them, warriors struck at white confidence and economic viability simultaneously. The attacks also served psychological warfare, proving that no settlement was safe and that Seminoles controlled territory far beyond their supposed confinement. Plantation owners fled to fortified towns or abandoned Florida entirely, leaving valuable land idle and demonstrating that military posts alone couldn't protect dispersed settlers.

The incorporation of liberated slaves into Seminole bands shifted the war's character. Black Seminoles brought military intelligence, knowledge of white tactics, and desperate resolve—they fought knowing recapture meant torture or death. Their presence enraged Southern slaveholders who demanded the Army prioritize slave recovery over Indian removal, complicating military objectives. General Thomas Jesup later acknowledged that suppressing Black Seminole resistance was harder than fighting the Seminoles themselves, calling them the primary obstacle to ending the war. The February raids proved this: by destroying plantations and freeing slaves, Seminoles both weakened their enemy and strengthened their own forces.

The plantation destruction carried long-term consequences. Sugar production along Florida's Atlantic coast collapsed and never fully recovered in the antebellum period. The raids forced the Army to spread thin protecting settlements rather than concentrating forces for offensive campaigns. Settlers who had believed military forts guaranteed safety learned otherwise, creating political pressure that prolonged the war by demanding protection the Army couldn't provide. The attacks also revealed that Seminole resistance wasn't defensive—it was offensive, calculated, and effective at disrupting colonization.

New warrior statues, whose original paints have been preserved, were discovered during ongoing excavations at the site of the Terracotta Army in Xian, one of China's mind-blowing archaeological discoveries. The presence of purple and green pigments sheds light on China's early dynasty dye technology.

The presence of purple pigment particularly surprised archaeologists because purple dye was rare and expensive in ancient times.

Dr. Zhang Wei from Shaanxi Archaeological Institute said, "These warriors must belong to the emperor's special guard unit. Purple is the imperial color in China.” 

Another riddle is where the purple paint comes from. Was it obtained from seashells or was it imported through pre-Silk Road trade?

Most Terracotta soldiers lose their color while underground. However, the reason for the preservation of the paints in these statues is:

🎨Clay layers: The statues are covered with a layer of moisture-proof clay.

🎨Minerals: Mercury (red), malachite (green) and hematite (purple) were used in the pigments.

🎨Sudden burial: fire and flood of 206 BC "sealed" the paints, leaving some of the statues airless.

The Qin terracotta warriors wore a variety of colors. Upper garments included shades of light green, vermilion, maroon, pink, light purple, sky blue, white, and ochre, while trousers were generally light green, though red, sky blue, light purple, and white were also common. In short, the terracotta warriors' clothing was brightly colored, but without a unified color scheme. Among the many colors, light green, vermilion, light purple, and sky blue were the most frequently used, suggesting these were the primary colors of the terracotta warriors' clothing.

The Qin terracotta warriors' painting technique also had many unique features. Observation of cross-sections of terracotta fragments proves that before firing, the surface of the terracotta warriors was coated with fine mud, and also with a thin layer of a glue-like substance (lacquer).  Unfortunately, due to the passage of time and exposure to air, the surface moisture of the terracotta warriors evaporated quickly, causing the lacquer to peel and flake off. What we see now are only the original color of the terracotta body.

One of the surprises was a green-faced terracotta warrior. This is the only terracotta warrior discovered to date whose face is entirely painted green with malachite green pigment, except for its black hair, beard, and pupils. The reason for this remains a mystery. Because of its immense value, this green-faced terracotta warrior (the last image) is the only one prohibited from being exhibited abroad.

THE FIRST "COMMANDOS" IN HISTORY-THE SKIRITES

Every hoplite had his position. But I will tell you about a little known regimen of the Spartan Army-The Skirites/Σκιριτες

When someone drives south to enter Laconia on the way to Sparta, he has to pass through a narrow mountain pass in South Arcadia. In Ancient times, the area was called “Skiritis”/Σκιριτης and the inhabitants were the Skirites. The etymology comes “skiros”/“Skliros”/meaning “hard”.

even though the Skirites weren’t Spartans, they were very valued in the Spartan Army. In fact, according to Diodorus Siculus, the Skirites were always towards the left of the phalanx (the most dangerous position) and around the Spartan King. They carried a shield of a white hawk in a black background.

The Fairchild-Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II: If you can hear it, it's already too late. 

The A-10 technically has an official name. It is even a good one. It inherits a proud title from a magnificent aircraft of an earlier war. But no one actually uses it. Not in practice. Not in the field. Everyone calls it the Warthog, because language evolves toward accuracy.

In an era where modern military aviation measures success in Mach numbers and contrails, the A-10 chooses a different unit of measurement entirely. My Fiat 500L can match its stall speed, and it would struggle to keep up with most civilian aircraft in a flat out race. While other aircraft climb toward the thin, antiseptic air of the stratosphere, the A-10 defines its universe as low and slow. It prefers the altitude where you can still smell the battlefield. It likes to linger. It likes to loiter. It behaves less like a fighter and more like a bad decision that refuses to leave.

Most aircraft experience what engineers politely call a RUDE, a Rapid Unexpected Disassembly Event, when introduced to a surface to air missile. The Warthog treats that encounter as a scheduling inconvenience. It has been documented returning home with an engine missing, half a wing shredded, a vertical stabilizer absent, and its hydraulic systems held together by stubbornness and cable tension. Its unofficial creed can be summarized simply: I did't hear no bell.

Designed to meet Soviet armored columns head on, it would have positively salivated at the sight of the 'forty mile convoy' during the Russian invasion of Ukraine. 

So many tanks, such straight lines and nowhere to go. When your people are pinned down in a desert somewhere and the radio crackles with panic, there is no more comforting sound than the distant roar of two General Electric TF34 turbofan engines. That is the sound of inevitability. You hear it before you hear the gun. And you already know which gun. There is only one.

The A-10 mounts a cannon. No... that statement is technically incorrect.

The cannon mounts an A-10.

The airframe exists because the weapon exists. Everything else is a negotiation with physics to keep that weapon on target and alive long enough to finish the conversation. The engines sit high so gravel and debris do not kill them when it lands on unfinished dirt airfields. The wings are broad so the aircraft can loiter like a patient vulture. The landing gear is brutal because roads-as-runways are a luxury for sexier aircraft. The cockpit is wrapped in titanium because the pilot is the most fragile component of the system.

In every conflict since its birth, the A-10 has been declared obsolete by people who have never needed one. In every conflict, it has then been sent out anyway and asked to do exactly what it was built to do: Destroy anything in front of its cannon and render close-air-support without equal.

It has done so with terrifying consistency.

The General Electric GAU-8/A Avenger is a thirty millimeter, hydraulically driven, seven-barrel rotary autocannon roughly the size and temperament of a Volkswagen Beetle with unresolved anger issues. Fully assembled, the gun system represents roughly sixteen percent of the aircraft’s total empty weight before ammunition is even considered. Because the cannon is so central to the aircraft’s balance and center of gravity, removing it requires installing a jack under the tail to keep the entire airplane from tipping backward onto its ass. The gun is not payload, it is infrastructure. 

When the Avenger spins up and starts spitting Redbull cans full of caffeinated hate, the recoil physically slows the aircraft. Newtonian physics files a grievance and the pilot has to increase power. The sound of the gun is not a bark or a crack but a continuous metallic roar that infantry recognize instantly and enemies never forget. The rounds arrive in such density that the target does not so much explode as vaporize. The GAU-8 is optimized for a specific distance, a specific dive angle, and a specific kind of problem. It does not spray. It carves its name into memories with 30mm precision.

Everything else the A-10 carries is just supportive doctrine. Mavericks for standoff tank murder. Laser guided bombs for modern diplomacy. Rocket pods for when nuance is not invited. Sidewinders for self defense against anything foolish enough to challenge an aircraft whose primary job description is “stay and fight.” Countermeasure pods, flares, and chaff hang beneath the wings. They do not make it invulnerable. They make it take a lot of effort to kill this thing, while it and everything in the area is trying to kill you right back. 

The A-10 doesn't' care much about air superiority or stealth corridors or anything like that. It cares about tanks, trenches, and people on the ground who need something loud and reliable to show up overhead when they are in trouble. 

Every attempt to retire it runs into the same problem: nothing else does this job the same way. Precision weapons can replace its reach. Drones can replace its persistence. Fighters can replace its flexibility. None of them replace its presence. When a Warthog arrives, the battlefield changes shape. Nothing this side of a Specter Gunship can do that, and the A-10 is so much more personal.

Dr. Melaku E. Bayen and the Institutionalization of Black Internationalism, 1900–1940

Dr. Melaku E. Bayen (1900–1940) occupies a critical yet underexamined position in twentieth-century Ethiopian and Black Atlantic history. An Ethiopian physician educated in the United States, Bayen became the principal architect of Ethiopia’s organized political relationship with African Americans and Afro-Caribbeans during the Fascist Italian occupation of Ethiopia (1936–1941). This essay examines Bayen’s early life, education, wartime service, and diasporic activism, with particular attention to his founding of the Ethiopian World Federation (EWF) in 1937. It argues that Bayen transformed diffuse diasporic sympathy for Ethiopia into an institutionalized, transnational political movement linking Ethiopian sovereignty to Black internationalism.

⸻

Introduction

The Italian invasion of Ethiopia in 1935 provoked one of the most significant episodes of global Black political mobilization in the twentieth century. While scholars have extensively documented the responses of African Americans and Afro-Caribbeans to the crisis, the Ethiopian agents who actively shaped and organized this mobilization remain less well studied. Among them, Dr. Melaku E. Bayen stands out as the most consequential.

Bayen was not merely a symbolic representative of Ethiopia abroad. Acting under imperial authority, he served as a diplomat, organizer, publisher, and institutional founder whose efforts helped anchor Ethiopia at the center of Black international political consciousness during the interwar period. His work laid the organizational foundations for later repatriation movements, citizenship discourse, and sustained diasporic engagement with Ethiopia.

⸻

Early Life and Education

Melaku Bayen was born on April 27, 1900, in Wollo Province, Ethiopia, to Grazmach Bayen and Woizero Desta. Following his family’s relocation to Harar Province, Bayen attended a church school where his intellectual aptitude attracted the attention of Crown Prince Tafari Makonnen. At a time when Ethiopia was deliberately cultivating a modern, internationally educated elite, Bayen was selected as one of three promising students—alongside Beshahwored Habtewold and Worku Gobena—to pursue education abroad.

In January 1921, the students were sent to British India, where they encountered colonial pedagogical environments that openly asserted the inevitability of European domination over Ethiopia. These experiences reinforced their resolve to continue their education either in Ethiopia or in the United States, which they perceived as politically distinct from European colonial powers.

Armed with a letter of introduction from Crown Prince Tafari Makonnen addressed to U.S. President Warren G. Harding, the students traveled to the United States. They were received at the White House, where Harding advised them to enroll at Marietta College in Ohio, his alma mater. All three were admitted and commenced their studies.

Upon completion of their undergraduate education, two of the students returned to Ethiopia. Bayen, however, remained in the United States, undertaking further studies at The Ohio State University before enrolling in the Howard University College of Medicine in Washington, D.C. His medical training at Howard placed him within one of the most significant intellectual and professional centers of African American life during the interwar period. Bayen graduated as a physician, becoming one of the earliest U.S.-trained Ethiopian doctors.

⸻

Service to Ethiopia and the Italian Invasion

In the early 1930s, Dr. Bayen returned to Ethiopia and entered public service as a physician. His return coincided with mounting international tensions as Fascist Italy prepared for military aggression. When Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, Bayen served as physician and aide to Emperor Haile Selassie I, assuming medical and logistical responsibilities connected to large numbers of Ethiopian combatants.

During the conflict, Bayen witnessed the Italian military’s systematic use of chemical weapons, including mustard gas, against Ethiopian soldiers and civilians. These atrocities were later cited by Emperor Haile Selassie in his historic address to the League of Nations in 1936, in which he condemned the aerial deployment of poison gas and appealed to the international community for justice and collective security.

⸻

Ethiopia’s Turn to the Black Diaspora

Following the occupation of Ethiopia, Haile Selassie and his advisers recognized that conventional European diplomacy had failed. As a result, they sought to mobilize global public opinion, particularly among people of African descent who viewed Ethiopia as a symbol of Black sovereignty and independence. Dr. Bayen was selected to carry out this mission in the United States.

Arriving in September 1936, Bayen established himself in Harlem, then the epicenter of African American political, cultural, and religious life. His strategy differed from earlier, more informal appeals to diasporic sentiment. Bayen emphasized organization, legal recognition, and sustained political pressure.

⸻

The Ethiopian World Federation

In 1937, Dr. Bayen founded the Ethiopian World Federation, Incorporated (EWF), an organization officially sanctioned by the Ethiopian government-in-exile. The EWF sought to unite Africans, African Americans, and Afro-Caribbeans in active support of Ethiopia’s liberation and future reconstruction.

The Federation functioned as a vehicle for political advocacy, fundraising, and public protest. Bayen also established The Voice of Ethiopia, a publication designed to disseminate information about the occupation and counter Fascist propaganda. Under his leadership, the EWF attracted the support of prominent African American intellectuals and activists, including W.E.B. Du Bois, as well as ministers, community leaders, and organizations throughout the Caribbean, the United States, and Europe.

Bayen explicitly framed Ethiopia’s struggle as inseparable from the global struggle for Black dignity and self-determination. This framing resonated deeply with African American and Afro-Caribbean communities already shaped by Pan-Africanism, Garveyism, and Ethiopianism. Through mass demonstrations—some numbering more than 20,000 participants—the EWF transformed diasporic sympathy into visible, organized resistance to Fascist imperialism.

⸻

Death and Legacy

Dr. Melaku Bayen’s relentless pace took a severe physical toll. In May 1940, at the age of forty, he died in New York from complications associated with extreme physical and emotional strain. He did not live to witness Ethiopia’s liberation in 1941, an outcome for which his efforts had played a meaningful role.

He was buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx, far from his homeland, yet firmly within the landscape of Black diasporic history. His legacy endured through the continued activities of the Ethiopian World Federation, which later became central to repatriation initiatives, land grants such as Shashamane, and enduring diasporic claims of moral and political relationship to Ethiopia.

⸻

Conclusion

Dr. Melaku E. Bayen occupies a pivotal place in the history of twentieth-century Black internationalism. More than a physician or exile activist, he served as a state-sanctioned architect of Ethiopia’s engagement with the Black Atlantic world. By institutionalizing diasporic solidarity through the Ethiopian World Federation, Bayen transformed Ethiopia from a distant symbol into an organized political cause embraced by African Americans and Afro-Caribbeans alike.

His life demonstrates that Ethiopia’s survival during one of its darkest periods depended not only on diplomacy among states, but on the mobilization of transnational Black political consciousness. Bayen’s work stands as a foundational chapter in the modern history of Ethiopia–diaspora relations and deserves sustained scholarly attention.
