في Avengers: Infinity War (2018)، كان دور سبايدرمان أكثر من مجرد دعم قتالي؛ كان القلب الإنساني وسط حرب كونية. يظهر بيتر باركر كبطل ما زال مراهقًا، لكنه لا يتردد لحظة عندما يرى سفينة ثانوس في سماء نيويورك. يندفع إلى المعركة بدافع المسؤولية الخالصة، حتى دون إذن، مؤكدًا أن البطولة عنده قرار فوري لا يحتاج حسابات.

مشاركته مع آيرون مان ودكتور سترينج في الفضاء أبرزت تطوّره الكبير. بدلة الـIron Spider منحتْه قدرات إضافية، لكن ما ميّزه فعليًا كان ذكاؤه وسرعة بديهته، خاصة في خطة إسقاط إيبوني ماو مستلهمًا أفكارًا من الثقافة الشعبية. وفي مواجهة ثانوس على تيتان، كان سبايدرمان عنصرًا حاسمًا في تنفيذ الخطة، متنقلًا بخفة بين الحطام ومحاولًا انتزاع قفاز اللانهاية.

أكثر لحظاته تأثيرًا جاءت في النهاية. مشهد تلاشيه بين ذراعي توني ستارك لم يكن مجرد خسارة بطل، بل لحظة كسرت الجمهور وأظهرت هشاشته رغم شجاعته. خوفه الواضح وهو يقول إنه لا يريد الرحيل جسّد أن سبايدرمان، مهما كان قويًا، يبقى شابًا يخاف الموت لكنه يواجهه بشجاعة.

في Infinity War، لم يكن سبايدرمان الأقوى في ساحة المعركة، لكنه كان أحد أكثر الشخصيات تأثيرًا عاطفيًا—بطل صغير في سنّه، عظيم في تضحيته.

Sud Bosne i Hercegovine je potvrdio optužnicu protiv optuženih Dragana Jevtića, Slavka Bogićevića i Damjana Lazarevića, koji se terete da su počinili krivično djelo genocid iz Krivičnog zakona Bosne i Hercegovine (KZBiH).
Optuženi se, između ostalog, terete da su, za vrijeme široko rasprostranjenog i sistematičnog napada preduzetog od 11. jula 1995. do 1. novembra 1995. godine, od pripadnika VRS-a i MUP-a RS, usmjerenog na pripadnike bošnjačkog naroda u Zaštićenoj zoni UN-a Srebrenica, tokom kojeg napada je izvedena operacija trajnog i prisilnog preseljenja cjelokupnog bošnjačkog civilnog stanovništva, operacija zarobljavanja, zatvaranja i pogubljenja vojno sposobnih muškaraca Bošnjaka i dječaka iz srebreničke enklave, te operacija njihovog ukopa, iskopa, te ponovnog ukopa na drugim lokacijama u cilju sakrivanja dokaza, svjesno pružili pomoć članovima udruženog zločinačkog poduhvata, na način da je, optuženi Dragan Jevtić u svojstvu v.d. komandira Inžinjerijske čete 1. zvorničke pješadijske brigade VRS-a, izdavao naređenja i prenosio naređenja njegovih nadređenih iz komande Zvorničke brigade, da se izvrše pripreme prije ubistava zatočenika na lokacijama za njihov ukop, kao i pripreme teške građevinske mehanizacije, te kopanje prostora za masovne grobnice.
Navedeno je podrazumijevalo naređivanje pripadnicima Inžinjerijske čete da izvrše pripremu i dopremu radnih mašina na mjesta egzekucija, zatim osiguravanje neophodnog goriva, te organiziranje ljudstva i mašinista za rad na kopanju jama prije i tokom ubijanja zarobljenika, da se u toku i odmah po završetku ubijanja izvrši ukop osoba lišenih života, upotrebom teške građevinske mehanizacije, koje naredbe su provodili Slavko Bogićević, u svojstvu pomoćnika komandira za moral i vjerske poslove, ujedno zamjenik komandira Inžinjerijske čete i Damjan Lazarević, u svojstvu komandira voda Inžinjerijske čete 1. Zvorničke pješadijske brigade, izvodeći pripremne radnje ukopa ubijenih, dajući konkretna uputstva na terenu pripadnicima Inžinjerske čete Zvorničke brigade VRS-a, tako što su lično na lokalitetima određivali precizne pozicije za kopanje primarnih grobnica, izdavali usmena uputstva mašinistima za kopanje i zagrtanje masovnih grobnica, te neposredno rukovodili procesom ukopavanja tijela ubijenih u jame radi prikrivanja tragova, neposredno nakon izvršenih streljanja zatočenika.
Tačkom 2. potvrđene optužnice optuženi Slavko Bogićević i Damjan Lazarević terete se da su tokom septembra i oktobra 1995. godine, zajedno sa drugim pripadnicima Inžinjerijske čete, po naređenjima viših starješina iz Zvorničke brigade i Glavnog štaba VRS, učestvovali u organiziranom premještanju posmrtnih ostataka iz primarnih masovnih grobnica u tzv. sekundarne grobnice, koja operacija je bila sastavni dio masovnih ubistava zatočenih Bošnjaka i dječaka iz Zaštićene zone Srebrenica, na način da su upravljali konkretnim operacijama na terenu, koordinirali izvođenje radova u dogovoru s organima bezbjednosti Zvorničke brigade i komandom Glavnog štaba VRS, te vršili organizaciju i angažovanje ljudstva uz nadzor nad tim aktivnostima, uključujući i lični nadzor nad radom teške mehanizacije pri formiranju sekundarnih grobnica i finalnom skrivanju masovnih grobnica, a sve s ciljem prikrivanja tragova i izbjegavanjem eventualnog otkrivanja pomenutih masovnih grobnica, saopćeno je iz Suda BiH.

Genocide is the story, not antisemitism
   
(John Menadue, Pearls and Irritations)

The Australian government’s response to Gaza, and its handling of President Isaac Herzog’s visit, has blurred the line between antisemitism and criticism of Israel. The result is deeper division, weaker democracy and greater risk to Jewish communities.

Following the state sanctioned violence in Sydney, Anthony Albanese told us that we need to lower the temperature. But it is Anthony Albanese who has raised the temperature with his scant concern for the murder of over 70,000 Palestinians, mainly women and children. He refuses to let the word genocide pass his lips.

Correspondence and analysis in The Lancet magazine suggests that in fact the number murdered at the hands of Israel and the IDF maybe as high as 240,000.

To add to his failure, Albanese then invites President Herzog to Australia. Herzog has, through both omission and commission abetted the Israeli genocide. He has told the world a litany of lies about the IDF protecting civilians and that Israel is obeying international law. He heads an apartheid, genocidal and criminal state that is deliberately killing women and children and breaches numerous international laws and decisions of the UN.

It is just not true – as Israel wants us to believe – that the Hamas attack in October 2023 started the war. Israel has been killing Palestinians and stealing their land for decades. In 1948 Palestinians owned 94 per cent of all land. Then came the Nakba and further occupation and ethnic cleansing. Now Palestinians own only 18 per cent of the land with annexation continuing in the West Bank. Even at the very time Herzog was getting red carpet treatment in Australia, the Israeli Finance Minister said that the moves on the West Bank “will continue to kill the idea of a Palestinian State.”

Anthony Albanese is rightly concerned for Jewish families after the horrible Bondi killings but surely an Australian rabbi would be more appropriate to console Jewish families in Australia? Why does the lobby always invoke Israel? Time and time again it blurs the distinction between Jews and the State of Israel. But it only blurs the distinction when it suits. It avoids invoking the link to Israel when it comes to genocide.

The lobby has been exercising destructive power for decades. Its role as an agent of foreign influence for Israel should be publicly examined.

Herzog has gone well beyond consolation for Jewish families which Albanese tells us is the reason for the visit. Much of Herzog’s public comments have been very political. He - said that he wanted to strengthen Australia’s relations with Israel. - accused pro-Palestinian protesters in Australia of undermining Israel. - expressed frustration that more was not being done to tackle antisemitism in Australia. - told Jews to “wear Zionism with pride”. - even pulled the rug from under our Prime Minister in saying that a two-state solution is not on the agenda.

In fact, the Israeli government along with Herzog is opposed to a two-state solution in any shape or form. That is why Netanyahu funded Hamas for years to weaken the influence of President Abas. Netanyahu did everything possible to destroy any popular Palestinian leadership. That is why the ‘Palestinian Mandela’, Marwan Barghouti has been brutalised in an Israel prison for 22 years. Over 6,000 Palestinian hostages are still in Israeli jails.

Herzog could not have been more political on this visit to Australia. Anthony Albanese sheepishly raised a few issues with Herzog but avoided any discussion of the genocide.

And then we had the shameful performance of the NSW Premier Minns who has for over two years supported the Zionist position and been highly critical of those who are concerned about the ceaseless killing of Palestinians. With his legislation on hate speech and support of the Zionist lobby it is not surprising that the NSW police went on a rampage. Many would be justified in thinking that Minns had their back.

The NSW Police Commissioner could tender his resignation, knowing it would be quite safe to do so. He would know that the Premier would not accept it. Instead, the Premier might present him with a medal! No surprise that Minns said there would be no independent inquiry!

Fortunately the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission has just announced that the actions of the NSW police will be examined. The LECC’s website says: “The Commission is separate from and completely independent of the NSW Police Force and NSW Crime Commission. Its principal functions are to detect, investigate and expose serious misconduct and serious maladministration within the NSW Police Force and the NSW Crime Commission.”

What a contrast Sydney was on Monday when all other protests around Australia were well managed by cooperation between protesters and the police. That he was not so in Sydney. Professor Ben Saul of Sydney University and UN Special Rapporteur of Human Rights and Counter Terrorism pointed out that “domestic rights have been suppressed by illegal laws and aggressive policing and NSW is now one of the most draconian anti protest jurisdictions in the democratic world”

Take a bow Premier Minns. The lobby must be well pleased.

For over two years we have had hundreds of peaceful protests across Australia against the genocide. There have been very few antisemitic incidents.

Undoubtedly some of the antisemitic behaviour in Australia is homegrown. Most of it, however, is the result of the barbaric cruelty inflicted by Israel on the Palestinian people. It is time Herzog, Albanese and others sheeted home responsibility to Israel for the spike in antisemitism which is occurring around the world. It will continue until there is peace with justice for Palestinians.

As Robert Manne put it so clearly about Israeli denial, “don’t mention the war.”

When will the Zionist lobbyists do some honest soul searching? Has it ever crossed their minds that Jews are less safe because of Gaza and their misuse and abuse of the term antisemitic?

Free speech and the right to organise and protest is also being challenged across the western world, as Professor Ben Saul has pointed out. A new McCarthyism is afoot. Now it is not communists under the bed – it is people who oppose genocide. In many Western countries universities and others are being threatened and defunded because of their support for Palestinians. We saw this McCarthyism at work recently directed against Grace Tame for her challenging speech at the Sydney rally.

Seventy thousand or even two hundred thousand murdered Palestinians is of little concern to our government. When Anthony Albanese and Chris Minns are prepared to mouth the word “genocide” the divisions they have created will begin to heal.

The Herzog visit exposed again the duplicity of Israel and the failure of our government to stand against genocide.

Criticism of Israeli genocide is not antisemitic.

GSU “G” COMPANY: THE PRESIDENTIAL GUARD UNIT 🇰🇪
GSU “G” Company is widely recognized as the elite Presidential Guard element within Kenya’s General Service Unit (GSU), a specialized paramilitary formation under the National Police Service. Unlike the more than 20 field companies that conduct regional security operations, G Company’s core mandate is the protection of the President, Deputy President, and key State installations. Its role places it at the highest tier of VVIP security within Kenya’s policing structure.
The General Service Unit itself was established in 1948 and reorganized in 1953 to enhance its operational effectiveness. Over time, it has grown into a highly trained paramilitary wing tasked with counter-terrorism, riot control, anti-banditry operations, and anti-poaching missions. Within this broader structure, G Company operates as a distinct and specialized formation dedicated almost exclusively to executive protection and the safeguarding of critical national leadership assets.
GSU field companies are alphabetically designated from “A” to “Y” (excluding O, P, and U), with most deployed across various regions to handle public order management and high-risk security operations. In contrast, G Company is primarily stationed at high-security installations such as State House Nairobi and other State Lodges. It frequently works alongside the elite Recce Company during high-threat situations, reinforcing Kenya’s top-level protective security framework.
As a result, GSU G Company remains one of the most discreet yet strategically vital units in Kenya’s security architecture — a silent shield around the country’s highest office.

Peter McAleese built a reputation as one of the most hard-edged figures ever associated with Britain’s elite forces, his life reflecting both exceptional soldiering skill and a turbulent personal record. Born in 1942, he began his military career as a teenager when he enlisted in the British Army and trained with the Parachute Regiment at Aldershot, going on to serve with 1 Para’s mortar platoon. In the early 1960s he passed selection for the Special Air Service and joined D Squadron, seeing operational service during the Aden Emergency in Aden. His time in the regiment, however, was punctuated by disciplinary problems that periodically returned him to conventional airborne duties, including postings to Cyprus and Bahrain.

McAleese later re-entered the SAS and served with 16 (Air) Troop, taking part in jungle operations in Borneo during the Indonesian Confrontation. Despite demonstrating strong fieldcraft and combat leadership, further misconduct again interrupted his special forces career, and he spent his final army period as a sergeant-instructor with 1 Para before leaving the service in 1969. The early 1970s proved troubled: he received prison sentences for violent offences, a phase he later acknowledged as a destructive chapter that contrasted sharply with his professional military competence.

After his release he sought a new start abroad, joining the National Liberation Front of Angola as a mercenary during the Angolan Civil War, where he briefly assumed command after the capture of Costas Georgiou. He subsequently moved to Rhodesia, serving as an NCO with the Rhodesian SAS and later with Special Branch, before continuing his career with the South African Defence Force’s 44 Parachute Brigade, helping develop reconnaissance pathfinder capabilities. McAleese’s life remains a striking study in extremes — battlefield professionalism set against personal controversy — and his name endures in military history discussions as a figure both respected and debated.

Why the Battle of Kettle Creek Was Significant

Even though it was a relatively small engagement, the Battle of Kettle Creek (February 14, 1779) turned out to be one of the most important Patriot victories in the Southern backcountry during the American Revolution.
1. It shattered British assumptions about Loyalist support
British commanders believed the Southern backcountry was full of Loyalists ready to rise up and join them. Kettle Creek proved that assumption wrong.
After the Loyalist militia was defeated, British officials realized they did not have the local support they expected, a miscalculation that weakened their entire Southern strategy.
2. It was a morale‑boosting Patriot victory
Patriot militia under Andrew Pickens were outnumbered yet still managed to overwhelm the Loyalist column. The win energized Patriot forces in Georgia and the Carolinas at a moment when British momentum seemed strong.
3. It disrupted the British plan to consolidate control of Georgia
The Loyalist force was marching to join British troops in Augusta. Their defeat helped convince the British commander in Augusta to abandon the city, undermining British control of the interior.
4. It weakened Loyalist recruitment
Many of the Loyalists who escaped the battle gave up the war effort entirely, reducing the pool of local fighters the British desperately needed.
5. It contributed to the eventual failure of the British Southern Campaign
Because the British misjudged Loyalist strength and lost a key militia force, their broader Southern strategy began to unravel—one of the factors that ultimately led to their surrender at Yorktown.

Campism and Chemical Denial: The Western Left’s Syria Failure

For 15 years to date, much of the Western “anti-imperialist” left has continued to insist that its hostility toward the Syrian revolution was principled. Leftists were opposing US intervention! Rejecting regime change! Refusing to be manipulated by another Iraq-style war narrative! 

Yet many of the same 'anti-imperialist' voices enthusiastically celebrated and defended the US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces, whose territorial survival depended on sustained American airpower and military partnership from 2014 onward. Those who rightly condemned indefinite detention at Guantanamo Bay detention camp were largely silent about tens of thousands, many of them women and children, held indefinitely for years without charge or trial in camps such as Al-Hol camp and Al-Roj camp. They denounced “imperialist propaganda,” yet amplified Kremlin-aligned conspiracy theories accusing Syrian revolutionaries of staging chemical attacks against themselves. The principle, it turns out, was less opposition to intervention than selective outrage dressed as doctrine.

From 2011 onward, Syrians rose against a hereditary dictatorship that had perfected detention, torture, and extermination over decades. As the uprising militarised, they found themselves fighting not only the Assad regime but also Iranian militias, Russian airpower, ISIS, and an international system increasingly willing to treat their struggle as a geopolitical inconvenience. They did so largely without sustained Western military backing.

Yet instead of solidarity, large segments of the Western left treated the revolution - while refusing to acknowledge it as a revolution -  primarily as a CIA project or a terrorist coup. Prominent figures including leftist elder statesmen like Seymour Hersh and Robert Fisk cast doubt on the regime’s responsibility for major chemical attacks, publishing accounts later dismantled by independent investigators. Jeremy Corbyn and Noam Chomsky echoed or entertained similar scepticism under the banner of resisting Western intervention. The effect was consistent: the burden of proof shifted from a regime with a documented history of mass torture to civilians resisting it.

The justification was familiar. To question the regime narrative was to resist US imperialism. To accept international investigations into chemical attacks was to risk becoming an instrument of Washington. The fact that Russia — not the United States — was the primary external military force reshaping Syria by that stage appeared to complicate the story less than one might expect.

At the same time, another armed actor in Syria was openly partnered with the United States. Originally known as the YPG, this PKK affiliate emerged in 2014 in coordination with US military leadership and operated for years under a US security umbrella. American airpower, logistics, and special forces were indispensable to its territorial control. Yet this arrangement did not provoke sustained anti-imperialist outrage. Instead, it was widely celebrated by the same leftists as a revolutionary democratic experiment. In 2015, the YPG attained a new name, the ‘Syrian Democratic Forces’, at the behest of then-U.S. Special Operations Commander General Raymond Thomas, who explained that he urged the YPG to "change their brand" as the YPG name was problematic due to Turkey's hostility to the PKK.  The YPG, along with other groups, became the core of the SDF in late 2015  in a bid to create a more inclusive, less Kurdish-centric image (although the SDF is still routinely referred to as “the Kurds”). The "Democratic" in Syrian Democratic Forces was specifically added to meet the rebranding suggestion, with General Thomas describing its inclusion as a “stroke of genius”.

The PKK, a longstanding Assad regime ally, had been designated for decades as a terrorist organisation by the United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom – this  history was disregarded while its affiliate proved useful for Washington. In areas under the SDF’s control in northeast Syria, meanwhile, dissent was silenced and rival Kurdish political parties reported harassment and attacks on offices. Assyrian media outlets and activists accused local Kurdish militia elements of abuses against minority communities worse than those of ISIS. Human rights organisations documented child recruitment, political suppression, torture, and disappearances by the SDF.

None of this erased the SDF’s role in fighting ISIS. But it certainly complicates the ‘anti-imperialist’ mythology.

More troubling still was the detention regime that developed in the aftermath of ISIS’s territorial defeat. As internationally respected human rights organizations, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the Syrian Network for Human Rights, documented in regular reports, tens of thousands of men, women, and children were held for years without charge or trial in prisons and camps across northeast Syria. Reports detailed arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, and in some cases torture. The system operated within the framework of the US-led anti-ISIS coalition.

Western activists who had marched against Guantanamo did not fill the streets over al-Hol. The War on Terror, it seemed, was objectionable when administered by Washington directly, but tolerable when subcontracted.

Recent developments have underscored the inconsistency. In early 2026, detainees considered active ISIS suspects began to be transferred for prosecution in Iraq through arrangements involving the US-led coalition and Syrian authorities. Plans were announced to close long-standing detention camps and resolve the status of the women and children who had languished there for years. Whatever one’s view of the new Syrian government, the shift toward conventional judicial processing stands in contrast to the indefinite limbo that preceded it.

The contrast is stark. Syrian revolutionaries — fighting Assad, Iran, Russia, and ISIS — were treated as potential extremists or imperial proxies. A US-partnered militia, rooted in an internationally designated armed movement, was framed as the embodiment of democratic resistance. Documented abuses were contextualised. Chemical attacks were questioned. Detention without trial became a regrettable necessity rather than a moral scandal.

Opposition to US militarism is not hypocrisy. Selective opposition is. If the standard is that foreign intervention and indefinite detention are wrong, then that standard must apply regardless of which faction benefits. If the principle is solidarity with oppressed people, then it must extend to Syrians who rose against a regime whose prisons became symbols of industrialised cruelty.

The Syrian revolution was not a branding exercise. It was a revolt against a hereditary dictatorship that met peaceful protest with bullets and later met defiance with barrel bombs and chemical agents. Syrians who endured siege, bombardment, fragmentation, and abandonment did not wait for Western intellectual approval. They persisted and endured unimaginable suffering and loss because the alternative was tyranny and further murderous subjugation for future generations.

Campist leftists and others, whose own worst suffering was a nasty look from policemen at a student protest, condescendingly treated Syrians’ heroic persistence as naivety. Others dismissed it as manipulation. A few insisted it was all a façade.

History has a way of clarifying such judgments, however. Those who faced airstrikes and torture chambers in pursuit of freedom require no mythology. They proved their seriousness and their heroism in the only arena that counts. Tankies can continue debating imperialism in theory. Syrians confronted it — in multiple forms — and won their freedom in practice.

"Sixty-two hours. Thirty events. One woman among 103 men. And when it was over, she'd rewritten history without saying a word.
First Lt. Gabrielle A. White didn't compete to make a statement. She competed to win.
At just 25 years old, the West Point graduate became the first woman ever to complete the Best Ranger Competition—a three-day gauntlet so brutal that 36 of the original 52 teams couldn't finish. Alongside her teammate, Capt. Seth Deltenre, she placed 14th. Every other team that started was made up of men.
The Best Ranger Competition isn't designed for completion. It's designed to break you.
Over 62 hours with minimal sleep, teams face relentless challenges that test every dimension of a soldier: water survival in full gear, obstacle courses that destroy your hands, marksmanship when your vision blurs from exhaustion, helocasting—leaping from helicopters into open water—and navigating 60+ miles of terrain while your body screams to quit. It's been called harder than the Ironman triathlon, the CrossFit Games, and multiple marathons combined—stacked back-to-back.
For four decades, it was considered a men's arena. The proving ground for the Army's most elite warriors.
White, already an infantry officer decorated with multiple honors and one of only eight women to earn both Ranger and Sapper tabs, approached it the same way she approaches everything: with quiet competence. No fanfare. No proclamations. Just preparation and performance.
She carried 40-pound rucks. She scaled rope bridges. She breached barriers. She fired weapons with precision while her muscles trembled. And when other teams dropped out—strong teams, experienced teams—she kept moving forward.
What makes this achievement extraordinary isn't that a woman did it. It's that she did it at the same standard required of everyone else, proving what should have always been obvious: excellence has nothing to do with gender and everything to do with will.
White graduated Ranger School in 2022, making her one of only 154 women to earn that distinction since the program opened to female soldiers in 2015. She was a basketball standout at West Point, a systems engineering graduate, and a soldier who understood that the only way to change what's possible is to do what hasn't been done.
When asked about making history, her response was simple: ""I didn't go into this to be the first. I went in to compete and to prove to myself that I could.""
The battlefield doesn't ask your gender. It asks if you can perform when everything is on the line.
First Lt. Gabrielle White answered that question for 62 straight hours.
And when the competition ended, 14 teams remained standing. She was among them—not because she's a woman who competed, but because she's a Ranger who excelled.
Sometimes the most powerful statements are made without words. Just action. Just results. Just showing up and getting it done.
That's what excellence looks like.

The Downfall of Achai Wiir: When the Money Faded: The Rise, Fall, and Silence Around Achai Wiir

The story of Achai Wiir feels like one of those sharp, cinematic rises and crashes that make you pause and rethink how fragile status really is.

She wasn’t just wealthy. She was visible. Achai Wiir became known as one of South Sudan’s most talked-about businesswomen — generous, flashy, and surrounded by people. Her home was a gathering place. Her phone never stopped ringing. When someone needed school fees, hospital bills covered, or startup capital for a small business, her name came up first. That kind of influence builds fast, and it builds loud.

Money can turn a person into an institution.

But institutions can crumble.

In what many describe as a shockingly short period of time, her financial empire reportedly began to unravel. Business ventures failed. Trusted associates allegedly mismanaged funds. Some say investments collapsed. Others whisper about lifestyle pressures and people draining resources faster than they were replenished. The details vary depending on who tells the story, but the pattern is common in economic history: rapid growth without durable foundations often leads to rapid decline. Wealth built on unstable networks can evaporate like mist under noon sun.

And then came the illness.

The woman who once carried others financially is now reportedly bedridden, fighting for her health. The same phone that once rang nonstop is now quieter. The same crowds that filled her space have thinned out.

That contrast is painful.

In the middle of this, South Sudanese singer Lady Kola stepped forward publicly. She used her Facebook page not to gossip, not to speculate, but to remind people of who Achai was when she had strength and resources. Her words were simple and heavy:

 “It truly breaks my heart. I remember when my sister Achai Wiir had money everyone was calling, checking in, trying to be close to her. Today, when she is at her lowest and fighting for her health, when she needs prayers, support, and encouragement the most, there is silence.
It hurts to see how quickly people disappear when there is nothing to gain. Support should not only come during good times. Real love and real community show up when someone is struggling.
I am deeply disappointed. In moments like this, we see who genuinely cares. I pray that one day we learn to stand with each other not only in prosperity, but also in pain.”

That message hit hard because it exposed something universal. Prosperity attracts proximity. Pain reveals loyalty.

Now, about the accusations.

Some people blame her downfall on alleged involvement with witchcraft or “signing herself to the devil.” That narrative is emotionally powerful, especially in communities where spiritual explanations often fill the gaps left by incomplete financial or medical information. But here’s the grounded truth: there is no verified evidence that supernatural contracts cause financial collapse or illness. Economic downturns, betrayal, poor financial planning, health conditions — these are observable, documented phenomena. Human beings prefer mystical explanations when reality feels too random or unfair. It gives chaos a storyline.

It’s more intellectually honest to say: we don’t have confirmed facts about the exact causes of her financial and medical struggles. Speculation may comfort some, but it doesn’t equal truth.

What is clear is this:

Many people who once depended on Achai Wiir financially are now quiet. The social ecosystem around wealth is transactional more often than we admit. When the resource center disappears, so do the orbiting satellites.

There’s a philosophical lesson here, and it’s not preachy — it’s practical. Wealth is a tool, not an identity. Popularity is a season, not a guarantee. Community that depends only on money is not community; it’s a marketplace.

Achai’s story forces a mirror in front of society. Who do we stand with when there’s nothing to gain? Who do we pray for when the cameras are gone?

In the long arc of human history, empires have fallen, tycoons have gone bankrupt, kings have died poor, and celebrities have faded into silence. What lasts is how people were treated when they were strong — and how they were treated when they were weak.

Her situation is not just gossip. It’s a social case study on loyalty, fragility, and the psychology of wealth.

And if there’s one forward-looking takeaway, it’s this: build systems, not hype. Build health, not just status. Build real relationships that survive economic weather. Because storms are not a possibility — they’re a certainty.

It frequently works alongside the elite Recce Company during high-threat situations, reinforcing Kenya’s top-level protective security framework.

Upper Nile Governors Are Only Good At Painting Shops 

By Dut Nyok - Pantem 

I don’t know whether our leaders bewitched us or we bewitched ourselves.
Once upon a time, Malakal was not just a town, it was a statement. Mention its name anywhere in South Sudan and people would nod with respect. Trade was alive. Streets had stories. Buildings stood with pride.
Today? Don’t be surprised if someone whispers, “Is Malakal still in South Sudan or did it relocate quietly?”
Since 2016, when the guns went silent in Malakal, we expected rebuilding. We expected healing. We expected development.
What did we get?
White paint.
Blue paint.
And more paint.
Our governors discovered their true calling  interior decorators of tragedy.
Businesses are forced to paint their shops white 🤍 and blue 💙. They say these are the “state colors.” Maybe they are. But I am still confused how paint replaces policy, and how decoration equals development.

Is the Ministry of Housing now the Ministry of Aesthetic Affairs?
Because if painting shops was an Olympic sport, Upper Nile would bring home gold, silver, and bronze.
Meanwhile.
Unoccupied houses are collapsing like tired elders. Some buildings were burned and never rebuilt. Entire neighborhoods look like abandoned movie sets. The town has become an ugly agglomeration of ruins and survival.
But at least the shops are color coordinated.

Maybe tourists will come and say,
“Wow, the destruction is painful. but the color balance is impressive.” How i hope for this day to come.
Development is not a paintbrush.
Leadership is not a color chart.
There are roads to fix.
Hospitals to equip.
Schools to rebuild.
Youth to empower.
Investors to attract.
Instead, we are measuring progress in liters of paint.
Let me be clear: this is not about colors. White is beautiful. Blue is peaceful. But peace is not painted; it is built. Growth is not brushed, it is planned.
Malakal deserves more than cosmetic governance.
We don’t need governors who specialize in repainting shops. We need leaders who can rebuild a city. Leaders who understand that revival is not about uniform colors but unified vision.
Because one day, if nothing changes, someone might genuinely ask:
“Was Malakal ever great, or was that just a story painted in white and blue?”
And that question.
will not be funny anymore.

Si Prof. Nur Misuari ay isang Tausog lider at politiko na kilala bilang tagapagtatag ng Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). Ipinanganak siya noong 1939 sa Tapul, Sulu. Bago pumasok sa pakikibaka, nagtapos siya sa kolehiyo at naging propesor sa University of the Philippines, na nagbigay sa kanya ng kaalaman sa pamahalaan, politika, at edukasyon.

Noong 1970s, itinatag niya ang MNLF bilang tugon sa mga hinaing ng mga Moro sa Mindanao na naglalayong magkaroon ng sariling pamahalaan at proteksyon sa kanilang kultura at relihiyon. Ang MNLF ay naging pangunahing grupo sa pakikipaglaban para sa karapatan ng mga Muslim sa rehiyon, lalo na sa ilalim ng pamahalaan ni Ferdinand Marcos. Ang kanyang pamumuno ay nagbigay sa kanya ng malaking impluwensya sa rehiyon at nagpatibay sa kilusan para sa Moro self-determination.

Noong 1996, lumagda ang MNLF at ang pamahalaan ng Pilipinas sa isang kasunduang pangkapayapaan sa administrasyon ni Fidel V. Ramos. Bilang bahagi ng kasunduan, itinalaga si Misuari bilang gobernador ng Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM). Ang hakbang na ito ay nagbigay daan sa kanya upang makilahok sa legal at pampulitikang proseso, sa halip na armadong pakikibaka, at nagsilbing simbolo ng pag-asa para sa kapayapaan sa rehiyon.

Gayunpaman, hindi naging madali ang kanyang pamumuno. Nasangkot si Misuari sa ilang armadong pag-aalsa at tensyon sa rehiyon, kabilang ang insidente sa Zamboanga City noong 2013, na nagresulta sa labanan sa pagitan ng kanyang mga tagasuporta at pwersa ng gobyerno. 

Sa kabuuan, si Nur Misuari ay isang mahalagang personalidad sa kasaysayan ng Mindanao at sa kilusan para sa Moro self-determination. Bagamat kontrobersyal, siya ay kinikilala bilang simbolo ng Moro nationalism at determinasyon. Ang kanyang buhay ay nagpapakita ng kahirapan at tagumpay ng mga kilusan para sa kultura, relihiyon, at politika sa rehiyon, at patuloy siyang pinag-aaralan bilang isa sa mga pangunahing lider ng Moro sa Pilipinas.

Press Release by the Chiefs, Elders, Youth Leaders, and Women Leaders of Panyang Payam

The people of Panyang Payam hereby issue this press release to respectfully inform the Government of South Sudan and humanitarian organizations operating in South Sudan about their return home and the challenges they are currently facing.

Late last year and early this year, the people of Panyang Payam witnessed horrific and undeserved suffering at the hands of the IO militia. Following the killing of Panyang leaders in Ayuai, the IO advanced to Pajut, where they captured the area, burned down homes, and looted properties, including essential medicines. Some members of the public may have seen images of individuals carrying bags on their heads, including women. These were not Panyang residents returning home; rather, they were individuals involved in looting properties from Panyang. We extend our congratulations and express our deep appreciation to Gen. Paul Nang and the SSPDF for restoring peace, stability, and hope to the resilient people of Panyang.

I had promised him I would keep an eye on Leo. I had promised him things would be fine. But as I watched the silver Lexus pull into our cracked driveway, I knew my promises were worth about as much as the damp cardboard boxes stacked against the siding. Mr. Sterling stepped out of his car, holding an umbrella that looked like it cost more than my monthly disability check. He didn't look like a man who enjoyed cruelty; he looked like a man who found it necessary for a clean ledger. He didn't look at the puddles or the peeling paint. He looked at his watch. Behind him, two men in work jumpsuits climbed out of a white van. They didn't look at anything at all. I walked down the steps, my knees popping in the cold, and met him halfway. Leo was already there, standing by the front door of their unit, clutching a plastic bin of LEGOs to his chest as if they were the only things keeping him anchored to the earth. The boy was seven, but in that gray light, he looked ninety. He was wearing his father’s old army fleece, which swallowed him whole, the sleeves dragging in the mud. He was shivering, a rhythmic, violent trembling that you could almost hear. Mr. Sterling didn't wait for a greeting. He simply pulled a folded packet of papers from his breast pocket. He didn't offer them to me. He held them out like a shield. Elias is still in the hospital, I said, trying to keep my voice from shaking. I spoke slowly, the way you speak to someone who might be dangerous, even if they're wearing a silk tie. The money is coming. The VFW is processing the emergency grant. It just takes time. Sterling sighed, a sound of profound boredom. Time is a luxury your friend doesn't have, he replied. The grace period ended at midnight. The management company has been very clear. We are taking possession of the unit today. You can't just throw a kid onto the street in this weather, I said, stepping closer. The air was turning from rain to sleet, sharp little needles of ice that stung the skin. Sterling finally looked at me, and his eyes were as flat as coins. I am not throwing him onto the street. I am removing unauthorized occupants from a property that is no longer under lease. Where he goes is not my concern. He looked over my shoulder at Leo. The boy hadn't moved. He was staring at the men from the van who were now unloading heavy-duty trash bags. Sterling walked past me, his expensive shoes crunching on the gravel. He reached the porch and looked down at the child. Move, he commanded. Leo looked up, his face pale and wet, his lips a faint shade of blue. My dad... he started, but his voice broke. Sterling didn't let him finish. He pointed a finger directly at my face as I stepped toward the porch. Don't you take another step, he warned me. This is a legal eviction. With a sharp, impatient sound, Sterling reached out and shoved the boy. It wasn't a punch, but it was hard—the kind of dismissal you'd give a stray animal. Leo stumbled backward, his oversized boots catching on the threshold. He fell off the low porch, landing hard on his knees in the freezing slush of the driveway. The plastic bin flew from his hands, and hundreds of colorful bricks scattered into the mud like broken teeth. The sound of his knees hitting the pavement was muffled by the rain, but I felt it in my own joints. That was the moment the world stopped. Buster, Elias’s old black Lab mix, had been lying under the porch, a silent shadow in the dark. He was twelve years old, mostly blind, and slow to move. But when Leo hit the ground and let out a sharp, choked sob, something in that old dog snapped. He didn't bark. He didn't give a warning. He lunged. It was a blur of graying fur and a low, guttural snarl that sounded like a saw cutting through bone. Sterling screamed, a high, thin sound of pure terror, as Buster’s teeth caught the fabric of his trousers, dragging him down into the same mud where Leo lay. Sterling fell back, his umbrella flying into the street, his dignity dissolving in a second as he scrambled away on his elbows, shouting for help. I stood there, frozen between the urge to help the boy and the dark, visceral satisfaction of watching the man crawl. The rain was coming down harder now, a curtain of ice that seemed to isolate us from the rest of the world. Just as one of the men from the van started toward Buster with a crowbar, the roar of a heavy engine cut through the sound of the storm. A black SUV, massive and gleaming even in the gloom, swung into the driveway, blocking Sterling’s Lexus. The tires threw up a spray of muddy water that soaked Sterling even further. The engine died, and for a heartbeat, there was only the sound of the wind. Then, the door opened. A man stepped out, his movements precise and heavy with authority. He wore a long, dark coat, and as he stepped into the light of the porch lamp, I saw the glint of gold on his lapel. He didn't look at Sterling, who was still gasping in the mud. He didn't look at me. He looked at Leo, who was crying silently while trying to gather his mud-covered LEGOs. The man walked over, knelt down in the freezing rain without a second thought for his clothes, and began to help the boy pick up the pieces. I knew then that the ledger was about to be balanced in a way Mr. Sterling hadn't calculated.

Montana, 1913. Joe Medicine Crow was born into a world where his people's traditions were dying.
The buffalo were gone. The open plains were fenced. The warrior culture that had defined the Crow Nation for generations was fading into memory and museum displays.
But Joe's grandfather, White Man Runs Him, refused to let it disappear.
White Man Runs Him had been a scout for George Armstrong Custer at the Battle of Little Bighorn in 1876. He'd witnessed the last great victory of the Plains tribes. Now, as an old man, he sat by the fire with young Joe and taught him the ancient ways.
He told Joe about the War Chiefs—the highest honor a Crow warrior could achieve. To earn that sacred title, a man had to complete four specific deeds in battle:

Lead a successful war party
Touch an enemy without killing him (counting coup)
Take an enemy's weapon in hand-to-hand combat
Steal an enemy's horse

Joe listened with a broken heart.
He was born too late. The age of horses and hand-to-hand combat was over. He'd never ride into battle. He'd never become a War Chief.
The tradition, his grandfather told him sadly, would likely die with the elders.
So Joe went to college instead. He studied anthropology at USC, determined to at least preserve his culture's history even if he couldn't live it.
Then Pearl Harbor happened.
December 1941. Joe Medicine Crow enlisted in the U.S. Army.
Before he shipped out, his grandfather called him close one final time. The old man's hands trembled as he painted traditional red war designs on Joe's arms.
"You will go to war," his grandfather whispered. "Remember who you are. Remember what I taught you."
Joe promised.
He wore the war paint under his Army uniform. He tucked a sacred eagle feather inside his steel helmet, hidden from view.
He was a modern American soldier preparing to fight Nazis with rifles and grenades.
But in his heart, he was a Crow warrior preparing for something far older.
Joe was assigned to the 103rd Infantry Division and shipped to Europe in 1944. The fighting in France and Germany was hell—machine guns, artillery, tanks rolling through burning villages.
Joe wasn't thinking about ancient traditions. He was trying to survive.
But sometimes destiny finds you anyway.
The First Deed: Lead a War Party
In France, Joe's commanding officer gave him an order: take seven men and scout through German-held territory. Gather intelligence. Return alive.
Joe led his squad through enemy lines using skills his grandfather had taught him—moving silently, reading the landscape, sensing danger before it appeared.
They avoided German patrols. Dodged landmines. Completed their mission.
Every single man returned safely.
His commanding officer called it excellent leadership.
Joe realized he'd just completed the first deed.
The Second and Third Deeds: Take a Weapon and Count Coup
In a bombed-out French village, Joe was scouting ahead when he turned a corner and collided directly with a German soldier.
Both men crashed backward. Joe's rifle flew from his hands and skidded across the rubble. The German still had his weapon.
For one frozen second, they stared at each other.
Then the German raised his rifle.
Joe didn't reach for his knife. He didn't run.
He charged.
Joe slammed into the German before the man could fire, knocking him to the ground. He grabbed the rifle barrel and wrenched it from the enemy's hands.
Now Joe stood over him, holding the German's own weapon. The man lay terrified on the ground, waiting to die.
Joe looked at him—young, scared, defeated.
He let him go.
In those chaotic seconds, Joe had completed two more deeds: he'd taken an enemy's weapon in hand-to-hand combat, and by touching the man in battle without killing him, he'd counted coup.
Three deeds completed. One remained.
The Final Deed: Steal an Enemy's Horse
This was the impossible one.
It was 1945. The German army used tanks, trucks, and motorcycles. Horses were relics of a previous century.
Joe figured the ancient tradition would end at three-quarters complete. Close, but not enough.
Then something unexpected happened.
As Allied forces pushed deeper into Germany, Nazi fuel supplies ran desperately low. In some areas, German officers began using horses again for transportation.
Early one morning, Joe's unit approached a farmhouse occupied by SS officers.
Through the morning mist, Joe spotted something that stopped his heart.
Behind the farmhouse was a stable. Inside were at least fifty horses—prized animals belonging to the German officers sleeping inside.
Joe stared at those horses and heard his grandfather's voice: Remember who you are.
This was it. This was his moment. The war would end soon. He'd never get another chance.
He waited for darkness.
German guards patrolled the perimeter. Joe moved like a shadow—silent, invisible, using every hunting skill he'd ever learned.
He slipped into the stable. The smell of hay and horses filled his lungs. It smelled like home. Like Montana. Like everything his grandfather had told him about.
He moved among the animals, calming them with soft words in the Crow language. He found the finest horse, fashioned a makeshift rope halter, and swung onto its bare back.
Then he gave a loud war cry—the same cry Crow warriors had used for centuries.
He kicked the horse into a gallop and burst through the stable doors, leading all fifty horses behind him in a thundering stampede.
German soldiers shouted and fired into the air, but it was too late. Joe was already riding hard toward American lines.
And as he rode—with bullets whizzing past, with fifty stolen horses thundering behind him, with the modern world exploding all around—Joe Medicine Crow began to sing.
He sang a traditional Crow war song. The same song his ancestors had sung two centuries earlier when they rode across the plains.
For that moment, the tanks and trenches disappeared.
He wasn't in Germany in 1945.
He was riding for his people, carrying their honor forward through time.
He arrived at American lines with the captured horses. His commanding officer was stunned. His fellow soldiers cheered—they'd just captured valuable enemy transportation.
But Joe knew what he'd really done.
He'd completed the four deeds. He'd honored his grandfather. He'd kept a tradition alive.
The Last War Chief
When the war ended, Joe returned to Montana. He went to the Crow elders and told them everything.
They listened in silence. They verified each deed. They consulted the ancient laws.
Then they held a ceremony that hadn't been performed in generations.
They painted his face with traditional designs. They placed the War Chief headdress upon his head. They danced and sang the old songs.
Joe Medicine Crow was named a War Chief of the Crow Nation.
He was the last man to ever earn that title.
Joe lived to be 102 years old. He became a renowned historian and author, writing extensively about Crow culture and Native American history. He completed his master's degree from USC. He advised presidents and spoke at the Smithsonian.
In 2009, President Barack Obama awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom, saying: "An act of extraordinary valor speaks for itself. So does a life."
But Joe always said the medals and honors were secondary.
What mattered was the continuity—that he'd kept his grandfather's traditions alive in the middle of the most modern war in history.
He proved something profound: heritage isn't about the past. It's about carrying meaning forward, even when the world around you has completely changed.
Joe Medicine Crow died in 2016 at age 102. He was buried with full military honors and traditional Crow ceremonies—a bridge between two worlds until the very end.
He was the last War Chief.
But his story ensures that what a War Chief represents—courage, honor, cultural pride, connection to ancestors—will never die.
Because sometimes the most powerful act of resistance is simply remembering who you are.

On February 15, 1989, the last Soviet armored column rumbled across the Friendship Bridge at Termez and out of Afghanistan.

Nine years earlier, they had entered in confidence — tanks gleaming, banners high, certain that a brief intervention would steady a faltering communist ally. Now they left in silence. No victory parade. No triumphal speech. Only exhausted conscripts and a superpower that no longer looked invincible.

The war had cost the Soviet Union roughly 15,000 dead, tens of thousands wounded, and untold billions of rubles. It cost something less measurable as well: prestige. Authority. The aura of inevitability that had hovered over Moscow since the end of the Second World War.

But to understand that bridge in 1989, you have to return to Kabul in 1978. That April, Afghan communists seized power in what became known as the Saur Revolution. They promised modernization. Land reform. Socialism. What they delivered instead was purges, internal feuding, and policies that trampled tribal structures and religious life in a fiercely traditional society.

The countryside ignited.

The rebels called themselves mujahideen — warriors in a holy struggle. They were not a single army but a patchwork of factions: tribal leaders, Islamists, nationalists, opportunists. What united them was resistance to a regime they saw as godless and imposed.

Moscow hesitated at first. But Soviet advisers were being killed. The regime in Kabul was unraveling. And within the Kremlin, hardliners warned that failure to act would invite instability across Central Asia. So on Christmas Eve, 1979, Soviet forces crossed the border, assassinated Afghan leader Hafizullah Amin, and installed the more pliable Babrak Karmal. But the intervention that was supposed to last months stretched into years.

In Washington, President Jimmy Carter viewed this all as naked aggression. Even before Soviet troops entered, his administration had authorized limited aid to Afghan rebels. Afterward, that support expanded. His national security adviser, Zbigniew Brzezinski, saw an opportunity: Afghanistan could become Moscow’s Vietnam.

When Ronald Reagan entered the White House in 1981, the policy intensified. Through Pakistan’s intelligence service, the CIA funneled money, weapons, and training to the insurgency. Saudi Arabia matched American funds. Volunteers from across the Muslim world arrived — the so-called “Afghan Arabs.” Among them was a wealthy young Saudi named Osama bin Laden.

In 1986, U.S.-supplied Stinger missiles began knocking Soviet helicopters from the sky. What had been a grinding occupation turned into a strategic bleed. Casualties mounted. Morale sagged. The myth of Soviet invulnerability cracked.

When Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985, he had inherited a war he could neither win nor justify. He called Afghanistan a “bleeding wound.” Reform at home required retreat abroad. The withdrawal agreement was signed. The columns rolled north.

And then the larger structure began to sway. Eastern Europe stirred. The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. Soviet republics asserted independence. In December 1991, the Soviet Union dissolved. Many factors brought about that collapse — economic stagnation, internal dissent, reformist overreach — but Afghanistan had drained blood and credibility from the empire, playing a major role. The rollback that began in the mountains reached all the way to Moscow.

Yet history rarely gives clean victories. The same pipeline that armed anti-Soviet fighters strengthened the most radical factions. Pakistan’s intelligence service favored hardline Islamists. Saudi money encouraged fundamentalist networks. The United States, focused on defeating its superpower rival, did not fully reckon with what it was helping to midwife.

When the Soviets left, Afghanistan did not find peace. It found civil war. From that chaos rose the Taliban. And from that soil emerged al-Qaeda — the organization bin Laden would later turn against the West.

History is seldom tidy. One empire’s humiliation can become another generation’s reckoning.

Panyang Community’s Humble Request to the Government of South Sudan and Humanitarian Organizations

Press Release by the Chiefs, Elders, Youth Leaders, and Women Leaders of Panyang Payam

The people of Panyang Payam hereby issue this press release to respectfully inform the Government of South Sudan and humanitarian organizations operating in South Sudan about their return home and the challenges they are currently facing.

It is with profound hope and sincere appreciation that we thank the Government of South Sudan for liberating our area from the IO militia. Late last year and early this year, the people of Panyang Payam witnessed horrific and undeserved suffering at the hands of the IO militia. The violence began in Ayuai, where our Paramount Chief and several other chiefs were killed while on a peaceful mission. Some individuals were captured unarmed and later tragically killed. These were civilians going about their daily lives who did not deserve such a fate. These events occurred before the SSPDF deployed troops to carry out rescue operations.

Following the killing of Panyang leaders in Ayuai, the IO advanced to Pajut, where they captured the area, burned down homes, and looted properties, including essential medicines. Some members of the public may have seen images of individuals carrying bags on their heads, including women. These were not Panyang residents returning home; rather, they were individuals involved in looting properties from Panyang. As a result, significant destruction occurred, and very little was left behind.

During these confrontations, soldiers and civilians lost their lives, many were displaced and scattered, and some families are still searching for missing loved ones. The suffering experienced by our community has been immense.

Fortunately, unlike in previous conflicts, this time the Chief of Defence Forces, Gen. Paul Nang, together with the SSPDF, took decisive leadership and successfully recaptured all the areas that had been taken by the IO. We extend our congratulations and express our deep appreciation to Gen. Paul Nang and the SSPDF for restoring peace, stability, and hope to the resilient people of Panyang.

Today, our people have finally returned home. However, they remain in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. The limited support received from a few community members in the diaspora and within South Sudan is not sufficient to facilitate full resettlement and recovery.

The community is currently facing serious challenges, including food shortages, a cholera outbreak, lack of shelter, inadequate clothing, limited access to clean water, and many other basic necessities. We therefore humbly and respectfully appeal to the Government of South Sudan, all humanitarian organizations operating in South Sudan, and relevant stakeholders to intervene and provide the necessary support to assist the people of Panyang in rebuilding their lives.

The people of Panyang Payam remain grateful for the restoration of security and stand ready to cooperate with the government and humanitarian partners in ensuring sustainable peace and recovery in our area.

The intellectuals, Chiefs, Elders, Youth Leaders, and Women Leaders

When Audie Murphy stood at the White House receiving his Medal of Honor—one of 33 medals he would earn in WWII—he did something no one expected. He didn't smile for the cameras. He didn't celebrate. Instead, he whispered to the officer beside him: "These belong to the men who didn't come home."
That's the burden carried by America's most decorated warriors. They don't see themselves as heroes. They see themselves as survivors who lived to tell the stories of those who didn't.
Audie Murphy (Army) earned 33 medals in WWII, including the Medal of Honor, making him the most decorated American combat soldier. But numbers don't tell the story. At 19 years old, he stood alone on a burning tank destroyer, holding off an entire German company for over an hour while wounded. He saved his entire battalion. When asked why he did it, he said simply: "They were my friends."
Matt Urban (Army) was wounded SEVEN times in WWII—and kept coming back. He earned 29 decorations, including the Medal of Honor. His men called him "The Ghost" because he'd disappear into the hospital with wounds that should have ended his war, then reappear on the battlefield weeks later, leading from the front. He refused to stop fighting until his friends came home.
Robert L. Howard (Special Forces) was recommended for the Medal of Honor THREE times in Vietnam—the only soldier ever to achieve this. He received it once, along with 8 Purple Hearts. During one mission, despite being wounded, he called in airstrikes on his own position to save his team, then fought his way through enemy lines carrying a wounded comrade. He survived. The enemy didn't.
Daniel Daly (Marine Corps) is one of only two Marines to receive TWO Medals of Honor—for heroism in China (1900) and Haiti (1915). During WWI at Belleau Wood, while under heavy fire, he allegedly shouted the most famous battle cry in Marine Corps history: "Come on, you sons of bitches, do you want to live forever?" Then he charged into machine gun fire. His men followed. They won.
Alvin York (Army) was a pacifist from rural Tennessee who didn't want to fight in WWI. But when his battalion was pinned down in France, something changed. Using his Tennessee sharpshooting skills, he systematically took out 28 German soldiers, then captured 132 more—with just seven men helping him. When asked how he did it, he said: "I was doing what needed doing."
Lewis "Chesty" Puller (Marine Corps) earned FIVE Navy Crosses—more than any Marine in history. His leadership philosophy was simple: "Take me to the brig. I want to see the real Marines." He believed the greatest warriors were the ones willing to break rules to protect their brothers. His men would have followed him into hell.
Edward Rickenbacker (Army Air Service) shot down 26 enemy aircraft in WWI, earning the Medal of Honor and the title "Ace of Aces." But his greatest test came in WWII when his plane crashed in the Pacific. He survived 24 days adrift at sea with his crew, catching rainwater and seagulls to survive. When rescued, his first words were: "How are my men?"
Smedley Butler (Marine Corps) received TWO Medals of Honor for extraordinary heroism. Later, he became one of the military's most controversial figures, writing "War is a Racket" and speaking out against military interventionism. He proved that true courage includes speaking truth even when it costs you everything.
Patrick Brady (Army) flew medevac helicopters in Vietnam, earning the Medal of Honor for rescuing over 60 wounded soldiers in a single day—through horrific weather and enemy fire that should have killed him a dozen times. He made trip after trip, refusing to leave wounded men behind. When his helicopter was too damaged to fly, he commandeered another and kept going.
Richard Bong (Army Air Force) became America's top flying ace in WWII with 40 confirmed kills. He could have stayed safe stateside as a flight instructor, but he volunteered to return to combat again and again. He died testing a new jet aircraft in 1945, still trying to serve.
These warriors didn't collect medals. They collected scars, nightmares, and the weight of survivor's guilt. They carried it so we wouldn't have to.
The next time you see a veteran, remember: the medals on their chest don't represent their greatest achievement. Their greatest achievement is that they came home when so many didn't—and they've spent every day since trying to be worthy of that gift.

The rich kid laughed, kicking the walker out from under the 78-year-old widow. "She slipped!" he lied to his girlfriend's camera as Martha writhed in agony on the oily concrete. But then, his coffee began to ripple. The ground shook. The kid froze as 20 Vagos MC bikers, led by a giant named Bear, surrounded the gas station, ready to teach him a lesson he'd never forget…
The heat in Bakersfield wasn't just weather; it was a sentence. It settled deep in the bones, making every movement feel like wading through invisible molasses. For Martha, seventy-eight years old and eighty-nine pounds soaking wet, the heat was a mortal enemy she battled every time she stepped out of her ancient 1998 Buick Century.
She hated stopping for gas. She hated the toxic smell of fumes, the complicated digital screens that asked too many questions, and the brutal impatience of the world rushing past her. But she had to go. It was Tuesday. Tuesday was the day she visited Henry.
Henry had been in the cold ground for five years, but Martha still talked to him about grocery prices and the leak in the roof. He was the only one who listened anymore.
Her hands, knobby with arthritis and mapped with blue veins, trembled as she reached for her walker in the passenger seat. It was a war—the metal legs caught on the torn upholstery, the rubber feet snagging the floor mat.
"Come on, you old thing," she whispered, her voice like dry autumn leaves. She finally wrestled the walker out onto the oil-stained concrete and hauled herself up. Her hip, the joint the doctors called a ticking time bomb, gave a sharp pinch of warning.
She swiped her credit card. Error. Please see cashier.
Martha let out a shaky sigh. She just wanted three gallons. Just enough to get to the cemetery and back.
That’s when the music assaulted her before the car did. A thumping bass that rattled the loose change in her pocket. An electric-blue BMW M3—bright and aggressive—swerved into the station, cutting the corner sharp and screeching to a halt right behind her Buick. The engine revved—a hungry, predatory growl.
Martha froze. She looked at the screen. See cashier. She needed to walk inside, but the blue shark was blocking her only path to the door.
The driver’s door flew open. The boy who stepped out looked like he belonged in a magazine ad for expensive cologne. Blonde hair perfectly coiffed, a varsity jacket despite the scorching heat, and a sneer that looked practiced in a mirror. He was maybe seventeen.
"Hey!" he shouted, slapping the roof of his car. "Move it, antique! You're blocking the only premium pump."
Martha turned slowly, clutching the handles of her walker for dear life. "I... I’m sorry, young man. The machine... it’s not working. I have to go inside."
The passenger door opened. A girl with long acrylic nails and a phone already held up in recording mode stepped out. She was chewing gum loudly. "Oh my god, Trey, she’s literally a fossil. Just tell her to move."
Trey, the driver, walked up to Martha. He towered over her. To Martha, he looked terrifying—a symbol of a world that had become too fast and too cruel for her to understand.
"I don't have all day," Trey snapped, glancing at the camera his girlfriend was holding. He was performing now. "I got places to be. Put it in drive and roll this junk heap forward."
"I can't walk that fast," Martha said, her voice trembling. "Please. I just need to pay."
"You shouldn't even be driving," Trey laughed, looking back at his friend in the backseat who was also live-streaming. "It's dangerous. You're a hazard."
"Please," Martha whispered, tears pricking her eyes. She felt so small. Henry would have said something. Henry would have protected her. But Henry was under six feet of dirt on the other side of town.
Trey looked at his girlfriend, grinned, and made a decision that would change the trajectory of his life forever, though he didn't know it yet. He wanted a viral moment. He wanted to look tough.
"Let me help you speed up," Trey said.
He pulled his leg back and kicked.
He didn't kick the car. HE KICKED THE WALKER.
His expensive sneaker connected with the aluminum frame. The sound was a harsh, metallic clatter. The walker flew out from under Martha’s grip, skidding ten feet across the asphalt.
For a second, Martha hung in the air, her eyes wide with shock. Then, gravity took her.
She hit the concrete hard. Her left shoulder took the brunt of it, followed by her fragile hip. A cry of pure, jagged pain tore from her throat—a sound so raw that the birds on the power lines scattered in fear.
"Oh, snap!" the boy in the backseat yelled, laughing. "World Star!"
The girlfriend giggled, zooming in on Martha as she curled into a ball on the dirty ground, gasping for air. "Trey, you are so bad!"
"She slipped," Trey said loudly, winking at the camera. "You all saw it. She slipped."
Martha couldn't breathe. The pain in her hip was a blinding white light. She tried to reach for her walker, but it was too far away. She was lying in a puddle of oil and grit, humiliated, broken, and utterly alone.
Henry, she thought, closing her eyes. I’m coming, Henry. I’m just so tired.
Trey stepped over her legs to get to the pump nozzle. "Whatever. I'm filling up. She can nap there."
He grabbed the nozzle. He was feeling like a king. He had the girl, the car, the power. He had just dominated the space.
Then, the coffee in the cup holder of his BMW started to ripple.
A low vibration began to hum through the soles of his limited-edition sneakers. It wasn't the bass from his car stereo. It was deeper. Guttural. LIKE THE EARTH ITSELF WAS GROWLING.
Trey paused, the nozzle in his hand. "What is that?"
The sound grew louder. A rhythmic, thunderous roar that drowned out the highway traffic. It wasn't one engine. It was an army.
The girlfriend lowered her phone, her face draining of color. "Trey..."
From the on-ramp, they appeared.
First one. A massive black Harley with ape-hanger handlebars, ridden by a man who looked like he was carved out of granite. Then two more. Then ten. Then twenty.
The Vagos MC.
They didn't just ride in; they flooded the lot like a tsunami. The sound was deafening, a mechanical thunderstorm that swallowed the air. They wore "cuts"—leather vests—with the green lizard patch on the back. These weren't weekend warriors. THESE WERE 1%ERS. The kind of men who didn't follow the laws Trey’s daddy paid to bend.
Trey swallowed hard, the nozzle slipping in his sweaty grip. "Babe, get in the car."
But he couldn't move.
The lead biker, the one on the front Harley, killed his engine. The silence that followed was heavier than the noise. He kicked down his stand and dismounted with a slow, terrifying grace. He was huge—easily six-four, with a grey beard braided down to his chest and arms covered in ink that faded into old scars.
His name was Bear. And he hadn't looked at Trey yet.
Bear walked straight toward the spot where Martha lay shivering on the ground. He didn't look at the BMW. He didn't look at the girl filming.
He stopped at Martha’s feet. He saw the walker thrown ten feet away. He saw the bruise forming on her arm. He saw the tears leaking from her shut eyes.
Bear’s eyes slowly lifted. He turned his head, just an inch, until he was locking eyes with Trey.
Trey tried to speak, but his voice was a squeak. "She... she fell."
Bear didn't blink. He just reached into his vest.
The other nineteen bikers dismounted in unison. The sound of nineteen kickstands hitting the concrete sounded exactly LIKE THE RACKING OF A SHOTGUN SLIDE...

LIBERIA’S LONG ROAD TO JUSTICE: War and Economic Crimes Court Set to Confront the Ghosts of 1989–2003

Liberia is standing at a historic crossroads.

More than two decades after the guns fell silent, the nation is finally preparing to confront one of the darkest chapters in its history — the Liberian Civil War (1989–2003), a brutal conflict that left over 250,000 people dead, displaced millions, and tore apart the very fabric of the state.

Now, with the establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, the long-awaited wheels of justice are beginning to turn.

A War That Devastated a Nation

The civil war erupted in 1989 when forces of the National Patriotic Front of Liberia (NPFL), led by Charles Taylor, launched an insurgency against the government.

What followed was more than a power struggle — it was a descent into chaos.

Multiple armed factions emerged, including the Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL) and various militia groups. Towns were overrun. Villages were burned. Families were shattered.

Civilians paid the highest price:
 • Massacres of entire communities
 • Widespread rape and sexual violence
 • Forced recruitment of child soldiers
 • Torture and inhumane treatment
 • Public executions

The violence was systematic, ruthless, and often fueled by greed.

Blood Diamonds, Timber & War Profits

The conflict was not driven by politics alone.

Liberia’s vast natural resources — diamonds, timber, rubber — became tools of war. Armed groups financed their campaigns by exploiting and exporting these resources, prolonging the bloodshed and enriching warlords while ordinary Liberians suffered.

Economic plundering turned the war into a business enterprise.

And for years, those responsible operated with near-total impunity.

The Truth Commission’s Revelations

In 2005, Liberia took a bold step by establishing the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC).

Its mission was clear:
 • Investigate the causes of the war
 • Document human rights violations
 • Identify perpetrators
 • Recommend prosecutions and reparations

The TRC’s findings were chilling.

It documented widespread atrocities — mass killings, torture, sexual slavery, and crimes against humanity. The commission named individuals and groups it believed bore responsibility and recommended their prosecution.

Yet for years, those recommendations gathered dust.

The War and Economic Crimes Court: A Turning Point

Now, Liberia is moving forward with the creation of a War and Economic Crimes Court.

This marks one of the most significant accountability measures in the country’s post-war history.

The court’s objectives include:
 • Prosecuting individuals accused of war crimes
 • Addressing crimes against humanity
 • Tackling economic crimes linked to the conflict
 • Delivering justice to victims and their families

For survivors, this moment is deeply emotional. For many, justice delayed has felt like justice denied.

The establishment of the court sends a powerful message:
Impunity will no longer be tolerated.

International Support and National Responsibility

The international community has expressed strong support for Liberia’s effort to pursue accountability. Global partners recognize that sustainable peace depends on justice and the rule of law.

However, the success of the court will depend largely on:
 • Political will within Liberia
 • Cooperation from state institutions
 • Protection of witnesses
 • Support from civil society
 • Continued international backing

This will not be an easy process.

Liberia remains a fragile post-conflict democracy. Reopening old wounds carries risks. But many argue that ignoring them carries even greater danger.

Justice, Healing, and the Future

The War and Economic Crimes Court represents more than prosecution — it represents a test of Liberia’s maturity as a democracy.

Can the nation confront its painful past?
Can it hold powerful figures accountable?
Can justice and reconciliation walk hand in hand?

For the victims — the mothers, the orphaned children, the survivors of unspeakable violence — this court is not about politics.

It is about recognition.
It is about dignity.
It is about truth.

After years of silence, Liberia may finally be ready to answer one of its most urgent questions:

Will the scars of war define the nation forever — or will justice help heal them?

There’s nothing like Igbo, Hausa, or Yoruba language that people sat down one day to establish. 

This post is just a little education for some of my people who take pride in ignorance. 

Hopefully, ignorance and pride will allow them to learn. 

What we call Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa, even English and Chinese are not single, heavenly voices that dropped from the sky. They are assemblages. Coalitions. Collections and networks of many dialects that politics, trade, religion, education, and media slowly molded into something we now call a standard.

The “correct” version people brag about today is just what gradually came together from different dialects to form a generally spoken language. 

Within the Igbo world alone, the differences in tone, pronunciation, and vocabulary from one community to another can be wide. Yet a standardized Igbo developed through schools, Bible translations, broadcasting, and literature, giving everyone a common meeting point. So when someone looks at another Igbo group and calls them sub-Igbo because they sound different, what they are really displaying is not cultural intelligence. It is ignorance. If speaking differently is a crime, then almost everybody will be deported from their own identity.

The same thing exists among the Yoruba. Listen carefully as people from Oyo, Ijebu, Ekiti, Ondo, or Ijesha speak. The rhythm changes. Some words bend. Intonations rise and fall differently. But nobody wakes up and says one group is not truly Yoruba because of that. A common written and broadcast form holds them together, and life goes on.

Hausa is no exception. Travel across cities, from Kano (Kananci) to Katsina (Katsinanci) to Bauchi (Guddiranci) to Zazzau / Zaria (Zazzaganci) and Daura (Dauranci) linked to Daura, an area important in Hausa historical traditions. You will hear shifts shaped by geography, history, and contact with other peoples. Yet trade networks, religion, and administration created a widely accepted standard that millions understand.

This is how languages survive. Not through uniformity, but through negotiation. A network of dialects. 

Now think about English. British English is not American English. Nigerian English is not Australian English. Accents, spellings, slang all vary. Imagine Manchester announcing that Texas is now sub-English because they pronounce words differently. It would sound absurd.

Yet we do the same thing to ourselves.

The truth many people avoid is this. What you call your language is a big umbrella covering many ancestral streams. The dialect you inherited is not proof of superiority. It is simply where history placed your people. 

Igbo, Hausa, Yoruba, etc. is no particular people’s language. It’s an assemblage of different similar dialects. Repeat that until it sinks.

If we start removing everyone who sounds different, we might soon discover that your own village does not qualify either.

And the people you are tempted to look down on may be preserving partss of the very history you claim to defend.

And unity did not come from sounding the same. Unity came from agreeing to belong together.

If that agreement breaks, pronunciation will not save anybody. Have sense and stop being an embarrassment to yourself.

It was an impossible decision for someone so young, yet her answer was calm and firm. She refused to betray her comrades. According to later accounts, her final words expressed faith that her fellow fighters would continue the struggle and prove that courage could not be silenced.

Her life ended soon after, but her story did not. After the war, she was honored as one of the youngest heroes of the resistance. Her name became a reminder that bravery is not measured by age, and that even in the face of fear, a single person can stand for something greater than themselves. In the quiet enclosure of Ichikawa City Zoo, a baby Japanese macaque named Punch was born last July—only to face rejection from his mother mere days later. Hand-raised by dedicated keepers who bottle-fed him through sleepless nights and cradled him when no troop would, he grew up knowing human hands more than monkey fur.

When the time came to join the others in January, the world of his own kind felt foreign. He lingered on the edges, unsure of the grooming rituals and playful chases that came so naturally to his peers—a quiet struggle common in primates denied those first, vital maternal bonds.

To ease the loneliness etched in his small eyes, the keepers offered a soft, oversized plush orangutan. What began as a simple comfort became his constant companion: carried on his back like an infant, groomed with tender care, clutched tight during moments of fear or uncertainty.

Punch still ventures out, still tries to belong, but that bright orange friend remains his anchor—a gentle reminder that love, even when stitched and surrogate, can help a heart keep beating through the ache of what was lost.

Captain Bol Deng represented the vast number of them.
