GSU “G” COMPANY: THE PRESIDENTIAL GUARD UNIT 🇰🇪
GSU “G” Company is widely recognized as the elite Presidential Guard element within Kenya’s General Service Unit (GSU), a specialized paramilitary formation under the National Police Service. Unlike the more than 20 field companies that conduct regional security operations, G Company’s core mandate is the protection of the President, Deputy President, and key State installations. Its role places it at the highest tier of VVIP security within Kenya’s policing structure.
The General Service Unit itself was established in 1948 and reorganized in 1953 to enhance its operational effectiveness. Over time, it has grown into a highly trained paramilitary wing tasked with counter-terrorism, riot control, anti-banditry operations, and anti-poaching missions. Within this broader structure, G Company operates as a distinct and specialized formation dedicated almost exclusively to executive protection and the safeguarding of critical national leadership assets.
GSU field companies are alphabetically designated from “A” to “Y” (excluding O, P, and U), with most deployed across various regions to handle public order management and high-risk security operations. In contrast, G Company is primarily stationed at high-security installations such as State House Nairobi and other State Lodges. It frequently works alongside the elite Recce Company during high-threat situations, reinforcing Kenya’s top-level protective security framework.
As a result, GSU G Company remains one of the most discreet yet strategically vital units in Kenya’s security architecture — a silent shield around the country’s highest office.

On Presidents Day, former President George W. Bush published a pointed essay honoring George Washington that had everyone reading between the lines. Bush centered his tribute on Washington's most defining act: walking away from power. Twice. Washington surrendered command of the Continental Army after the Revolution, then willingly stepped down from the presidency after two terms. "Our first president could have remained all-powerful, but twice he chose not to," Bush wrote. "In doing so, he set a standard for all presidents to live up to." Those words are impossible to read without thinking of a man who tried to overturn a lost election and is now floating the idea of a third, constitutionally prohibited term.

Bush didn't stop there. He went on to celebrate Washington's commitment to humility, restraint, and placing the nation above personal ambition, qualities that read less like historical praise and more like a pointed checklist of everything Trump lacks. Washington "carried himself with dignity and self-restraint, honoring the office without allowing it to become invested with near-mythical powers," Bush wrote. The contrast with a president who has compared himself to Jesus and demands loyalty oaths could not be more glaring.

The "In Pursuit" project will also feature essays from Barack Obama and Bill Clinton, along with Chief Justice John Roberts. Notably, Bush is not giving interviews. He doesn't need to. The essay speaks loudly enough on its own, according to former National Archivist Colleen Shogan, who now helps oversee the project after being abruptly fired by Trump in early 2025. "The lesson of presidential humility transcends time," she said. On this Presidents Day, with a would-be king sitting in the Oval Office, that lesson has never felt more urgent.

“From Collaboration to Sovereignty.”

By Lorcan Black

Seven years ago, in 2019, I was the architect of something that had never been done before in our corner of the world. A daily devotional… for Satanists. Not a prayer book. Not a grovel-at-the-altar guide. Not a collection of pious mutterings to some invisible sky tyrant. But a 365-day book of wicked wit, sharp observations, irreverent humor, and grounded, nontheistic perspective.

It was called Satan Calling: 365 Days of Wicked Witticism & Wisdom.

And whether people want to admit it or not, it was historical.

It was the first of its kind, a collaboration between members of the Church of Satan, offering daily passages that uplifted without kneeling, inspired without begging, and reflected the Satanic spirit of individualism, strength, skepticism, and dark humor. It proved something important, that “devotional” does not have to mean submissive. It can mean intentional. It can mean reflective. It can mean sharpening your own blade daily rather than dulling it on dogma.

Overall, the project was a success. It reached people. It entertained people. It stirred discussion. It even stirred controversy, because of course it did. When you put the word “Satan” on a book and ask people to read something daily from a place of personal sovereignty instead of servitude, you’re going to rattle cages.

But controversy never frightened me. If anything, it confirms impact.

What mattered more to me, personally, was something far quieter and far more uncomfortable.

My contributions were not where they should have been.

They didn’t suck. Let’s be clear. They were competent. They were clever at times. They carried the voice I had at the time. But they were not the best I was capable of becoming. And when you are the architect of an idea that shines as brightly as that one did, you feel it when your own bricks don’t match the glow of the blueprint.

The idea itself outshined my content.

That realization did not embitter me. It refined me.

Because Satanism demands ruthless self-honesty. If you can’t look at your own work and say, “This could have been stronger,” then you’re not practicing individualism, you’re practicing ego worship. There is a difference.

I could have coasted. I could have leaned forever on the fact that I helped build something historic. I could have told myself, “Good enough.” Many people do. Many people stop at the first hill they climb and build a monument to mediocrity.

But that is not who I am.

After Satan Calling, I made a decision. If I ever put out another book, it would have to be superior. Not just different. Not just louder. Superior. It would have to reflect growth. It would have to reflect discipline. It would have to reflect years of sharpening thought, refining voice, strengthening structure.

It would have to be al mine.

And so, after years of thinking, writing, discarding, rewriting, questioning, and evolving, The Satanic Gospels were born.

This time, there are no collaborations. No additional voices. No shared authorship. No room for someone else’s missteps, controversies, or off-stage behavior to spill onto my stage. No dilution. No compromise.

Just me.

That is not arrogance. That is ownership.

When you collaborate, you share brilliance, but you also share risk. And while I do not regret Satan Calling, I learned from it. I learned that when you tie your name to something, you are tying it not only to the content but to every moving piece connected to it. If one piece falters, the entire machine feels it.

With The Satanic Gospels, there is no confusion about authorship. If you love it, that’s on me. If you hate it, that’s on me. If it succeeds, it succeeds because of my discipline. If it fails, it fails because of my shortcomings.

That level of accountability is liberating.

And it has been fun. Incredibly fun.

Writing these books has not felt like obligation. It has felt like ignition. It has felt like finally speaking with a voice that has been tempered through years of reflection. The essays are sharper. The structure is stronger. The humor is more deliberate. The arguments are deeper. The contradictions are intentional rather than accidental.

This time, I did not rush the blade.

Of course, even now, as the books approach release, the whispers begin. They always do.

“He didn’t write it himself.”
“He used AI.”
“It’s not authentic.”
“It’s manufactured.”

My response?

Think whatever you want.

Next.

I do not exist to satisfy the suspicions of strangers. I do not write to appease critics who have never built a thing in their lives. And I certainly do not halt forward motion because someone on the sidelines feels insecure about it.

If you believe I used tools, good. Tools are extensions of human will. The hammer does not build the house, the carpenter does. The pen does not write the book, the mind does. The instrument is irrelevant. The architect matters.

But let’s be honest, the accusation itself is not about technology. It is about dismissal. It is easier to say, “He didn’t really write it,” than to admit, “He improved.”

Improvement makes people uncomfortable. Growth threatens those who remain stagnant.

I have spent years refining my craft. Years studying language. Years pushing myself to think deeper, write clearer, argue stronger. The difference between 2019 and now is not magic. It is work.

Relentless work.

You would think after all these years the critics would understand something about me. I cannot be swayed. I cannot be shamed into silence. I cannot be discouraged into quitting.

I am a fighter.

Persistence is not just a personality trait for me, it is a principle. Satanism is about disciplined self-creation. It is about becoming more formidable with time, not less. It is about forging identity deliberately rather than inheriting it passively.

When people try to bash The Satanic Gospels, they are not attacking a fragile ego. They are testing a will that has already survived far more than criticism.

And here is the truth.

If I had allowed the controversies surrounding Satan Calling to define me, I would have stopped writing.

If I had allowed dissatisfaction with my early contributions to shame me, I would have stopped creating.

If I had allowed rumors about AI or authenticity to intimidate me, I would have halted this project before it began.

But that would not be Satanic.

Satan represents self-determination. The refusal to kneel before the collective’s expectation. The audacity to continue when others demand retreat. The willingness to evolve without asking permission.

I am not here to preserve comfort. I am here to build.

The Satanic Gospels are not an attempt to erase the past. They are proof of growth beyond it. They are what happens when an idea that once shined brighter than my content meets a version of me who has finally caught up to his own vision.

And let’s be clear about something else.

No one can stop this.

Not critics.
Not gossip.
Not accusations.
Not pearl-clutching traditionalists worried about titles.
Not outsiders pretending to guard a philosophy that is, at its core, about individual sovereignty.

Love it or hate it, my words are coming.

They are coming sharpened.
They are coming refined.
They are coming with more effort poured into them than anything I have produced before.

This time, I did not rely on novelty. I relied on discipline.

This time, I did not lean on collaboration. I leaned on accountability.

This time, I did not allow the idea to outshine the execution. I made sure the execution could stand on its own.

And if someone still wants to dismiss it, that is their right. Satanism is not about forced admiration. It is not about recruitment. It is not about unanimous approval.

It is about standing alone when necessary.

Seven years ago, I built  something historic. Today, I am building something personal. Something stronger. Something fully owned.

Satan Calling was a spark.

The Satanic Gospels are the fire.

I am not the same writer I was in 2019. I am sharper. I am more disciplined. I am more deliberate. And I am far less interested in playing small to make others comfortable.

After all these years, if there is one thing the “haters” should have learned, it is this, I do not stop, I do not bend, I do not ask permission to create.

I am Lorcan Black.

I am persistent.

I am accountable to my own standards.

And I AM a Satanist.

……The books are coming.

The Tiger and the Empty Chair

By : Phillip Dau Bul

They call him the Tiger. Not because he roars every day, but because his shadow alone has kept the jungle from tearing itself apart.

Mock him if you want. Laugh at the hat, the walk, the silence. Say he moves slowly. Say he speaks less. Say he looks tired. But ask yourself one question — what happens when the Tiger is no longer there?

Some of you think the problem is the Tiger. But look closer. Is it the Tiger, or is it the crowd feeding around him? The same people who hide behind his name, use his authority, and quietly build their own kingdoms while he carries the weight of history on his shoulders.

If he leaves today, it will not be poetry. It will be panic.

The smiling men will stop smiling. The loyal men will choose new loyalties. The quiet ambitions will become loud. And suddenly, everyone who pretended to serve will begin to compete to rule.

You see an old man walking. History sees a survivor of the bush. You see silence. History hears endurance. You see one man. Reality sees the last wall holding back a storm of unfinished ambitions.

Mock the Tiger if you wish. But remember this: when the jungle loses its Tiger, it does not become peaceful. It becomes open season.

And on that day, many will realize too late that stability was not as cheap as they thought.

🇷🇴A venit timpul să depășim modelul de stat construit la începutul anilor ’90 și să construim o țară care să funcționeze cu adevărat pentru români.

🇷🇴Sub conducerea lui Ion Iliescu și a Frontul Salvării Naționale, s-a consolidat un sistem care a permis perpetuarea unor privilegii și formarea unor rețele de influență în politică, economie și administrație.

🇷🇴De-a lungul anilor, practici clientelare au afectat sectoare esențiale, agricultura, energia, industria, educația, sănătatea și infrastructura. Contractele publice au fost adesea percepute ca fiind direcționate preferențial, iar această realitate a alimentat un sentiment profund de nedreptate socială. Astfel s-a conturat un sistem în care conexiunile politice au contat mai mult decât competența. Relația dintre politică și mediul de afaceri a devenit adesea prea strânsă, iar contractele cu statul au favorizat, nu de puține ori, aceleași cercuri. Pentru unii a însemnat prosperitate, pentru mulți alții stagnare și frustrări.

🇷🇴În acest context, anul 2025 aduce o tentativă reală de schimbare. Prin agenda de reforme propusă de Ilie Bolojan: eliminarea privilegiilor nejustificate, limitarea contractelor „cu dedicație”, abordarea problemei pensiilor speciale, se încearcă, pentru prima dată după mult timp, o reașezare a priorităților statului. Sunt măsuri de bun-simț, pe care majoritatea românilor le așteaptă de ani de zile.

🇷🇴Nu este surprinzător că aceste inițiative întâmpină rezistență din partea unor structuri politice consolidate, inclusiv din zona Partidul Social Democrat, dar și din partea unor actori instituționali sau politici care se tem de pierderea avantajelor. Am văzut blocaje procedurale, opoziție vocală și tentative de amânare a reformelor, un semn clar că miza este mare.

🇷🇴În ultimii 35 de ani, schimbările profunde au fost adesea întârziate. Totuși, pare că societatea începe să devină mai atentă și mai exigentă. Este încurajator să vezi că inclusiv susținători ai AUR sau PSD recunosc necesitatea acestor măsuri, chiar dacă nu împărtășesc aceleași simpatii politice. Dincolo de diferențe, tot mai mulți oameni înțeleg că este nevoie de un stat mai corect, mai eficient și mai apropiat de cetățeni.

🇷🇴În lunile și anii care urmează, se va contura tot mai clar o alegere: între continuarea unui sistem bazat pe privilegii acordate selectiv sau asumarea unei reforme reale, în interes public. Cred că românii sunt pregătiți pentru o resetare. Nu una distrugătoare, ci una constructivă.

🇷🇴Este momentul să lăsăm în urmă reflexele vechiului sistem și să construim o țară în care regulile sunt aceleași pentru toți și în care statul lucrează, cu adevărat, pentru români.

تحلّ علينا هذه الأيام الذكرى الخامسة عشر لثورة السابع عشر من فبراير، تلك المحطة الوطنية الفارقة في تاريخ ليبيا المعاصر، والتي جسّدت إرادة الشعب الليبي في التغيير، والتطلع إلى دولة القانون والمؤسسات، والكرامة والعدالة. كما نستقبل في الوقت ذاته نفحات شهر رمضان المبارك، شهر الرحمة والمغفرة والتسامح، بما يحمله من معاني السمو الروحي وتجديد العهد مع القيم الإسلامية التي يقوم عليها مجتمعنا.

وبهذه المناسبة الوطنية والدينية الجليلة، يتقدم رئيس ونائبا جهاز الحرس الرئاسي الليبي، وكافة الضباط وضباط الصف والجنود ومنتسبي الحرس، بأصدق التهاني وأطيب التبريكات إلى أبناء الشعب الليبي كافة، سائلين الله العلي القدير أن يعيد هذه المناسبات على وطننا بالأمن والاستقرار، وعلى شعبنا بالخير والوئام.

إن ثورة السابع عشر من فبراير لم تكن مجرد حدث عابر في مسار التاريخ، بل كانت تعبيرًا عن إرادة شعبٍ يتطلع إلى بناء دولة حديثة، تُصان فيها الحقوق، وتُحترم فيها السيادة، ويعلو فيها صوت القانون فوق كل اعتبار. وإذ نستحضر هذه الذكرى، فإننا نستذكر تضحيات الشهداء، ومعاناة الليبيين عبر سنوات صعبة من الانقسام والتحديات الأمنية والاقتصادية والسياسية.
ورغم ما يمر به الوطن من تحديات جسام، فإننا نؤمن يقينًا بأن الأوطان قد تمرض ولكنها لا تموت. وستنهض ليبيا من جديد، بإذن الله، وتعود وطنًا آمنًا مستقرًا، سيدًا مستقلًا، بسواعد أبنائها المخلصين، وبعزيمة رجالها الذين لم يفقدوا الأمل يومًا في مستقبل أفضل.

وفي هذا السياق، يؤكد الحرس الرئاسي الليبي التزامه الثابت بمهامه الوطنية في حماية المؤسسات الشرعية، وتأمين المقرات السيادية، والمساهمة في ترسيخ الاستقرار، انطلاقًا من عقيدة مهنية وطنية خالصة، تضع مصلحة ليبيا فوق كل اعتبار، وتعمل بروح الانضباط والمسؤولية في خدمة الوطن والمواطن.

نسأل الله أن يكون شهر رمضان المبارك فرصة لتعزيز روح التسامح والتآخي بين الليبيين، وأن يجمع كلمتهم على الحق، ويوحّد صفوفهم، ويوفق الجميع لِما فيه خير البلاد والعباد.

حفظ الله ليبيا، ومنَّ عليها بنعمة الأمن والاستقرار، وجعل مستقبلها أكثر إشراقًا وعدلاً وازدهارًا.

Sa kanyang pahayag, diretsahan niyang kinuwestiyon ang naging aksyon ni Bosita sa lungsod:

“Nakapagtataka talaga — sa laki ng Pilipinas, dito pa sa Davao napiling umeksena ni Mr. Bosita.”

Ipinunto rin niya ang umano’y paraan ng pakikitungo nito sa mga city employees:

“Kung makasigaw sa mga city employees na maayos namang ginagawa ang trabaho nila, akala mo siya ang inihalal ng mga Dabawenyo para mamuno sa siyudad. You were not elected here. Our people chose their leaders. Respect that.”

Binigyang-diin din ni Duterte ang legal na basehan ng pagpapatupad ng regulasyon:

“For your information, may City Ordinance No. 0334-12, the Comprehensive Transport and Traffic Code of Davao City. Hindi ito basta trip lang ng LGU. It exists to protect public order — especially against excessively loud modified exhaust systems na wala namang dulot kundi istorbo, ingay, at alarma lalo na sa gabi.”

Dagdag pa niya, mahalaga umano sa lungsod ang katahimikan at disiplina:

“Davao values discipline. Davao values peace and quiet. Hindi ito about pagpapasikat. It’s about protecting communities — especially families, elderly residents, at mga batang natutulog sa gabi.”

Hinimok din niya ang tamang proseso ng adbokasiya:

“Kung gusto mong mag-advocate, gawin mo sa tamang paraan. Dialogue, not drama. Policy discussion, not public spectacle.”

Nagbigay pa siya ng halimbawa upang idiin ang epekto ng maiingay na tambutso:

“At kung sa tingin mo harmless ang bora-bora pipes, pwede naman siguro nating subukan — dalhin natin sa tapat ng bahay mo, sabay-sabay paandarin sa dis-oras ng gabi. Tan-awon nato kung dili ka mabwisit. Principle is easy to defend when it’s not your neighborhood affected.”

Nanawagan din siya sa mga motorista:

“Sa mga Dabawenyong motorista, sumunod tayo sa batas. Kung may kailangang amyendahan ang ordinansa, may proseso. The local government is open to consultation. That’s how governance works — not through shouting matches, but through legislation and public dialogue.”

At nagtapos siya sa mas matapang na pahayag:

“Criticism is welcome. Arrogance is not. Davao will always choose order over noise. Ayaw'g siyagit siyagit diri bay kay ikaw ray bungol.”

Samantala, wala pang inilalabas na opisyal na pahayag si Bosita kaugnay sa mga alegasyon at pahayag na ibinato laban sa kanya.

Supreme Court Dismisses Rivers State University Appeal, Upholds Muslim Students’ Right to Worship on Campus
ABUJA, Feb. 10, 2026.

The Supreme Court has dismissed the appeal filed by Rivers State University (RSU), ending a long legal dispute that started in 2012 over the right of Muslim students to pray and have a place of worship on campus.

The case was brought by Umaru Wazuru and 98 other Muslim students, who complained that the university authorities prevented them from observing prayers and establishing a mosque, even though churches were already operating within the campus.

In 2013, the Federal High Court in Port Harcourt ruled in favour of the students. The court held that denying Muslim students a place of worship violated their constitutional right to freedom of religion.

RSU appealed the judgment, but in 2017, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and affirmed the High Court’s decision.

The university went further to the Supreme Court. On February 10, 2026, the Supreme Court unanimously dismissed the appeal, confirming that Muslim students have the right to worship freely and should be allocated a suitable space on campus.

This decision is final and binding, and the university is expected to comply with the court’s ruling.

I say this because one of the things that is being used against me is the fact that I actively engage on social media, and Facebook in particular. Information that was relayed to me by the Darfurian.

In one of our previous conversations, I was following up on a request for a meeting through him. I knew this meeting had the influence of the former minister's son, attached to it, based on the response i got from the Darfuri guy. The Dafuri responded by telling me that the moment he mentioned my name, the Honorable Special Envoy drastically changed her facial expression and her mood dropped suddenly.

What a freaking lie.

Hon. Adut is a politician and a natural born leader. Leaders never show emotions. That is how we were oriented from a young age. To suggest that a woman of her standing, a Kiir by blood and a product of the SPLM school of politics, would wear her emotions on her sleeve because of a name is not just an insult to her. It is an insult to the institution of leadership itself. This man manufactures narratives to suit his agenda, and unfortunately, some people buy into them.

As much as my loyalty is questioned today by some of my fellow countrymen and women because of some of the political decisions I made along my journey, I remain steady. My views have never changed, and my deep appreciation to Gen. Taban Deng Gai. He is a leader who looks at the youth through a future perspective, a leader who sees beyond the immediate and invests in what is to come. He inspires me not because of positions, but because of his vision.

Yes, I briefly joined the SPLM-IO in 2015. And in the few months I was there, I felt no difference at all. I was accorded the same nationalistic spirit in Pagak that I was accorded in Juba. When we came back in December 2015, barely months after joining the opposition, my impact was already visible. I had already made my mark.

Let me remind people of who I am. I was the former Chairman of the Greater Bahr el Ghazal Youth Union, an initiative I undertook back in 2011. I also served as a former NBGS youth leader 2008-2011, working alongside fellow youths whom are now tasked with national duties at various institutions of our government.These are men of substance, and we worked together for the youth.

Anyway, just to come back to my point. I am now truly feeling the weight of the Darfurian's words. He made me reflect on my unfavorable circumstances, and in doing so, I see a pattern of destruction that goes beyond just me.

My brother Agel Ring should also look deep into his own stagnant situation. He was introduced to this same Darfurian guy by the same childhood friend of mine. The same one I first introduced the Dafurian guy to from our circle and the one I mentioned in my previous piece. Agel is a man of potential, yet here he sits, stuck in place, while the very people he was connected to move forward or block his path entirely. This is not a coincidence, it's a design.

To keep this conversation moving, in Part Three I will begin to mention a few names. Cde. Akot Lual. Cde. Benjamin Bol Mel. And a couple more people whom also relate to this conversation. 

Forward we move.

On this day in 1943, a thirty two year old Polish woman was murdered in Auschwitz after just three months and seven days of imprisonment.

Her name was Sylwia Nistenberger.

Before the camp reduced her to a number, she was a clerk. She had habits, conversations, perhaps small daily frustrations and ordinary hopes. She moved through a world that still believed in tomorrow.

Auschwitz was first established in 1940 as a concentration camp for Polish prisoners. By 1943 it had become the largest killing center in Europe, but it remained a place where ethnic Poles, Jewish Poles, Roma, and others were imprisoned under a racial regime that measured human worth according to ideology.

Three months and seven days. That is all the Third Reich allowed her.

When we say “millions,” we lose faces. When we say “victims,” we risk abstraction. But Sylwia was not an abstraction. She was a woman with a name, a profession, and a life that did not deserve to end behind barbed wire.

Memory resists reduction. It restores the singular.

Today we remember Sylwia Nistenberger not as a statistic, but as a human being whose life was violently taken, and whose name must not disappear into silence.

I can’t even put into words how bad this hurts. This loss hit different. It’s a pain that sit heavy on my chest. If somebody really knew our bond, they’d understand why this one broke me the way it did.

You wasn’t just my best friend… you was my brother. Chosen family. My right hand. My safe place.

Every morning my phone would ring, and it’d be you. “You good? Mental straight?” Even when you had your own battles, you still made sure I was okay. That’s the type of heart you had. You carried everybody, even when nobody knew you needed carrying too.

To know you was to love you. Solid. Loyal. About your family. About your paper. But most of all, about your people. You would defend somebody’s name in a room they wasn’t even in. You stood on business and you stood on love.

And what hurt the most… you made sure everybody else was straight, even when you wasn’t.

I miss them calls.
I miss them talks.
I miss laughing with you.
I miss knowing I could reach for my phone and you’d answer.

There’s a hole here now that can’t be filled.

But I promise you this as long as there’s breath in my body, your name will never die. I’m going to speak it. I’m going to honor it. I’m going to live in a way that make you proud. Your legacy not stopping here.

Thank you for being my brother.
Thank you for love you gave everyone 
Thank you for being solid when the world wasn’t.

In my eyes, you forever a legend.

I love you. I miss you. And I carry you with me every day.

WHAT HAS NOT YET BEEN DONE TO THE APC?

Sheriff Mahmud Ismail

On Monday, 16th Februrary, 2026, the ruling Sierra Leone Peoples Party (SLPP) presided over a political charade that borders on bewilderment and shambolism. In the process, they produced images that are as stark as they are unforgettable, depicting the weaponization of the judiciary. 

Lansana Dumbuya, Secretary General of the main opposition All Peoples Congress (APC), steps down from the back of a sealed prison truck, wrists bound in handcuffs. Why? Dumbuya accused President Bio of stealing the 2023 elections.

But President Koroma was heckled and insulted in New York by known SLPP supporters and stakeholders using the same words Dumbuya used to describe President Bio's actions relating to the 2023 elections. The insulting hecklers returned home. No one was invited by the police. No one was questioned, detained, cuffed or charged to court.

The mistreatment of the APC Nationsl Secretary-General was meant to cow him to bow, but he emerged strong, courageous, and inspiring. In that single moment of lifting his hands high in defiance, he becomes more than a detainee. He becomes a symbol of courage, strength, and resistance.

But there is also another symbolism that is jarring. The Magistrate Court stands just beside Pademba Road Prison. A connecting passage was built to allow detainees to move quietly and with dignity from cell to courtroom. But that path was not used. Instead, Dumbuya was loaded into a sealed prison vehicle, paraded through public view, and brought out from the rear like a dangerous convict. For a man accused over political comments, the message felt deliberate, the humiliation unmistakable.

And yet, even with his cuffed hands, he demonstrated that strength does not come from the abuse of state apparatus. Dumbuya demolished tyranny without saying a word. In that gesture of raising his handcuffs, he said it all: You may shackle my hands, but you cannot break my spirit, you cannot silence my voice, or dim my mind. It was a moment that stirred both sympathy and pride.

What deepens the unease is the sequence of events that led there. The Political Parties Regulation Commission (PPRC) had already fined the APC heavily over the comments attributed to Dumbuya, a penalty the party paid. Still, he was detained for a whole day at the Criminal Investigation Department (CID). Then, he was rearrested on Thursday, arraigned, and remanded at the Pademba Road Prison. To many, it feels like double jeopardy - punishment layered upon punishment for the same matter.

Therefore, on the day of his second court appearance, lawyers, supporters, and observers gathered from 9 a.m., expecting the case at 10 a.m. The time kept shifting. Hours passed. By about 3 p.m., confusion gave way to disbelief. There had been no hearing. No proceedings. No formal explanation. The faint - hearted magistrate had abducated and fled hurriedly through the back door. That act of cowardice by someone deemed to be in cohoot with the belligerent should be seem as a gutwrenching symbolism of how frail the oppressor could be. .

This is not the first such mistreatment of APC leaders. Two years ago, there was another image, equally haunting, poignant, and hair-stirring. A former president of the republic standing quietly in the dock, shoulders squared, hands behind him, framed by wooden rails. A man who once led a nation being subjected as a defendant before it, then forced out of his country? Whether one supports him or not, the symbolism is profound. It portrays a public spectacle choreographed to mock, lacerate, and drain the APC of dignity, strength and morale.

Placed side by side, the scenes form a pattern many cannot ignore. They throwback the painful memories of those nauseating Commissions of Inquiry (COIs) many believe were politically motivated, which were used to strip leaders of assets and standing. There were those endless legal battles that drained resources, those actions that deprived access to frozen bank accounts, severance benefits and tenured jobs.

Still, there were the travel bans that reportedly resulted in some individuals being unable to seek urgent medical treatment abroad because of restrictions and delays, and lives were reportedly lost. 

Then, there was the removal of elected APC Members of Parliament, replaced by their SLPP opponents who were runners up, without the cleansing of constitutionally mandated by-elections- topped by the imposition of a Speaker. There was the firing of life rounds at the APC headquarters, killing an innocent health worker who was there to help save lives. And there iwas the crux of the matter - the premature announcement of ‘statistically inconsistent’ elections results before the counting of ballots was completed in many parts of the country. 

Back on to the Monday 16 Februray charade, an observer’s words, shared widely on social media, captured the shock: 

“I have never seen this happening. Lawyers are in court, the Magistrate adjourned without them knowing. He left through the chambers’ back door. The Registrar comes out and tells the court that matter is adjourned. How was the adjournment done? No proceedings? Nothing. For fairness sake, even if you want to adjourn, you should call the defendant’s representatives or the lawyers present and tell them that you are adjourning for whatever reasons. But even that courtesy couldn’t be extended to your legal colleagues. Wow!”

The lead defence counsel for Dumbuya, Joseph Fitzgerald Kamara, speaking to journalists outside the courtroom, re-echoes this undisputable fact. He described the situation as “a sad day for justice in Sierra Leone,” stressing that the legal team had been ready to vigorously defend their colleague but were deprived from doing so.

“The matter was not adjourned formally, and the accused was whisked off without our knowledge or the opportunity of knowing the adjournment date,” Kamara said.

He added that the defence will file a petition with the Chief Justice over the incident and warned that they would challenge what he described as an attempt to weaponise the judiciary.

“We will vigorously challenge any institution that will weaponise the judiciary of this country,” he asserted.

But it is the APC Acting National Chairman, Osman Foday Yansaneh’s words that every Sierra Leonean must remember: The party has exercised “tremendous patience,” he said, before reinforcing Kamara’s sentiments that the handling of the court process did not follow proper procedures for adjourning a matter. 

To the observer, it might feel like a slow tightening grip, an unrelenting pressure meant to weaken and weary. To the APC, state institutions have been compromised, instrumentalised to persecute, to extort, to exhaust, to cripple.

And yet history sits quietly in the background, offering a mirror of what the APC faced during the era of the National Provisional Ruling Council (NPRC) military junta, a dictatorship the current president was a part of and a period associated with suppression, extra-judicial killings, and hardship. That memory now hangs over the present. It raises difficult questions about whether the lessons of the past are being remembered. The country’s post conflict reflections spoke in broad terms about the dangers of exclusion, of intolerance, of the misuse of power, and the closing of democratic space. They warned that humiliation, marginalisation, and the erosion of trust were among the roots of national tragedy. They urged fairness, restraint, and inclusion to ensure the past would not return.

The warning is particularly poignant in the face of the irony that many find impossible to ignore. That irony relates to the façade of an elaborate so-called “National Remembrance Day.” On that day, citizens and leaders were entreated to reflect on how and why the country must never return to those dark chapters. But the images on the ground seem to tell another story. The National Secretary -General of the main opposition party in chains for words he uttered! Two years earlier, a former president from the same party in the dock! The APC, it leaders and supporters under relentless pressure!

One is tempted to ask:
Is there no one in the SLPP that understands the warning that power is never permanent - that the same state machinery used today can be inherited tomorrow - that the same precedents set in one era can return in another?

Is there no one in the SLPP that remembers that the APC party endured arrests, pressure, and extra - judicial killings. But it survived. It stood back up. It reorganised. It returned. And, in many ways, it emerged stronger?

Is there no one in the SLPP that believes that if the APC prevailed before, it will do so again?

Or is it because the SLPP knows that the APC is not vengeful, that when in power, they concentrate on working for the common good rather political witch hunt?

Whatever the motivations for SLPP's amnesia, it is instructive not to ignore the simple words of the APC Acting National Chairman: "the party has exercised tremendous patience."

Imagine your husband worships gods you consider demons.
Every day, he prays to Jupiter. To Mars. To Mercury. To Celtic deities and Scandinavian gods. To statues of stone, wood, and metal. To some strange sea god that's part man, part beast, part bull.

And you? You're a Catholic. A devout believer in the one true God.
This was Clotilde's reality when she married Clovis, King of the Franks, around 493 AD.
Clotilde was a Burgundian princess who had endured tragedy. Her uncle Gundobad had murdered her father and drowned her mother. He'd forced one of Clotilde's sisters into a convent. The family was torn apart by violence and ambition.
But Clotilde survived. And when another uncle, Godegisel, found himself in a precarious political position, he decided to ally with the powerful Frankish king Clovis by offering him his exiled niece in marriage.

Clovis was about 27 years old, already king of the Salian Franks for roughly 12 years. He was a brutal, effective warrior. Gregory of Tours, writing decades later, described Clovis as personally capable of splitting a man's head open with an axe if anyone demeaned his honor.

But Clovis was also politically shrewd. A marriage alliance with the Burgundians was strategically valuable.
So Clotilde, the Catholic princess, married Clovis, the pagan king.

And from the moment of their marriage, Clotilde had a mission: convert her husband.
According to Gregory of Tours, Clotilde used "florid rhetoric" to argue with Clovis, trying to persuade him to abandon paganism. She told him about the Christian God. About salvation. About truth.

Clovis resisted. He wasn't some rabid anti-Christian (after all, he'd married a Christian and allowed her to practice her faith), but he wasn't interested in converting either.
Then Clotilde became pregnant with their first son.
She begged Clovis to let the child be baptized.
He refused.

So Clotilde had the baby baptized in secret, without Clovis's knowledge.
Days later, the child died.
Clovis exploded in rage. He blamed the baptism. He blamed Clotilde's God. He blamed the "magical Christian water." He swore he would never allow another child to go through that ritual.

The grief must have been overwhelming for both of them. But for Clotilde, it was compounded by her husband's fury and his rejection of everything she believed had meaning.

When their second son, Chlodomer, was born, Clotilde faced an impossible choice.
She baptized him anyway. Again without Clovis's permission.
And again, disaster struck. The child fell desperately ill immediately after the baptism.
Clovis was furious. His worst fears confirmed. This Christian God was killing his sons.
But Clotilde prayed. Frantically, desperately, she prayed for her son's life.
And Chlodomer survived. He recovered.

This, Gregory of Tours suggests, began to shift something in Clovis's mind. Not enough to convert. But enough to wonder.

For years, this continued. Clotilde arguing, pleading, reasoning. Clovis resisting, worshipping his pagan gods, remaining skeptical.
The turning point came around 496 AD (though some historians now argue it was as late as 508 AD).

Clovis led his Franks into battle against the Alemanni, a fierce pagan Germanic tribe living along the Rhine near modern-day Germany and Belgium.
The battle went badly. The Franks were being slaughtered. Clovis's forces were on the verge of total defeat.

And in that moment of desperation, Clovis did something he'd never done before.
He cried out to Clotilde's God.
He promised that if the Christian God would give him victory, he would convert. He would abandon his pagan gods. He would be baptized.
According to the accounts, the tide of battle immediately turned. The Alemanni king was killed. His army, seeing their leader fall, surrendered.
Clovis had his victory.

And now he had a promise to keep.
According to tradition, Clovis was baptized on Christmas Day, either in 496 or (more likely according to modern scholars) in 508, in a small church near what would become the Abbey of Saint-Remi in Reims.

The ceremony was orchestrated by Bishop Remigius of Reims, a learned and holy man who Clovis had been meeting with secretly for religious instruction.
The city of Reims was decorated lavishly for the occasion. White banners hung throughout the streets. It was a festive, public spectacle.
Clovis processed through the city to the church, accompanied by 3,000 of his warriors who would also be baptized.

As Clovis approached the baptismal font to renounce his Frankish idols, Bishop Remigius spoke words that would echo through history:
"Bow thy head, adore what thou hast burned, and burn what thou hast adored!"
Clovis was baptized. He affirmed the Nicene Creed, accepting the Holy Trinity. He was marked with holy chrism oil with the sign of the cross.

And with him, 3,000 Frankish warriors went into the waters of baptism.
There's a charming legend about the ceremony. They say that in the haste to accommodate the king and thousands of warriors, someone forgot to bring the holy oil needed for the anointing. But miraculously, a white dove appeared carrying a vial of oil from heaven.
Whether true or not, the symbolism was powerful: God himself had anointed this barbarian king.

For Clotilde, it must have been the culmination of years of prayer, argument, and heartbreak.
Her first son had died. Her second son had nearly died. She had endured her husband's rage, his mockery of her faith, his devotion to gods she considered demonic.
But she had persevered. And now, watching her husband emerge from the baptismal waters, she had won.
Or had she?

Here's the uncomfortable truth that historians have long grappled with: Clovis's baptism changed very little about his actual behavior.
French historian Ernest Lavisse noted: "The conversion of Clovis in no way changed his character; the gentle and peaceful moral of the Gospel did not touch his heart."
Another historian declared: "Instead of Odin, he invoked Christ and remained the same."
After his conversion, Clovis systematically murdered every potential rival to his throne. 

He exterminated relatives "to the sixth degree." He betrayed allies. He ordered assassinations.
He convinced Prince Chlodoric to murder his own father, then had Chlodoric killed. He bribed the retainers of his old ally Ragnachar, then executed Ragnachar and his brother.
Reminiscent of Constantine after his supposed conversion, Clovis used Christianity as a political tool while continuing to behave like a ruthless warlord.
But here's what his conversion did change: the entire political and religious landscape of Western Europe.

By converting to Nicene Catholic Christianity (as opposed to Arian Christianity), Clovis made a brilliant strategic move.
Most other Germanic tribes were Arian Christians. The Visigoths, Ostrogoths, Burgundians, Vandals. They all followed Arianism, which taught that Jesus was subordinate to and created by God the Father.
The Catholic Church had declared Arianism a heresy at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.
By converting to Catholicism instead of Arianism, Clovis aligned himself with:

The Gallo-Roman Catholic majority in Gaul
The powerful Catholic bishops who controlled administrative networks
The Pope and the institutional Church

He became the champion of orthodox Christianity against the Arian "heretics."
In 507, Clovis defeated the Arian Visigoths in battle, extending Frankish power to the Pyrenees. He positioned himself as the protector and liberator of Catholics in Western Europe.

The Catholic bishops enthusiastically endorsed his authority. The Church's administrative machinery helped him consolidate control over conquered territories.
And when Clovis died in 511 AD (or possibly 513), he left a kingdom that would become the foundation of medieval France.

His descendants, the Merovingian dynasty, would rule for nearly two centuries. Eventually, the Carolingians would replace them, culminating in Charlemagne being crowned Holy Roman Emperor by the Pope in 800 AD.

All of this traced back to Christmas Day 496 (or 508), when a pagan warrior king went into baptismal waters because his Catholic wife had spent years arguing with him and because he'd made a desperate battlefield promise.
Clotilde was later venerated as a saint by both the Catholic Church and Eastern Orthodox Church for her role in converting Clovis.

When Clovis died, he was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles that he'd built in Paris, next to Saint Geneviève. Years later, Clotilde was buried beside him.
The determined Catholic princess and the brutal pagan king, together in death as they had been in life.

The marriage that changed Europe.
Because one woman refused to give up on converting her husband.

Legal scholars point out that much of this expansion predates any individual president and reflects long-standing tensions between the branches of government. Polémique aux JO d’Hiver 2026 : Le commentateur suisse Stefan Renna démonte l’équipe israélienne de bobsleigh

Les Jeux Olympiques d'hiver de Milano Cortina 2026 ont accouché d'un commentaire aussi savoureux qu'embarrassant pour la délégation israélienne. Entre deux virages sur la piste de bobsleigh, c'est une voix suisse qui a osé rappeler que l'étoile de David traîne dans son sillage un charnier nommé Gaza. La performance sportive ? Médiocre, pour ne pas dire catastrophique. La charge politique ? Dévastatrice.

La mécanique du ridicule

Il fallait voir ce bob israélien négocier la piste de Cortina comme un éléphant dans un magasin de porcelaine. Adam Edelman, fier pilote sioniste « jusqu’à la moelle » comme il aime le clamer sur ses réseaux sociaux, et son freineur Menachem Chen ont offert au monde une démonstration de médiocrité technique aussi spectaculaire qu’involontaire. Leur engin, orné aux couleurs nationales, a caressé chaque paroi de glace avec une insistance maladroite, transformant cette descente en parcours du combattant contre les lois de la physique. Résultat des courses : une dernière place acquise avec la conviction des vaincus qui singent les vainqueurs, bras levés et sourire aux lèvres, comme si terminer loin derrière les Allemands méritait des célébrations nationales.

Le micro qui tue

C’est là que Stefan Renna, commentateur pour la Radio Télévision Suisse, a transformé l’essai. Tandis que l’image montrait ce ballet de médiocrité, sa voix posée a choisi de ne pas jouer le jeu de l’omerta olympique. Il a cité Edelman, ce pilote qui se revendique « sioniste jusqu’à la moelle ». Il a évoqué ses publications enflammées sur les réseaux, où l’homme qualifie l’intervention militaire à Gaza de « guerre la plus moralement juste de l’histoire ». Il a rappelé, sans trembler, que des instances internationales parlent de génocide. En deux minutes chrono, Renna a fait ce que le Comité international olympique refuse obstinément : établir un lien entre le sport et la réalité. Entre le bob qui dérape et les bombes qui tombent.

L’hypocrisie olympique

Car voilà l’os que ce commentaire a déniché : comment se fait-il que la Russie, bannie pour son intervention en Ukraine, reste au ban des nations pendant qu’Israël défile fièrement sous le drapeau étoilé ? Où est passée la cohérence du CIO, cette institution si prompte à moraliser quand il s’agit d’exclure Moscou, mais muette comme une tombe quand Tel Aviv perpétue ce que les experts qualifient de nettoyage ethnique ? Le sport, ce miroir aux alouettes, révèle soudain ses coutures idéologiques. La performance israélienne, aussi dérisoire soit-elle, devient symbole : celui d’une impunité que même la glace italienne ne parvient pas à geler.
Ces deux minutes de bob malmené auront accompli ce que des années de rapports onusiens peinent à produire : une prise de conscience collective, fût-elle fugace, que l’olympisme a deux poids, deux mesures. Et que certaines étoiles, sur fond bleu, brillent plus que d’autres dans l’indifférence complice des instances.

In the Ruweng Administrative Area, the promise of South Sudan’s future is slipping away. Underage students and jobless youth are being swept into military by the Chief of Ruweng’s command. This is more than a leadership failure; it is a violation of international law and a deep betrayal of an entire generation. The cruelest cut of forced recruitment is its hypocrisy. While the children of the poor are marched to war, the sons and daughters of leaders study safely in Kampala and Nairobi. This is not an unrelated headline for me; it is the story of my own life. On April 10, 2011, I was one of 254 children taken from Parieng County and forced to march ten hours to Buoth Training Center in Mayom County. Many boys beside me never made it home, their lives lost in unmarked graves, stolen by a war they could not understand. Seeing this tragedy repeat in 2026 shows that some leaders still believe they can hold onto power by sacrificing the young.

South Sudan deserves an army built on respect, not one assembled by ripping children from their classrooms. A true national force is formed by willing adults, paid fairly and treated with dignity, not by converting schools into hunting grounds for recruits. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child is a solemn promise, not a mere suggestion. We must shield our schools and guarantee that no child is ever targeted or forced into service.

I call on the Chief of Ruweng and the central government in Juba to end forced recruitment now. Every detained child must be released, welcomed back to school, and given the support to heal. An independent investigation must bring those responsible to justice. Real security for South Sudan cannot be built on the pain of its children. Our youth need classrooms, not weapons; they deserve hope, not heartbreak. I speak for those lost in 2011 and for those whose futures are still at risk.

The cold didn’t bother me as much as the silence. In our house, silence wasn’t peace; it was the heavy, suffocating weight of things unsaid. It was the way my father looked at his shoes when Cynthia raised her voice. It was the way the air seemed to vanish whenever I walked into a room she had already claimed as her own.

I was ten years old, and I had become an expert at being invisible. I knew which floorboards creaked. I knew that if I held my breath long enough, I could disappear into the shadows of the hallway. But today, the mud had betrayed me. A single track of wet earth on the pristine white rug of the entryway—a rug that cost more than my mother’s old car, or so Cynthia reminded us every day.

“Look at this,” she whispered. Her voice was never louder than a prayer, which made it all the more terrifying. It was a sharp, clinical sound. “Leo, look at what you’ve done to my home.”

I didn’t look at the rug. I looked at her shoes—sharp, pointed heels that looked like they could draw blood. I tried to apologize, but the words died in my throat. My father was in the kitchen, the clinking of his coffee spoon against the ceramic the only sign he was even there. He didn’t come out. He never came out.

Before I could move, her hand was on my collar. It wasn’t a gentle grip. It was the grip of someone taking out the trash. She hauled me toward the front door, the wood grain blurring under my feet. 

“You want to be a pig?” she hissed, her face inches from mine. I could smell her expensive peppermint gum and the metallic scent of her hairspray. “Then go live in the dirt where you belong.”

The door swung open to the grey, drizzling Tuesday afternoon. With a strength that surprised me, she shoved. I didn’t have time to catch my balance. My sneakers slipped on the wet porch steps, and I went down hard. 

The impact with the garden bed was a dull thud that rattled my teeth. Cold, slick mud filled my mouth and coated my jeans. For a moment, the world was just the smell of wet earth and the stinging heat in my scraped palms. I looked up, blinking through the rain, hoping to see my father standing in the doorway. 

But there was only Cynthia. She stood on the top step, looking down at me with a disgust so pure it felt like a physical weight. I started to cry—not the loud, demanding cry of a child who wants attention, but the quiet, rhythmic sobbing of a child who knows no one is coming to help.

“Stop that noise,” she snapped, stepping down onto the first gravel path. “You’re pathetic. Just like her.”

I knew who 'her' was. My mother. The woman whose pictures Cynthia had systematically removed from every frame in the house until the only place she existed was in the back of my mind.

I tried to scramble backward, my hands sliding in the muck. Cynthia reached for me again, her hand raised high. I closed my eyes, bracing for the sting I knew was coming. I waited for the sharp contact, the familiar humiliation of being silenced. 

But the strike never landed.

Instead, there was a sound I had only heard through the walls of the house across the street—a low, vibrating rumble that seemed to come from the earth itself. It wasn’t a bark. It was a warning. 

I opened one eye. 

Buster was there. The dog from across the street. The one the neighborhood kids called 'The Beast.' He was a Belgian Malinois, lean and scarred, belonging to Mr. Henderson, the veteran who never left his house except to sit on his porch and stare at nothing. 

Buster wasn’t biting. He wasn’t attacking. He had simply... appeared. He stood directly between me and Cynthia, his body a rigid line of muscle. He didn’t growl again; he just stood there, his golden eyes fixed on Cynthia’s raised hand. His presence was a wall of fur and teeth that made the world go silent.

Cynthia froze. Her hand stayed suspended in the air, her fingers trembling slightly. The mask of controlled fury she wore cracked, revealing a jagged edge of genuine fear. 

“Get away,” she breathed, her voice finally losing its calm. “Get that animal away from me!”

Buster didn’t move. He didn't even blink. He leaned back slightly against my mud-covered chest, his warmth seeping through my soaked shirt. It was the first time in years I felt something protecting me.

Then, from the shadows of the porch across the street, a voice drifted over—gravelly, tired, and carrying the weight of a thousand miles. 

“He doesn’t like it when people raise their hands, Ma'am,” Mr. Henderson said. He was leaning against a pillar, his old army jacket damp from the mist. He wasn’t looking at Cynthia. He was looking at me. “He’s seen enough of that to last ten lifetimes.”

Cynthia stepped back, her heel catching on a stone. “Your dog is a menace! I’ll have him put down! He’s threatening me on my own property!”

“He’s standing on the sidewalk,” Mr. Henderson replied quietly. “And he hasn’t moved an inch toward you. He’s just standing guard. Funny thing about Buster... he always knows who the victim is.”

I looked at the dog. Buster turned his head just a fraction, his wet nose brushing my cheek. In that moment, the mud didn't feel so cold anymore. I looked past Cynthia, past the house that wasn't a home, and saw my father finally standing at the window. He was watching. For the first time, he saw everything. 

But he didn't move. He just watched as the 'traumatized' dog and the 'broken' soldier did the one thing he couldn't do. They stood up for me.

Royal Mail Group Members,

You may have seen that the BBC has recently reported that Liam Byrne, Labour MP and Chair of the Business and Trade Select Committee, has written to the CEO of Royal Mail. In the letter, he has outlined the quality of service crisis and given the company two weeks to answer a series of questions regarding the service, including whether the company is prioritising parcels over letters. A copy of the letter is attached to this email.

This is a serious investigation from the government, spurred on by the thousands of our members who have written to their MPs over the past few months, as part of the CWU’s letter writing campaign. We are pleased that the government has not accepted Royal Mail’s attempts to explain away these issues as though this is a short-term problem.

We all know this is a company that has orchestrated a long-term UK wide crisis in customer quality, staff turnover/shortages and overtime bans. The reason being there are very senior managers still wedded to a strategy that accelerates letter decline – makes Royal Mail just another parcel courier – replicating the exploitative employment models of the competitors.

In response to this important parliamentary intervention, the union is stepping up our engagement with politicians from all political parties to ensure the voices of postal workers are fully heard by Westminster.  It is therefore vital that we take any opportunity to represent the views of frontline postal workers to both the government and the public. As such, we will contact members and branches with further initiatives in due course.

CWU meeting with the Government and EP Group

We also want to report that a tripartite meeting between the CWU, EP Group and the government took place on Monday the 16th of February. Daniel Kretinsky and the Secretary of State for Business and Trade attended this meeting, where we discussed the major problems facing our members, the company and the service.

As a result of this meeting, both parties have agreed to enter a period of intensive negotiations for four weeks, facilitated by the Government. These negotiations aim to resolve all outstanding issues, including the USO reform deployment, equalisation of terms and conditions and the full implementation of the agreement reached between EP Group and Royal Mail. We will be keeping members and branches updated throughout these talks.

Next Steps

This is a moment where the union needs to mobilise and come together to do whatever is necessary to defend our members, customers and the UK postal service. 

Our objective is to ensure that all parties, EP Group/Royal Mail and the CWU, honour and deliver the commitments made in Rebuilding Royal Mail Parts One and Two. The positive vision of the future that was laid out in these agreements is the only sustainable way forward for Royal Mail and we need all stakeholders- Royal Mail, Ofcom and the government to come together with the union and align on this vision.

We will be briefing your local union representatives imminently and in the near future, we will be asking you to support further key activities that the union will be undertaking to defend your job and the service.  Further communications will be sent to you next week.

With your support we will influence the future in a positive way.

Yours in solidarity,

Dave Ward

General Secretary

"GET YOUR FILTHY, MANGY MUTT AWAY FROM MY STORE BEFORE I CALL THE COPS ON YOU BOTH," HE SCREAMED, HIS FINGER TREMBLING WITH RAGE JUST INCHES FROM MY FACE. I STOOD THERE IN MY WEATHERED ARMY JACKET AS MY THREE-YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER LILY SOBBED, HUGGING THE SHIVERING STRAY DOG TO HER CHEST UNDER THE MERCILESS MIDDAY SUN, COMPLETELY UNAWARE THAT THE CHIEF OF POLICE HAD JUST WITNESSED EVERY SECOND OF HIS CRUELTY.

The asphalt was soft under the August sun, a shimmering black sea that swallowed the sound of the traffic on 4th Street. I felt the heat rising through the soles of my boots—boots I’d owned since my third tour, worn thin but still holding together by habit and stubbornness. I didn’t mind the heat. Heat I understood. It was the silence of the people passing by that always got to me. 

"Did you hear me?" the man shouted. 

His name was Marcus. I knew it because it was embroidered in gold thread on the polo shirt stretched tight over his chest. He was the manager of the upscale bistro behind us, a place where a glass of water probably cost more than the rations I’d lived on for months at a time. He was red-faced, the kind of red that suggests a lifetime of getting exactly what you want and exploding when you don't. 

He wasn't looking at me, not really. He was looking at the dog. 

It was a scruffy thing, a mix of terrier and something else, with ribs that pushed against its matted fur like the hull of a sinking ship. We’d found him shivering behind a dumpster three blocks back. Despite the hundred-degree heat, the poor creature was shaking. 

My daughter, Lily, hadn't let go of him since we picked him up. She was three years old, with eyes that saw the world as a series of things to be loved or things to be healed. Right now, she was huddled on the sidewalk, her small arms wrapped around the dog’s neck. She was crying, a quiet, hiccupping sound that tore at my chest more than any shrapnel ever could. 

"Sir, we’re just catching our breath," I said. My voice was low, gravelly. I tried to keep the military posture out of it, tried to look as small as society expected a man in a faded field jacket to look. "The dog is dehydrated. We’re just giving him a little water."

I pointed to the plastic lid I’d filled with lukewarm water from my canteen. The dog was lapping at it, his tail giving a single, pathetic wag. 

"I don't care if it's dying," Marcus hissed, stepping closer. His finger was trembling as he pointed it at my chest, then at Lily. "This is a place of business. Look at you. You’re a vagrancy hazard. You’re scaring the customers. That animal is a health code violation, and you’re using my storefront as a kennel."

I looked at the customers sitting behind the glass. Some looked away, suddenly fascinated by their salads. Others held up their phones, recording the scene like it was a piece of street theater. No one stood up. No one said a word. 

"We aren't bothering anyone," I whispered. I could feel the old pressure behind my eyes, the phantom weight of a rifle I hadn't carried in years. I had to stay calm. For Lily. 

"You're a disgrace," Marcus said, his voice dropping to a jagged, cruel register. "Coming out here, using a kid and a mutt to beg for sympathy? I bet that jacket isn't even yours. I bet you never spent a day in uniform. You're just another grifter looking for a handout."

The world went very still. I could hear the dog’s heavy breathing and the distant hum of an air conditioner. I looked at Marcus’s manicured hands, then at my own—calloused, scarred, and currently shaking with the effort of not closing into fists. 

Lily looked up at me, her face streaked with dirt and tears. "Daddy, is the man mad at the puppy?" 

"No, baby," I said, though it was a lie. "He's just... in a hurry."

"I'm calling the precinct," Marcus declared, reaching for his phone with a flourish of triumph. "I want you cleared off this block. I want that dog in a pound where it belongs."

He didn't notice the black SUV that had pulled up to the curb thirty seconds ago. He didn't see the door open. He was too busy enjoying the sight of me standing there, defeated, as I began to pack the canteen back into my bag. 

"Go ahead and call them, Marcus," a new voice said. 

It was a heavy, authoritative voice, the kind that didn't need to shout to be heard. A man stepped onto the sidewalk. He was tall, wearing a crisp white shirt and a silver badge clipped to his belt. Chief Miller. 

Marcus froze, his face shifting from rage to a greasy, performative smile in a heartbeat. "Chief! Thank God you're here. I was just about to report this... this situation. These people are a nuisance. They're—"

Chief Miller didn't even look at Marcus. He walked straight over to me. He looked at my jacket, then at the unit patch on my shoulder—the 10th Mountain Division. Then he looked me in the eye. He didn't see a vagrant. He saw a brother. 

"Sergeant?" the Chief asked quietly. 

I stood up straight then. The heat didn't feel so heavy anymore. "Yes, sir."

"Is there a problem here?" the Chief asked, his eyes finally shifting to Marcus. 

Marcus started to stammer. "I... I was just protecting the property value, Chief. You know how it is. We can't have people just... sitting here."

Chief Miller looked at Lily, who was still shielding the dog. He knelt down in the dirt, ruining the crease of his expensive trousers, and looked at the shivering stray. 

"That looks like a brave dog," the Chief said to Lily. 

"He's sick," Lily whispered, her voice trembling. "The mean man wants to take him away."

The Chief stood back up and turned to Marcus. The manager actually took a step back. The air around the Chief was suddenly very cold. 

"This man served more years for this country than you've spent behind that counter, Marcus," the Chief said, his voice like iron. "And if I hear one more word out of your mouth that isn't an apology to this child, I'm going to have the fire marshal do a floor-to-ceiling inspection of your kitchen every single day for the next month. Do I make myself clear?"

Marcus turned a shade of white that matched his chef's apron. He looked at me, then at the crowd watching from the windows. The power had shifted so fast the ground felt like it was tilting. 

But the story didn't end there. As the Chief reached out to help me gather our things, he whispered something that made my blood run cold. 

"Elias, I need you to come with me. Not because of him. There’s something you need to see at the station. It’s about your old unit."

"Over My Dead Body, Sir" — The Black Women Who Defied a General

The 6888th Central Postal Directory Battalion was the only all-Black Women's Army Corps unit deployed overseas during World War II. In February 1945, 855 Black women (with some members of Mexican and Puerto Rican descent) arrived in Birmingham, England, to face warehouses stacked floor-to-ceiling with undelivered mail — some letters and packages three years old. The U.S. Army estimated clearing the backlog would take six months. Working in unheated warehouses with broken windows, infested with rats, the women of the 6888th worked three rotating shifts, seven days a week, processing an average of 65,000 pieces of mail per shift. They cleared the six-month backlog in three months. Their unit motto was "No Mail, Low Morale" — they understood their mission wasn't just sorting letters; it was keeping troop morale alive by connecting soldiers with their families. Major Charity Adams, who became the first Black woman commissioned as an officer in the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps on July 13, 1942, commanded the battalion and rose to lieutenant colonel, making her the highest-ranking Black woman in the entire U.S. military during WWII. According to her memoir "One Woman's Army," when a general tried to send a white first lieutenant to take command of her unit, Adams responded without hesitation: "Over my dead body, sir." She stood down a general and won. The 6888th served in Birmingham, then moved to Rouen, France (after V-E Day), and finally Paris. When they returned to the U.S. in March 1946, they received no welcoming ceremony. The battalion wasn't officially honored until 2009 — 64 years after the war ended — when three surviving members attended a commendation ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. On March 14, 2022, President Biden signed legislation awarding the 6888th the Congressional Gold Medal, making them the only women's military unit ever to receive that honor.

WES GOVERNOR MEETS VICE PRESIDENT, ADVOCATES FOR ROAD DEVELOPMENT

 The Governor of Western Equatoria State, His Excellency Daniel Badagbu Rimbasa, on Wednesday met with Vice President Taban Deng Gai in Juba to discuss key development priorities, including the rehabilitation of major road networks linking the state to other parts of South Sudan.

Speaking to the media after the meeting, Governor Rimbasa emphasized the urgent need to improve roads connecting Yambio to Tambura and onward to Wau, as well as access routes linking the state to Juba. He noted that upgraded road infrastructure would boost trade, facilitate the movement of people, and enhance service delivery.

“We discussed the road from Yambio to Tambura and from Tambura to Wau, and the meeting was very fruitful,” the governor said, stressing that improved connectivity is vital for business growth and regional integration.

Vice President Taban Deng Gai welcomed the governor’s proposals and highlighted the strategic importance of the road network to national development. “These roads are very important and should be treated as a priority,” he said. “

I congratulate you on your appointment as Governor of Western Equatoria State, and I will support initiatives that link the state with Wau and Juba.”

Western Equatoria is widely regarded as one of South Sudan’s major agricultural hubs, supplying food to several regions. 

Both leaders noted that improved transport infrastructure would strengthen markets, enhance the movement of agricultural produce, and contribute to economic growth.

The meeting concluded with a shared commitment to prioritize road rehabilitation to improve access to services and promote development across Western Equatoria and neighboring states.

A fierce Washington, D.C., grandmother brought the crowd to its feet at President Trump's Black History Month celebration Wednesday, delivering an impassioned defense of the president against charges of racism—and earning his immediate endorsement to run for office.

Forlesia Cook, whose grandson Marty William McMillan Jr. was mur*dered in 2017, took the stage in the East Room and didn't hold back.

The crowd erupted in applause and cheers.

"He really was special, with lots of personality, grit and street smarts," Trump said.

He also announced that Ben Carson, an adviser to his administration, will soon receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor.

Forlesia Cook's passionate defense of Trump highlights the complex relationship between the president and Black Americans—some of whom support his policies while others condemn his rhetoric. Dear Residents, Ratepayers, Friends and Chums

From the outset, I would like to express my sincere, heartfelt gratitude to the fine people of the Tamworth Region who stood by me during a recent dark period of my life.  The hundreds of telephone calls, messages, texts, emails and people stopping me in the street to offer their support, telling me not to give up and keep going, has warmed the cockles of my heart during a time when I really needed it.

On a different topic, the numerous accusations that have been thrown at me from all angles and the manner in which they have been feverishly pursued over the last 12 months, would give cause to any reasonably minded person to start believing in conspiracy theories.

That there is a small cabal of people from certain sections of our community that would like nothing more than for me to just shut up and go away, trying to stop me from drawing attention to subjects and finely laid plans that others would prefer not to be highlighted, resulting in a clutching at straws, desperation to find the most effective way to carry out the task of banishing me into the abyss. Whilst I do not subscribe to this theory, I do know that my advocacy and stance on several issues on behalf of the people who elected me, upsets some people within our community.

Let me be absolutely clear, how ever they come after me, I will continue strongly to be your advocate and stand up for the issues you care about. He couldn't speak. He just bowed his head and wept.
It was July 3, 1863.
Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.

General Robert E. Lee had just ordered a massive, frontal assault right into the center of the entrenched Union line. He wanted 15,000 men to march across nearly a mile of open, sun-baked ground, directly into the mouths of dozens of Union cannons.

The man tasked with executing this order looked at the field. He did the math. He knew exactly what was about to happen.
His name was James Longstreet. He was Lee’s most trusted commander. Lee called him his "Old War Horse." After Stonewall Jackson died, Longstreet was the undisputed heavy hitter of the Confederate Army.

But unlike Jackson or Lee, Longstreet didn't believe in glorious, romantic, dying-for-the-cause frontal assaults. He was a thoroughly modern general. He believed in the power of the defensive trench. He believed in flanking.

He looked at Lee and said, "General, I have been a soldier all my life. I have been with soldiers engaged in fights by couples, by squads, companies, regiments, divisions, and armies, and should know, as well as any one, what soldiers can do. It is my opinion that no fifteen thousand men ever arrayed for battle can take that position."

Lee refused to listen. The "glory" of the charge blinded him. He ordered Longstreet to send the men forward.
When General George Pickett rode up to Longstreet and asked for the order to advance, Longstreet was so overcome with grief that he couldn't form the words. He simply nodded his head.

The assault forever known as Pickett's Charge was a massacre. It was the high-water mark of the Confederacy, and it broke the back of Lee's army. Longstreet had been absolutely, tragically right.

But surviving Gettysburg wasn't Longstreet's defining moment.
His defining moment came after the war was lost.

Following the surrender at Appomattox, the South needed a scapegoat. They couldn't blame the aristocratic, saintly Robert E. Lee for losing the war. So, the architects of the "Lost Cause" myth rewrote history. They blamed Longstreet. They said his hesitation at Gettysburg cost them their independence.

Longstreet didn't help his own popularity in the South. In fact, he did the unthinkable.
He accepted defeat.

He looked at the devastated nation and decided the fighting was over. He joined the Republican Party the party of Abraham Lincoln. He endorsed his old pre-war friend, Ulysses S. Grant, for President of the United States.

The South was horrified. They called him a traitor. They called him a "scalawag." They erased him from their monuments and their history books.

But Longstreet didn't stop there.
In 1874, the city of New Orleans was boiling over. A violent, white supremacist paramilitary group called the White League launched an armed rebellion to overthrow the Reconstructionist state government.

James Longstreet put on the uniform of the United States government. He rode out to meet them.

He commanded a biracial state militia and the city's integrated police force. The man who had once been the greatest tactical commander of the Confederacy was now ordering armed, African American soldiers into combat against white Southerners who were trying to destroy the peace.

He was shot, pulled from his horse, and taken prisoner during the Battle of Liberty Place before federal troops finally arrived to crush the rebellion.

He died in 1904. For over a century, while statues of Lee and Jackson were erected in every town square in the South, Longstreet was largely forgotten or openly despised by the people he had bled for.

He taught us that it requires one kind of courage to charge into enemy cannon fire, but it requires an entirely different kind of courage to tell your own side they are wrong.

He was the brilliant tactical genius who correctly predicted the slaughter of Gettysburg, only to become a pariah in the South because he realized that the only way to heal a broken nation was to surrender his pride.
