Deported for the Reich: The Forced Labor of Polish Civilians: 

When people speak about German crimes in occupied Poland, public memory understandably moves first to ghettos and extermination camps, to places whose names have become synonymous with mechanized murder, and yet alongside those centers of annihilation there operated a vast, deeply organized, and structurally indispensable system of forced labor that uprooted millions of Polish civilians and integrated their coerced bodies into the machinery of the German war economy.

Between 1939 and 1945, approximately 2.7 to 2.8 million non-Jewish Polish civilians were deported to the German Reich for compulsory labor, a number established through postwar demographic studies and supported by German administrative records preserved in the Bundesarchiv, and these deportees were not prisoners of war captured on battlefields but farmers, students, teachers, clerks, mechanics, and adolescents taken from towns and villages under occupation and transported westward under threat, coercion, and administrative compulsion.

The removal of these civilians followed formal labor quotas imposed upon occupied communities, with villages ordered to produce a designated number of workers and local officials pressured to supply names, while failure to comply could invite fines, arrests, or collective punishment, thereby transforming labor recruitment into a mechanism of social control that reached into the most ordinary corners of daily life.

By 1940 the German labor administration, working in coordination with the SS and regional occupation authorities, had begun to systematize these transfers in order to compensate for labor shortages in agriculture, mining, heavy industry, and armaments production, and as Ulrich Herbert demonstrates in Hitler’s Foreign Workers, the German war economy evolved into a structure increasingly dependent upon foreign forced labor, with Polish civilians forming one of the earliest, largest, and most tightly regulated categories within that hierarchy of exploitation.

On March 8, 1940, the regime codified this hierarchy through the issuance of the Polen-Erlasse, the so-called Polish Decrees, which formalized racial discrimination into everyday legal reality and established a distinct and inferior status for Polish laborers inside the Reich, subjecting them to restrictions that were both humiliating and severe.

Polish workers were required to wear a purple letter “P” stitched onto a yellow diamond-shaped background, displayed prominently on their clothing so that they could be instantly identified in public spaces, and this visible marker functioned not merely as administrative classification but as a deliberate instrument of segregation and stigma, reinforcing racial ideology while facilitating surveillance and denunciation.

The decrees imposed strict curfews, limited freedom of movement, restricted access to public transportation, prohibited attendance at most German social or religious institutions, and criminalized intimate relationships between Polish laborers and German citizens under the regime’s racial laws, with alleged violations often resulting in imprisonment, transfer to concentration camps, or execution.

Richard Overy, in his analyses of the German war economy, emphasizes that foreign labor was not a marginal supplement but a structural pillar sustaining wartime production, and by 1944 foreign workers comprised roughly one quarter of the total labor force within Germany, a proportion that underscores the extent to which the Reich’s military and agricultural output rested upon the coerced labor of occupied populations.

Archival documentation preserved in the Bundesarchiv, alongside testimonies and court records published by the Institute of National Remembrance, reveals patterns of physical abuse, sexual violence, arbitrary confinement, and punitive transfers to concentration camps for infractions that ranged from alleged insubordination to minor breaches of curfew, illustrating how the boundary between forced labor and camp incarceration could dissolve quickly under accusation.

Many of those deported were teenagers whose removal severed families and disrupted entire communities, and the psychological consequences of years spent in coerced labor, marked publicly as inferior and deprived of basic autonomy, extended long after the war’s conclusion, shaping postwar lives in ways that rarely entered official narratives.

Understanding this dimension of occupation requires attention not only to the spectacular sites of mass murder that dominate global memory but also to the administrative networks, decrees, payroll systems, transport lists, and identification badges that sustained a slower, pervasive form of dehumanization, one that reduced millions of Polish civilians to regulated labor units within a racial state that denied their equal humanity.

The trains that carried Polish workers westward, the red “P” stitched onto worn coats, the curfews enforced by local authorities, and the wage slips marked by deductions all formed part of a coherent system whose purpose was exploitation embedded within ideology, demonstrating how occupation functioned simultaneously through terror and bureaucracy.

Remembering this history restores scale to what was done and to whom it was done, and it complicates any narrative that confines destruction to isolated sites, because the dismantling of Polish society unfolded as much through coerced labor, economic plunder, and administrative degradation as through overt execution, leaving behind records that testify not only to suffering but to the organized nature of that suffering within the structure of the Third Reich.

“Power, peace deal and the ballot box”: S. Sudan digs in as Machar’s trial tests fragile unity

South Sudan’s government has drawn a firm line in the sand over the fate of suspended First Vice President Riek Machar, insisting that only the courts, not foreign governments, will decide his future, even as pressure mounts from across the continent.

The pushback follows a call from Nigeria for Machar’s “immediate and unconditional release,” made during a high-level African Union meeting in Addis Ababa. 

Nigerian officials framed the detention as a destabilizing move that risks undermining South Sudan’s already fragile peace.

But in Juba, Information Minister Ateny Wek Ateny countered that sovereignty comes first.

“Dr. Riek is under a competent court,” Ateny said, stressing that the executive would not interfere in judicial proceedings. “The decision will come from that court.”

A Trial at the heart of a political storm

Machar, 73, has been under house arrest since March 2025 and faces treason charges before a special court, alongside seven co-accused. 

Prosecutors allege he backed the White Army militia during clashes in Upper Nile State, claims his party strongly denies.

The case strikes at the core of the 2018 peace agreement that returned Machar to government as first vice president under President Salva Kiir. 

Critics argue the prosecution contradicts the spirit, if not the letter, of that deal, especially as violence has again flared in parts of the country.

AU divisions emerge

The diplomatic dispute has exposed fractures within the African Union’s mediation framework. The C5 committee, comprising Algeria, Chad, Nigeria, Rwanda, and South Africa, is chaired by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and mandated to support regional peace efforts led by IGAD.

Ateny dismissed Nigeria’s stance as an individual position rather than a unified AU directive, signaling that Juba sees no binding continental consensus demanding Machar’s release.

Elections over everything

Despite the turbulence, the government insists the December elections will go ahead. Ateny claimed that 13 of the African Union’s 15 member states involved in discussions support proceeding with the vote.

“There is no other way for the government to draw its legitimacy,” he said, arguing that postponement could trigger instability.

To meet the timeline, the government now plans to “delink” key provisions of the 2018 agreement, specifically a national census and the adoption of a permanent constitution. Ateny compared the constitutional process to Kenya’s decades-long reform journey, suggesting South Sudan cannot afford similar delays.

High stakes for a young nation

At stake is more than one man’s trial. Machar’s prosecution has become a litmus test for judicial independence, national sovereignty, and the durability of South Sudan’s peace framework.

The courtroom, and the ballot box—may together determine whether the world’s youngest nation moves toward stability or slips deeper into political deadlock, as the country approaches its long-delayed elections.

In October 2011, before the sun rose over the mountains of Afghanistan, 1st Lt. Ashley White-Stumpf prepared for another mission. Her gear was secured. Her expression was steady. At just 24 years old, she was stepping into danger alongside some of the military’s most elite units.

She had chosen this path.

After graduating from college, Ashley commissioned into the Army as a Medical Service Corps officer. She was drawn to service — to the camaraderie, the discipline, and the sense of purpose that came from being part of something greater than herself. While others looked for comfort, she looked for meaning.

She found it in uniform.

Assigned to the 230th Brigade Support Battalion, Ashley volunteered for an even more demanding role: a Cultural Support Team (CST) attached to a Joint Special Operations Task Force. At the time, women were not formally assigned to direct combat roles. Yet CST members accompanied Special Operations units on dangerous missions, engaging with Afghan women and gathering critical information.

No spotlight.
No special protection.
No guarantees.

To do her job, Ashley walked the same roads, entered the same compounds, and faced the same threats as the men beside her.

She never hesitated.

During a mission that October, the assault force advanced carefully through hostile terrain. Every step carried risk.

Then an improvised explosive device detonated.

The blast changed everything.

Ashley was mortally wounded, becoming the first Cultural Support Team member killed in action in Afghanistan.

The news traveled quietly — another young service member lost, another folded flag presented to a grieving family.

For her courage and service, she was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star, the Purple Heart, the Meritorious Service Medal, the Afghanistan Campaign Medal, and the Combat Action Badge.

The medals recognized her bravery.

But they could not replace a daughter.

Those who knew Ashley remember her as humble and kind — someone who never sought praise or attention, only the opportunity to serve. She walked into war when she did not have to. She stood beside warriors when policy had yet to fully recognize women in combat.

Her legacy is larger than the moment she was lost.

She showed that courage has no gender.
That sacrifice has no age.
And that quiet strength can change history.

Ashley White-Stumpf gave her future in service to her country — and she deserves to be remembered.

February 19, 1777 — In the weeks after the stunning victories at Trenton and Princeton, Washington found himself commanding an army that had won the winter but was nearly spent by it. Enlistments had evaporated, recruiting lagged, and officers were scattered across the states trying to pull men back from hospital furloughs. From Morristown, he warned Congress that the army lacked the senior leadership needed to survive the coming campaign. Congress responded on this day by elevating William Alexander, Thomas Mifflin, Arthur St. Clair, Adam Stephen, and Benjamin Lincoln to major general — a move driven not by politics or personal slight, but by Washington’s urgent effort to rebuild a fighting force before spring. Benedict Arnold, senior to several of them, bristled at the decision, yet the moment was shaped far more by necessity than by wounded pride.

Here is how each officer strengthened that effort: William Alexander, “Lord Stirling,” whose rearguard stand at Long Island helped prevent the army’s destruction; Thomas Mifflin, the first Quartermaster General whose logistical skill and mercantile networks built the army’s early supply system; Arthur St. Clair, known for his strategic withdrawals, including the necessary evacuation of Fort Ticonderoga; Adam Stephen, a dependable battlefield commander at Trenton and Princeton promoted for meritorious service; and Benjamin Lincoln, the steady New England officer who helped secure Saratoga and later accepted the British surrender at Yorktown. Though this leadership spine was fragile — with Stephen dismissed and Mifflin sidelined by year’s end — together they provided the structure Washington needed to rebuild the army for the hard campaign ahead.

In March 1884, in a dimly lit St. Paul theater, Sitting Bull watched something he'd never seen before.

A woman—barely five feet tall—was doing impossible things with a rifle.

She split playing cards edge-on from 30 paces. Shot corks clean off bottles. Snuffed out candles with bullets, one after another, never missing.

Her name was Annie Oakley. She was 23 years old.

Eight years earlier, Sitting Bull had led the Lakota and Cheyenne warriors who defeated George Custer's cavalry at Little Bighorn. He was the most feared and respected Native American leader in the country—a man who had defended his people against an army.

But that night, he was captivated.

After the show ended, Sitting Bull sent $65 to Annie's hotel—a small fortune in 1884—hoping to buy an autographed photograph.

Annie sent his money back.

But the next morning, she appeared at his door with the photograph as a gift.

What happened next would surprise everyone who knew their histories.

Sitting Bull, moved by her extraordinary skill and her character, symbolically adopted Annie as his daughter. He gave her a Lakota name that would follow her for life: Watanya Cicilla—Little Sure Shot.

Then he gave her something more precious than money could buy.

The moccasins from the Battle of Little Bighorn. Made by his own daughter, who had died not long after that battle. Annie was about the same age she would have been.

"He asked me to take the place of the daughter he lost," Annie would later write. "When he gave me those moccasins he treasured so deeply, I understood."

Their friendship deepened when Sitting Bull joined Buffalo Bill's Wild West show in 1885. For four months, the Lakota chief and the Ohio sharpshooter traveled across America together, performing side by side.

In an era when Native Americans and white settlers were locked in bitter conflict, when treaties were broken and wars raged across the frontier, these two found something rare: genuine respect.

Annie called him "my dear, faithful old friend." But more than that, she understood him in ways few white Americans bothered to.

"He fought justly for his people," she wrote. "They had been driven from their God-given inheritance and were living upon broken promises."

When Sitting Bull was killed in 1890 during a botched arrest, Annie's words were unflinching: "If Sitting Bull had been a white man, someone would have hung for his murder."

She carried the name Little Sure Shot with fierce pride for the rest of her life—a gift from a chief who looked past the divisions tearing his world apart and saw something extraordinary in a young woman with a rifle.

Two people from vastly different worlds. One, the spiritual leader of the Sioux nation. The other, a sharpshooter from rural Ohio.

They proved that respect, admiration, and true friendship don't ask where you come from or what uniform you've worn.

Even when everything around you insists you should be enemies, the human heart knows better.

In the corridors of power, few names evoke as much admiration and as much scrutiny as Nasir Ahmad El-Rufai. From his tenure as Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) under President Olusegun Obasanjo (2003–2007) to his eight years as Governor of Kaduna State (2015–2023), El-Rufai has carved a reputation as a reformer unafraid of confrontation. Yet, alongside the accolades lie decades of allegations, controversies, and now, an unprecedented multi-agency crackdown that has thrust him once again into the national spotlight.

El-Rufai’s first major clash with anti-corruption authorities came in 2008 when the EFCC declared him wanted over alleged misappropriation of N32 billion during his FCT tenure. Accused of defying court orders, he fought back with legal action, a prelude to the tense dance between authority and accountability that would mark his career.

By 2010, allegations of manipulating Abuja’s Master Plan surfaced, with claims that he had revoked land titles from state entities and funneled them to friends and family. Despite the controversies, El-Rufai returned from self-imposed exile, his political ambitions undeterred.

Fast forward to 2023, El-Rufai’s nomination as a minister under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu met resistance. A negative security assessment by the DSS cited human rights abuses, including the 2015 Zaria clashes involving Shiite leader Ibrahim El-Zakzaky’s followers, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary demolitions, alleged embezzlement, and a history of backstabbing political allies. The report, coupled with petitions from human rights groups, forced him to withdraw, suggesting Jafaru Sani as a replacement.

The controversies did not end with ministerial politics. In late 2024, the Kaduna State Government accused El-Rufai of embezzling N423 billion during his governorship. Despite the gravity, the EFCC had not pressed formal charges. By February 2025, El-Rufai claimed in an ARISE News interview that the ICPC had cleared him, but that officials were pressured to implicate him. He further accused National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu of orchestrating a campaign against him, framing the allegations as politically motivated maneuvers in Nigeria’s high-stakes power game.

February 2026 marked a dramatic escalation. On the 16th and 17th, El-Rufai was detained by the EFCC over alleged corruption. Protests erupted at EFCC headquarters, met with tear gas as citizens and supporters clashed with security forces. Administrative bail was short-lived, DSS operatives immediately intercepted him, accusing him of illegally intercepting communications linked to NSA Ribadu. Critics questioned the legality of the arrest, which occurred without a court order.

Today for Blak Friday I am honouring Vanessa Turnbull-Roberts — a proud Bundjalung Widubul-Wiabul woman who has dedicated her life to protecting our children and standing up for our people.

Vanessa is a human rights lawyer, author, Fulbright Scholar and survivor. Removed from her family at just 10 years old, she knows what it means to live inside systems that harm the very children they claim to protect. She has turned that experience into tireless advocacy, fighting child removal, criminalisation, sexual exploitation, and the pipeline from so-called “care” into custody.

In 2024, she became the ACT’s inaugural Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Commissioner, a historic appointment she carried with strength and dedication.

But here’s what too often happens to strong Blak women who choose to stand up.

A badly informed media hit piece targeted Vanessa over absences at work. Instead of respecting her privacy and extending her the benefit of the doubt, damaging speculation was published about her.

Under that pressure, Vanessa was forced to disclose that she had been sexually assaulted and harassed in her workplace.

No survivor should have to reveal their trauma just to defend themselves. But that is what she was forced to do.

I can relate to Vanessa’s experience. When I was targeted in the media over absences from Parliament, I was forced to disclose that I had been violently assaulted and required surgery and time off, something I had wanted to keep private.

First Nations women are too often treated as suspect before we are treated as human. We are spoken about instead of listened to. Our leadership is questioned. Our integrity is doubted.

And when we try to protect ourselves quietly, it is weaponised against us.

Vanessa has always stood for children’s safety, for mothers, for families, and for all First Peoples. She works every day to bring this country together.

That is who she is. A staunch Blak woman of courage and integrity, who keeps showing up for our people, even when the cost is personal.

I stand with you sis.

The work continues 🖤 ✊🏾

Wesley Clark realized he had been relieved of NATO command only when a staffer mistakenly handed him a briefing folder detailing the timeline for his successor.

He scanned the pages, closed the folder, and immediately understood that Washington had decided his fate without informing him.

The political consequences were already in motion.

The moment came at the height of the Kosovo conflict. Clark had been pressing for a tougher approach against Serbian forces, even raising the possibility of ground troops—an option several senior officials firmly rejected. Strategy meetings grew strained. Clark argued that air power alone would not halt ethnic cleansing. The Pentagon urged restraint.

He did not yield.

The internal struggle escalated when Clark ordered British and French forces to secure Pristina airport before Russian troops could take control. Moscow dispatched its own convoy toward the runway. The standoff edged dangerously close to armed confrontation.

London was alarmed.

Washington was alarmed.

Clark did not retract the directive.

British General Mike Jackson pushed back, delivering the now-famous response: “I’m not going to start World War Three for you.” He refused to move his troops forward. In that instant, the unity of command visibly cracked.

Privately, some senior officials viewed Clark as too willing to escalate.

Clark believed he was blocking a strategic Russian foothold in the Balkans.

Each side was convinced of its judgment.

Only one side, however, held authority over his position.

The replacement schedule inside that misplaced folder confirmed what Clark had sensed. By the time he was formally notified, allied leaders had already been briefed. He completed his tenure without public protest and stepped aside.

Years later, some diplomats acknowledged that Clark’s concerns about the airport were not unfounded. Had Russian forces secured it uncontested, the balance of negotiations might have shifted in Moscow’s favor.

The episode revealed the essence of Wesley Clark.

He was not removed for incompetence.

He was removed because he would not retreat from a strategy he believed would protect lives and strengthen NATO’s position.

Clark believed leadership required moral conviction rather than political caution.

That conviction defined his successes, fueled his conflicts, and ultimately led to the briefing folder that signaled his departure before anyone officially said so.

El-Rufai and the Rhetoric of Hell

By: Folorunso Fatai Adisa 

(Published in the Punch Newspapers on Friday, 20 February, 2026). 

I first encountered the name Joseph Goebbels in a lecture hall at Moshood Abiola Polytechnic, Abeokuta. It was during my Diploma programme some decades ago, and I recall my communications lecturer, Dr. Sina Julius Aina, introducing his work long before politics taught me why he still matters. Goebbels spoke for power, engineered perception, shaped truth, and disciplined dissent through language. That short man who was nicknamed “the poison dwarf” was the evil genius who gulled all of Germany into following Adolf Hitler. Consequently, history now remembers him as a propagandist and as proof that words can govern minds long before authority governs territory.

Whenever political speech begins to sound less like communication and more like orchestration, one quickly recalls the timeless caution of George Orwell, whose intellectual clarity still cuts through the fog of power. In his book titled “Politics and the English Language,” Orwell delivered a verdict that has since become a cornerstone of political communication theory: “Political language is designed to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable, and to give an appearance of solidity to pure wind.” This is both literary brilliance, and a diagnostic tool. It explains how rhetoric can be used to soften brutality, disguise intention, and manufacture legitimacy. When language is bent long enough, truth begins to wear the apparels of falsehood, and falsehood marches about dressed as truth. Power then no longer needs to coerce openly because it has already persuaded silently. Such is the danger when words cease to describe reality and begin instead to redesign it.

It is within this tradition of language as an instrument of power that one must examine Nasir El-Rufai, a man who, like Goebbels, is as rhetorically potent as he is physically slight. I ask my readers to forgive this brief lapse into body shaming (this essayist, too, is of modest height) but the observation is only a reflection of Mallam’s own style. It was, after all, El-Rufai himself who recently chose to dismiss a security operative at the airport by describing him as “one fat officer.”

While appearing as a guest on Arise TV Station’s Prime Time programme on 13th February, 2026, El-Rufai once again displayed his instinct for political communication as strategy rather than expression. His language was sharp, deliberate, and calibrated to frame, dominate, and control the interpretive space of political discourse. The comparison here is not of ideology or historical weight, but of communicative method. Like seasoned political tacticians everywhere, he understands that in modern contests for power, perception often outruns reality.

El-Rufai does not practice the politics of silence. Where others cultivate mystique through withdrawal, he chooses aggressive exposure. Mallam’s words operate less as conversation and more as tactical positioning. As such, admirers see intellectual boldness in him, but critics see calculated ambiguity. Either way, this visibility is both his greatest weapon and his most glaring vulnerability.

During that same broadcast, El-Rufai claimed he had access to a conversation involving the National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu. When the interviewer noted that such interception would be illegal, he did not deny it. This admission is chilling. Intercepting private communication without judicial authorisation constitutes a serious legal breach. Even proximity to such an act raises profound questions about legality, judgment, and respect for institutional boundaries. If such surveillance occurred, under whose authority did it happen, and how extensive was it? These are not idle curiosities, but questions that strike at the very heart of public trust and lawful power. In other words, Mallam is a malware within our national security architecture. 

Worrying as the wiretapping allegations may be, they are no greater than what the botched arrest says about the state’s waning authority. A nation weakens when enforcement becomes a spectacle. And whenever the state fails to execute an arrest in a controlled environment like an airport, it signals weakness to those who would challenge the law. It tells them that the state can be tested, and once that test begins, disorder spreads quietly before it erupts visibly.

From numerous indications, El-Rufai’s recurring public confrontations with Nuhu Ribadu suggest more than an ordinary personal disagreement. On February 24, 2025 ,exactly one year ago this month, Ribadu declared on his Facebook page that he would not "join issues" with El-Rufai, urging the public to disregard the statements made against him. Of course, in politics, clashes between former allies often show deeper struggles over influence, legitimacy, and the control of institutional power. Power rarely fractures without consequence. Mallam El-Rufai clearly harbors grievances he has yet to fully air regarding Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, and as spectators to their high-stakes maneuvering, we wait to watch their performance as it moves from scene to scene until it climaxes.

Ahistorically, many Nigerians romanticise political actors, repeatedly investing hope in figures whose histories they fail to interrogate. Memory, however, must not be selective. It was under this same El-Rufai governorship that tensions with dissenting voices became frequent and severe. From reports of crackdowns to legal pressure against critics, a pattern of hostility emerged that cannot be ignored. Political intolerance rarely announces itself with trumpets. It reveals itself through repetition.

El-Rufai is notorious for his history of fabrications, most notably his 2014 claim that he was seventh on a “hit list” of targets to be executed by snipers under President Goodluck Jonathan’s administration. These bogus assertions are part of a familiar political tactic in which dramatisation is used to court relevance and false alarms are used to capture attention. Serious observers treat such claims with the skepticism they deserve.

Empirically, reports and commentaries over the years have consistently documented El-Rufai’s rhetorical aggression toward his opponents. The pattern shows a governing temperament deeply uneasy with dissent. During his tenure, journalists faced arrest, activists faced intimidation, and criticism was often interpreted as hostility rather than democratic engagement. Names such as Luka Biniyat, Midat Joseph, and Jacob Dickson remain part of that history, alongside documented cases like that of cleric Bello Yabo. Sheikh Ibrahim El-Zakyzaky will not soon forget the treatment he suffered during those years, and it would require the highest form of human kindness for him to offer forgiveness.

One begins to wonder how a political actor becomes so hardened by conflict that he resorts to the language of death as metaphor and mockery. El-Rufai appears unusually fluent in this register. During an APC stakeholders’ meeting in Kaduna, he once warned his opponents: “I have fought with two presidents. Umaru Yar’Adua ended up in his grave, while President Goodluck Jonathan ended up in Otuoke.”

This is the text-book definition of the Dunning-Kruger effect. For an individual to imply he single-handedly determined the death of one president and the defeat of another reveals a profound delusion of grandeur. It is therefore unsurprising that when security operatives approached him at the airport, his reflex was to declare, “Not even the president can…”

However, words have consequences beyond the podium. Correlation is not proof, but political climates often leave fingerprints without signatures. If El-Rufai is powerful enough to link his conflicts to a President's grave, he cannot simultaneously plead ignorance regarding the fate of Abubakar Idris Dadiyata. The vanishing of Dadiyata remains the darkest shadow of El-Rufai’s era. To now recast Dadiyata solely as a critic of Abdullahi Ganduje is a convenient distortion. Dadiyata was a broad critic of the northern establishment, including El-Rufai.

In Yoruba thought, metaphor often exposes truth more sharply than argument: “Eegun atiro wọle, eeyan atiro jade.” (The limping masquerade enters, and the limping man emerges). The disguise has dissolved. The loudest critics of intolerance often mirror the very instincts they condemn, and that is exactly what El-Rufai is currently doing. 
Power is judged not only by what it does, but by what it permits. A government unable to protect its fiercest critic cannot convincingly claim to protect its citizens. Nigerian politics has long blurred the line between authority and intolerance. For many who have tasted power, dissent becomes an irritation to be silenced rather than a voice to be engaged. Intolerance travels easily across offices and across alliances.

The unresolved mystery surrounding Dadiyata’s disappearance is grisly haunting. El-Rufai has now attributed the disappearance to the Kano State Government under Ganduje. Whether true or not, such claims heighten public unease. If Daditaya is not found within the coming months, he will reach the seven-year threshold to be judicially presumed dead under Section 164 of the Evidence Act. That a citizen can vanish so completely, while both state and federal authorities claim ignorance, remains a profound indictment of institutional failure, and an inexcusable scar on our democracy.

We need to realistically understand that El-Rufai does not stand outside the political culture he now interrogates. He is its most refined personification, strategic and forceful, shaped by the very logic of power he now critiques. And in the blood-sport of Nigerian politics, language is rarely innocent because those who master it often, unconsciously, disclose the deepest truths about themselves in their fiercest declarations. They forget that while power speaks, language, like the elephant, remembers.

Consequently, before anyone rushes to cuddle El-Rufai’s new truth-teller persona, they must understand that he is not a saint. He is not a reformer. Mallam is a power player who, like many before him, is simply repositioning himself for his next political move.

The adjournment of proceedings to February 25 in the case against suspended First Vice President Riek Machar and seven senior members of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In Opposition (SPLM-IO) marks yet another critical moment in South Sudan’s fragile pursuit of justice and stability.

This is not an ordinary court case. It is a test of whether our nation will tolerate the use of armed violence as a political tool.

Prosecutors allege that forces affiliated with the Sudan People’s Liberation Army-In Opposition (SPLA-IO), in alliance with the White Army militia, launched a coordinated and deadly assault on the Nasir garrison in March 2025. The attack reportedly claimed the lives of 257 soldiers from the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF), including senior commander Gen. David Majur Dak. Military equipment worth approximately $58 million was allegedly destroyed or seized.

If proven in court, these are not mere battlefield incidents. They represent a direct assault on the sovereignty of the state and the lives of men and women sworn to defend it.

South Sudan cannot afford to normalize cycles of armed confrontation driven by political rivalry. For too long, power struggles have translated into bloodshed. For too long, civilians and soldiers alike have paid the price of elite competition. The Nasir attack, as alleged, underscores the urgent need to draw a firm line between lawful political engagement and violent insurrection.

Accountability is not revenge. Accountability is deterrence. Holding individuals responsible—regardless of rank or political influence—sends a clear message: leadership does not grant immunity from the law.

The special court must proceed independently, transparently, and without intimidation. The integrity of this process will shape public confidence not only in the judiciary but in the broader peace framework of the country.

South Sudan stands at a crossroads. Either the rule of law prevails, or the cycle of armed power contests continues.

Justice must not be delayed. Justice must not be selective. And justice must not bow to political pressure.

The future stability of the nation depends on it.

The forceful recruitment of young men into the army in Ruweng Administrative Area represents something far more serious than a simple administrative decision. It signals a crisis of responsibility at the level of leadership. And responsibility, if we are to speak plainly, is the foundation upon which any sovereign state stands.

South Sudan is not a militia. It is not a loose collection of armed interests. It is meant to be a constitutional order with institutions, procedures, and moral legitimacy. Recruitment into the armed forces must be voluntary, structured, and lawful. When a government resorts to compulsion outside transparent institutional frameworks, it reveals weakness, not strength. Force is what you use when you have failed to persuade. And persuasion fails when trust has been eroded.

The young men being targeted are not abstractions. They are the primary economic backbone of their families. They farm. They study. They provide. They carry responsibilities that many leaders have long since delegated to others. To remove them by force is not merely to fill barracks. It is to destabilize already fragile households. It is to deepen poverty in communities that are barely surviving.

Here is the deeper question. What moral claim does a government have to demand sacrifice from citizens to whom it has not fulfilled its basic obligations? Education in RAA struggles. Healthcare remains inadequate despite oil wealth and corporate financing. Youth unemployment persists. Soldiers themselves reportedly go unpaid. Their children struggle. Their families suffer. When the state cannot properly care for those already in uniform, what justification does it have to compel more into the same uncertainty?

Authority is not the same thing as power. Authority is earned through competence and service. Power can be imposed. But imposed power without moral legitimacy breeds resentment, fear, and eventually instability. History has already shown South Sudan the cost of political miscalculation. Lives lost. Families broken. Generations growing up in uncertainty. Have those lessons been integrated, or merely endured?

There is also a painful asymmetry that ordinary citizens observe. Many in leadership ensure safety, education, and stability for their own families. Meanwhile, the sons of struggling households are expected to sacrifice for structures that have not tangibly improved their lives. That imbalance corrodes trust. And when trust collapses, the very thing leaders claim to be defending becomes fragile.

RAA has existed for more than a decade with considerable resources at its disposal. Yet the measurable transformation in education, healthcare, and economic empowerment remains limited. If governance does not translate resources into human development, then it forfeits the moral high ground required to ask for loyalty and sacrifice.

A state worthy of defense is one that first demonstrates competence. It provides functioning schools. It ensures healthcare access. It pays its soldiers. It protects families. Only then can it call upon citizens and reasonably expect voluntary commitment. People will willingly defend a system that defends them. They will resist one that merely extracts from them.

This is therefore a call to the authorities in RAA. Reconsider this path. If recruitment is necessary, make it transparent, lawful, and voluntary. Announce it openly. Establish clear criteria. Guarantee welfare, training, and fair compensation. Respect the dignity and agency of the youth.

Compulsion is a short term instrument. Legitimacy is a long term foundation. If leadership cannot yet provide services that stabilize society, it should first put its own house in order before demanding further sacrifice from an already burdened population.

The young men of RAA are not expendable assets in a political calculation. They are the future architects of whatever South Sudan becomes. Undermine them, and you undermine the future. Strengthen them through education, opportunity, and dignity, and you build a nation that does not need to rely on force to secure loyalty.

The choice before the authorities is not merely administrative. It is existential. They can choose coercion, which breeds fragility. Or they can choose responsibility, competence, and voluntary allegiance, which builds something that can endure.

Clinton Nyapara Mogesa wanted a change of pace. At 29, this Kenyan living in Qatar thought he had found a professional opportunity in Russia. 

A few months later, he was killed on the Ukrainian front, having been conscripted into the Russian army after responding to what appeared to be a simple job offer. His story illustrates the growing dangers of online recruitment that promises a bright future but leads to war.

In an article published on its website, the BBC reports that Ukrainian authorities announced on Monday, February 2nd, the death of Clinton Nyapara Mogesa, a Kenyan citizen killed during an attack in eastern Ukraine. "After brief training, Clinton Mogesa was killed in a 'sacrificial assault' in Donbas," stated the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (HUR) in a message posted on Telegram. 

His body has not been recovered, and his family, who remain in Kenya, are still awaiting answers and possible repatriation.

Like him, many Africans are drawn to advertisements circulating on social media and job platforms. These offers tout civilian, industrial, or security positions in Russia, with attractive salaries and accommodation included. Programs such as 𝐀𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐮𝐠𝐚 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 contribute to this illusion of a stable and well-paid future. But behind these promises often lie opaque contracts, signed abroad, which can lead to forced or disguised military recruitment.

Journalistic investigations and NGOs describe a well-oiled system that exploits economic insecurity and hopes for social advancement. Once there, refusing to fight becomes almost impossible, under threat of detention or even imprisonment.

On the front lines, these foreign recruits are frequently treated as cannon fodder. Poorly equipped and poorly trained, they are sent to the front lines with a very low survival rate. Their families are left without news or support.

Clinton Mogesa's fate serves as a stark warning: behind the false promises of jobs in Russia, a deadly trap sometimes lurks.

I always trust my gut. Fifteen years in Special Operations teaches you that your instincts are the most reliable weapon you have. And as I stood outside the Pentagon briefing room, every nerve in my body was screaming.

This wasn't a standard briefing. This was a summons.

The fluorescent lights of the conference room cast long, harsh shadows across the polished oak table. General James Harrington sat alone, a man whose face was a roadmap of conflicts I’d only read about in classified files. His silence was heavier than any reprimand.

"Thank you for coming on such short notice," he said, his voice carrying the weight of his 65 years. He motioned for me to sit.

His eyes, sharp and calculating, studied me from across the table. I’d seen that look before in men who were about to ask you to do the impossible.

"Your record speaks for itself, Captain," he began. "Three tours in Afghanistan, two in Iraq. Distinguished Service Cross for that extraction in Kandahar." He paused, his gaze softening almost imperceptibly. "Your father would have been proud."

A familiar pang of grief hit my chest. Master Sergeant William Reeves, my dad, never got to see me follow in his footsteps. A heart attack took him five years ago, leaving behind a legacy of service and the survival skills he’d drilled into me during our hunting trips in the Montana mountains.

"Thank you, sir," I managed to say.

General Harrington slid a folder across the table. The stark red "CLASSIFIED" stamp seemed to glare at me under the cold lights.

"What do you know about domestic militia movements, Captain?"

The question was so far out of left field it almost threw me off balance. "They've been increasing in number and sophistication, sir. Most operate under the radar."

He leaned forward slightly. "And Colonel Victor Reynolds?"

The name hit me like a physical blow. Victor Reynolds. My former mentor. The man who recruited me for this life, who saw something in me I didn't see in myself. The man who vanished three years ago.

"Colonel Reynolds was one of our best tactical minds, sir," I said, keeping my composure locked down. "My understanding was that he retired due to health concerns."

General Harrington's expression hardened. "That was the official story." He opened the folder, revealing satellite photos of a compound nestled deep in the remote Montana wilderness. My wilderness.

Guard towers. Training facilities. Heavy weapons that had no business being in civilian hands.

"We've been tracking a domestic extremist group calling themselves the 'Guardians' for 18 months," Harrington continued, his voice low and grave. "They've been recruiting former military personnel, stockpiling weapons, and plotting to 'purify' America through controlled chaos."

My unease grew as I studied the photos. "And Colonel Reynolds?"

"He calls himself 'Patriot' now," the General said, letting the words hang in the air. "He's their leader."

Ice water seemed to flood my veins. Victor Reynolds, a true patriot, had turned against the very country he served with such distinction? It didn't make sense. Nothing made sense.

"We need confirmation of their activities and intel on an operation they're calling 'Project Awakening'," Harrington said. "This isn't officially sanctioned, Captain. On paper, this conversation never happened."

"Why me, sir?"

"Because Reynolds trusts you. Because you know that terrain better than anyone. Because if anyone can reach whatever remains of the man you once knew, it's you."

An unsanctioned mission against a former superior officer. No official support. Deep in the Montana wilderness where I grew up. It was a suicide mission.

"This is strictly volunteer, Captain," he said. "I wouldn't blame you for walking away."

I thought of my father. I thought of the oath I swore. And I thought of the Victor Reynolds who had pinned my first set of captain's bars on my uniform, his eyes shining with pride.

"Who would be on my team, sir?"

الدفاع يطالب بإبطال الأدلة الجنائية الرقمية في محاكمة مشار ______________________

أُرجئت جلسات محاكمة النائب الأول لرئيس الجمهورية الموقوف الدكتور ريك مشار وسبعة متهمين آخرين، لإتاحة الفرصة لهيئة المحكمة لدراسة قانون الجرائم الإلكترونية لجنوب أفريقيا لعام 2020، الذي يستند إليه فريق الدفاع في طلبه اعتبار الأدلة الجنائية الرقمية المقدمة في القضية «باطلة ولاغية».

وكان فريق الدفاع قد اعترض، خلال جلسة الاثنين الماضي، على قبول الحقيبة الدبلوماسية التي استُخدمت لنقل أجهزة إلكترونية إلى جنوب أفريقيا ضمن مستندات الاتهام. وطلب الادعاء ترقيم الحقيبة كمستند ادعاء رقم "9-ه"، غير أن الدفاع عارض ذلك، معتبراً أن خبير الأدلة الجنائية الرقمية راتلهوغو بيتر كالفين رافادي لا يملك الاختصاص القانوني لإعداد التقرير وفقاً لقانون الجرائم الإلكترونية الجنوب أفريقي.

وطلب القاضي رئيس الجلسة الدكتور جيمس ألالا دينق من هيئة الدفاع تقديم نصوص القانون المشار إليه للاطلاع عليها، وحدد يوم الجمعة 20 فبراير موعداً للنطق بالقرار بشأن قبول الأدلة من عدمه.

وخلال الجلسة الثالثة والخمسين التي انعقدت يوم الجمعة 20 فبراير، قرر القاضي تأجيل الإجراءات إلى 25 فبراير، موضحاً أن بعض أعضاء هيئة المحكمة يتلقون علاجاً طبياً ولم يتمكنوا من دراسة القانون بشكل كافٍ، لا سيما المواد من 42 إلى 52 التي استند إليها الدفاع في دفوعه.

ويتضمن تقرير الأدلة الجنائية ستة مرفقات، من بينها طلبات دعم فني موجهة إلى جنوب أفريقيا، وخطابات من وزارتي العدل والخارجية، ومواد أُرسلت عبر القنوات الدبلوماسية لجنوب السودان.

ويؤكد الادعاء أن التقرير يشكل ركناً أساسياً في القضية، التي تتهم مشار والمتهمين الآخرين بالتخطيط لهجوم وقع في مارس 2025 على حامية تابعة لقوات دفاع شعب جنوب السودان في مقاطعة الناصر بولاية أعالي النيل. وبحسب الاتهام، نفذت الهجوم قوات تابعة للحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان/المعارضة متحالفة مع مليشيا «الجيش الأبيض»، ما أسفر عن مقتل 257 جندياً وتدمير أو الاستيلاء على معدات عسكرية تُقدَّر قيمتها بنحو 58 مليون دولار.

ويواجه مشار ورفاقه تهماً من بينها الخيانة العظمى والقتل، فيما نفى جميع الاتهامات الموجهة إليه واعتبر المحاكمة ذات دوافع سياسية.

The Woman who killed Custer. Buffalo Calf Road Woman (Cheyenne)
Most history books tell you Custer met his end at the hands of Lakota and Cheyenne warriors. What they often leave out is the story of Buffalo Calf Road Woman, a Northern Cheyenne warrior who fought beside them, and who, according to Cheyenne oral history, struck the final blow that brought Custer down.

Buffalo Calf Road Woman wasn’t new to battle. Just days earlier, at the Battle of the Rosebud, she’d fearlessly rode onto the battlefield to rescue her brother, Comes in Sight, who had fallen from his horse. Her courage turned the tide of that fight, inspiring the warriors to push back the U.S. Army.

At the Battle of the Little Bighorn, when Custer’s 7th Cavalry attacked their camps, she fought again, this time not just to protect her family, but her entire people. According to Cheyenne oral tradition, Buffalo Calf Road Woman was the one who struck the blow that knocked General Custer from his horse, delivering the decisive blow that ended George Armstrong Custer.

Most of the written history about the Battle of the Little Bighorn comes from U.S. military reports and white historians, who ignored or erased Native perspectives, especially the contributions of women in battle. But among the Cheyenne, Buffalo Calf Road Woman’s bravery is celebrated, not forgotten.

I have been following the Großglockner case and the proceedings in Innsbruck concluded. I do not enjoy writing about real people in real tragedies. But when decisions contribute to an outcome, there are lessons there, and avoiding that conversation helps no one.

I wrote about this case back in December, and a few of you remember that post and have asked how I see it now that the court has ruled. The Innsbruck court has found Thomas Plamberger guilty of gross negligent manslaughter. The sentence was suspended, and there was no finding of intent to kill. I had already formed my view on leadership responsibility before the verdict. After reviewing what was presented in court and seeing the judge’s decision, my position has not changed. This is not about internet judgment. It is about decision making under stress and what we can learn from it.

Same lane as last time. I am not a high altitude technical mountaineer, and I am not here to play judge. I am here to examine decisions. I teach survival mindset, hands on practical skills, and I lead people in remote environments where small decisions stack up fast. In training, I intentionally introduce controlled stress so people can see how they react and build better responses before the stakes are real. That is the world I work in.

Here is what the court process clarified and why it aligns with what I have been saying.

Plamberger maintained he was not a guide, had no formal alpine training, and that they planned the tour together. He described it as an exception situation and claimed she told him to go for help. The judge challenged parts of his account based on how she was found. Reporting described her hanging on the rope with loose crampons and open snowboard boots, which indicates severe physical decline and impaired judgment. The medical examiner confirmed hypothermia as the cause of death and noted viral pneumonia and ibuprofen in her system, without concluding how much that affected performance. Her parents defended him and spoke to their belief in her capability. The prosecution argued he was the more experienced partner and that the situation should never have progressed to the point where she was left alone near the summit.

The court’s decision reinforces a distinction many people blur. Murder requires intent. Negligent manslaughter is about decisions, duty, and a serious failure of judgment that contributes to a death.

Sometimes things go catastrophically wrong in the mountains with no clear human error. Avalanches, sudden weather shifts, rockfall, icefall. Nature does what it does. We just saw that in California where an avalanche killed multiple people. On the other side, when you are solo, the risk calculus is different because you are only accountable for yourself.

This was different. This was not an unpredictable force wiping out a team. It was a chain of human decisions inside a partnership where experience was uneven. In harsh environments, uneven experience changes the dynamic. The stronger partner becomes the stabilizing force whether it is formally assigned or not. When one person begins to fade, shared decision making stops being equal. Hypothermia, exhaustion, fear, altitude, and cold stress strip away judgment quickly. The person still thinking clearly becomes the decision maker. That is physiology.

Much of the public argument has centered on one moment. Should he have stayed with her or left to get help. If he stayed, he might have died too. If he left, he might save himself and possibly her.

I do not see that as the core issue. When you are that high, that late, in deteriorating weather, and one partner is in advanced cold stress, the situation is already catastrophic. By the time he walked away, or even by the time staying became the only remaining option, the good choices were already gone. That moment was not the beginning of the problem. It was the final step in a chain that had already boxed them in.

They should never have gotten that far.

And here is why.  In advanced hypothermia at that elevation, at night, in exposed winter terrain, survival without immediate shelter and aggressive rewarming is extraordinarily unlikely. By the time he descended, the window for reversal was almost certainly closing or already closed. That is why the focus has to stay on the earlier decisions that allowed it to reach that point.

Once she collapsed near the summit, both options at that point were bad because earlier decision points had already been missed. Late start. Gear questions. Continuing upward as fatigue showed. Continuing as daylight faded. Continuing as conditions shifted. In leadership, when you ignore early warning signs, you eventually get forced into two terrible options. At that point, you are no longer managing risk. You are absorbing consequences.

Most accidents are not one dramatic failure. They are a stack of small decisions that keep working until they do not. Many inexperienced adventurers look competent right up until the first real emergency. Repeated success can create an illusion of capability that collapses under real stress.

I respect that her family wants to defend him. That is human. No parent wants their daughter’s final chapter reduced to headlines and arguments. That does not remove the role leadership failures can play in an outcome.

One detail that still gives me pause is the phone. Court reporting described him silencing it after an initial contact, with rescue teams making repeated attempts to reach him that went unanswered. I wanted full context before drawing conclusions, but that clarity never really came. In environments like that, a phone can be a lifeline depending on signal, battery, and conditions. Was it dead. Was he conserving power. Was there no reception. Was it a judgment call. I still do not know.

The legal system has made its determination, and the leadership lessons remain. My focus stays where it has always been. Experience is not about summits or photos. It is about recognizing decline in your partner before they recognize it in themselves. It is about turning around early enough that the decision feels boring instead of heroic.

Winter changes the rules. Time changes the rules. Fatigue changes the rules. Love changes the rules because sometimes it makes people push when they should turn.

Physics and physiology make the final decision, not confidence or narrative. The court labeled it gross negligent manslaughter. From a leadership perspective, that assessment makes sense.

A demand for Dr. Riek Machar’s unconditional release while ignoring atrocities resulting from his armed wing’s offensive is not peacemaking. It is a reward for rebellion, Africa cannot afford such a precedent.

By Dr. Sunday de John

At last week’s C-5 Plus Summit in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, Nigeria’s Vice President Kashim Shettima presented a demand on behalf of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu: the “immediate and unconditional release” of South Sudan’s detained First Vice President, Dr. Riek Machar Teny Dhurgon. While this demand was projected as a friendly gesture toward peace, it was perceived as excessive interference in the internal matters of South Sudan and, others thought that it served as a diplomatic lifeline to an armed insurgency.

By all accounts, Nigeria’s statement failed to mention the March 2025 Nasir attack, a coordinated deadly assault by the “White Army”, a militia group affiliated with Dr. Riek Machar Teny’s SPLM/A-IO on a South Sudan People’s Defence Forces (SSPDF) garrison (Wec Yar Adiw), which triggered this crisis.

It did not address the SPLM/A-IO’s subsequent rampage across the country, including the attacks on Torit in Eastern Equatoria, the border crossings at Nadapal, the overrunning of Panyume in Morobo County, the assaults on Pajut in Jonglei, and the seizure of Waat and Yuai in Greater Akobo, towns whose civilian populations bore the brunt of an insurgency that Nigeria’s demand statement chose to ignore.
The demand statement did not condemn the SPLM/A-IO’s January 2026 declaration to capture Juba. Basically, the statement required nothing from the armed opposition, it demanded everything from the government. This method does not truly reflect a balanced diplomacy; it is a typical exertion of disproportionate pressure to one side in an ongoing conflict.

Dr. Riek Machar Teny is not a political prisoner, his case is criminal by the definition of his current predicament. He is undergoing a criminal investigation and trial concerning a potential command responsibility for the violence involving the joint SPLM/A-IO-White Army militia, which resulted in the deaths of South Sudanese soldiers, including the decorated General David Majur Dak. He faces the same legal standards that the International Criminal Court applies to commanders and heads of state who are charged with genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and other atrocities globally.

Nigeria’s demand for his release before any investigation concludes, with no accountability framework in place while his armed wing continues to advance militarily, does not uphold international legal norms. It dismantles them. And if the message sent to every armed movement on this continent is that launching offensives earns you international sympathy while the government defending itself earns condemnation, Africa will reap this despicable and unpalatable harvest for decades.

The warlords will get emboldened, and they would allude to the fact that, If picking up a gun guarantees a diplomatic shield from Abuja, South Sudan will never run short of active armed factions engaging its government.

Looking at it critically, there is a painful irony in Nigeria taking this position. This is because we are aware that Abuja spent decades defending its own territorial integrity and fragmentation against armed separatist movements, at enormous human cost, on the fundamental principle that no armed faction may dictate political outcomes by military means.

An episode of this kind, teaches us that by Nigeria’s standing, history was bought with blood. If so, why is Nigeria asking Juba to do what it would never do? Nigerian leaders are aware that sovereignty is not a courtesy extended to governments that fulfill their counterparts' preferences.

Nigeria does understand well that the continent cannot tolerate the overthrow of a legitimate government through military coups. Actions of that kind, although violated by some ECOWAS member states, have a bearing on West African internal mechanisms for changing leaderships. ECOWAS has zero tolerance to unconstitutional change of governments. This is the basis, why Nigeria recently, upon request by President Patrice Talon, helped the Republic of Benin thwart a military coup on December 7, 2025.

This means, defense of the territorial integrity and sovereignty is the structural precondition of every functioning state on this continent; this must be defended consistently, or it means nothing.

Through the perspectives of neutral observers, President Salva Kiir Mayardit is not hindering the peace process. He in fact, acquiesced to Dr. Riek Machar Teny's adamant demands regarding the implementation of the agreement, even though it was fraught with significant challenges that made it difficult to implement, therefore, the basis of multiple extensions. This is one of the indicators that South Sudanese government has not obstructed progress on the path of peace.

It has lately committed to holding elections in December 2026 and has made constitutional amendments to resolve the sticky issues that have stalled the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement.

The government has engaged, and is continuously engaging with cooperative opposition groups that have opted for politics over the military incursions. These actions do not show a government with intention of dismantling peace; they reflect an effort to establish it, even in the face of an armed opponent that has openly declared its goal of regime change through military means.

The central question is not whether South Sudan should hold elections; there is a consensus that it should happen so that a futile cycle of extending agreements is broken democratically. The real issue is whether elections can be conducted while an armed faction, equipped with lethal artillery and infantry, is actively advancing toward the capital.

No democracy in the world can successfully hold credible elections under such grueling circumstances. Nigerian diplomats are aware of this reality. The path to the December 2026 elections does not pass through Dr. Riek Machar Teny’s cell but through a ceasefire. The demand for ceasefire from the SPLM/A-IO with the same urgency Abuja has shown toward Juba is necessary now.

Given this, one would conclude that the path to the December 2026 elections is not optional and must run through an enforceable ceasefire, one that demands all armed actors cease equally, not just the government defending its capital city.

As I express this, I am not placing South Sudan’s government beyond scrutiny. However, accountability must apply equally to all sides. A wise person would say that scrutiny without balance is not principled; it is merely a political manipulation. Observing closely, it appears that Nigeria’s current stance, politically rewards the party that chose war while penalizing the party attempting to maintain stability.

I acknowledge that Nigeria is a major power with genuine ethical authority on the continent of Africa, and it also has a capacity to exercise this power shrewdly. Here is a clear path forward: Nigeria should advocate for a bilateral or multilateral ceasefire and encourage all armed factions to engage equally. Also, it is indispensable for Nigeria to recognize and support the Kenya-led Tumaini mediation process in Nairobi; this should be done with the aim of arriving at a comprehensive and sustainable peace in favor of the citizens.

Also, Nigeria ought to provide resources to support South Sudan’s electoral commission in order to achieve its concern about her younger, sisterly state; instead of issuing unnecessary ultimatums and ensure that the courts in Juba can operate free from external political interference.

Nigeria should take note that South Sudan does not require rescue from its sovereignty. It needs partners who will respect it and hold all parties in this conflict to the same standard of accountability. This is what true African solidarity means. Nigeria, more than any other country, should understand this well.

Till then, yours truly, Mr. Teetotaler!

We are told to believe them when they claim the point blank range shot was “not supposed to” break a jaw, or gauge out an eye.  The gas was “not supposed to” trigger the life threatening asthma  attack.  The guns were fired because they felt “endangered” by the weaponless woman in the car.  

We are told to ignore the evidence of our own eyes, and that the man twitching in reaction when multiple bodies piled on as he struggled to take a breath, deserved an assassination by firing squad when he lay subdued and powerless on the street.

We are told to believe that they were “boxed in” when they rammed the car into the vehicle driven by a weaponless observer.   We are told to suspend logic and disbelief to accept that it is a common everyday thing for a man in zip ties to run headfirst into a cement wall and give himself multiple skull fractures, including most mysteriously, the ones on the sides of his head where he must have gone back multiple times to smash that cement wall from multiple angles.

We are supposed to lay still and take it.  Perhaps offer compliments on how fast and hard and thorough and brutal it all is ….

The “greatest ever” in terms of mass sadistic torture and rape.  How the troops flooded the physical zones and stopped just being armies of Russian bots.   How clever the recruiting scheme was, when they found addicted brainwashed young men steeped in a misogynistic culture of resentment, dissatisfaction and hatred, and lured them step by step into a matrix of distorted non reality where massacring people in real life felt just as good as a “Call of Duty” video game.

We are told that sometimes people must be forced to do what they don’t want.    That it is all for some future someone’s greater wealth and power, or the efficiency of a world where robber barons merged with crypto kings, and cartel overlords mingled and entwined with techno fascist children who became perpetually lost in their own delusions.  

We are told that we really should try the plot lines for the Terminator movies and this time it will be super cool because they will do a better job at being the masters who control the on/off switch. 

We are told that sometimes “they” don’t know what they “really” want….Those people in Ukraine or Gaza, Greenland or Minneapolis.   The activists and pacifists and democracy minded, naive, leftover from the old world, remnants. 

Sometimes “they” just need “a little encouragement.” The threat from an enforcer, the broken arm or leg, the bombing of the entire region, the city lost in flames…the “small genocide that will assure victory for the conquerors.   

Eventually those that remain will “adjust,” or so they tell us.  

If they remain unwilling or unable to assimilate, they can continue to be the targeted “others” for the rest of “us.”   They will be the pacifists forced to the front lines and told to fire at the human in front of them or be targeted by the militia member holding a weapon at their back.

We are told so many things that we fall like dominos, while those seizing power are terrified if anyone mentions that the momentum can go the other way…

That we can prop each other up and become each other’s strength.   That we can be the courage for another when we feel the most frightened for ourselves.  That our efforts to help “them” succeed, may offer a future doctor to us when we are in need.   That the food we once seeded and offered, became the crop that kept us alive when the drought hit. 

Somehow, somewhere in your mind and heart you know that polarities can be reversed. Death spirals can become layers of civilization and efforts set on climbing.  The worst unleashed in people, can become an era where people commit to nurturing and giving to support the best in what can be created together, and the capacity for love and integrity within themselves.   

You know that buoyant things pushed down eventually feel compelled to rise. You know that even when the world seems to be flooded with lies, the truth has its’ own inevitability that is beyond any “sides.”

Is there a way to shift that polarity?  

A way to move from extraction to contribution.  From taking to giving.   From hatred to loving… 

From cycles of mass assured destruction, into a will to create the conditions that offer us a cumulative shared increasing good, and the hope for future survival?

Is there a way to shift that momentum and bring it to reversing course? 

A way to change having measurements built on how little we can force “them” to have as we struggle everyday to make the rent and pay the bills, into wanting the best for “them” in the hope that overflowing tables in an abundant expansive world offers us dreams and gifts that we can not even begin to imagine beyond anything a billionaire could buy. 

Is there a way to turn systems, so that the peace activist in Russia who is forced to the front lines in a war they stood against, and now must confront a “kill the person in front of you or be murdered by the man behind you” choice….  

And switch that into a reverse, where the man he has has been told to kill turns and becomes unmasked as the researcher who is working on the cure that would save his life.   As the peace activist “opposition dissident,” is revealed to be the musician who would have created the most incredible best selling album, danced to and treasured by the man who would have been his greatest fan, standing with the gun behind him…. 

Is there a way to reverse the fall of dominos and turn them into the support beams for a future capable of offering all of us shelter?   

This road they try to force us down is littered with pain, destruction and horror.    

If there is even the smallest hope that we can reverse it, let us come together and try it.
