For those of you who are tiring of auld Wilton, please bear with me; a fresh topic is visible on the horizon! To get there, however, we have a few more forgotten thoroughfares to tackle first.

This week it’s Pathhead, a street name once given to a row of houses at the top of Wilton Path, of which two buildings survive as 1 and 5 Langlands Road. 

Adam Scott is recorded as living there in 1739, while in 1764, an important meeting regarding the division of Wilton Common was held at the Crown Inn, across the water in Hawick, providing us with two more Pathhead residents:  Robert Scott, hosier; and Thomas Ferguson, labourer, who was born in the late 1600s.

‘James Blaky in Hawik’ paid tax there in 1791, and Hector Blaikie, boatman at the Coble Cauld and a wright in ‘Pathhead near Wilton Church’, was named in a court action against the Duke of Buccleuch in 1795. William Scott was a stocking weaver on Pathhead, according to ballots for the militia in Wilton Parish in 1799 and 1801. Tam Ferguson (b.1772), a likely descendant of the earlier Thomas, is also recorded as a spinner at Pathhead on the same roll. He was one of two men chosen in 1842 to point out the old marches of Wilton.

A rare contemporary newspaper advert details ‘Roughheugh Pathhead’ in 1809 as being the “eastmost house with room for a garden at the back… [a] house west of lot 15, with garden ground,” plus two further houses extending into what is now Langlands Road, “with further ground for let suitable for house building.”

Sergeant Waugh, recruiting officer for the Dumfries Militia, loaned his sash that same year for use by the rebel Cornet, John Tully. He also tried to take the coach to Selkirk to find musicians for the rebel party, but was pushed off the coach at Pathhead, the guard having been paid off by the opposing ‘royalist’ party!

Elliot’s 1810 sketch shows conjoined two-storey tenements, an adjoining cottage to the west, and a gap to Saut Ha’ (see The Hawick Paper, March 24, 2017), while Wood’s 1824 town map has four adjoining buildings at Pathhead belonging to James Oliver. 

One of the street’s most famous sons was Robert Lamb, born at Pathhead in 1832. He trained as a woollen hosiery dresser, like his father John, and emigrated to Galt, Ontario, along with his older brother Adam. They later moved to MacGregor, Manitoba, where they were among the first white settlers. Robert farmed there and gave two acres of his land to establish a school, which he called Path Head School (The Hawick Paper, August 9, 2019) after his birthplace. There is a cairn marking the location of the school which operated from 1891 until 1965.

Other pre-census residents of Pathhead were William Cairns, a handloom weaver, and Rob Scott, a stockingmaker and noted supporter of the strikers during the Lang Stand Oot of 1822 (The Hawick Paper, December 22, 2023). Across the road was Francis Ballantyne’s garden house which, given its isolated position in 1832, was listed as a real possibility for a cholera hospital. This ground would later be sold to become the Free Kirk Manse, now Marfaux.

Around 1841, Pathhead was demolished and rebuilt as a row of tenements. 

In 1845 the small street played host to high drama when Thomas Bell, a native of Ecclefechan and a suspected thief, “took leg-bail” from Pathhead and evaded police on an epic chase through Silverbuthall and Stirches, before eventually being apprehended at Sunnyside near Ormiston. Described by the Carlisle Patriot newspaper as “one of the best contested races on record,” Bell received nine months at Jedburgh Jail for his troubles.

For the 1841 census, Pathhead was occupied by William Henderson, carter, along with his wife Margaret and their children. He could be the same William as the coach-driver who was an early member of Allars Kirk. Another resident at the time was George Wallace, a former inkle weaver and ‘parish pauper’.

Moving forward a decade, Alexander Hogg, foreman in Hawick, bid at Pathhead. In 1871 he donated to the museum “autograph letters of the late Lord Napier, Thirlestane, Lord Jeffrey, the Ettrick Shepherd, and Sir Walter Scott.” He also gave a talk on incidents in the life of Sir Walter Scott, including an account of the Carterhaugh Ba’. This contained personal recollections such as watching the arrival of the Hawick contingent just after dawn. Although only 14 years old, and intending to just watch the game, he did have an opportunity to handle the first ball, and later met Sir Walter when walking over the hills from Selkirk to Hawick.

The 1858 Ordnance Survey (OS) map shows ‘Path-head’ as a row of four buildings bookended by a warehouse and tenter fields at Salt Hall roadend, plus a larger warehouse to the rear of modern-day 76 Princes Street. Up the lane ahint no.1 were a further two buildings, while a rectangular path led directly behind here to Salt Hall. No.2 was in use as a stable or byre with a hayloft. 

To the south of the tenter fields, but east of Langlands Bank, were Wilton Cottage and two large gardens reaching to the rear of properties in Wilton Path. The cottage was home to Margaret Turnbull (née Dalgleish) who ran it as the Image Garden School around the 1840s. It was later home to James Turnbull, Wilton schoolmaster. 

Langlands Road itself, although not a lost street name, was once known as ‘the kirk road from Wilton to Langlands’, and was named around 1868. 

It’s unclear when Pathhead gave way to the naming convention of 1 to 5 Langlands Road, but the Balmoral Bar was one of its longest tenants at no.1, in an amputated, slim, three-storey tenement with a long extension to the rear which consumed at least one of the older properties in the lane.

Back in 1897 the bar switched hands from James Murray to Robert Beattie, and in 1903 the licence transferred from George Paterson to Robert M. Crosby. William Taylor was the owner in 1908, followed by T.P. McLean, and then Spencer Hancox in 1912. 

Ownership had transferred to Thomas Fernie by 1926. During his tenure, the Balmoral was gutted by fire, in February 1933, resulting in the rescue of his wife Helen and their children from the flat above. Neighbours were told to move their furniture while the blaze was brought under control, and the reported cost of the damage was £2,000. 

Undeterred, Thomas reopened the pub on July 27, 1933. Less than a year later he was dead. The licence was then transferred to his widow Helen, who sold the property to a former Greens player, John C. Haig, in 1934. At that time he was the licensee of the Wheat Sheaf Hotel in Swinton but was keen to return home to Wilton where his father lived at Ladylaw Place.

Haig remained in charge of the Balmoral well into the 1950s but I’ve been unable to determine who had the licence in the following two decades. By the early 1980s, Scottish & Newcastle Inns Ltd owned the pub and it was managed by John Robertson and then Wullie Boyle. The last licensee for whom I have a name is Carlos Nunes, circa 1999.

The Balmoral kept its doors open until the Great Recession of 2008-09, with the former function suite upstairs doubling as a restaurant for a time. It had one of the town’s last dummy waiters, too. In August 2016 the Bamboo Box takeaway opened in its place, ending an association stretching back over 150 years.

Other wee snippets regarding Pathhead include the refusal of a grocer’s licence there, in 1863, for William Robson, as there were already two shops within 50 yards of the property. One newspaper reports two apartments to let at 21 Wilton Pathhead, in 1904, which suggests that the tenements were divvied up into smaller properties.

Across the lane to the east, the warehouse from the 1858 OS map existed for more than six decades prior to being bought by William Flockhart, along with the two homes in front of it (nos. 2 and 4 Ladylaw Place), in 1919. Despite extensive research, I’ve been unable to find out exactly who had it and for what purpose. Answers on a postcard, please!

William was a yarnman for A.P. Innes & Co, hosiery manufacturers, who went out on his own after the First World War to found the Hawick Knitwear Manufacturing Company, initially in a couple of rooms at Old Dovemount, prior to purchasing the Ladylaw Place warehouse. Indeed, Flockhart became synonymous with the mill as he was the first to expand it at street level, being known both as Flockhart Mill and Flockhart Works.

Dr Martin joined as partner of the rebranded Hawick Knitwear Ltd in 1927, and the pair remained in charge until William’s death in 1951, after which the good doctor took the helm, selling the firm on to Thistle Industrial Holdings in 1961. 

Alfreton Knitting Mills (later called Dalkeith Mills) acquired Hawick Knitwear in the early 1960s, which prompted a significant expansion of their Hawick and Greenlaw mills, in April 1965, and the replacement of original machinery. The footprint of the Hawick mill was described thus: “These buildings comprise of a three-storey factory building with a stone and render frontage... The site slopes up to the rear (north-west) resulting in a change of ground levels between the front and rear of the building. The factory building to the rear is single storey and there are a number of rendered single storey outbuildings to this side.”

Sometime prior to March 1983, the site was purchased by or let to Clan Douglas, cashmere producers, with Lindes Contracts as a neighbouring tenant. A shop was then created at ground level, with the Crofters Kitchen above, as part of a revamp overseen by new parent conglomerate, the Pitlochry Knitwear Company. Guided tours were also a staple. 

In December 1989, Clan Douglas was visited by the Princess Royal in her role as president of British Knitting and Clothing and Export Council. By 1991, however, challenging economic circumstances saw the firm being saved by Reid’s woollen mill, albeit briefly, as Clan Douglas went into receivership in April 1992 with the threat of 70 job losses.

A month later the company was sold to Murray Allan, of Innerleithen, under the watchful eye of parent company Toyoboshi Kogyo.

May 1996 once again saw Clan Douglas Knitwear, or CDK Realisations Ltd, face insolvency proceedings. By the end of the millennium, though, the rejuvenated firm boasted 120 workers and a significant share of the American cashmere market, worth over £5million to the Wilton-based factory. Clan Douglas also took over Mansfield Mill for a time to keep up with demand.

That which goes up must come down, and so it was in 1999 that CDK was threatened with mass redundancies because of a six-year-long trade dispute between Europe and the United States over the import of bananas which affected other tariffs. 

Clan Douglas survived the so-called banana wars and merged with Lyle & Scott, in 2001, to form an independent knitwear business, Hawick Knitwear, a continuation of Flockhart’s original brand – which has sadly been dormant since the demise of the new firm in 2016. 

The Princes Street premises were then taken over by Lochcarron, the world’s leading tartan manufacturer and designer of many Hawick tartans, following their removal from Huddersfield Street, Galashiels, in 2006. The Hawick mill became their main knitwear centre but it, too, was closed in the wake of the Great Recession of 2008-09. Lochcarron remains alive and well in Selkirk. 

In 2012, Scottish Borders Council gave the green light to transform the old Flockhart Mill into a gym and fitness studio with multiple units. This work was later carried forward by A1 Border Moves, with further tenants following in the shape of Glenmac Builders Ltd, Hawick Boxing Club, LMDA Dance School, Welding Specialists, and Lawrie Roofing.

Next week we skip across the lane to Ladylaw Place.

In December 2013, a massacre occurred in Juba, where Dinka-led government forces and militias targeted Nuer civilians, resulting in the deaths of between 20,000 to 47,000 people, mostly women and children.¹ ²

The violence was characterized by house-to-house searches, targeted killings, and ethnic cleansing. The Nuer people were subjected to mass killings, rape, and abduction. The SSPDF, led by President Salva Kiir, was accused of orchestrating these atrocities, with some reports suggesting that the Mathiang Anyoor militia was involved.³

In addition to the 2013 massacre, there have been other instances of violence against the Nuer people, including:
- The Gudele Massacre: Over 400 Nuer men, women, and children were killed in a police station.
- The Bentiu Massacre: SPLM-IO forces killed about 200 mostly non-Nuer civilians in April 2014.
- Uror County Massacre: Over 200 women and children were abducted, and at least 287 people were killed in Murle-Nuer clashes in 2020.

Maps covered the long table. Intelligence reports sat in neat stacks. The smell of cigars and coffee filled the air.

These men had just conquered France in 6 weeks. They felt unstoppable. A junior officer spread photographs across the table. The pictures showed soldiers boarding ships in a place called Halifax far across the ocean in Canada. The generals leaned forward to look. Then something unexpected happened. They started to laugh.

One general picked up a photo and shook his head. He said the Canadians looked like farmers and lumberjacks playing soldier. Another general joined in the joke. He said Canada was sending boys to do men's work. The room erupted with laughter. The sound echoed off the walls. The generals had good reason to feel confident.

Their army, the Vermacht, had just crushed. The French military in record time. The numbers told an amazing story. German losses in France were 27,000 dead. French losses were 290,000 dead. That meant France lost more than 10 times as many men. The German war machine had rolled through Belgium, the Netherlands, and France like a hot knife through butter.

Nothing could stop them, or so they thought. One general tapped his finger on an intelligence report about Canada. The paper said the first Canadian division had landed in Britain back in December 1939. That was 7 months ago. The division had 7,400 men. The general read the details out loud. Average height of Canadian soldiers was 5'9 in.

Many came from farms in small towns. Most had never seen combat. They had almost no battle experience. The general set down the paper and smiled. His own Vermach divisions had 15,000 soldiers or more. And these were veteran troops who had fought in Poland and France. They knew how to fight. They knew how to win.

Another officer pulled out more intelligence photos. These showed Canadian soldiers during training exercises. The Germans studied the images carefully. They saw men in simple uniforms. They saw men carrying old rifles. They saw men who looked nothing like the hardened German troops who had conquered Europe. One general made another joke.

He said the Canadians probably spent more time milking cows than shooting guns. More laughter filled the room. The mockery continued. These German commanders could not imagine that soldiers from a distant country like Canada could ever challenge their mighty army. But the generals missed something important in those photographs, something they would not understand until it was too late.

The Canadian soldiers in the pictures had powerful builds. Their shoulders were broad. Their arms looked powerful. These men came from a hard land. They chopped down trees in freezing forests. They worked on farms from sunrise to sunset. They mined coal and copper deep underground. Their bodies were built by years of difficult work.

The Germans saw farmers and lumberjacks. They were right, but they did not understand what that really meant. The meeting ended. The generals collected their papers and left. They walked out confident and pleased. They had conquered France. They had conquered Belgium. They had conquered the Netherlands. Who could stop them now? Certainly not Canada.

The very idea seemed like a joke. Their intelligence told them Canada had a tiny professional army before the war started. Only 4,500 regular soldiers. Germany had 4.7 million men under arms. The math was simple. Canada was no threat. The generals returned to planning their next moves. Some would go to North Africa. Some would prepare for other campaigns.

They put the Canadians out of their minds. There were bigger enemies to fight. The British Empire still stood. The Soviet Union loomed to the east. Why waste time thinking about Canadian farm boys? But time has a way of teaching hard lessons. Four years would pass. Four long years of brutal war. And in that time, everything would change.

Those same German generals who laughed in June 1940 would find themselves in a very different situation. Many would become prisoners of war. They would be shipped to camps far from home and those camps would be run by Canadians. The guards at those camps would tower over them. These guards would stand 6 feet tall or more.

Their arms would be thick with muscle. Their eyes would be hard from seeing battle. The German generals would have to look up at these men. They would have to take orders from the very soldiers they had mocked. The generals would stand in those prison camps and wonder, "How did this happen? How did they get it so wrong? How did the farmers and lumberjacks become the ones holding the keys?" The intelligence reports had been so clear.

The Canadians were supposed to be weak. They were supposed to be no threat. They were supposed to be a joke. But the joke was on Germany because the men from the north turned out to be some of the toughest, strongest, and most determined soldiers of the entire war. The question that would haunt those German commanders was simple but painful.

How did they so badly underestimate the huge Canadian soldiers who would one day guard their prison camps? Canada had fought in war before. 23 years earlier in April 1917, Canadian soldiers climbed a muddy hill in France called Vimemy Ridge. The French army had tried to take that hill for 3 years. They failed. The British army tried too.

They also failed. Then the Canadians came. In 4 days they captured what no one else could. They fought together as one unit for the first time. They planned carefully. They trained hard. They fought brave. When the smoke cleared, Vimemy Ridge belonged to Canada. The victory made Canada famous as a fighting nation.

But that was a long time ago. By 1939, most people had forgotten. The Canadian military had become very small after the first war ended. [snorts] When Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, Canada's entire military was smaller than a single German division. A Canadian farmer could walk through his whole country and barely see any soldiers.

In Germany, armies marched through the streets every day. The contrast was clear to everyone. German intelligence officers kept files on every potential enemy. They had thick folders about France, Britain, and Poland. The folder on Canada was thin, very thin. Inside, the report said Canada was just a colonial militia with limited combat value.

The Germans wrote that Canadian soldiers were not real warriors. They were farmers who picked up rifles when needed. German military thinking focused on professional soldiers, modern tanks, and experienced leaders. Canada seemed to have none of these things. The German files got locked away in cabinets. Nobody thought they mattered. Then everything changed.

September 10th, 1939, Canada declared war on Germany. Recruiting stations opened across the country. What happened next surprised everyone. Young men lined up outside the doors. The line stretched down city blocks. In Toronto, the recruiting office processed 1,000 volunteers in just the first week. The same thing happened in Montreal, Vancouver, and Winnipeg.

Men wanted to fight, but Germany only saw the numbers on paper. They did not see the quality of the men signing up. Canada had something special that the Germans did not understand. The country was huge and the population was small. That meant recruiting stations could be picky about who they accepted. Britain needed so many soldiers that they took almost anyone.

Their minimum height requirement was 5' 3 in. Canada set their minimum at 5'6 in. That was 3 in taller. It does not sound like much, but it made a big difference. Taller men were often stronger men. Canada could afford to choose only the strongest because so many wanted to join. The average age of Canadian recruits was 26 years old.

British recruits averaged 21. Those five extra years mattered. A 26-year-old man was fully grown. His body was at peak strength. Many had worked hard jobs for years.
